kingdom-of-tamassos.t: Inland Cypriot kingdom built on rich copper mines, whose last king sold his realm to the king of Kition for fifty talents.
kingdom-of-tamassos.o: Tamassos lay in the Pediaios valley at the foot of the copper-rich Troodos mountains and was settled from the Bronze Age. Its copper may be the 'Temese' of Homer's Odyssey. By the 7th century BCE it was an independent kingdom; its king Admetus appears among the Cypriot rulers listed by Esarhaddon of Assyria.
kingdom-of-tamassos.r: The kingdom's wealth came from copper mining and smelting. Its royal tombs of the 6th century BCE are built of fine ashlar masonry imitating wooden houses, and a sanctuary of Apollo and the Mother of the Gods has yielded much sculpture. Tamassos used Greek and Phoenician alongside each other.
kingdom-of-tamassos.e: In the 4th century BCE King Pasicyprus sold Tamassos to Pumiyaton of the Kingdom of Kition for fifty talents. Alexander the Great later gave it to the king of Salamis. Tamassos survived as a town under Ptolemaic and Roman rule.

kingdom-of-surrey.t: A short-lived Saxon territory south of the Thames whose name, the 'southern district', survives as the county of Surrey.
kingdom-of-surrey.o: Surrey, Suthrige, probably began as the southern part of a larger Middle Saxon territory on both sides of the Thames. In the 7th century it lay between Kent, Wessex, Sussex and Mercia and was ruled by local leaders under one or another of them.
kingdom-of-surrey.r: The only known ruler is Frithuwold, a sub-king under Wulfhere of the Kingdom of Mercia, who around 672 to 674 endowed Chertsey Abbey, founded by Bishop Eorcenwald. The charter shows estates, minsters and Mercian overlordship but no independent dynasty.
kingdom-of-surrey.e: Surrey never had a lasting royal line. Control passed between Mercia and Wessex, and in the 9th century it became a West Saxon shire, keeping its name and much of its boundary.

kingdom-of-morocco.t: The independent Moroccan monarchy, in which the Alaouite kings have kept central power through decades of political change and the Western Sahara dispute.
kingdom-of-morocco.o: After the French protectorate in Morocco and the Spanish protectorate in Morocco ended in 1956, Sultan Mohammed V of the Alaouite Sultanate adopted the title of king in 1957. Tangier, Tarfaya in 1958 and Ifni in 1969 were reintegrated.
kingdom-of-morocco.r: Hassan II, king from 1961 to 1999, introduced constitutions but kept firm control, surviving coup attempts in 1971 and 1972 and repressing opposition during the Years of Lead. His Green March of 1975 began Moroccan control of most of Spanish Sahara, leading to war with the Polisario Front. The economy rests on phosphates, agriculture, tourism and remittances.
kingdom-of-morocco.e: Mohammed VI succeeded in 1999, reforming family law in 2004 and approving a new constitution after the 2011 protests, though the king retains wide powers. Morocco remains a monarchy, claiming Western Sahara.

kingdom-of-gera.t: The southernmost Gibe Oromo kingdom, remembered for holding the Italian explorers Cecchi and Chiarini captive in 1879 to 1880.
kingdom-of-gera.o: Gera emerged as a monarchy around 1835 in the forested highlands south of the Gibe, bordering the Kingdom of Kaffa. Like the other Gibe states it was formed when Oromo settlers adopted hereditary kingship and settled government.
kingdom-of-gera.r: Gera's kings ruled from Chala through officials, with an economy of coffee, honey, civet and slaves traded north to the markets of the Kingdom of Jimma. The ruling family adopted Islam. In 1879 the court seized the Italian explorers Antonio Cecchi and Giovanni Chiarini, who was held there until his death; Cecchi was freed in 1880 after Ethiopian intervention.
kingdom-of-gera.e: In 1887 Gera was conquered by the forces of Menelik II and annexed to the Ethiopian Empire.

kalahandi-state.t: A Naga dynasty state in western Odisha, once known as Karond, whose Maharajas ruled from Junagarh and later Bhawanipatna until 1948.
kalahandi-state.o: Tradition holds that the Naga dynasty was founded around 1005 by Raghunath Sai, with its capital at Junagarh. The early history of the state is known mainly from family tradition and later records.
kalahandi-state.r: Kalahandi was a largely rural state of rice fields and forest with a large Kondh population. In the 18th century it became tributary to the Bhonsles of the Nagpur Kingdom, and in 1849 the capital moved to Bhawanipatna. It passed to British supervision with Nagpur in 1853, and a Kondh uprising in 1882 was put down by British troops.
kalahandi-state.e: Maharaja Pratap Keshari Deo signed the merger agreement, and Kalahandi joined Orissa on 1 January 1948. It is now a district of Odisha.

kazakh-ssr.t: The vast Soviet republic of the Kazakhs, scene of the Virgin Lands campaign, nuclear testing at Semipalatinsk and the Baikonur space launches.
kazakh-ssr.o: The Kazakh ASSR became a union republic, the Kazakh SSR, under the Soviet constitution of December 1936, with its capital at Alma-Ata. It emerged from the famine of the early 1930s with Kazakhs a minority in their own land.
kazakh-ssr.r: The republic received deported peoples, including Koreans, Volga Germans and Chechens, and many Gulag camps such as Karlag. From 1954 Nikita Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign ploughed millions of hectares of steppe for wheat, bringing in Russian and Ukrainian settlers. The Soviet nuclear test site near Semipalatinsk carried out over 450 tests from 1949 to 1989, and Baikonur launched Sputnik and Yuri Gagarin. Dinmukhamed Kunaev led the republic from 1964 to 1986.
kazakh-ssr.e: Kunaev's replacement by a Russian sparked the Jeltoqsan protests of December 1986. Nursultan Nazarbayev became leader in 1989, and on 16 December 1991 the republic, the last to leave the Soviet Union, declared independence as Kazakhstan.

kingdom-of-kinda.t: A central Arabian tribal kingdom that briefly united the Bedouin of Najd under Himyarite patronage and produced the poet Imru al-Qays.
kingdom-of-kinda.o: Kinda was a tribe from the borders of Hadramawt that moved into central Arabia. In the 5th century the Himyarite Kingdom installed its chief Hujr Akil al-Murar as king over the Ma'add tribes of Najd, giving Himyar indirect control of the interior. Qaryat al-Faw, a caravan town on the edge of the Empty Quarter, is often linked with the kingdom.
kingdom-of-kinda.r: Kindite kings ruled as overlords of shifting tribal alliances rather than through fixed institutions, collecting tribute and leading raids. Under al-Harith ibn Amr in the early 6th century, Kinda reached its peak and even held al-Hira for a time at the expense of the Lakhmid Kingdom, with Byzantine diplomatic support.
kingdom-of-kinda.e: After al-Harith was killed around 528, his sons divided the tribes and were defeated by the Lakhmids and rival tribes. The kingdom had collapsed by about 540. Its memory survives through Imru al-Qays, son of the last king Hujr, whose ode is one of the Mu'allaqat.

kingdom-of-tio.t: The Teke kingdom on the plateaus north of Malebo Pool, whose king signed the 1880 treaty that founded French rule on the Congo.
kingdom-of-tio.o: The Tio or Teke kingdom formed on the sandy plateaus north of Malebo Pool by the 15th century. Portuguese sources of the 16th century call it Anziku and describe wars with the Kingdom of Kongo for control of the Pool, the hub of river trade between the interior and the Atlantic coast.
kingdom-of-tio.r: The king, known as the Makoko, ruled from Mbe as a sacred figure whose power came from the national shrine of Nkwe Mbali and the royal nkobi, a box of sacred relics. Real power was shared with territorial lords who controlled trade at the Pool. The kingdom traded slaves, ivory and copper downriver in exchange for cloth, guns and shells, and was famed for its raffia textiles.
kingdom-of-tio.e: In 1880 Makoko Iloo I signed a treaty with Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza placing his lands under French protection, which gave France its foothold on the Congo and its new post of Brazzaville. The kingship survives as a ceremonial office in the Republic of the Congo.

kingdom-of-york.t: The Viking kingdom centred on Jorvik, a prosperous Anglo-Scandinavian town whose kings were often also rulers of Dublin.
kingdom-of-york.o: The Great Heathen Army captured York in 866 to 867, and in 876 Halfdan shared out the land of Northumbria south of the Tees among his followers. Danish kings ruled from York, with Guthfrith in the 880s accepting Christianity. Early in the 10th century the Norse dynasty of the Kingdom of Dublin took over.
kingdom-of-york.r: Jorvik grew into a major town of craftsmen and traders, with goods from Scandinavia to the Middle East, as the Coppergate excavations show. Its kings minted coins, some with Christian symbols, and cooperated with the archbishops of York. Scandinavian settlement left hundreds of place-names across Yorkshire.
kingdom-of-york.e: Aethelstan seized York in 927, but Norse kings such as Olaf Guthfrithson, Amlaib Cuaran and Eric Bloodaxe returned repeatedly. Eric's expulsion and death in 954 ended the kingdom, and York became part of the Kingdom of England as an earldom.

klein-vrystaat.t: A tiny Boer republic on the Swazi border, created from a land grant by the Swazi king Mbandzeni.
klein-vrystaat.o: Around 1886 a group of Boer farmers who had obtained grazing and land concessions from the Swazi king Mbandzeni in the southwest of his kingdom set themselves up as an independent republic, the Little Free State, around the area of the later town of Piet Retief.
klein-vrystaat.r: Very little is recorded beyond its small Volksraad and a population of a few dozen farming families. Its existence was one example of the concessions that left much of the Swazi Kingdom in the hands of outsiders.
klein-vrystaat.e: Klein Vrystaat was incorporated into the South African Republic in 1891.

kingdom-of-matamba.t: An Mbundu kingdom east of Ndongo, often ruled by women, which Queen Njinga made the base of her long resistance to Portugal.
kingdom-of-matamba.o: Matamba lay in the upper Kwango valley and was a tributary of the Kingdom of Kongo in the early 16th century. It was ruled by queens in the later 16th century. Around 1631 Njinga Mbande, driven out of the Kingdom of Ndongo, conquered Matamba and made it the centre of her state.
kingdom-of-matamba.r: Njinga ruled with the support of Imbangala warriors, trading captives to the Dutch during their occupation of Luanda and later to the Portuguese after the peace of 1656. She accepted Christian missionaries, and Santa Maria de Matamba became her capital. After her death in 1663 her sister Barbara and later rulers continued the line, and the kingdom served as a slave-trading intermediary between the interior and Portuguese Angola.
kingdom-of-matamba.e: Matamba remained independent through the 18th and 19th centuries, sometimes at war with Portugal or the Kingdom of Kasanje. Portuguese forces finally occupied it in 1909, and it was absorbed into Portuguese Angola.

kingdom-of-the-hwicce.t: An Anglo-Saxon sub-kingdom of the lower Severn valley around Worcester, ruled by its own kings under Mercian overlordship.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.o: The Hwicce took shape in Gloucestershire, Worcestershire and western Warwickshire after the West Saxon victory at Dyrham in 577 opened the region to English settlement. By the 7th century the area was ruled by a local dynasty, possibly installed or confirmed by Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.r: Hwiccan kings such as Osric and Oshere founded minsters including Bath, Gloucester and Pershore, and a bishopric was created at Worcester around 680 to serve the people. The territory was rich in salt from Droitwich and in farmland, and its charters are among the earliest English documents.
kingdom-of-the-hwicce.e: Hwiccan rulers were downgraded from kings to ealdormen in the late 8th century under Offa. The kingdom's boundaries survived as the medieval diocese of Worcester, preserving its outline for centuries.

kingdom-of-kourion.t: Cypriot kingdom on a clifftop above the south coast, remembered for the sanctuary of Apollo Hylates and for its king's betrayal at the Battle of Salamis in 497 BCE.
kingdom-of-kourion.o: Kourion arose in the Episkopi area of southern Cyprus, near a Late Bronze Age settlement, in the 11th century BCE. Its Greek inhabitants claimed descent from settlers from Argos. By the 7th century BCE it was one of the island's city-kingdoms, listed among the Cypriot rulers who paid tribute to the Assyrian king Esarhaddon.
kingdom-of-kourion.r: The kings ruled a fertile territory along the Kouris river. The sanctuary of Apollo Hylates, god of the woodland, was its chief cult centre, and rich tombs yielded the gold and silver of the so-called Kourion treasure. Kourion followed the Cypriot syllabary and Greek institutions, under Assyrian and then Achaemenid overlordship.
kingdom-of-kourion.e: In the Ionian Revolt, King Stasanor deserted to the Persians at the Battle of Salamis in 497 BCE. Later King Pasicrates aided Alexander at Tyre. The monarchy was abolished under Ptolemy I c. 312 BCE, and Kourion flourished as a Roman and early Christian city until earthquakes in the 4th century CE.
kingdom-of-kourion.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Hylates

kingdom-of-corsica.t: The eight-month kingdom of Theodore von Neuhoff, a German adventurer crowned by Corsican rebels against Genoa in 1736.
kingdom-of-corsica.o: Corsicans had been in revolt against Genoese rule since 1729. In March 1736 Theodore von Neuhoff, a Westphalian baron, landed with arms and money from Tunis, and in April the rebel leaders crowned him king at the convent of Alesani, with a constitution limiting his power.
kingdom-of-corsica.r: Theodore set up a court at Cervione, created orders of knighthood, minted coins and issued titles, but failed to take the Genoese-held coastal towns. Promised foreign aid did not arrive, and his support among the rebel chiefs waned.
kingdom-of-corsica.e: In November 1736 Theodore left Corsica to seek help. His later attempts to return failed, and he ended in a London debtors' prison, dying in 1756. The revolt continued and later produced the Corsican Republic.

kingdom-of-tunisia.t: Tunisia's brief monarchy after independence, in which the last Husainid bey reigned as king while Habib Bourguiba held power.
kingdom-of-tunisia.o: When the French protectorate of Tunisia ended in March 1956, the bey Muhammad al-Amin, known as Lamine Bey, became head of an independent kingdom. Habib Bourguiba, leader of the Neo-Destour party, became prime minister after elections to a constituent assembly.
kingdom-of-tunisia.r: Real power lay with Bourguiba, who sidelined the monarchy and the rival Youssefist faction. In August 1956 the government issued the Code of Personal Status, abolishing polygamy and reforming divorce, among the most progressive family laws in the Arab world. Religious courts were unified and lands of religious endowments reformed.
kingdom-of-tunisia.e: On 25 July 1957 the constituent assembly abolished the monarchy and proclaimed a republic, with Bourguiba as president. Lamine Bey was placed under house arrest, ending the Husainid dynasty, which had ruled since 1705.

kingdom-of-syunik.t: A south Armenian mountain kingdom that outlasted the fall of Ani, home to the great monastery of Tatev.
kingdom-of-syunik.o: The Siunid family had governed the mountainous province of Syunik since antiquity. Around 987 Smbat, a prince of its Baghk branch, took the title king with the backing of Bagratid Armenia, forming a kingdom in the southern highlands between Lake Sevan and the Araxes.
kingdom-of-syunik.r: Kings ruled from fortresses such as Kapan over a land of deep valleys, mines and pasture. The monastery of Tatev, seat of the bishops of Syunik, held many villages and grew into a centre of learning. The kingdom acknowledged the kings of Ani and later paid tribute to the Seljuk Empire while defending its fortresses.
kingdom-of-syunik.e: Seljuk conquests stripped away fortress after fortress in the 12th century, and in 1170 the Eldiguzids took Baghaberd, ending the kingdom. Local princely families such as the Orbelians later restored Armenian rule in Syunik under Georgian and Mongol overlords.

kingdom-of-hana.t: Hana, a kingdom of the middle Euphrates centred on Terqa, which filled the gap left by Mari's fall and preserved its old traditions.
kingdom-of-hana.o: After the Babylonian Empire destroyed Mari c. 1760 BCE, local rulers at Terqa, a few kilometres upstream and long the seat of the god Dagan, created the kingdom of Hana. It controlled the Euphrates valley between the Khabur river and the Babylonian frontier.
kingdom-of-hana.r: Its kings, such as Isharlim and Kashtiliashu, issued land contracts in a distinctive Hana style and kept the Mari-era cult of Dagan. Excavations at Tell Ashara found a scribe's house with a jar of cloves, which must have travelled from south-east Asia. Some rulers bore names suggesting links with the Kassites.
kingdom-of-hana.e: Hana fell under the Mitanni Empire in the 15th century BCE and later the Assyrian Empire, surviving as a province and a regional name. Its successor on the middle Euphrates was the Land of Suhu.

kingdom-of-nepal.t: The Himalayan kingdom of the Shah dynasty, created by the Gorkha conquest of the Kathmandu Valley and abolished in 2008.
kingdom-of-nepal.o: Prithvi Narayan Shah of the Gorkha Kingdom conquered the Kathmandu Valley in 1768 to 1769 and made Kathmandu his capital. His successors extended the kingdom from the Teesta river to the Sutlej, absorbing the Kumaon Kingdom, the Kingdom of Palpa and many hill states, before war with China in 1792 and Britain in 1814 to 1816 checked expansion.
kingdom-of-nepal.r: The Treaty of Sugauli in 1816 fixed Nepal's borders and made it a semi-isolated buffer. From 1846 the Rana family held hereditary power as prime ministers, with the king a figurehead; Jang Bahadur Rana issued the Muluki Ain law code in 1854. Gurkha soldiers served in the British army. The monarchy regained power in 1951 and Mahendra imposed the partyless panchayat system in 1960.
kingdom-of-nepal.e: Popular movements in 1990 restored multiparty democracy. A Maoist insurgency from 1996, the royal massacre of 2001 and King Gyanendra's seizure of power in 2005 led to mass protests in 2006. The Constituent Assembly abolished the monarchy in 2008, creating the Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal.

kwararafa.t: Jukun power of the Benue valley whose armies raided deep into Hausaland in the 16th and 17th centuries.
kwararafa.o: Kwararafa is the name used in Hausa and Bornu sources for a power centred on the Jukun people of the middle Benue. Its origins are obscure; it emerged by the 14th century, perhaps as a confederacy of Jukun and neighbouring groups along the river valleys south of the Hausa states.
kwararafa.r: The Jukun king, the Aku Uka, was a sacred ruler whose wellbeing was bound to the harvest and who was secluded from ordinary view. Kwararafa's strength was military: the Kano Chronicle records attacks that forced Kano to pay tribute, and in the 17th century its armies raided Katsina, Kano and even threatened the Kanem-Bornu Empire.
kwararafa.e: Kwararafa declined in the 18th century under pressure from Bornu, internal division and later the Fulani jihad. Its successor, the Kingdom of Wukari, kept the Jukun kingship, and the Aku Uka still reigns at Wukari in Taraba State.

kolhapur-state.t: The senior surviving Maratha state of Shivaji's line, founded by Queen Tarabai and made famous by the social reformer Shahu Maharaj.
kolhapur-state.o: After the Maratha succession dispute that followed the release of Shahu in 1707, Tarabai, widow of Rajaram, set up a rival court for her son Shivaji II, settling at Kolhapur by around 1710. The Treaty of Warna in 1731 divided the Maratha kingdom between Satara and Kolhapur.
kolhapur-state.r: The Chhatrapatis of Kolhapur ruled the fertile Panchganga valley. Shahu, who reigned from 1894 to 1922, founded schools and hostels, reserved posts for non-Brahmin and backward castes in 1902, and supported the Satyashodhak movement. It was a nineteen-gun salute state.
kolhapur-state.e: Kolhapur merged into Bombay Province in 1949 and became part of Maharashtra in 1960. The royal family remains influential in the city.

kharsawan-state.t: A small Singh Deo state of Chota Nagpur, remembered for the police firing on Adivasi protesters at its merger in 1948.
kharsawan-state.o: Kharsawan was founded by a younger branch of the Singh Deo family of Porahat, the line that also ruled Seraikela State. The register dates its separate existence to around 1650.
kharsawan-state.r: The Rajas governed a small forested territory largely inhabited by Ho and other Adivasi communities, with some iron and copper resources. It came under British protection in the early 19th century and later the Eastern States Agency.
kharsawan-state.e: On 1 January 1948, as Kharsawan was merged into Orissa, police fired on an Adivasi gathering opposing the merger, killing many. The state was transferred to Bihar later that year and now lies in Seraikela Kharsawan district of Jharkhand.

karauli-state.t: The Jadaun Rajput state of eastern Rajasthan, whose rulers claimed descent from Krishna's Yadava clan and whose capital grew around the Madan Mohan temple.
karauli-state.o: The Jadaun Rajputs, claiming descent from the Yadavas, ruled around Bayana and Timangarh before the 14th century. In 1348 Arjun Pal founded the town of Karauli, which became the capital of the state.
karauli-state.r: Karauli was a hilly, largely rural state on the Chambal ravines. Its Maharajas accepted Mughal overlordship and later paid tribute to the Marathas. The temple of Madan Mohan, a form of Krishna, made the town a pilgrimage centre, and red sandstone from local quarries was used for its palaces. In 1817 Karauli signed a treaty with the British.
karauli-state.e: Karauli joined the Matsya Union in 1948, which merged into Rajasthan in 1949. It is now a district of Rajasthan.

kingdom-of-fetu.t: Small Akan kingdom of the Gold Coast in whose lands Cape Coast Castle and other European forts were built.
kingdom-of-fetu.o: Fetu, or Efutu, was a kingdom of Guan and Akan speakers inland from present-day Cape Coast. It existed by the time Portuguese traders reached the coast in the late 15th century, and the coastal town of Oguaa, later Cape Coast, belonged to it.
kingdom-of-fetu.r: Its king drew wealth from renting land to European traders and taxing their commerce in gold and slaves. The Swedes built Carolusborg at Cape Coast in 1653, later taken over by the English as Cape Coast Castle, and the Danes built a fort on a nearby hill. Fetu's rulers played the companies against one another.
kingdom-of-fetu.e: Fetu declined around 1700 under pressure from the Fante and wars among European companies, and its lands were absorbed into the Fante states. Cape Coast became the headquarters of the British on the Gold Coast.

khadga-dynasty.t: A Buddhist dynasty of Samatata in south-eastern Bengal, known from copper plates and the reports of Chinese pilgrims.
khadga-dynasty.o: The Khadgas emerged in the 7th century in Samatata, the region around modern Comilla in south-eastern Bangladesh, after the collapse of the Gauda Kingdom. The line was founded by Khadgodyama, and its capital is named in inscriptions as Karmanta, probably modern Barakamta.
khadga-dynasty.r: The Khadgas were Buddhists and are known from copper plates found at Ashrafpur, which record grants to Buddhist monasteries, and from a few other inscriptions. The Chinese pilgrim Yijing reported that King Rajabhata of Samatata supported thousands of monks and recited Buddhist texts daily. Samatata had trade links with the Bay of Bengal coast.
khadga-dynasty.e: The Khadga line fades from the record in the early 8th century. Samatata later came under the Deva dynasty and then the Chandra dynasty and the Pala Empire.

kingdom-of-arrapha.t: A Hurrian kingdom around modern Kirkuk, vassal of Mitanni, whose town of Nuzi left thousands of tablets on family life, land and law.
kingdom-of-arrapha.o: Arrapha, the ancient name of Kirkuk, became the capital of a Hurrian kingdom east of the Tigris in the 15th century BCE, when the region fell within the sphere of the Mitanni Empire. Its kings ruled the plain between the Lesser Zab and the Zagros foothills as Mitannian vassals.
kingdom-of-arrapha.r: The best evidence comes from Nuzi (Yorghan Tepe), a provincial town excavated in the 1920s and 1930s, where over 5,000 tablets were found. Written in a local Akkadian with many Hurrian words, they record family archives such as that of Tehip-tilla, adoptions used to transfer land, slave contracts, marriage settlements and lawsuits. Society was dominated by the palace and by chariot-owning families. Kings such as Kipi-Teshup and Ithi-Teshup are named in seal impressions and documents.
kingdom-of-arrapha.e: As Mitanni weakened in the mid-14th century BCE, Nuzi was burnt around 1340 BCE, probably by Assyrian forces, and Arrapha was soon absorbed by the Assyrian Empire, later becoming an Assyrian province.

kwanyama-kingdom.t: The largest Ovambo kingdom, straddling the Angola–Namibia border, whose last king Mandume ya Ndemufayo fought both Portugal and South Africa.
kwanyama-kingdom.o: Oukwanyama formed by the 18th century on the floodplains around the Kunene and Cuvelai rivers, under kings drawn from a royal matriclan. It grew into the most populous of the Ovambo kingdoms, with its royal seat in the area of modern Ondjiva.
kwanyama-kingdom.r: Kings held wide power over land and justice, ruling through district headmen and maintaining armed retainers. The economy combined millet farming, cattle, salt and iron, and in the 19th century the kingdom traded cattle and captives for guns and horses with Portuguese and Boer traders. German and Finnish missionaries worked in the kingdom from the 1880s.
kwanyama-kingdom.e: Mandume ya Ndemufayo, king from 1911, resisted Portuguese advances, but after the Portuguese victory at Mongua in 1915 he withdrew south. He was killed fighting South African forces in 1917, and the kingdom was divided between Portuguese Angola and South West Africa.

kapurthala-state.t: The Ahluwalia Sikh state of the Doaba region of Punjab, known for its Francophile Maharaja Jagatjit Singh and his Versailles-style palace.
kapurthala-state.o: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, leader of the Ahluwalia misl and a commander of the Dal Khalsa, briefly held Lahore in 1761 and took Kapurthala in the 1770s. His successor Fateh Singh Ahluwalia was an ally of Ranjit Singh.
kapurthala-state.r: Kapurthala sided with the British after the First Anglo-Sikh War and in 1857, gaining estates in Awadh. Jagatjit Singh (1877–1949) travelled widely, admired France and built the Jagatjit Palace modelled on Versailles. Unusually the Sikh ruler governed a majority-Muslim population, and the state was known for religious tolerance, including a Moorish-style mosque he funded.
kapurthala-state.e: Kapurthala acceded to India in 1947 amid Partition violence and in 1948 joined the Patiala and East Punjab States Union, which merged into Punjab in 1956.

kingdom-of-khurda.t: The Odia kingdom that kept the Gajapati title and guarded the Jagannath temple at Puri under Mughal, Maratha and British overlords.
kingdom-of-khurda.o: After the Karrani Afghans overthrew independent Odisha in 1568, Ramachandra Deva I, of the Bhoi family, established himself at Khurda near Puri. Akbar's general Man Singh recognised him as Raja of Khurda in 1592, and his successors took the Gajapati title of the former kings.
kingdom-of-khurda.r: The Khurda rajas were acknowledged as the first servants of Jagannath at Puri, a role that gave them prestige across Odisha. They ruled a small hill-and-forest territory with paika militia soldiers who held land for service. They paid tribute to the Mughal Empire and, from 1751, to the Marathas of Nagpur.
kingdom-of-khurda.e: The British East India Company took Odisha in 1803. The raja Mukunda Deva II joined a revolt and Khurda was annexed in 1804. Resentment over land settlements led to the Paika Rebellion of 1817. The Puri Gajapati family still holds ritual rights at the Jagannath temple.

kathiri-sultanate.t: The sultanate of the Kathiri tribe in Wadi Hadramawt, which ruled Seiyun and Tarim for centuries and was absorbed into South Yemen in 1967.
kathiri-sultanate.o: The Kathiri tribe rose in Hadramawt in the late 14th and 15th centuries, taking control of the valley's towns. In the 16th century Sultan Badr Abu Tuwayriq expanded Kathiri rule across Hadramawt and into Dhofar, using firearms and troops obtained through Ottoman contacts.
kathiri-sultanate.r: Kathiri sultans ruled from Seiyun, whose mud-brick palace still dominates the town, and from Tarim, the religious centre of the valley's sayyid families and Shafi'i scholarship. Their power depended on tribal alliances and later on remittances from Hadrami emigrants in Java, Singapore and Hyderabad. In the 19th century they lost the coast and much of the valley to the Qu'aiti Sultanate.
kathiri-sultanate.e: An agreement of 1918 with the Qu'aiti and Britain placed the sultanate within the British sphere, later the Aden Protectorate. In 1967 the National Liberation Front took over Hadramawt, abolished the sultanate and incorporated it into South Yemen.

kingdom-of-lihyan.t: The Lihyanite kingdom of al-Ula, whose kings taxed the incense road through the Hejaz and carved monumental statues at Dedan.
kingdom-of-lihyan.o: Lihyan succeeded the Kingdom of Dedan at the oasis of al-Ula, probably in the late 6th or 5th century BCE, after the Babylonian occupation of the Hejaz ended. Its kings ruled from Dedan and drew their wealth from caravans carrying incense from south Arabia towards the Mediterranean.
kingdom-of-lihyan.r: Dadanitic inscriptions record a succession of Lihyanite kings, temple offerings and taxes paid to the god Dhu Ghabat. Large sandstone statues of kings and nobles from the sanctuary at al-Khuraybah show contact with Egyptian and Hellenistic art. Minaean traders from the Kingdom of Ma'in lived alongside the local population and kept their own officials.
kingdom-of-lihyan.e: Lihyan declined as the Nabataean Kingdom extended its control over the caravan trade and took Hegra (Mada'in Salih) to the north. By the 1st century BCE its independence had ended, though the dynasty's exact fate is uncertain. The Lion Tombs and statues at al-Ula are among the region's best-known monuments.

kingdom-of-serbia.t: Serbian kingdom that doubled its territory in the Balkan Wars, endured the First World War and became the core of Yugoslavia.
kingdom-of-serbia.o: Prince Milan Obrenović of the Principality of Serbia, independent since 1878, proclaimed himself king in 1882 with the support of Austria-Hungary. His reign brought defeat by Bulgaria at Slivnitsa in 1885 and domestic unrest, and he abdicated in 1889 in favour of his son Alexander.
kingdom-of-serbia.r: The unpopular Alexander Obrenović was murdered with his queen by army officers in the May Coup of 1903, and Peter I Karađorđević became king. Under the 1903 constitution and Nikola Pašić's Radical Party, Serbia became a parliamentary state, freed itself from Austrian economic control after the Pig War of 1906, and in the Balkan Wars of 1912 to 1913 gained Kosovo and Vardar Macedonia.
kingdom-of-serbia.e: After the Sarajevo assassination, Austria-Hungary attacked Serbia in 1914. Overrun in 1915, its army retreated through Albania to Corfu and returned via the Salonika front in 1918. On 1 December 1918 Serbia joined the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, then called the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

kingdom-of-kasa.t: Bainuk kingdom of the lower Casamance river, whose king's title, Kasa Mansa, gave the region its name.
kingdom-of-kasa.o: Known mainly from Portuguese sources. When Portuguese traders reached the Casamance in the 15th century, they found a kingdom of the Bainuk (Banyun) people on the south bank of the river, whose ruler was called the Kasa Mansa, 'king of Kasa', a title shaped by Mandinka usage.
kingdom-of-kasa.r: Kasa traded rice, wax, cotton cloth and slaves with Portuguese and Luso-African traders who settled at riverside ports. Its rulers dealt with merchants through local intermediaries, and the kingdom sat on the margins of the Kaabu Empire's sphere of influence.
kingdom-of-kasa.e: Kasa declined in the 17th century as Mandinka, Balanta and Jola expansion and the slave trade reshaped the region. Its name survives in the Casamance river and region of southern Senegal.

kingdom-of-dawro.t: An Omotic kingdom of south-western Ethiopia, known for the great defensive stone wall attributed to its kings.
kingdom-of-dawro.o: Dawro, also called Kullo, lay west of Wolaita between the Omo and Gojeb rivers. Its royal dynasty is known from oral tradition, which places its consolidation in the 16th century, after the earlier Christian presence in the region had faded. The kingdom was closely related in language and culture to its neighbours Wolaita and Konta.
kingdom-of-dawro.r: The kawo (king) ruled with regional officials and clan leaders. Dawro is best known for the Halala Kella, a stone wall running for well over 100 kilometres, attributed in tradition to King Halala and built to defend the realm. Its people farmed ensete and grain and traded with Kaffa and the Gibe kingdoms.
kingdom-of-dawro.e: In 1891 Dawro was conquered by the armies of Menelik II and annexed to the Ethiopian Empire. The Dawro Zone today keeps the name, and the Halala Kella wall is a significant heritage site.

khanate-of-kalat.t: The Brahui-led khanate of Balochistan, the paramount power of the region for nearly three centuries until merged into Pakistan.
khanate-of-kalat.o: Around 1666 the Ahmadzai chief Mir Ahmad Khan I established a Brahui-led confederacy based at Kalat, in the highlands of central Balochistan, on the borderlands of Safavid Persia and Mughal India.
khanate-of-kalat.r: The Khan ruled through a tribal confederacy of Sarawan and Jhalawan chiefs. Mir Nasir Khan I, who reigned for much of the late 18th century, organised the army and administration and extended rule to the coast. In 1839 British troops stormed Kalat and killed Mehrab Khan; later treaties made it a British-protected state, with Kharan State and other chiefdoms as feudatories.
khanate-of-kalat.e: Khan Ahmad Yar Khan declared independence in 1947 but acceded to Pakistan in March 1948. Kalat joined the Baluchistan States Union and was absorbed into West Pakistan in 1955.

kishtwar-kingdom.t: A mountain kingdom on the upper Chenab, famed for saffron, whose Rajas converted to Islam in the 17th century before the Dogras of Jammu annexed it.
kishtwar-kingdom.o: Tradition holds that a Rajput named Kahan Pal founded the dynasty around 1100. The kingdom occupied the high valleys of the upper Chenab between Kashmir and the Jammu hills.
kishtwar-kingdom.r: Kishtwar exported saffron and lay on routes between Kashmir, Chamba and Ladakh. In the 17th century the Sufi saint Shah Farid-ud-din came to Kishtwar, and Raja Kirat Singh converted to Islam, after which the dynasty and much of the population became Muslim. The Rajas were tributaries of the Mughal emperors.
kishtwar-kingdom.e: Gulab Singh, Dogra ruler of Jammu under the Sikh Empire, conquered Kishtwar in 1821. It became part of Jammu and Kashmir (princely state) in 1846 and is now a district of Jammu and Kashmir.

kingdom-of-marion.t: Cypriot kingdom on the north-west coast that grew rich on copper trade with Athens until Ptolemy I destroyed it in 312 BCE.
kingdom-of-marion.o: Marion grew near modern Polis Chrysochous in north-west Cyprus, close to the copper mines of Limni, in the early Iron Age. It emerged as a city-kingdom in the Cypro-Archaic period, facing Anatolia and the Aegean across the sea.
kingdom-of-marion.r: Marion exported copper and imported large quantities of Athenian painted pottery, found in its cemeteries. Its kings, some with Greek names such as Stasioikos and others possibly Phoenician, issued coins in the 5th and 4th centuries BCE. Inscriptions use the Cypriot syllabary for Greek.
kingdom-of-marion.e: Its last king, Stasioikos II, sided with Antigonus against Ptolemy I, who destroyed Marion in 312 BCE and moved its people to Paphos. Ptolemy II refounded the site as Arsinoe c. 270 BCE, and the modern town of Polis stands there today.
