kingdom-of-lower-egypt.t: The predynastic Nile Delta, remembered by later Egyptians as a kingdom of the red crown centred on Buto before unification with the south.
kingdom-of-lower-egypt.o: Later Egyptian tradition held that before unification the Delta formed a kingdom of its own, with its capital at Buto (Pe and Dep) and the red crown as its emblem. Archaeologically the region was home to the Buto-Maadi culture of the 4th millennium BCE, with settlements at Buto, Maadi and Tell el-Farkha.
kingdom-of-lower-egypt.r: Whether the Delta was ever a single kingdom is debated; many scholars see a cluster of chiefdoms and trading towns gradually absorbed by Naqada culture spreading from the south around 3400 to 3300 BCE. The Palermo Stone lists names of early northern kings, but they cannot be checked. Buto was home to the cobra goddess Wadjet, and Maadi traded copper, wine and oil with Canaan.
kingdom-of-lower-egypt.e: The north was brought under southern rule around 3100 BCE, remembered as its conquest by Narmer or Menes and the founding of Early Dynastic Egypt. The red crown and Wadjet survived as emblems of Lower Egypt in royal regalia and titles for three thousand years.

kingdom-of-qataban.t: An incense kingdom of south Arabia centred on Wadi Bayhan and its capital Timna, rival of Saba and Hadramawt for five centuries.
kingdom-of-qataban.o: Qataban emerges in Sabaean inscriptions of the 7th century BCE as a junior ally of the Kingdom of Saba. As Sabaean power waned, its rulers asserted independence by the 5th or 4th century BCE, ruling from Timna (modern Hajar Kuhlan) in Wadi Bayhan, at the start of the caravan route north.
kingdom-of-qataban.r: The kingdom taxed the incense trade and built irrigation systems in Wadi Bayhan. Its most famous text, the market law of Shahr Yagil Yuhargib on a stele at Timna, regulated trade and taxes. Qatabanians worshipped the god Amm and wrote Qatabanic. At its height it reached the Gulf of Aden coast and Wadi Markha.
kingdom-of-qataban.e: Qataban weakened in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE as sea trade grew. Timna was burnt, and around 175 CE the Kingdom of Hadramawt and the Himyarite Kingdom divided its lands. Excavations by American teams in the 1950s made Timna one of the best-known south Arabian sites.

kingdom-of-zazzau.t: Southernmost of the seven Hausa states, famed for the warrior queen Amina and for its role in raiding and trade toward the Niger and Benue.
kingdom-of-zazzau.o: Zazzau emerged by the 11th century among Hausa farming communities on the southern edge of Hausaland and is counted among the Hausa Bakwai. Its early capital was Turunku. Tradition holds that Zaria, the later capital, was founded in the 16th century by Queen Bakwa Turunku and named after one of her daughters.
kingdom-of-zazzau.r: Zazzau's position on the frontier made it the Hausa state of war captives and expansion: its rulers raided and taxed peoples to the south and controlled routes to the Nupe and Kwararafa lands. Queen Amina, remembered as a 16th century conqueror, is credited with walled camps across the region. Islam spread among the ruling class from the 15th century.
kingdom-of-zazzau.e: In 1808 the jihadist Malam Musa took Zaria, which became the Zaria Emirate under the Sokoto Caliphate. The Hausa royal house fled south and founded the Abuja Emirate at Zuba, today's Suleja. Zaria remains an emirate and a major city of northern Nigeria.

kalingga-kingdom.t: A Javanese kingdom on the north coast of Central Java, famed in Chinese records for the strict justice of its Queen Shima.
kalingga-kingdom.o: Chinese histories of the Tang dynasty describe a kingdom called Ho-ling on Java that sent envoys from the 7th century. Most historians place it on the north coast of Central Java, near Jepara. Its beginnings are not recorded, and the register's dates are approximate.
kalingga-kingdom.r: The New Book of Tang tells of Queen Shima, chosen in 674, whose rule was so just that a bag of gold left in the road went untouched for three years until her own son touched it with his foot, for which she ordered his punishment. Ho-ling was also a Buddhist centre: the monk Huining worked there with the Javanese scholar Jnanabhadra in 664 to 665 to translate scriptures.
kalingga-kingdom.e: Kalingga's later history is obscure. Its people and court traditions are thought to have passed into the Medang Kingdom, founded by Sanjaya in 732 in the interior of Central Java. The legend of Shima remains a popular story of good government in Indonesia.

kingdom-of-the-netherlands.t: The Dutch constitutional monarchy, shaped by the 1848 constitution, colonial empire, neutrality, war and post-war reconstruction into a founding EU member.
kingdom-of-the-netherlands.o: The Kingdom of the Netherlands took its present shape when William I accepted Belgian independence in the Treaty of London of 1839. Constitutional revision in 1848, drafted under Johan Rudolf Thorbecke, introduced ministerial responsibility and direct elections, establishing parliamentary government.
kingdom-of-the-netherlands.r: The colonial empire, above all the Dutch East Indies, brought wealth through the cultivation system, criticised in Multatuli's Max Havelaar. Society was organised in 'pillars' of Protestants, Catholics, socialists and liberals. The country stayed neutral in the First World War but was occupied by Germany from 1940 to 1945, while Queen Wilhelmina led the government from London.
kingdom-of-the-netherlands.e: Indonesia became independent in 1949. After the North Sea flood of 1953 the Delta Works were built. The Netherlands co-founded NATO and the European Communities, and since 1954 the Kingdom has included Caribbean countries. Willem-Alexander became king in 2013.

kingdom-of-agbor.t: Ika kingdom west of the lower Niger, ruled by the Dein of Agbor and long within the sphere of the Benin Empire.
kingdom-of-agbor.o: Agbor lies in the forest between Benin City and the Niger, among the Ika, an Igboid-speaking people with strong ties to the Edo. Its kingship is believed to date from around the 15th century, when Benin influence spread east toward the river, and its traditions combine Edo and Igbo elements.
kingdom-of-agbor.r: The Dein of Agbor ruled with title-holding chiefs and age-grade associations over yam-farming villages. Agbor paid tribute to the Oba of the Benin Empire and adopted Benin titles and regalia, while keeping its own dynasty and local religious practices.
kingdom-of-agbor.e: After the British conquest of Benin in 1897, Agbor came under British control and was incorporated into Southern Nigeria. The Dein of Agbor remains the traditional ruler of Agbor in Delta State.

kingdom-of-manu-a.t: The island realm of the Tuʻi Manuʻa in eastern Samoa, whose title was revered as the oldest and most sacred in Samoan tradition.
kingdom-of-manu-a.o: The Manuʻa group, the islands of Taʻu, Ofu and Olosega, lies at the eastern end of the Samoan archipelago. Samoan tradition holds that the god Tagaloa created the islands and that the first Tuʻi Manuʻa was his descendant, so the title predates the great titles of Upolu and Savaiʻi. Its early history is known only from oral genealogies.
kingdom-of-manu-a.r: The Tuʻi Manuʻa lived on Taʻu and was surrounded by strict taboos: commoners could not look on him directly, and a council of chiefs (fono) handled daily affairs. Villages lived from taro, breadfruit, coconut and fishing. Manuʻa stood somewhat apart from the wars over titles in western Samoa, and its prestige rested on ancestry and ritual rather than conquest. Christian missionaries arrived in the 1830s and most islanders converted.
kingdom-of-manu-a.e: After the Samoan islands were divided in 1899, Tuʻi Manuʻa Elisala signed a deed of cession to the United States in 1904, bringing Manuʻa into what became American Samoa. After his death in 1909 the American authorities discouraged the title, which fell into abeyance.

kingdom-of-israel.t: The northern Kingdom of Israel, a wealthy Iron Age state centred on Samaria, home of prophets Elijah and Amos, conquered by Assyria.
kingdom-of-israel.o: After Solomon's death c. 930 BCE, the northern tribes rejected his son and made Jeroboam I king, splitting the United Kingdom of Israel. Jeroboam set up shrines at Bethel and Dan to rival Jerusalem. Omri founded a new capital at Samaria c. 880 BCE.
kingdom-of-israel.r: Israel was larger and richer than Judah, with olive oil, wine and trade links to Tyre. Ahab fielded 2,000 chariots at Qarqar in 853 BCE, and the Black Obelisk shows Jehu paying tribute to Shalmaneser III. The prophets Elijah, Amos and Hosea condemned its kings' religious and social policies.
kingdom-of-israel.e: After a revolt against the Assyrian Empire, Shalmaneser V besieged Samaria, which fell in 722 BCE; Sargon II deported over 27,000 people and made Israel a province. The exiles became the legend of the ten lost tribes, while the Samaritans claim descent from those who remained.

kingdom-of-dhanyawadi.t: The first kingdom of Arakan in the Rakhine chronicles, remembered as the home of the Mahamuni image, the most revered Buddha statue in Myanmar.
kingdom-of-dhanyawadi.o: Rakhine chronicles place the founding of Dhanyawadi far back in antiquity, with a line of kings ruling from a walled city in the Kaladan valley. Historians date the excavated city, with its brick walls and palace site, to the early centuries CE, and the register's 1st to 4th century span follows the later chronicle chronology.
kingdom-of-dhanyawadi.r: Dhanyawadi was a rice-growing and trading kingdom on the Bay of Bengal, open to Indian influence. Its fame rests on the Mahamuni Buddha, which tradition says was cast in the Buddha's lifetime under King Chandrasuriya. Sanskrit inscriptions and coins of the following Chandra kings show Indian-style kingship.
kingdom-of-dhanyawadi.e: According to the chronicles, power shifted south to the new city of Waithali around 370. The Mahamuni image remained at Dhanyawadi until 1784, when the Konbaung dynasty carried it to Mandalay, where it is still a major pilgrimage site.

kingdom-of-abkhazia.t: A western Georgian kingdom whose rulers, though Abkhaz in origin, built a Georgian church and culture and through Bagrat III united Georgia in 1008.
kingdom-of-abkhazia.o: Around 778 Leon II, ruler of the Principality of Abasgia, broke from the Byzantine Empire with Khazar help, took the title king and joined Abasgia to Egrisi, the old lands of Lazica. He moved his capital to Kutaisi, shifting the state's centre into the Georgian-speaking interior.
kingdom-of-abkhazia.r: Over the 9th century the kings replaced Greek with Georgian in church and government and separated the western Georgian church from Constantinople. Under George II and Constantine III the kingdom expanded into Kartli and fought the Armenian Bagratids. Churches such as Mokvi and Bedia show its wealth, and the kingdom controlled the Black Sea coast and Rioni valley.
kingdom-of-abkhazia.e: In 978 the throne passed to Bagrat III, son of the Bagratid Gurgen and an Abkhazian princess. In 1008 he inherited Kartli as well, founding the united Kingdom of Georgia.

krivichs.t: A large East Slavic tribal union on the upper Dnieper, Dvina and Volga, whose towns became Smolensk and Polotsk.
krivichs.o: The Krivichs settled the forested watershed between the Dnieper, the Western Dvina and the upper Volga between the 6th and 8th centuries, mixing with the Baltic and Finnic peoples already there. Archaeologists link them with the culture of long burial mounds. The Primary Chronicle names their towns Smolensk, Polotsk and Izborsk.
krivichs.r: They were organised in clans and districts around fortified centres, governed by elders and tribal assemblies. Their lands lay on the river route from the Baltic to the Black Sea, so trade with Scandinavians brought silver and goods. According to the chronicle, the Krivichs joined the Ilmen Slavs and Finnic tribes in inviting Rurik and his Varangians to rule them.
krivichs.e: In 882 Prince Oleg took Smolensk on his way south to Kiev, and the Krivichs were drawn into Kievan Rus', paying tribute and serving in its armies. Their territory later formed the Principality of Polotsk and the Principality of Smolensk, and their name survives in Latvian as the word for Russians, krievi.

kanjuruhan-kingdom.t: A small Hindu kingdom near modern Malang in East Java, known from a single Sanskrit inscription of 760 and the temple of Badut.
kanjuruhan-kingdom.o: Kanjuruhan is known almost entirely from the Dinoyo inscription of 760, found near Malang. It tells how King Gajayana, son of Dewasimha, built a temple to the sage Agastya and replaced an old wooden image with one of black stone. It is the oldest known kingdom of East Java.
kanjuruhan-kingdom.r: The inscription shows a Shaivite court with Brahmin priests, gifts of land and cattle, and a cult of Agastya brought from southern India. Candi Badut, one of the oldest temples in East Java, is thought to be the shrine it describes.
kanjuruhan-kingdom.e: No later record names Kanjuruhan as an independent kingdom. In the 9th and 10th centuries inscriptions mention a Rakai Kanuruhan as a title within the Medang Kingdom, suggesting the area had been absorbed and its rulers became regional lords.

kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia.t: The short-lived realm of the Amorite king Shamshi-Adad I, who united northern Mesopotamia from the Zagros to the Euphrates and ruled through his sons.
kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia.o: Shamshi-Adad, an Amorite chief, seized Ekallatum on the Tigris and then the city of Assur around 1808 BCE. He went on to take Mari on the Euphrates and the Khabur plains, creating the first state to unify Upper Mesopotamia, with its capital at Shubat-Enlil (Tell Leilan).
kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia.r: Shamshi-Adad ruled as 'king of the universe', placing his elder son Ishme-Dagan at Ekallatum and his younger son Yasmah-Addu at Mari. The Mari archives preserve his letters, in which he scolds Yasmah-Addu for idleness and directs campaigns, censuses and harvests. The kingdom was a network of fortified cities, tribal allies and vassals, held together by the king's personal energy. Later Assyrian tradition counted him among the kings of the Assyrian Empire.
kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia.e: After Shamshi-Adad died around 1776 BCE, the kingdom fell apart. Zimri-Lim recovered Mari, local kings rose at Andarig, Karana and Kurda, and Ishme-Dagan kept only the core around Ekallatum and Assur.

khanate-of-tabriz.t: The khanate of the great city of Tabriz in the turbulent half-century after Nader Shah, ruled for much of it by the Kurdish Donboli family.
khanate-of-tabriz.o: Tabriz, the chief city of Azerbaijan, came under local khans after the death of Nader Shah in 1747, as rivals including Azad Khan Afghan and Fath Ali Khan Afshar fought over the region. Under Karim Khan of the Zand Empire, Najaf Qoli Khan of the Donboli family was confirmed as governor and ruled largely independently.
khanate-of-tabriz.r: Najaf Qoli Khan rebuilt Tabriz after the devastating earthquake of 1780, constructing new walls and gates. The city remained a major centre of trade between Iran, the Ottoman Empire and Russia, famous for its bazaar and crafts. The khans balanced between the Zands, the Donbolis of Khoy and other neighbours.
khanate-of-tabriz.e: Agha Mohammad Khan's Qajar Iran took Tabriz in the 1790s, and from 1799 the city became the seat of the Qajar crown prince, notably Abbas Mirza, as governor of Azerbaijan.

kel-gres.t: A Tuareg confederation pushed south from Aïr that settled on the borderlands of Hausaland, mixing pastoral and agricultural life.
kel-gres.o: The Kel Gres lived in the Aïr mountains in the early modern period, with ties to the Sultanate of Agadez. Pressure from the Kel Ewey drove them south, and by the 18th century they had settled in the region between Tahoua and Madaoua on the northern edge of the Hausa kingdoms.
kel-gres.r: The Kel Gres combined camel and cattle herding with control over farming villages worked by dependent and servile groups. They traded in salt and livestock and were drawn into the wars of the Kingdom of Gobir and its neighbours, and later into rivalries with the Iwellemmeden Kel Dinnik. Muslim scholarly lineages had high prestige.
kel-gres.e: The French conquered the region around 1900, and Tuareg resistance during the First World War was suppressed by 1917. The Kel Gres are today part of Niger's Tuareg population.

karafuto-prefecture.t: Japan's colony on the southern half of Sakhalin island, won from Russia in 1905 and lost to the Soviet Union in 1945.
karafuto-prefecture.o: The Treaty of Portsmouth that ended the Russo-Japanese War in 1905 gave Japan Sakhalin south of the 50th parallel. Japan set up the Karafuto Agency in 1907, with its seat at Toyohara, the former Russian settlement of Vladimirovka.
karafuto-prefecture.r: Karafuto was run by a governor under the home government. Japanese settlers came to fish herring and salmon, cut timber and work in pulp and paper mills and coal mines, and the population reached about 400,000 by the 1940s, including Korean labourers. Ainu, Nivkh and Uilta communities were pressed to assimilate. In 1943 Karafuto was made part of Japan proper.
karafuto-prefecture.e: Soviet forces invaded in August 1945 and occupied the territory, and the Japanese population was repatriated by 1949, though many Koreans were left behind. Japan renounced its claim in 1951, and the area is now part of Russia's Sakhalin Oblast.

kingdom-of-pengwern.t: A shadowy British kingdom of the Shropshire borderlands, remembered in the Welsh poems lamenting Cynddylan and the ruin of his hall.
kingdom-of-pengwern.o: Pengwern is known almost entirely from Welsh poetry, notably the Canu Heledd, a 9th or 10th century cycle of poems lamenting Cynddylan, a 7th century prince. Its centre is uncertain; later tradition placed it at Shrewsbury, while scholars suggest the Wrekin area or Din Gwrygon.
kingdom-of-pengwern.r: Nothing reliable is recorded of its government. The poems describe Cynddylan's hall at Eglwysau Bassa and his wars against the English, and he may have been an ally of Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia. The kingdom was probably one of several successors to the Cornovii tribal region.
kingdom-of-pengwern.e: Pengwern seems to have fallen to Mercian expansion in the mid 7th century; Cynddylan's death is lamented in the poems. Its lands became Mercian, while its memory survived in Welsh literature as a symbol of loss.

kingdom-of-saxony.t: Kingdom of the Albertine Wettins created under Napoleon, a German industrial heartland around Dresden, Leipzig and Chemnitz.
kingdom-of-saxony.o: Elector Frederick Augustus III of Saxony changed sides after Prussia's defeat at Jena and joined the Confederation of the Rhine in December 1806, taking the title King Frederick Augustus I. Napoleon also made him Duke of Warsaw in 1807.
kingdom-of-saxony.r: Saxony fought for Napoleon until Leipzig in 1813, and at the Congress of Vienna it lost about three-fifths of its territory to Prussia. A constitution followed the unrest of 1830, and the May Uprising in Dresden in 1849 was crushed with Prussian help. Textiles, machine building and mining made Saxony one of Germany's most industrialised regions, and Leipzig was a centre of publishing and music.
kingdom-of-saxony.e: Saxony sided with Austria in 1866, then joined the North German Confederation and in 1871 the German Empire. King Frederick Augustus III abdicated in November 1918, and the state became the Free State of Saxony.

kingdom-of-gandhara.t: An ancient kingdom of Taxila and the Peshawar valley, gateway between India and Iran, before it became a province of the Achaemenid Empire.
kingdom-of-gandhara.o: Gandhara, praised in the Rigveda for its sheep's wool, became one of the sixteen mahajanapadas by the 7th and 6th centuries BCE. It covered the Peshawar valley and the land across the Indus around Taxila, in modern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan, and controlled the routes linking the Ganges plain with Bactria and Iran.
kingdom-of-gandhara.r: Buddhist texts record its king Pukkusati, said to have exchanged envoys and gifts with Bimbisara of Magadha and later to have become a monk. Taxila was already a centre of learning, where teachers taught the Vedas, medicine and statecraft to students from across northern India. Excavations at the Bhir Mound reveal the early city with its irregular streets.
kingdom-of-gandhara.e: Around 518 BCE Gandhara appears as a subject land in the Behistun inscription of Darius I, conquered by Cyrus or Darius, and it paid tribute to the Achaemenid Empire. Under Persian rule the Kharoshthi script developed from Aramaic. Local rule resurfaced later in the Kingdom of Taxila that Alexander met.

korean-empire.t: Korea's last independent monarchy, proclaimed by King Gojong in 1897 to assert equality with China and Japan, and annexed by Japan in 1910.
korean-empire.o: After Japan's victory over Qing China in 1895 ended Korea's tributary ties, Japanese agents murdered Queen Min, and King Gojong took refuge in the Russian legation in 1896. Returning to his palace in 1897, he proclaimed the Great Han Empire and took the title of emperor, choosing the era name Gwangmu.
korean-empire.r: The Gwangmu reforms carried out land surveys, issued land titles and brought electricity, telegraphs, a tramway and the first railway to Seoul, while strengthening imperial power. The emperor suppressed the reformist Independence Club in 1898. Korea became a prize in rivalry between Russia and Japan, and Japan's victory in the war of 1904 and 1905 left it exposed.
korean-empire.e: The Eulsa Treaty of 1905 made Korea a Japanese protectorate under Resident-General Ito Hirobumi. Gojong sent secret envoys to The Hague in 1907 and was forced to abdicate for his son Sunjong; the army was disbanded, and Japan annexed Korea in 1910.

kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.t: Early Welsh kingdom of the Tywi valley in Carmarthenshire, conquered around 730 by Ceredigion to form the realm of Seisyllwg.
kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.o: Ystrad Tywi, 'the vale of the Tywi', covered the fertile river valley and surrounding uplands of what is now Carmarthenshire, including the old Roman town of Moridunum, Carmarthen. After Roman rule ended around 410 it seems to have emerged as a separate territory, sometimes held by the kings of the neighbouring Kingdom of Dyfed.
kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.r: Very little is known about its rulers or government, and no secure king list survives. The Tywi valley was among the best farmland in south-west Wales, with major church sites such as Llandeilo Fawr, home of the gospel book now known as the Lichfield Gospels before it left Wales.
kingdom-of-ystrad-tywi.e: Around 730 Seisyll ap Clydog of the Kingdom of Ceredigion conquered Ystrad Tywi, forming a larger kingdom named Seisyllwg after him. This passed in the 10th century to Hywel Dda and became part of Deheubarth, whose later princes ruled from Dinefwr in the Tywi valley.

kingdom-of-kaan.t: The Snake Kingdom, the most powerful Classic Maya state, which from Dzibanche and later Calakmul built a network of allies to encircle Tikal.
kingdom-of-kaan.o: The snake-head emblem dynasty of Kaan is first firmly attested at Dzibanche in southern Quintana Roo in the 5th and 6th centuries. Around 635 the dynasty moved its seat to Calakmul in Campeche, a large city whose own earlier lords had used a different emblem.
kingdom-of-kaan.r: Kaan exercised power through hegemony rather than direct rule: subject kings at Caracol, Naranjo, Dos Pilas, El Perú-Waka', La Corona and Cancuén acknowledged its overlords. Under Yuknoom Ch'een II, who reigned from 636 to about 686, it reached its height, and Calakmul holds more stelae than any other Maya city. Its alliance defeated Tikal in 562.
kingdom-of-kaan.e: Tikal's victory over Yuknoom Yich'aak K'ahk' in 695 broke Kaan's dominance, and its network fragmented in the 8th century. Calakmul raised its last monuments around 900. The kingdom remained little known until its glyphs were deciphered in the 1990s.

kingdom-of-albania-medieval.t: Angevin kingdom on the Albanian coast created by Charles I of Anjou in 1272 as a base for his ambitions against Byzantium.
kingdom-of-albania-medieval.o: Charles I of Anjou, king of Sicily, acquired claims to the Albanian coast through the Treaty of Viterbo of 1267. In 1272 Albanian nobles and the city of Durrës accepted him, and he proclaimed himself King of Albania (Regnum Albaniae).
kingdom-of-albania-medieval.r: The kingdom was governed by Angevin captains-general and marshals from Durrës, with Albanian nobles granted titles and privileges. It served as a bridgehead for Charles's planned attack on Byzantium, but the Angevin army was defeated at the siege of Berat in 1281. Thereafter it was reduced mostly to Durrës and its surroundings, held by the princes of Achaea and Taranto.
kingdom-of-albania-medieval.e: Albanian lords and the Serbian Empire took much of the land in the 14th century. In 1368 Karl Thopia seized Durrës, ending Angevin rule and founding the Principality of Albania (medieval).

kowoj.t: A Maya group of the Petén lakes that claimed descent from Mayapan and rivalled the Itza until both fell to Spain in 1697.
kowoj.o: According to their own traditions, the Kowoj (Couoh) migrated south from Mayapan to the Petén lakes after its fall around 1441, arriving by about 1450. They settled the north-eastern shores of Lake Petén Itzá and nearby lakes, with Zacpetén on Lake Salpetén as an important centre.
kowoj.r: The Kowoj were led by their own lords and at times allied with, and at times fought, the Itza kingdom of Nojpetén. Their towns show architecture modelled on Mayapan, with temple assemblages and colonnaded halls. Excavations at Zacpetén revealed ritual deposits and evidence of warfare. Kowoj leaders were involved in the Itza succession struggles of the 1690s.
kowoj.e: The Spanish conquest of Nojpetén in 1697 ended Kowoj independence. Many fled into the forests, and the survivors were gathered into colonial mission towns around the lake.

kingdom-of-han-206-bc.t: The remote kingdom Xiang Yu gave Liu Bang in 206 BCE, from which Liu fought his way out to defeat Xiang Yu and found the Han dynasty.
kingdom-of-han-206-bc.o: Liu Bang, a minor Qin official turned rebel, was first to enter the Qin heartland and accepted the surrender of Ziying. Xiang Yu, wary of him, made him King of Han in 206 BCE, ruling the isolated Hanzhong, Ba and Shu regions from Nanzheng. Liu Bang burned the plank roads behind him to show he had no ambitions.
kingdom-of-han-206-bc.r: With the chancellor Xiao He managing supplies and the general Han Xin commanding the army, the kingdom became a base for war. Xiao He kept the Qin records and grain stores, and Sichuan's resources fed the campaigns.
kingdom-of-han-206-bc.e: In 206 BCE Liu Bang conquered the Three Qins, then fought Western Chu for four years, losing at Pengcheng but recovering. After Xiang Yu's death at Gaixia in 202 BCE, Liu Bang took the title of emperor, and his kingdom gave its name to the Han Dynasty and to the Han Chinese.

khanate-of-gilan.t: A short-lived khanate on the Caspian coast whose ruler Hedayat-Allah Khan built up Rasht before falling to Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar.
khanate-of-gilan.o: Hedayat-Allah Khan, of a notable family from Fuman, became governor of Gilan under Karim Khan of the Zand Empire around 1762 and soon ruled the province as an autonomous khanate with its centre at Rasht.
khanate-of-gilan.r: Gilan was rich from silk, rice and Caspian trade with Russia, and Hedayat-Allah Khan developed Rasht as a commercial town. He was caught between the Zands, the rising Qajar leader Agha Mohammad Khan and Russia, whose navy and merchants were active on the Caspian; he invited Russian help and briefly lost and regained his province.
khanate-of-gilan.e: In 1786 Agha Mohammad Khan invaded Gilan. Hedayat-Allah Khan fled and was killed, and Gilan became part of the emerging Qajar Iran.

kingdom-of-gwent.t: Welsh kingdom between the Usk and the Wye, heir to the Roman town of Caerwent, which fell to the Normans after 1067.
kingdom-of-gwent.o: Gwent took its name from Venta Silurum, Caerwent, the Roman capital of the Silures. After Roman rule ended a kingdom formed in the land between the Usk and the Wye, with traditions of a founder named Caradog Freichfras. Its kings were often the same as those of the Kingdom of Glywysing, the two realms passing between branches of one dynasty.
kingdom-of-gwent.r: The Llandaff charters record grants by its kings to churches and show a landscape of royal estates and small monasteries. Brochfael ap Meurig submitted to Alfred of Wessex, according to Asser. The kingdom lay on the English border, and its rulers alternately fought and allied with the Mercians and later the English kings, while the fertile Usk valley and coastal levels provided its wealth.
kingdom-of-gwent.e: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn seized Gwent in the 1050s. After the Norman Conquest William FitzOsbern built Chepstow Castle from 1067 and pushed west. Its last king, Caradog ap Gruffudd, was killed at the battle of Mynydd Carn in 1081, and Gwent became Norman marcher lordships, later Monmouthshire.

kingdom-of-allada.t: Aja kingdom of the Slave Coast, the leading slave-trading state of the area in the 17th century and the ancestral seat of Dahomey's kings.
kingdom-of-allada.o: Allada was founded by Aja migrants from Tado, west of the Mono river, traditionally in the 15th century. Tradition links its royal line, descended from the founding ancestor Agassu, to the later rulers of the Kingdom of Dahomey and the Kingdom of Porto-Novo, which branched off from Allada in the 17th century.
kingdom-of-allada.r: Allada's king, known to Europeans as the king of Ardra, controlled the coast through the port of Offra and dealt with Portuguese, Dutch, English and French traders, becoming a major source of enslaved people by the 1640s. In 1670 Allada sent an ambassador to the court of Louis XIV. Vodun cults and royal ancestor worship underpinned kingship.
kingdom-of-allada.e: In 1724 Agaja of Dahomey conquered Allada, and its ruling family fled to the Kingdom of Porto-Novo. The town remains a ritual centre, and the Allada dynasty is recognised as the ancestor of Benin's royal houses.

kingdom-of-bhutan.t: The Himalayan Buddhist monarchy of the Wangchuck dynasty, known for its policy of Gross National Happiness.
kingdom-of-bhutan.o: After decades of civil strife in Zhabdrung Bhutan, Ugyen Wangchuck, penlop of Trongsa, defeated his rivals and gained British favour. In 1907 an assembly of monks, officials and nobles at Punakha elected him the first hereditary king, the Druk Gyalpo, ending the dual system of rule.
kingdom-of-bhutan.r: The Treaty of Punakha in 1910 placed foreign affairs under British guidance, a role later taken by India in 1949. Jigme Dorji Wangchuck created a national assembly in 1953 and began modernisation, and Thimphu became the capital. Jigme Singye Wangchuck promoted Gross National Happiness and preserved traditional culture. The expulsion of many Lhotshampa of Nepali descent in the early 1990s remains controversial.
kingdom-of-bhutan.e: Jigme Singye Wangchuck devolved power and abdicated in 2006 in favour of his son Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck. Bhutan held its first parliamentary elections and adopted a constitution in 2008, becoming a constitutional monarchy.

cr.a: See File history below for details.

kirghiz-ssr.t: The Soviet republic of the Kyrgyz in the Tian Shan, the direct forerunner of today's Kyrgyzstan.
kirghiz-ssr.o: Under the Soviet constitution of December 1936 the Kirghiz ASSR was made a union republic, the Kirghiz SSR, with its capital at Frunze, the former Pishpek and today's Bishkek.
kirghiz-ssr.r: The republic was a land of mountain pastures, livestock farming, mining and some industry, with a large Russian population in Frunze and the north and Uzbeks in the south around Osh. Kyrgyz culture was promoted in Soviet form, including the epic of Manas and the novels of Chingiz Aitmatov. Turdakun Usubaliyev led the party from 1961 to 1985. Ethnic clashes between Kyrgyz and Uzbeks in Osh in 1990 killed hundreds.
kirghiz-ssr.e: The physicist Askar Akayev became president in 1990. After the failed Moscow coup, the republic declared independence on 31 August 1991 as the Republic of Kyrgyzstan.

kingdom-of-orleans.t: Short-lived Merovingian kingdom of Clovis' son Chlodomer, which vanished when he fell in battle in 524.
kingdom-of-orleans.o: In the division of 511 Clovis' second son Chlodomer received lands along the Loire, with Orléans as his capital, together with Tours, Bourges and part of Aquitaine.
kingdom-of-orleans.r: Chlodomer ruled for only thirteen years. Little is known of his government beyond his wars against the Kingdom of the Burgundians, during which he had the captured King Sigismund and his family killed in 524.
kingdom-of-orleans.e: Chlodomer was killed later in 524 at the Battle of Vézeronce. His uncles Childebert I and Chlothar I murdered two of his young sons and divided his kingdom. The third son, Clodoald, escaped and became a monk; the town of Saint-Cloud near Paris is named after him.

kotda-pitha-state.t: A minor Kathi chiefship of central Kathiawar, one of the clan estates under British supervision.
kotda-pitha-state.o: Kotda Pitha was a small estate in central Kathiawar held by a Kathi family from around 1700. Its founding is known mainly from local tradition.
kotda-pitha-state.r: The Darbar held a few villages and, after 1807, came under British supervision in the Kathiawar Agency. Little else is recorded in standard works.
kotda-pitha-state.e: Kotda Pitha merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960.

krusevo-republic.t: Ten-day revolutionary government in the mountain town of Kruševo during the Ilinden Uprising of 1903, celebrated in North Macedonia as a founding moment.
krusevo-republic.o: On 2 August 1903, the feast of Saint Elijah, the Internal Macedonian-Adrianople Revolutionary Organisation launched the Ilinden Uprising against Ottoman rule in Macedonia. Rebels under Nikola Karev and Pitu Guli seized Kruševo, a prosperous mountain town of Slav, Aromanian and Greek-oriented Orthodox families, and proclaimed a provisional government.
krusevo-republic.r: Karev headed a council that included members of the different communities, and the town's administration, courts and supplies were reorganised for defence. The Kruševo Manifesto, attributed to the rebels, called on the local Muslim population to join the struggle against tyranny rather than against neighbours. The republic lasted about ten days.
krusevo-republic.e: An Ottoman army retook Kruševo around 12 August 1903; Pitu Guli died defending the Mečkin Kamen position and much of the town was burnt. Bulgaria and North Macedonia both claim the uprising, and the Ilinden memorial at Kruševo is a national symbol of North Macedonia.

koliya-republic.t: A small clan republic in the Himalayan foothills, home of the Buddha's mother and neighbour and kin of the Shakyas.
koliya-republic.o: The Koliyas lived east of the Shakya republic, across the Rohini river in the Terai of modern Nepal and India. They emerged as a self-governing clan by the 7th or 6th century BCE, with their main town at Ramagrama. The two clans intermarried, and Buddhist tradition makes Maya, mother of the Buddha, a Koliya princess.
koliya-republic.r: Like the Shakyas, the Koliyas were governed by an assembly of clan heads. They grew rice on land watered by the Rohini, and Buddhist texts tell how a quarrel with the Shakyas over its water nearly led to war until the Buddha reconciled them. They were dependent on the larger Kingdom of Kosala.
koliya-republic.e: After the Buddha's death the Koliyas received a share of his relics and built a stupa at Ramagrama, which survives in Nepal. They were absorbed by Kosala and then by Magadha in the 5th century BCE.

kingdom-of-armenia-orontid.t: The first Armenian dynasty, the Orontids or Yervandunis, ruled Armenia as Persian satraps and then as kings for over three centuries before the Seleucids took over.
kingdom-of-armenia-orontid.o: After the fall of the Kingdom of Urartu, Armenian-speaking groups dominated the highlands. The Orontid family appears as governors of the satrapy of Armenia under the Achaemenid Empire, and the Behistun inscription of Darius I records fighting in Armenia in 521 BCE. The traditional start of the dynasty in the 6th century BCE is uncertain.
kingdom-of-armenia-orontid.r: The Orontids ruled as satraps closely tied to the Persian court, sending horses as tribute, while Xenophon described the villages and wheat beer of Armenia in 401 BCE. After Alexander the Great, they ruled as effectively independent kings from Armavir and then Yervandashat. Their culture blended Iranian religion and Aramaic administration with local traditions.
kingdom-of-armenia-orontid.e: Around 200 BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus III defeated Orontes IV and divided the land between his generals Artaxias and Zariadres. After the Seleucid defeat at Magnesia in 190 BCE, Artaxias founded the Kingdom of Armenia (Artaxiad), which kept many Orontid traditions.

kingdom-of-ngoyo.t: A small Kongo coastal kingdom around Cabinda whose port grew into one of the busiest Atlantic slave-trading harbours north of the Congo River.
kingdom-of-ngoyo.o: Ngoyo was one of three Kikongo-speaking kingdoms on the coast north of the Congo estuary, alongside the Kingdom of Loango and the Kingdom of Kakongo. Its people, the Woyo, recognised the seniority of Loango in early times but by the mid-16th century Ngoyo was ruled by its own king, the Mangoyo, from Mbanza Ngoyo.
kingdom-of-ngoyo.r: The king was a sacred figure who, by tradition, could not see the sea, and was elected by senior lineages. Royal officials managed trade at the port of Cabinda, where Dutch, English, French and Portuguese ships bought slaves, ivory and copper brought from the interior. The trade made local merchant families rich and weakened the crown.
kingdom-of-ngoyo.e: After the Atlantic slave trade ended, the kingdom declined. In 1885 local princes signed the Treaty of Simulambuco, placing the area under Portuguese protection, and it became the Cabinda exclave of Portuguese Angola.

kataghan-khanate.t: An Uzbek khanate of northern Afghanistan centred on Kunduz, a slave-raiding power under Murad Beg until absorbed by the Afghan Emirate.
kataghan-khanate.o: The Qataghan Uzbeks had settled in the region of Kunduz in the 17th and 18th centuries. In the early 19th century their leader Murad Beg built a powerful state from Kunduz, taking Balkh, Badakhshan and neighbouring Tajik districts around 1815 to 1820.
kataghan-khanate.r: Murad Beg ruled with an army of Uzbek horsemen and grew rich from raiding and slaving, deporting Tajiks of Badakhshan to the marshy Kunduz plain. The British traveller Alexander Burnes and William Moorcroft described his court in the 1820s and 1830s. Successors were weaker and paid tribute to Bukhara or Kabul.
kataghan-khanate.e: After Murad Beg's death in the 1840s the khanate declined. In 1859 Dost Mohammad Khan's son Muhammad Afzal Khan conquered Kunduz for the Emirate of Afghanistan, ending its independence.

kazakhstan.t: The world's largest landlocked country, a resource-rich steppe state that built a new capital at Astana and balances between Russia, China and the West.
kazakhstan.o: The Kazakh SSR was the last Soviet republic to declare independence, on 16 December 1991, under Nursultan Nazarbayev, who had led it since 1989. The new state inherited the Semipalatinsk test site, which was closed, and a large nuclear arsenal, which it gave up by 1995.
kazakhstan.r: Nazarbayev ruled as president for nearly three decades, building a strong presidential system with little political competition. Oil from fields such as Tengiz and Kashagan, gas, uranium and metals brought rapid growth. The capital moved from Almaty to Astana in 1997. The state promoted Kazakh language and culture while keeping Russian widely used and managing a large ethnic Russian minority in the north.
kazakhstan.e: Nazarbayev resigned in 2019 in favour of Kassym-Jomart Tokayev but kept influence until the January 2022 unrest, when protests over fuel prices turned violent and Russian-led troops were briefly deployed. Tokayev then curbed Nazarbayev's family and introduced constitutional changes.

kingdom-of-ormus.t: The island kingdom of Hormuz, which controlled the mouth of the Gulf and its horse and spice trade until Persia and England expelled the Portuguese.
kingdom-of-ormus.o: Arab and Persian traditions say the kingdom was founded in the 11th century on the mainland near modern Minab by a ruler from Oman. Around 1300, harried by Mongol-era raids, its king moved the capital to the barren island of Jarun, which took the name Hormuz.
kingdom-of-ormus.r: Hormuz lived by trade, taxing ships between India, Persia, Arabia and East Africa and shipping Arabian horses to India. Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta visited it. Kings controlled ports on both sides of the Gulf, including Qalhat, Muscat and Bahrain, and paid tribute to stronger mainland powers. Water and food had to be brought to the island.
kingdom-of-ormus.e: Afonso de Albuquerque attacked in 1507 and in 1515 made Hormuz a vassal of the Portuguese Empire, which built a fortress and controlled its customs. In 1622 an Anglo-Persian force under Shah Abbas I of the Safavid Empire captured the island, ending the kingdom; trade moved to Bandar Abbas.

kingdom-of-epirus.t: Kingdom of the Molossians in north-west Greece, whose Aeacid kings led the Epirote peoples and produced Pyrrhus, Rome's most famous Greek opponent.
kingdom-of-epirus.o: The Molossian kings claimed descent from Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, and were called Aeacids. Their kingdom in the mountains of Epirus emerges into history in the 5th century BCE; King Tharyps, educated at Athens, introduced Greek institutions and letters. The Molossians gradually led the other Epirote tribes, the Chaonians and Thesprotians, in an alliance.
kingdom-of-epirus.r: Kings ruled alongside an assembly and annual magistrates, swearing to govern by law. The economy rested on pastoralism, with Dodona's oracle of Zeus as the great religious centre. Alexander I, brother of Olympias and uncle of Alexander the Great, campaigned in southern Italy until his death in 331 BCE. Pyrrhus (297-272 BCE) made Ambracia his capital and won costly victories over Rome.
kingdom-of-epirus.e: After Pyrrhus died at Argos in 272 BCE, his successors struggled against Macedon and the Aetolians. The last of the royal line, Deidamia, was killed around 232 BCE and the monarchy was replaced by the Epirote League. Pyrrhus survives in the phrase 'Pyrrhic victory'.

karystos.t: City of southern Euboea, forced into the Delian League by Athens and later famed for its green-veined Cipollino marble.
karystos.o: Karystos lay at the southern end of Euboea, below Mount Ochi. Greek tradition held that its people were Dryopes, later joined by Ionian settlers. It grew in the early Iron Age as a farming and seafaring community, controlling the channel between Euboea and Andros.
karystos.r: The Persians forced Karystos to submit in 490 BCE, and it fought on their side in 480 BCE. Athens then compelled it to join the Delian League c. 472 BCE. In the 4th century BCE it produced the physician Diocles, and later the writer Antigonus. Its green-veined marble, Cipollino, was quarried heavily in Roman times.
karystos.e: Karystos passed between Macedonian kings and Athens in the Hellenistic period and came under Roman control by 146 BCE. Its marble quarries remained important under the Empire, and the modern town keeps the ancient name.

kotharia-state.t: A small Jadeja Rajput estate near Rajkot in Kathiawar, a cadet branch of the Rajkot ruling house.
kotharia-state.o: Kotharia was held by a branch of the Jadeja Rajputs of Rajkot, who granted lands to younger sons as their share. The register dates its separate existence to around 1700.
kotharia-state.r: The Thakor ruled a small group of villages and, after 1807, came under British supervision in the Kathiawar Agency as a minor non-salute state. Little else is recorded in standard references.
kotharia-state.e: Kotharia merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960. It is now a suburb area of Rajkot.

katosan-state.t: A minor chiefship of the Mahi Kantha country in northern Gujarat, one of its many small hereditary holdings.
katosan-state.o: Katosan was one of the petty estates of the Mahi Kantha region whose rulers held a small group of villages from around 1600. Its origins are known mainly from local tradition and colonial gazetteers.
katosan-state.r: The Thakor paid tribute through the Gaekwads of Baroda and was supervised by the British Mahi Kantha Agency. Standard references record little beyond its status as a minor non-salute state.
katosan-state.e: Katosan was merged into Bombay Province in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960, in present Mehsana district.

kingdom-of-murcia.t: A Castilian frontier kingdom in south-eastern Spain, formed after the reconquest of Murcia and kept as a historical unit until 1833.
kingdom-of-murcia.o: After the Mudéjar revolt of 1264-1266, James I of Aragon conquered Murcia on behalf of his son-in-law Alfonso X of Castile, ending the Third Taifa of Murcia. Alfonso X resettled the territory with Castilians and Catalans and kept it as a separate kingdom within the Crown of Castile.
kingdom-of-murcia.r: Murcia was a frontier facing both the Emirate of Granada and the Crown of Aragon, which took its northern districts by the Treaty of Torrellas in 1304. The irrigated huertas produced silk, fruit and grain, the Mudéjar population declined, and Cartagena grew into the main naval base on the Mediterranean.
kingdom-of-murcia.e: The kingdom was a historical title and administrative unit rather than a self-governing state. In 1833 Javier de Burgos's reform divided Spain into provinces, splitting the old kingdom into the provinces of Murcia and Albacete.

khandpara-state.t: A small Garhjat state on the Mahanadi in central Orissa, founded by a branch of the Nayagarh ruling family.
khandpara-state.o: Khandpara was established around 1599 when a younger member of the Nayagarh ruling house received the territory as his own principality. It lay south of the Mahanadi, near the gorge where the river leaves the hills for the coastal plain.
khandpara-state.r: Its Rajas governed a small agrarian state of rice villages and forest, with Khond and other tribal communities in the hills. After 1803 Khandpara was one of the Orissa Tributary Mahals under British paramountcy, later in the Eastern States Agency. Little else of its internal history is widely recorded.
khandpara-state.e: Khandpara joined the province of Orissa on 1 January 1948, with the other Garhjat states. Its territory lies in present-day Nayagarh district.

kingdom-of-tondo.t: A Tagalog trading polity on Manila Bay, named in the Laguna Copperplate Inscription of 900 and ruled by Lakandula when the Spanish arrived.
kingdom-of-tondo.o: The Laguna Copperplate Inscription, dated 900 and the oldest known document from the Philippines, mentions a leader of Tundun, generally identified with Tondo. The settlement grew on the northern shore of the Pasig River delta, trading with Chinese merchants, who knew the region as Lusong.
kingdom-of-tondo.r: Tondo was ruled by a lakan or paramount chief over a society of maginoo nobles, maharlika warriors and dependants. It traded rice, cotton and gold for Chinese porcelain and silk and had close ties with Brunei. By the 16th century parts of the elite had adopted Islam, while most people kept indigenous beliefs.
kingdom-of-tondo.e: After Miguel Lopez de Legazpi took Maynila in 1571, Lakandula accepted Spanish rule and was baptised. In 1587 to 1588 his relatives led the Tondo conspiracy to expel the Spanish, which was discovered and its leaders executed or exiled. Tondo became a district of Manila in the Captaincy General of the Philippines.

kingdom-of-buhweju.t: A small mountain kingdom of western Uganda, incorporated into Ankole by the British in 1901.
kingdom-of-buhweju.o: Buhweju occupied the hills north-west of Mbarara. Its traditions link its rulers to the Chwezi of the Empire of Kitara, and it emerged as a separate kingdom around the 17th century, remaining independent of its larger neighbours Ankole and Bunyoro for much of its history.
kingdom-of-buhweju.r: Buhweju was a small state of farmers and herders ruled by a king with clan leaders. It was known for iron working and for its rugged, defensible terrain. Little else is reliably recorded.
kingdom-of-buhweju.e: Under the Ankole Agreement of 1901 the British merged Buhweju into the Kingdom of Ankole. It is now a district of western Uganda.

kish.t: A powerful city of northern Sumer whose name became a title of supreme rule: to be 'king of Kish' meant to hold hegemony over Mesopotamia.
kish.o: Kish lay on the Euphrates in northern Babylonia, east of later Babylon. The Sumerian King List names it as the seat of the first dynasty after the flood. Enmebaragesi, who ruled around 2600 BCE, is the earliest king in the list confirmed by his own inscriptions.
kish.r: Kish had a mixed population, and its early texts show a strong Semitic element alongside Sumerian. Its kings exercised influence far beyond the city: Mesalim of Kish acted as arbiter in the border dispute between Lagash and Umma, and later rulers of other cities, including Eannatum of Lagash, adopted the title 'king of Kish' to claim wider authority. Its patron god was the warrior Zababa.
kish.e: Under Ur-Zababa, the cupbearer Sargon rose to power and founded the Akkadian Empire around 2334 BCE, absorbing Kish. The city survived as a cult centre under later rulers, including Hammurabi and the Neo-Babylonian kings, and the prestige of its royal title outlasted it by centuries.

kingdom-of-tethba.t: A midland Irish kingdom spanning Longford and Westmeath, held by branches of the southern Ui Neill and later by the O'Farrells and O'Quinns.
kingdom-of-tethba.o: Tethba appears in the earliest Irish annals as a territory in the Irish midlands, divided by the River Inny into northern and southern parts. Its rulers in the early medieval period came from Cairpre and Maine, sons of Niall of the Nine Hostages, making it part of the southern Ui Neill world centred on Mide.
kingdom-of-tethba.r: Tethba was a small overkingship of several local peoples, often subordinate to the kings of Mide. Monasteries such as Ardagh and Clonmacnoise's daughter houses stood in or near its lands. In the 11th and 12th centuries local families, the Ui Cuinn and the Ui Fergail, rose to power in the northern part, later known as Annaly.
kingdom-of-tethba.e: After the Norman invasion much of southern Tethba was granted to Hugh de Lacy within the Lordship of Meath. Annaly survived under the O'Farrells until the 16th century, when it became County Longford.

kingdom-of-libya.t: Independent Libya under King Idris, a poor federal monarchy transformed by oil discoveries and overthrown by Gaddafi in 1969.
kingdom-of-libya.o: Under a UN resolution, Libya became independent on 24 December 1951 as a federal kingdom uniting Tripolitania, Cyrenaica and the Fezzan, with Idris al-Senussi, ruler of the Emirate of Cyrenaica, as King Idris I.
kingdom-of-libya.r: At independence Libya was among the poorest countries in the world, depending on foreign aid and rent from British and American bases such as Wheelus Air Base. The discovery of oil in 1959 and exports from 1961 brought sudden wealth. In 1963 the federation was abolished in favour of a unitary state. The king ruled conservatively, relying on Cyrenaican tribes.
kingdom-of-libya.e: On 1 September 1969, while Idris was abroad, army officers led by Muammar Gaddafi seized power and declared a republic. Idris died in exile in Egypt in 1983, and his flag was revived by the rebels of 2011.

kingdom-of-afghanistan.t: The Afghan monarchy of Amanullah and Zahir Shah, which pursued modernisation and neutrality for nearly half a century.
kingdom-of-afghanistan.o: Amanullah Khan, who had won full independence from Britain in 1919, took the title king (padishah) in 1926, turning the Emirate of Afghanistan into a kingdom. He launched ambitious reforms, including a constitution, schools for girls and the unveiling of women, inspired by Atatürk's Turkey.
kingdom-of-afghanistan.r: Amanullah's reforms provoked a revolt that drove him out in 1929, and after the brief Saqqawist Emirate, Mohammad Nadir Shah took the throne. After his assassination in 1933 his son Mohammad Zahir Shah reigned for forty years, at first through his uncles and then his cousin Mohammad Daoud Khan as prime minister. Afghanistan stayed neutral in the Second World War, received aid from both the Soviet Union and the United States, and adopted a liberal constitution in 1964.
kingdom-of-afghanistan.e: In July 1973, while Zahir Shah was in Italy, Daoud Khan seized power in a bloodless coup and abolished the monarchy, proclaiming the Republic of Afghanistan (1973-1978).

kingdom-of-anga.t: An eastern kingdom with its capital at the river port of Champa, the first great conquest of Magadha.
kingdom-of-anga.o: Anga lay east of Magadha in modern Bihar, around Champa near Bhagalpur on the Ganges. It is mentioned in the Atharvaveda as a distant eastern people and by the 6th century BCE it was listed among the sixteen mahajanapadas. Buddhist texts say Anga once dominated Magadha, and a king named Brahmadatta is said to have defeated Bimbisara's father.
kingdom-of-anga.r: Champa was counted among the six great cities of the Buddha's day. It was a river port from which merchants were said to sail to Suvarnabhumi in Southeast Asia, and its wealth rested on trade and the farming of the Ganges plain. Little is known of its government beyond the names of a few kings in Buddhist and Jain tradition.
kingdom-of-anga.e: Around 540 BCE the young Bimbisara of the Kingdom of Magadha conquered Anga, and Champa was governed for a time by his son Ajatashatru. The conquest began Magadha's rise to dominance over the Ganges valley.

klaipeda-region.t: The Memel Territory, detached from Germany after the First World War, seized by Lithuania in 1923 and annexed by Hitler in 1939.
klaipeda-region.o: The Treaty of Versailles separated the land north of the Neman, including the port of Memel (Klaipėda), from Germany, placing it under the Allies in 1920 with a French administration. In January 1923 Lithuanian irregulars staged the Klaipėda Revolt, and the Allies accepted Lithuanian sovereignty.
klaipeda-region.r: Under the Klaipėda Convention of 1924, the region was an autonomous part of the Republic of Lithuania, with its own parliament and directorate. Most inhabitants were German-speaking or bilingual Lietuvininkai, and conflicts between German parties and the Lithuanian governor were constant. The port was Lithuania's only outlet to the sea.
klaipeda-region.e: Nazi groups grew strong in the 1930s. In March 1939 Germany issued an ultimatum, and Lithuania ceded the region, which was annexed to the Reich on 23 March 1939. After the Second World War it became part of the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic, and its German population fled or was expelled.

kiautschou-bay-concession.t: Germany's naval colony on the Shandong coast, centred on Tsingtao, whose transfer to Japan in 1919 triggered China's May Fourth Movement.
kiautschou-bay-concession.o: Using the murder of two German missionaries in Shandong in 1897 as a pretext, Germany occupied Kiautschou Bay and in 1898 forced the Qing Empire to grant a ninety-nine-year lease, together with railway and mining rights in Shandong.
kiautschou-bay-concession.r: Uniquely among German colonies, it was run by the navy, with a naval officer as governor. Tsingtao was planned as a model colony, with modern harbour works, sewerage, schools, German-style architecture and a brewery founded in 1903, and the railway to Jinan opened in 1904. Chinese and European residential areas were kept separate.
kiautschou-bay-concession.e: When the First World War began, Japan, supported by British troops, besieged Tsingtao, which Governor Alfred Meyer-Waldeck surrendered in November 1914. The Treaty of Versailles gave German rights to Japan, provoking the May Fourth protests of 1919; Japan returned the territory to China in 1922.

kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.t: A kingdom without a king, created by Germany and Austria-Hungary in occupied Poland during the First World War, which handed power to Pilsudski in 1918.
kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.o: After driving the Russians out of Congress Poland in 1915, the Central Powers proclaimed an independent Kingdom of Poland by the Act of 5 November 1916, hoping to recruit Polish soldiers. Its borders and future king were left undecided.
kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.r: A Provisional Council of State, including Jozef Pilsudski, was set up in 1917, but real power remained with the German governor-general in Warsaw. When Pilsudski's legionnaires refused an oath of loyalty to the Central Powers, he was interned at Magdeburg. A Regency Council of Archbishop Aleksander Kakowski, Prince Zdzislaw Lubomirski and Jozef Ostrowski then governed, building Polish courts, schools and offices.
kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918.e: As Germany collapsed in November 1918, the Regency Council handed command of the army and then all authority to Pilsudski, freshly released, and dissolved itself. Its institutions passed to the Second Polish Republic.

kingdom-of-buganda.t: The largest and most centralised of the Great Lakes kingdoms, which gave its name to Uganda and still survives as a cultural monarchy.
kingdom-of-buganda.o: Buganda began around the 14th century as a small state on the northern shore of Lake Victoria, near modern Kampala. Its traditions trace the royal line to Kintu, the first man, and Kato Kimera. It was long overshadowed by Bunyoro, but from the 17th century the kabakas (kings) steadily expanded their territory at Bunyoro's expense.
kingdom-of-buganda.r: The kabaka ruled through appointed chiefs rather than hereditary clan heads, giving Buganda an unusually centralised government with a large standing army and a war-canoe fleet on Lake Victoria. Plantains provided a reliable food base. In the 19th century Mutesa I admitted Arab traders and Christian missionaries, and rivalry among Muslim, Catholic and Protestant factions led to civil war under Mwanga II.
kingdom-of-buganda.e: The Buganda Agreement of 1900 made the kingdom a privileged part of the Uganda Protectorate. Its kabaka Mutesa II became the first president of independent Uganda, but in 1966 Milton Obote attacked the palace and in 1967 abolished the monarchies. Buganda was restored as a cultural kingdom in 1993 under Ronald Muwenda Mutebi II.

kanva-dynasty.t: A short-lived Brahmin dynasty of four kings that ruled Magadha after the Shungas, in the twilight of Pataliputra's ancient power.
kanva-dynasty.o: Around 73 BCE Vasudeva Kanva, a Brahmin minister of the last Shunga king, Devabhuti, had his master killed and took the throne. The Kanvas inherited a shrunken kingdom in Magadha and the middle Ganges plain, ruled from Pataliputra.
kanva-dynasty.r: The dynasty is known almost entirely from the Puranas, which list four kings, Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana and Susharman, ruling for a total of 45 years. Coins bearing the name Bhumimitra may belong to the second king. Nothing reliable is known of their government.
kanva-dynasty.e: According to the Puranas, Susharman was killed around 28 BCE by a king of the Andhras, usually taken to be a ruler of the Satavahana dynasty. Magadha then broke into small local principalities until the Gupta Empire revived it in the 4th century.

kingdom-of-connacht.t: Western Irish province-kingdom whose O'Connor kings, Toirdelbach and Ruaidrí, became high kings before Anglo-Norman conquest reduced it.
kingdom-of-connacht.o: The Connachta, who gave the province its name, claimed descent from Conn of the Hundred Battles. By the 6th century their branches, the Uí Briúin and Uí Fiachrach, ruled the west, with kings inaugurated at Cruachan, the great ritual site of Rathcroghan in Roscommon. The Uí Briúin gradually took control of the over-kingship.
kingdom-of-connacht.r: Kings ruled through a network of subject kingdoms such as the Kingdom of Ui Maine. The Ua Conchobair, O'Connor, line rose in the 11th century; Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair, king from 1106 to 1156, built bridges and castles, divided Munster and claimed the high kingship. His son Ruaidrí became the last High King of Ireland and agreed the Treaty of Windsor with Henry II in 1175.
kingdom-of-connacht.e: Anglo-Norman lords led by the de Burghs received a grant of Connacht in 1227, and the O'Connors were confined to Roscommon. Splits between rival O'Connor branches in the 14th century weakened the kingship further, and the title faded out in the later 15th century.
kingdom-of-connacht.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-madanda.t: A small Shona kingdom in central Mozambique between the Buzi and Save rivers, on the edge of the Mutapa and Uteve world.
kingdom-of-madanda.o: Madanda emerged around 1500 as one of the Shona-speaking states between the Zimbabwe plateau and the coast, south of the Kingdom of Uteve. Its rulers were probably linked by origin to the Mutapa dynasty, but the kingdom appears only occasionally in Portuguese records.
kingdom-of-madanda.r: Little is known of its government. Like its neighbours, it was probably ruled by a sacred king advised by spirit mediums, and its people farmed, herded cattle and traded ivory and gold with Portuguese posts at Sofala and on the Zambezi.
kingdom-of-madanda.e: In the 19th century Madanda came under the domination of the Gaza Nguni state. In the 1890s its territory passed to the Mozambique Company and was absorbed into Portuguese Mozambique.

kingdom-of-arakan-lemro-period.t: Six centuries of Arakanese kingdoms in the Lemro river valley, between the fall of Waithali and the founding of Mrauk U.
kingdom-of-arakan-lemro-period.o: Rakhine chronicles date the start of the Lemro period to 818, when King Khittathin founded Pyinsa on the Lemro river after Waithali's decline. Over the following centuries the capital shifted between several towns in the valley, including Parein, Hkrit, Pyinsa again and finally Launggyet, founded in 1251.
kingdom-of-arakan-lemro-period.r: The Lemro kingdoms ruled the Rakhine coast through rice cultivation and Bay of Bengal trade, with strong links to Bengal and to the Pagan Kingdom, which at times claimed overlordship. Theravada Buddhism became dominant, and kings built pagodas and patronised monks. Political history was turbulent, with frequent succession disputes and invasions.
kingdom-of-arakan-lemro-period.e: In 1406 forces of the Ava Kingdom drove King Min Saw Mon from Launggyet into exile in Bengal. With help from the Bengal Sultanate he regained the throne in 1429 and founded a new capital at Mrauk U, opening the period of the Mrauk U Kingdom.

kahuripan.t: The East Javanese kingdom of Airlangga, who rebuilt Javanese royal power after the fall of Medang in 1016.
kahuripan.o: When Haji Wurawari destroyed the court of Dharmawangsa Teguh of the Medang Kingdom in 1016, his young son-in-law Airlangga, a prince from Bali, fled to the forest with a few followers. In 1019 priests consecrated him king, and over the next two decades he reconquered East Java from rival lords.
kahuripan.r: Airlangga's Pucangan inscription of 1041 tells his story in Sanskrit and Old Javanese. He built dams on the Brantas River, encouraged trade through the port of Hujung Galuh, and patronised Hindu and Buddhist clergy. The poet Mpu Kanwa wrote the Arjunawiwaha, seen as an allegory of his reign.
kahuripan.e: Before retiring as an ascetic, Airlangga had his kingdom divided around 1045, tradition says by the sage Mpu Bharada, between two sons: Janggala in the east and Kediri, or Panjalu, in the west. He died around 1049, and is believed to be buried at Belahan, on Mount Penanggungan.

kingdom-of-bussa.t: Borgu kingdom on the Niger where the Scottish explorer Mungo Park met his death in the rapids in 1806.
kingdom-of-bussa.o: Bussa was one of the kingdoms of Borgu, a region straddling the middle Niger, and claimed seniority among them. Its rulers traced their descent to Kisra, a legendary conqueror from the east whose story is shared across Borgu. The kingdom probably took shape by the 16th century.
kingdom-of-bussa.r: The king of Bussa ruled over Busa-speaking and Bariba subjects and controlled crossings and rapids on the Niger. Borgu warriors were feared horsemen and archers, and the region resisted both the Oyo Empire and the Fulani jihad. Mungo Park drowned in the Bussa rapids in 1806, and the Lander brothers passed through in 1830.
kingdom-of-bussa.e: Bussa was claimed by both Britain and France and was assigned to Britain by the Anglo-French Convention of 1898, becoming part of Northern Nigeria. The old town was flooded by the Kainji Dam in 1968, and its people moved to New Bussa.

kalmar-union.t: Personal union of Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one monarch, created by Queen Margaret I in 1397 and broken by Sweden's secession in 1523.
kalmar-union.o: Margaret I, daughter of Valdemar IV of Denmark and widow of Haakon VI of Norway, became ruler of Denmark and Norway and, after defeating King Albert of Mecklenburg in 1389, of Sweden too. In 1397 her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania was crowned king of all three realms at Kalmar.
kalmar-union.r: The union shared a monarch and foreign policy, but each kingdom kept its own laws, councils and nobility. Danish dominance and wars with the Hanseatic League and Holstein caused resentment in Sweden, where the Engelbrekt rebellion of 1434 began a century of conflict. Swedish regents of the Sture family often ruled in practice.
kalmar-union.e: Christian II reconquered Sweden in 1520 and executed some eighty nobles and clergy in the Stockholm Bloodbath, provoking a revolt led by Gustav Vasa, who was elected king of Sweden in 1523. The union ended, while Denmark and Norway continued together as Denmark-Norway.

kingdom-of-noricum.t: A Celtic kingdom in the eastern Alps, famed for its iron and steel, that became a Roman ally and then a Roman province without a major war.
kingdom-of-noricum.o: Noricum grew out of a union of Celtic tribes in the eastern Alps, led by the Norici, during the 2nd century BCE. Its core lay in modern Carinthia and Styria, around the Magdalensberg and a centre the Romans called Noreia. In 113 BCE Rome defended it against the migrating Cimbri, who defeated a Roman army at Noreia.
kingdom-of-noricum.r: The kingdom was ruled by kings over a federation of tribes and was known across the Mediterranean for ferrum Noricum, a high-quality steel produced from local ores. Italian merchants settled at the Magdalensberg trading post, and Noricum minted its own silver coins. Close ties with Rome made it a client kingdom; its king Voccio sent cavalry to Julius Caesar in 49 BCE.
kingdom-of-noricum.e: Around 16 BCE Noricum was absorbed peacefully into the Roman Empire, becoming the province of Noricum with towns such as Virunum and Celeia. Roman rule lasted until the late 5th century, when the Life of Saint Severinus records the last Roman communities before their evacuation in 488.

knidos.t: Dorian port city on a Carian peninsula, home of Praxiteles's Aphrodite, the astronomer Eudoxus and a renowned school of medicine.
knidos.o: Dorian Greeks settled Knidos at the tip of a long peninsula in south-west Anatolia in the early first millennium BCE. It belonged to the Dorian Hexapolis with Kos, Halicarnassus and the three Rhodian cities of Lindos, Ialysos and Kamiros, which met at the sanctuary of Apollo at Triopion in Knidian territory.
knidos.r: Knidos was an oligarchy run by a council of sixty, and grew rich on trade, wine and its double harbour. When the Persian general Harpagus advanced c. 545 BCE, the Knidians tried to cut through their isthmus but submitted. The city later produced the astronomer Eudoxus, the physician Ctesias and Sostratus, architect of the Pharos of Alexandria; its treasury and clubhouse stood at Delphi.
knidos.e: Off Knidos in 394 BCE Conon's Persian-backed fleet destroyed Spartan sea power. In the 4th century BCE the city moved to the cape, where Praxiteles's nude Aphrodite drew visitors. It joined the Roman province of Asia in 129 BCE as a free city.

kingdom-of-ailech.t: Kingdom of the northern Uí Néill based at the stone fort of Grianan of Aileach, whose Cenél nEógain kings often held the high kingship of Ireland.
kingdom-of-ailech.o: Ailech emerged in the early medieval period as the kingdom of the northern Uí Néill, descendants of Niall of the Nine Hostages who expanded into the north-west in the 5th and 6th centuries. It took its name from the hilltop stone fort of Grianan of Aileach on the Inishowen peninsula, which served as a royal centre.
kingdom-of-ailech.r: The kingdom was dominated by the Cenél nEógain, who displaced the Cenél Conaill from the kingship in the 8th century and alternated the high kingship with the southern Uí Néill. Kings such as Áed Findliath and Niall Glúndub, killed fighting the Vikings of Dublin in 919, were among the most powerful in Ireland. The Mac Lochlainn line, notably Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn, held the high kingship in the 12th century.
kingdom-of-ailech.e: In 1101 Muirchertach Ua Briain of Munster demolished Grianan of Aileach in revenge for an earlier attack on Kincora. Power within Cenél nEógain passed from the Mac Lochlainns to the Ua Néill, and the kingdom of Ailech became the O'Neill kingdom of Tír Eógain, Tyrone.

kololo-kingdom.t: A Sotho conquest state on the upper Zambezi, visited by Livingstone, whose language still shapes Lozi speech.
kololo-kingdom.o: Sebetwane led the Kololo, a Sotho group displaced in the 1820s, on a long migration across Botswana. Around 1840 they conquered the Lozi kingdom of Barotseland on the upper Zambezi floodplain, setting up their capital at Linyanti in the Chobe swamps.
kololo-kingdom.r: Sebetwane ruled with skill, incorporating Lozi and other subjects and spreading his Sotho language, which became the basis of modern Silozi. The Kololo lived from cattle, Lozi labour and tribute in grain, fish and ivory. David Livingstone reached Sebetwane in 1851 and later travelled to the Atlantic and Indian Ocean coasts with Kololo porters provided by Sekeletu.
kololo-kingdom.e: Sebetwane died in 1851; under his sickly son Sekeletu, malaria thinned the Kololo and loyalty collapsed. After Sekeletu's death in 1863 a Lozi rising led by Sipopa killed most Kololo men in 1864, restoring the Lozi monarchy.

kingdom-of-middag.t: A multi-village alliance of indigenous peoples on Taiwan's central plain, called a kingdom by the Dutch, which kept its autonomy until the Qing crushed it in 1732.
kingdom-of-middag.o: The alliance, centred among the Papora, Babuza, Pazeh and other plains peoples around modern Taichung, is known chiefly from Dutch East India Company records of the 1640s. Its origins are obscure; it is traditionally said to have formed in the mid-16th century.
kingdom-of-middag.r: The Dutch described a chief they called the King of Middag, Kamachat Aslamie, who presided over some fifteen to twenty-seven villages. Villages kept their own leaders, while the paramount chief led in war and diplomacy. In 1645 the Dutch forced him to accept a treaty acknowledging their authority, though the alliance stayed largely self-governing.
kingdom-of-middag.e: Middag kept its autonomy under the Kingdom of Tungning and early Qing rule. Rising Chinese settlement and labour demands provoked the Dajia-Shalu revolt of 1731, which Qing forces suppressed in 1732, ending the alliance.

kingdom-of-cambrai.t: Small Frankish kingdom around Cambrai, ruled by Clovis' kinsman Ragnachar until Clovis eliminated him.
kingdom-of-cambrai.o: Cambrai was taken by the Salian king Chlodio in the mid 5th century, and by the 480s it was the seat of a separate Frankish king, Ragnachar, a relative of Clovis. Known almost only from Gregory of Tours.
kingdom-of-cambrai.r: Ragnachar joined Clovis against Syagrius and the Domain of Soissons in 486. Gregory portrays him as a debauched ruler who lost the loyalty of his warriors.
kingdom-of-cambrai.e: Around 509 Clovis bribed Ragnachar's followers with armlets of gilded bronze passed off as gold, defeated him and killed him and his brother Richar with his own axe. Cambrai was absorbed into the Kingdom of the Franks.

kingdom-of-prussia.t: Hohenzollern kingdom that rose from scattered lands to a great power, defeated Austria and France and united Germany under its rule.
kingdom-of-prussia.o: Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg crowned himself King in Prussia at Königsberg on 18 January 1701, with Emperor Leopold I's consent. The title rested on the Duchy of Prussia, outside the Empire, but it was applied to all Hohenzollern lands, including Brandenburg, Pomerania and territories in the Rhineland and Westphalia.
kingdom-of-prussia.r: Frederick William I built a large army and efficient bureaucracy. Frederick II seized Silesia in 1740 and survived the Seven Years' War, then gained West Prussia in the First Partition of Poland. After defeat at Jena in 1806, the Stein and Hardenberg reforms modernised the state. Prussia gained the Rhineland in 1815, led the Zollverein, and under Bismarck defeated Denmark, Austria and France.
kingdom-of-prussia.e: In 1871 King William I became German Emperor, and Prussia formed the dominant state of the German Empire. William II abdicated in November 1918, and Prussia became the Free State of Prussia, abolished by the Allies in 1947.

kushano-sasanian-kingdom.t: Sasanian princes who ruled the former Kushan lands of Bactria and Gandhara as 'Kushanshahs', blending Persian, Kushan and Buddhist traditions.
kushano-sasanian-kingdom.o: After Ardashir I founded the Sasanian Empire, he and his son Shapur I conquered Bactria and much of the Kushan Empire in the mid-3rd century. Government of the region was entrusted to Sasanian princes who took the title Kushanshah, King of the Kushans, ruling from Balkh.
kushano-sasanian-kingdom.r: The Kushanshahs issued gold and copper coins in the Kushan style, often showing the god Oesho (Shiva) with the bull Nandi, alongside Sasanian crowns and Middle Persian or Bactrian legends. They held trade routes through the Hindu Kush, and Buddhist monasteries in Bactria continued to flourish under them. At times they acted nearly independently of the main Sasanian court.
kushano-sasanian-kingdom.e: In the mid-4th century the Chionites and the Kidarite Kingdom overran Bactria, ending Kushano-Sasanian rule. Their coinage strongly influenced the coin types of these later Hunnic rulers.

kalachuris-of-tripuri.t: A central Indian dynasty ruling the Chedi country from Tripuri near Jabalpur, which briefly became the strongest power in northern India under Lakshmikarna.
kalachuris-of-tripuri.o: The Kalachuris of Tripuri, who claimed descent from the legendary Haihaya king Kartavirya Arjuna and from the Kalachuris of Mahishmati, rose in the late 9th century under Kokalla I. He ruled the Chedi country around Tripuri, modern Tewar near Jabalpur, and strengthened his position through marriage alliances with the Rashtrakuta dynasty.
kalachuris-of-tripuri.r: Gangeyadeva took the title Vikramaditya and expanded the kingdom in the early 11th century. His son Lakshmikarna, ruling from about 1041 to 1073, campaigned in Bengal, Kalinga and Malwa and helped defeat Bhoja of the Paramara dynasty. The Kalachuris patronised Shaiva monasteries of the Mattamayura order and built temples such as the Chausath Yogini temple at Bheraghat. They used the Kalachuri-Chedi era of 248.
kalachuris-of-tripuri.e: After Lakshmikarna the kingdom declined under pressure from the Chandela dynasty, the Paramaras and the Gahadavalas. The last known king, Vijayasimha, ruled until about 1212, after which the region passed to the Chandelas and other powers.
