kingdom-of-cambodia.t: Present-day Cambodia, a constitutional monarchy restored in 1993 after decades of war, dominated in practice by Hun Sen and the Cambodian People's Party.
kingdom-of-cambodia.o: After the UN-supervised elections of May 1993, a constituent assembly adopted a new constitution, and on 24 September 1993 Norodom Sihanouk returned to the throne of a restored Kingdom of Cambodia. Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen became joint prime ministers of a coalition government.
kingdom-of-cambodia.r: The king reigns as head of state with limited powers; Sihanouk abdicated in 2004 in favour of his son Norodom Sihamoni. Hun Sen ousted Ranariddh in fighting in 1997 and dominated politics for decades. The last Khmer Rouge forces surrendered in 1998. Garment exports, tourism to Angkor and Chinese investment drove growth, while the main opposition party was dissolved in 2017.
kingdom-of-cambodia.e: The kingdom continues today. In 2023 Hun Sen handed the premiership to his son Hun Manet, while remaining president of the Senate. Cambodia joined ASEAN in 1999.

kingdom-of-diarra.t: Soninke kingdom of the Sahel north of the Senegal and Niger headwaters that outlived the Ghana Empire by nearly seven centuries.
kingdom-of-diarra.o: Diarra, or Diara, arose in the Kingaga region around present-day Nioro du Sahel as the Ghana Empire fragmented. Tradition dates it to 1076, the year associated with the Almoravid Empire's attack on Ghana. Its first ruling house was the Niakhate clan, later replaced by the Diawara.
kingdom-of-diarra.r: Diarra's Soninke rulers governed a mixed population of farmers and herders and profited from the trade between the desert and the savanna. The kingdom was usually a vassal of a larger power, first of the Mali Empire and then of the Songhai Empire, while keeping its own dynasties.
kingdom-of-diarra.e: In the 18th century Diarra was overrun by the Bambara of Kaarta, who took its lands in 1754, according to the register's dating. The Diawara remain a recognised Soninke clan in western Mali.

kingdom-of-biram.t: Hausa state east of Kano, traditionally the oldest of the seven Hausa kingdoms and seat of their legendary founder's eldest son.
kingdom-of-biram.o: Biram, centred on Garun Gabas, appears in the Bayajidda legend: the hero is said to have had a son named Biram by a Bornu princess before reaching Daura, so the kingdom was counted first among the Hausa Bakwai. Its origins probably lie in the 11th century, on the borderland between the Hausa plains and the Kanem-Bornu Empire.
kingdom-of-biram.r: Tradition gives Biram the role of seat of government among the Hausa states, but in practice it was small and strongly influenced by Bornu, to which it paid tribute for long periods. Its records are sparse, and its rulers are known only from late lists.
kingdom-of-biram.e: Fulani forces of the jihad overran Biram in the first decade of the 19th century, and its lands were incorporated into the Hadejia Emirate. Garun Gabas survives as a town in Jigawa State.

kingdom-of-ndorwa.t: A kingdom of the highlands between Rwanda and Uganda, remembered for its queen Kitami and as the cradle of the Nyabingi spirit cult.
kingdom-of-ndorwa.o: Ndorwa lay in the hills of today's south-western Uganda and northern Rwanda. Traditions from the region describe it as a kingdom of the 17th century, linked by marriage and war with the Kingdom of Rwanda, the Kingdom of Mpororo and the states of Ankole. Its history is known only from oral accounts.
kingdom-of-ndorwa.r: Little is known of its government. Traditions remember a queen, Kitami, whose spirit became Nyabingi, the focus of a powerful healing and resistance cult that spread across the region and later inspired revolts against colonial rule in the early 20th century.
kingdom-of-ndorwa.e: Ndorwa broke up in the 18th century and was conquered by Rwanda around 1800. Its lands were later divided by the colonial border between Rwanda and Uganda's Kigezi district.

khedivate-of-egypt.t: Egypt under the khedives, which opened the Suez Canal, fell into debt and came under British occupation in 1882 while remaining nominally Ottoman.
khedivate-of-egypt.o: In 1867 the Ottoman sultan granted Ismail Pasha, grandson of Muhammad Ali, the title of khedive and greater autonomy, transforming Egypt under Muhammad Ali into the Khedivate. Ismail aimed to make Egypt part of Europe, rebuilding Cairo on Parisian lines.
khedivate-of-egypt.r: The Suez Canal opened in 1869, and the cotton boom funded railways and schools, but borrowing became ruinous. Ismail sold his canal shares to Britain in 1875 and accepted Anglo-French financial control before being deposed in 1879. Ahmed Urabi's nationalist revolt led Britain to invade in 1882, and Lord Cromer effectively governed Egypt from 1883 to 1907.
khedivate-of-egypt.e: When the Ottoman Empire joined the First World War in 1914, Britain deposed Khedive Abbas II, ended Ottoman sovereignty and declared a protectorate, creating the Sultanate of Egypt under Hussein Kamel.

kingdom-of-galicia.t: The north-western Iberian kingdom centred on Santiago de Compostela, sometimes ruled by its own kings but usually joined with León and Castile.
kingdom-of-galicia.o: When Alfonso III of Asturias was deposed in 910, his son Ordoño II took Galicia as his kingdom. Galicia had been the core of the Kingdom of the Suebi and a part of the Asturian realm, and the cult of St James at Compostela had made it famous across Europe.
kingdom-of-galicia.r: Galicia was dominated by a powerful nobility and the church, above all the archbishops of Santiago such as Diego Gelmírez. It had its own kings at times, among them García II from 1065 to 1071, and Alfonso VII was crowned king of Galicia at Santiago in 1111. Galician-Portuguese became a major literary language, used for the troubadour lyric and the Cantigas de Santa Maria.
kingdom-of-galicia.e: From 1230 Galicia was permanently part of the Crown of Castile, though it kept the title of kingdom and from the 16th century its own Junta. The provincial reform of 1833 abolished it as an administrative unit, but Galicia today is an autonomous community.

kingdom-of-kiziba.t: The northernmost Haya kingdom west of Lake Victoria, ruled by a Bito dynasty linked to Bunyoro.
kingdom-of-kiziba.o: Kiziba lay on the Kagera river at the northern edge of today's Tanzania. Its rulers belonged to the Babito clan, which traditions link with the royal house of the Kingdom of Bunyoro, and it emerged as a separate kingdom by the 17th century.
kingdom-of-kiziba.r: The mukama governed a Haya farming society growing bananas and coffee, which was chewed as a stimulant and used in rituals. Kiziba kept its independence among rival Haya states and had close contacts with Buganda to the north. Its court and royal rituals resembled those of other Great Lakes kingdoms.
kingdom-of-kiziba.e: Kiziba became a subordinate chiefdom under German East Africa and then British Tanganyika Territory, ruled through its kings as a native authority. It ceased to exist when Tanganyika abolished the chieftaincies in 1963.

kingdom-of-loango.t: The Vili kingdom of the Loango coast, a major Atlantic trading power known for its raffia cloth, copper and ivory and later for slaves.
kingdom-of-loango.o: Loango emerged among the Vili north of the Congo River, probably by the 15th century, and by the mid-16th century had shaken off any dependence on the Kingdom of Kongo. Its king, the Maloango, ruled from Mbanza Loango (Buali) near Loango Bay, the kingdom's main harbour.
kingdom-of-loango.r: The Maloango was a sacred ruler chosen from princes of the royal matrilineage, assisted by ministers responsible for trade, war and the coast. Loango exported fine raffia cloth, used as currency in the region, together with copper from the Mindouli mines, ivory and dyewood. From the 17th century Dutch, English and French ships bought slaves at Loango Bay in large numbers.
kingdom-of-loango.e: The end of the slave trade and long interregnums left the crown weak in the 19th century. In 1883 the coast came under French protection, and the area became part of the French Congo. The Maloango title survives as a traditional office.

kingdom-of-gonja.t: A savanna kingdom in northern Ghana founded by Mande horsemen, whose divisional chiefs rotated the paramount title and whose Muslim scholars wrote its chronicle.
kingdom-of-gonja.o: Gonja tradition credits its foundation to Ndewura Jakpa, leader of Mande cavalry from the Niger region, who conquered the lands between the Black and White Volta rivers in the mid-17th century. The invaders, the Ngbanya, ruled over many older peoples, and Jakpa divided the conquests among his sons, creating the divisions that formed the kingdom.
kingdom-of-gonja.r: The paramount chief, the Yagbumwura, was chosen in rotation from the ruling divisions and resided at Nyanga (Yagbum). Society was layered into the ruling estate, Muslim scholars of Mande origin and commoners. Gonja controlled the kola trade of Salaga and Kafaba, linking the Ashanti Empire with Hausa traders. Muslim clerics wrote the Kitab Ghanja, an 18th-century chronicle of the state.
kingdom-of-gonja.e: The Ashanti Empire defeated Gonja in 1751-1752 and took tribute until 1874, when Salaga revolted. In the 1890s Britain and Germany divided the area, and most of Gonja became part of the Northern Territories of the Gold Coast. The Yagbumwura still heads the traditional state in Ghana.

kingdom-of-waterford.t: A Norse town-kingdom at the mouth of the Suir, the oldest city in Ireland, until its storming by the Anglo-Normans in 1170.
kingdom-of-waterford.o: Vikings raided the south-east in the 9th century, and in 914 a large fleet under Ragnall established a base at Waterford, Vedrafjordr. The settlement grew into a fortified trading town ruled by Norse kings or jarls, sometimes linked to the Kingdom of Dublin.
kingdom-of-waterford.r: Waterford traded wine, slaves and goods across the Irish Sea and to France. Its rulers became Christian and accepted bishops consecrated at Canterbury from 1096. Irish overkings of Munster, especially the O'Briens, often controlled the town, and Reginald's Tower recalls its Norse defences.
kingdom-of-waterford.e: In 1170 Strongbow and Raymond le Gros stormed the town, and Strongbow married Aoife, daughter of Diarmait Mac Murchada, there. Henry II landed at Waterford in 1171 and made it a royal city in the Lordship of Ireland.

kanker-state.t: A small Gond-country princely state in the hills of present-day Chhattisgarh, ruled from Kanker until 1948.
kanker-state.o: Kanker has inscriptions of local Somavanshi rulers from the 12th and 13th centuries; tradition dates the later ruling family to 1385. Its early history is only partly known.
kanker-state.r: Kanker was a forested state with a mainly Gond population. In the 18th century it came under the Bhonsles of the Nagpur Kingdom, passing under British control in 1853 and becoming one of the Chhattisgarh Feudatory States.
kanker-state.e: Kanker merged into the Central Provinces, later Madhya Pradesh, in 1948 and is now a district of Chhattisgarh.

kumul-khanate.t: A semi-autonomous Uyghur principality at Hami, loyal to the Qing for over two centuries, whose abolition in 1930 set off a major revolt in Xinjiang.
kumul-khanate.o: The Muslim ruling family of the Hami oasis, threatened by the Dzungar Khanate, submitted to the Kangxi Emperor in 1696 and helped Qing armies against the Dzungars. Its leader Abd Allah Beg was rewarded with a hereditary rank, and his descendants became princes (wang) of Hami under the Qing Empire.
kumul-khanate.r: The khans governed the Turkic Muslim inhabitants of the oasis through their own begs, collected taxes in kind and corvée from their subjects, and supplied the Qing with troops and provisions. They kept their position through the Qing conquest of Xinjiang in 1759 and the turmoil of Yettishar, and were regarded as one of the most loyal frontier houses.
kumul-khanate.e: After the death of the last khan, Maqsud Shah, in 1930, the Xinjiang governor Jin Shuren abolished the khanate and imposed direct rule and new taxes. The resulting Kumul rebellion of 1931 drew in the Hui warlord Ma Zhongying and helped spark the First East Turkestan Republic.

kingdom-of-lamjung.t: A hill kingdom of central Nepal from whose ruling house the Shah kings of Gorkha, and thus of Nepal, descended.
kingdom-of-lamjung.o: Lamjung emerged around 1500 in the hills of the Marsyangdi valley, ruled by a dynasty that claimed Rajput descent. Its kings gained prominence among the Chaubise Rajya, the twenty-four principalities of central Nepal. In 1559 Drabya Shah, a younger son of the Lamjung ruler, founded the Gorkha Kingdom to the east.
kingdom-of-lamjung.r: Lamjung was a small agricultural state of terraced fields with a Gurung population and a Hindu ruling family. Its kings competed with their Gorkha kinsmen for influence and allied at times with the Kingdom of Tanahun and the Kingdom of Palpa against Gorkha expansion. Few detailed records survive.
kingdom-of-lamjung.e: After Prithvi Narayan Shah's conquests, Lamjung was annexed by the Kingdom of Nepal in 1782. It is now Lamjung district.

kingdom-of-iarmumu.t: The early medieval kingdom of West Munster around Killarney's lakes, ruled by the Eoganacht Locha Lein, rivals of the Munster kings at Cashel.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.o: Iarmumu took shape in south-west Ireland by the 6th century, when the Eoganacht Locha Lein, a branch of the dynasties ruling Munster, established themselves around Loch Lein, the Lower Lake at Killarney. Their territory covered much of later Kerry and west Cork, absorbing earlier peoples such as the Corcu Duibne.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.r: The kings of Iarmumu sometimes claimed the kingship of all Munster, but were usually excluded from the rotation of Cashel's Eoganacht branches. Inisfallen on Loch Lein became an important monastery, later home of the Annals of Inisfallen. Cattle wealth and client peoples supported the dynasty.
kingdom-of-iarmumu.e: By the 8th and 9th centuries the dynasty weakened, and other lineages gained ground in Kerry, notably the Ui Donnchada. In the 12th century the area fell within the Kingdom of Desmond under the MacCarthys, with the O'Donoghues as local lords around Killarney.

kachari-kingdom.t: The kingdom of the Dimasa people of Assam, which moved from Dimapur to Maibang and finally Khaspur in the Barak valley.
kachari-kingdom.o: The Dimasa Kacharis ruled the Dhansiri valley from Dimapur, whose carved stone pillars survive, by the 13th century. Repeated wars with the Ahom kingdom, which sacked Dimapur in 1536, pushed the kings south to Maibang in the North Cachar hills, and in the 18th century to Khaspur in the plains of Cachar.
kachari-kingdom.r: The kings ruled a Dimasa society organised in clans and gradually adopted Hindu kingship; in 1790 Krishnachandra and his brother were formally initiated as Hindus, taking the name Heramba. Courts and land records came to use Bengali. The kingdom alternated between tribute to the Ahoms and independence, and fought Manipur and the Jaintia kingdom.
kachari-kingdom.e: Burmese invasions in the 1810s and 1820s ravaged Cachar. After Govinda Chandra, the last king, was assassinated in 1830 without an heir, the British East India Company annexed the plains in 1832. The hill areas followed later, and the region is now part of Assam.

kingdom-of-khotan.t: The jade-rich Buddhist kingdom of the southern Silk Road, whose Saka-speaking kings lasted more than a thousand years until the Kara-Khanid conquest.
kingdom-of-khotan.o: Khotan, Yutian in Chinese, grew in the oasis watered by rivers from the Kunlun Mountains on the southern edge of the Taklamakan. Its own legends trace the founding to Indian and Chinese settlers, including a son of the emperor Ashoka. It appears in Han records from the 2nd century BCE, already trading the white and green jade of its rivers.
kingdom-of-khotan.r: Khotan's people spoke Khotanese, an Eastern Iranian Saka language preserved in many Buddhist texts. Its kings, of the Visa dynasty, made it a major centre of Mahayana Buddhism, and tradition says a Chinese princess smuggled silkworm eggs to it in her headdress. Under the Tang Dynasty it was one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi; in the 10th century King Li Shengtian kept close ties with Dunhuang.
kingdom-of-khotan.e: After a long war, the Muslim Kara-Khanid Khanate conquered Khotan around 1006. Its Buddhist culture was replaced by Islam and the Turkic language, but manuscripts from Khotan and Dunhuang preserve Khotanese literature.

kingdom-of-rhufoniog.t: Small early Welsh kingdom between the Conwy and Clwyd valleys, named in legend after a son of Cunedda, later a cantref of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-rhufoniog.o: Welsh tradition, preserved in genealogies written down centuries later, says the district took its name from Rhufon, one of the sons of Cunedda who came from the north to settle north Wales in the 5th century. The story is a later origin legend, but Rhufoniog existed as a distinct territory in the uplands of what is now Denbighshire.
kingdom-of-rhufoniog.r: Very little is known of its rulers or government. It was one of several small early kingdoms of north Wales whose local dynasties appear in medieval genealogies, and its territory included the hills around Denbigh. Farming and cattle-rearing were the mainstay of a thinly settled land.
kingdom-of-rhufoniog.e: By the 9th century Rhufoniog had been absorbed into the Kingdom of Gwynedd and later formed one of the cantrefi of the Perfeddwlad, the borderland between Gwynedd and England contested by Welsh princes and English kings until 1283.

kingdom-of-janjero.t: A small kingdom of the Yem people in south-western Ethiopia, known for its sacred kingship and its position between Kaffa, Ennarea and the Gibe states.
kingdom-of-janjero.o: Janjero, the kingdom of the Yem people, lay in the valley of the Omo and Gibe rivers. It appears in Ethiopian chronicles from the 16th century as a tributary of the emperors, and Jesuit writers of the 17th century describe its rulers. Its own traditions are poorly recorded.
kingdom-of-janjero.r: Janjero was ruled by a sacred king whose person was surrounded by taboos, and European travellers reported elaborate royal rituals, including stories of sacrifice that may be exaggerated. Its people farmed ensete and grain and traded with neighbouring Oromo kingdoms and Kaffa. It spoke Yemsa, an Omotic language.
kingdom-of-janjero.e: In 1894 Janjero submitted to Menelik II, partly through the intervention of Abba Jifar II of the Kingdom of Jimma, and it was incorporated into the Ethiopian Empire. The Yem people today form a special woreda in southern Ethiopia.

kingdom-of-altava.t: A Christian Berber kingdom of western Algeria whose king Kusaila killed the Arab conqueror Uqba ibn Nafi.
kingdom-of-altava.o: After the death of Garmul of the Kingdom of the Moors and Romans in 578, Berber rulers continued to hold the region of Altava and the plains of western Algeria. By the 7th century the dominant group was the Awraba, a Berber confederation whose leader Kusaila (Kasila) was Christian.
kingdom-of-altava.r: Almost nothing is known of the kingdom between 578 and the 680s. Arab writers say Kusaila was captured by the commander Abu al-Muhajir, converted to Islam and accompanied the Arab army, but was humiliated by Uqba ibn Nafi. In 682 or 683 he ambushed and killed Uqba at Tahuda near Biskra, then took Kairouan and ruled Ifriqiya for several years.
kingdom-of-altava.e: Kusaila was killed around 688 to 690 in battle against Zuhayr ibn Qays, and the Umayyad Caliphate subdued the region by 708. The Awraba converted to Islam and later welcomed Idris I at Volubilis, helping found the Idrisid dynasty.

kingdom-of-bundu.t: A Muslim clerical state between the Senegal and Faleme rivers, among the first in West Africa to be ruled by an almamy, and a model for later Fulbe imamates.
kingdom-of-bundu.o: Bundu was founded around 1690 by Malik Sy, a Torodbe cleric from Futa Toro, who obtained land from the ruler of the Kingdom of Gajaaga and drew settlers to his community. He took the title almamy, and his descendants, the Sisibe, ruled after him. Its creation came a generation before the jihads of Futa Jallon and Futa Toro.
kingdom-of-bundu.r: Bundu was governed by almamys of the Sisibe lineage, whose succession was often contested between rival branches. Its towns, Boulebane and Koussan among them, were centres of Islamic learning. Lying near the Bambuk goldfields and on the routes from the upper Senegal to the Gambia, it profited from caravans of gold, slaves, cloth and salt, and it warred repeatedly with Kaarta, Khasso and Gajaaga.
kingdom-of-bundu.e: In the 1850s Bundu was caught between Umar Tall and the French. Almamy Bokar Saada sided with France, and Bundu became a French protectorate in the 1880s before being absorbed into French Senegal, its almamys reduced to local chiefs by about 1905.

kingdom-of-great-britain.t: The kingdom created by the union of England and Scotland in 1707, which became Europe's leading maritime and commercial power in the 18th century.
kingdom-of-great-britain.o: The Acts of Union of 1707, passed by the Kingdom of England and the Kingdom of Scotland, merged them into one kingdom with a single Parliament at Westminster, while Scotland kept its own law, church and education. The two countries had shared a monarch since 1603.
kingdom-of-great-britain.r: Great Britain developed cabinet government under Robert Walpole and the Hanoverian kings from 1714. It defeated Jacobite risings in 1715 and 1745. Trade, the Bank of England and naval power built an empire in North America, the Caribbean and India, and the Seven Years' War brought Canada. The American colonies were lost in 1783, while the Industrial Revolution began.
kingdom-of-great-britain.e: The Acts of Union of 1800 joined Great Britain with the Kingdom of Ireland to form the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland on 1 January 1801.
kingdom-of-great-britain.re: Christianity; Church of England, Church of Scotland

kingdom-of-saloum.t: Serer and Wolof kingdom of the Saloum delta in Senegal, rich from salt and trade, ruled by the Guelowar dynasty from Kahone.
kingdom-of-saloum.o: Saloum was founded around 1494 by Mbegan Ndour, a warrior who seized power in the region east of the Kingdom of Sine with the support of Muslim clerics and the Guelowar lineage. The capital was set at Kahone, near present-day Kaolack, and the kingdom broke free of the Jolof Empire in the following decades.
kingdom-of-saloum.r: The Buur Saloum ruled with a council of great titled chiefs and the Lingeer, a royal woman of high rank. Saloum controlled salt pans in the delta and trade routes to the Gambia river, and became the most extensive Serer-Wolof state. In the 1860s the jihadist Maba Diakhou Ba conquered much of it, spreading Islam.
kingdom-of-saloum.e: France made Saloum a protectorate and absorbed it into the colony of French Senegal in 1891. Its kings served as colonial chiefs until the monarchy lapsed in the 20th century. Kaolack became a centre of the groundnut trade.

kingdom-of-meirionnydd.t: Early Welsh kingdom between the Mawddach and the Dyfi, named after a grandson of Cunedda, which gave its name to the later county of Merioneth.
kingdom-of-meirionnydd.o: According to Welsh genealogical tradition, Meirionnydd took its name from Meirion, a grandson of Cunedda, who was granted the land between the rivers Mawddach and Dyfi in the 5th century. Like other Cunedda stories, this is a later legend, but a separate royal line for Meirionnydd is recorded in medieval genealogies.
kingdom-of-meirionnydd.r: Little is recorded of its government. The kingdom covered a mountainous coastal region including Cadair Idris, with farming on the valley floors and the coast, and its people were linked by sea with the rest of Cardigan Bay. Its kings appear to have been subordinate to the more powerful rulers of the Kingdom of Gwynedd for much of their history.
kingdom-of-meirionnydd.e: Meirionnydd was absorbed into the Kingdom of Gwynedd, probably by the 10th century, becoming one of its cantrefi. After the English conquest of 1283 it formed the core of the county of Merioneth, and the name survives in the region of Meirionnydd today.

kingdom-of-poland-1385-1569.t: Jagiellonian Poland, which with Lithuania defeated the Teutonic Knights, built a powerful noble democracy and enjoyed a Renaissance golden age.
kingdom-of-poland-1385-1569.o: In 1385 the Union of Krewo arranged the marriage of Queen Jadwiga to Jogaila, grand duke of Lithuania, who was baptised and crowned in 1386 as Wladyslaw II Jagiello. His dynasty linked the Polish Crown to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and for a time also ruled Bohemia and Hungary.
kingdom-of-poland-1385-1569.r: Together, Poland and Lithuania crushed the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410, and the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 brought Royal Prussia and the port of Gdansk under the Crown. The nobility won growing privileges, and the 1505 statute Nihil novi required the consent of the Sejm for new laws. Krakow became a Renaissance centre, home to Copernicus and to Italian builders at Wawel castle.
kingdom-of-poland-1385-1569.e: Sigismund II Augustus, last of the male Jagiellons, had no heir. To preserve the union, the Union of Lublin in 1569 merged the kingdom with Lithuania into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, with a common elected king and Sejm.

kingdom-of-buellt.t: Small Welsh kingdom around Builth Wells, ruled by a dynasty claiming descent from Vortigern, and later the place where Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed.
kingdom-of-buellt.o: Buellt lay in the middle Wye and Irfon valleys around modern Builth Wells. The Historia Brittonum of about 829 says Ambrosius granted Buellt and Gwrtheyrnion to Pascent, son of Vortigern, and names Fernmail as the ruler of both in the author's own day. Among its wonders it lists Carn Cabal, a cairn said to bear the footprint of Arthur's hound.
kingdom-of-buellt.r: Little is recorded of its government. It was a small upland kingdom of river valleys and hill grazing, generally ruled together with the Kingdom of Gwrtheyrnion and lying between the larger realms of the Kingdom of Powys, the Kingdom of Brycheiniog and the south-western kingdoms.
kingdom-of-buellt.e: Buellt was absorbed by larger Welsh kingdoms in the 10th century and later became a cantref contested between Welsh princes and Norman lords, with a castle at Builth. In 1282 Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, last native Prince of Wales, was killed near Cilmeri in Buellt.

kingdom-of-buleleng.t: North Balinese kingdom founded by the warrior Panji Sakti, whose defeat in 1849 began the Dutch conquest of Bali.
kingdom-of-buleleng.o: Buleleng was founded around 1660 by Gusti Panji Sakti, a noble of the Gelgel court who built a power base on the north coast of Bali. He made Singaraja his capital and extended his rule across the strait to Blambangan in eastern Java in 1697, making Buleleng briefly the leading Balinese state.
kingdom-of-buleleng.r: The kingdom looked outward through its north-coast harbours, trading rice, cattle and slaves with Bugis, Chinese and European merchants. It was ruled by a Hindu raja and his noble kin, with Brahmana priests at court. In the 18th century it passed for a time under the control of the Kingdom of Karangasem.
kingdom-of-buleleng.e: Disputes over the plunder of shipwrecks led the Dutch to attack in 1846 and 1848, when the patih Gusti Ketut Jelantik defeated them at Jagaraga. A third expedition in 1849 conquered Buleleng, and Singaraja became the Dutch administrative centre for Bali and Lombok.

kingdom-of-mukish.t: Mukish, the kingdom of Alalakh in the Amuq plain, best known for King Idrimi, whose statue tells the story of an exiled prince who won back a throne.
kingdom-of-mukish.o: Alalakh, at Tell Atchana near Antakya, was a town of the fertile Amuq plain by the early 2nd millennium BCE. In the 18th century BCE Abba-El of Yamhad granted it to his brother Yarim-Lim, making it a dependent kingdom of Aleppo. Leonard Woolley's excavations from 1937 recovered palaces and archives from this period.
kingdom-of-mukish.r: Alalakh's palace archives record a society of nobles who owned chariots, free farmers and dependent labourers, written in Akkadian with many Hurrian names. After a Hittite destruction c. 1600 BCE, Idrimi, a refugee prince from Aleppo, took the city and ruled Mukish as a vassal of the Mitanni Empire, as his inscribed statue relates.
kingdom-of-mukish.e: Suppiluliuma I of the Hittite Empire conquered Mukish in the 14th century BCE and gave some of its land to Ugarit. Alalakh was abandoned around 1200 BCE, during the collapse of the Late Bronze Age, and its region later formed part of Patina.

kingdom-of-kianja.t: A Haya kingdom near Bukoba, split from Kyamutwara around 1800, whose king Kahigi became a leading ally of German rule.
kingdom-of-kianja.o: Kianja was formed around 1800 when succession disputes divided the Kingdom of Kyamutwara in the Kagera region west of Lake Victoria. A branch of the Hinda dynasty took control of the new kingdom, which became one of the largest of the Haya states.
kingdom-of-kianja.r: The mukama ruled over a dense population of banana and coffee farmers through chiefs drawn from royal and noble lineages. In the 1890s King Kahigi II welcomed the Germans and used their support to extend his power over neighbouring Haya states, a policy that made Kianja the most favoured native authority in the region.
kingdom-of-kianja.e: Kianja remained a native authority under German East Africa and British Tanganyika Territory. It ceased to exist in 1963, when independent Tanganyika abolished the chieftaincies.

kingdom-of-buna.t: Kingdom of north-eastern Ivory Coast, founded by a Dagomba-linked dynasty over the Kulango and known for its Muslim scholarly community.
kingdom-of-buna.o: Buna traditions say the kingdom was founded around 1600 by Bunkani, a prince linked to the Kingdom of Dagbon, who imposed his rule over the Kulango farmers of the upper Comoe and Black Volta region. The town of Bouna became its capital.
kingdom-of-buna.r: The king ruled over Kulango villages whose earth-priests kept their religious role. Muslim Dyula traders and scholars settled in Bouna, which became a centre of Islamic learning on the routes between the Niger bend and the Akan goldfields. Buna was at times a tributary of the Ashanti Empire.
kingdom-of-buna.e: In 1896 the forces of Samori Ture sacked Bouna. The French took control shortly afterwards, and Buna became part of French Ivory Coast. A king of Bouna remains a traditional ruler.

kingdom-of-serbia-medieval.t: Nemanjić Serbia as a kingdom, which gained its own church, grew rich on silver mines and expanded south to become the Balkans' leading power.
kingdom-of-serbia-medieval.o: Stefan, son of Stefan Nemanja and ruler of the Grand Principality of Serbia, was crowned king in 1217 with a crown sent by Pope Honorius III, earning the name Stefan the First-Crowned. In 1219 his brother Sava obtained an autocephalous Serbian archbishopric from the Patriarch at Nicaea.
kingdom-of-serbia-medieval.r: The king ruled through royal courts that moved between residences, with nobles holding land in return for service. Uroš I invited Saxon miners, opening silver mines at Brskovo and Novo Brdo that made Serbia rich and supplied Ragusa's trade. Royal foundations such as Mileševa, Sopoćani and Gračanica have celebrated frescoes. Milutin (1282–1321) took northern Macedonia from Byzantium, and Stefan Dečanski crushed Bulgaria at Velbazhd in 1330.
kingdom-of-serbia-medieval.e: Stefan Dušan, who took the throne in 1331, conquered much of Byzantine Macedonia, Albania and Epirus and in 1346 was crowned emperor at Skopje, turning the kingdom into the Serbian Empire.

kolathunadu.t: The kingdom of the Kolathiri rajas of northern Kerala, heirs of the ancient Mushika line and rivals of the Zamorins of Calicut.
kolathunadu.o: Kolathunadu emerged as an independent chiefdom in northern Malabar after the decline of the Chera kingdom of Mahodayapuram in the early 12th century. Its Kolathiri rulers claimed descent from the earlier Mushika dynasty of Ezhimala and controlled the coast around Cannanore and the pepper-growing hinterland.
kolathunadu.r: Power was shared within a large matrilineal royal family whose branches held separate seats, and Nair warriors formed the backbone of society. The kingdom traded pepper and spices with Arab merchants, and later with the Portuguese, who built Fort St Angelo at Cannanore in 1505. The Ali Rajas of the Arakkal kingdom began as Muslim ministers and admirals of the Kolathiris.
kolathunadu.e: Internal division split the realm into several branch seats, with Chirakkal the senior one. Hyder Ali of the Kingdom of Mysore overran Malabar in 1766, and in 1792 the region passed to the British East India Company. The Chirakkal family survived as pensioned landholders.

kingdom-of-bithynia.t: Bithynia, a Hellenistic kingdom of north-western Anatolia that invited the Galatians in, sheltered Hannibal and was bequeathed to Rome.
kingdom-of-bithynia.o: The Bithynians, a people of Thracian origin, lived south of the Bosporus and the Sea of Marmara. Their dynast Zipoetes I resisted Lysimachus and the Seleucid Empire, and in 297 BCE he took the title king, founding a dynasty that lasted over two centuries.
kingdom-of-bithynia.r: Nicomedes I founded Nicomedia as his capital in 264 BCE and invited Celtic warriors into Asia, who settled in Galatia. Prusias I expanded the kingdom, founded Prusa and sheltered Hannibal, who took poison at Libyssa in 183 BCE rather than be handed to Rome. The kings promoted Greek city life.
kingdom-of-bithynia.e: Nicomedes IV, restored to his throne by Rome, left Bithynia to the Roman Republic in his will in 74 BCE. The bequest provoked the Third Mithridatic War with the Kingdom of Pontus, and Bithynia became a Roman province.

kingdom-of-jibei.t: A fragment of the old state of Qi given to Tian An in 206 BCE, destroyed within months when Tian Rong reunited Qi by force.
kingdom-of-jibei.o: Tian An, a grandson of King Jian, the last king of the State of Qi, captured several towns north of the Ji River during the war against the Qin dynasty and followed Xiang Yu to Julu. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Jibei, with his capital at Boyang in central Shandong.
kingdom-of-jibei.r: Jibei was one of three kingdoms into which Xiang Yu split Qi, alongside the Kingdom of Jiaodong and Qi (206 BC), to weaken the powerful Tian clan. It lasted too short a time for any government to take shape.
kingdom-of-jibei.e: Tian Rong, the Qi strongman excluded from Xiang Yu's settlement, attacked the three kingdoms in 206 BCE, killed Tian An and reunited Qi under himself, provoking Xiang Yu's invasion of Qi.

kingdom-of-sonbai.t: Atoni kingdom of West Timor whose rulers held a ritual supremacy over the interior and were courted in turn by the Portuguese and the Dutch.
kingdom-of-sonbai.o: Sonbai grew out of the Atoni (Meto) chiefdoms of the West Timor highlands, where its lords were recognised as senior ritual rulers over neighbouring domains such as Mollo and Amanuban. By the 17th century it was drawn into the rivalry between the Portuguese-allied Topasses of Lifau and the Dutch East India Company at Kupang, and in the 1650s it split in two.
kingdom-of-sonbai.r: A branch known as Small Sonbai moved near Kupang and became a Company ally, while Great Sonbai remained in the mountains. Power rested on sacred kingship, alliances of lineages and tribute in kind, and the realm supplied sandalwood and beeswax to foreign traders. Most people followed the indigenous Atoni religion centred on ancestors and the earth.
kingdom-of-sonbai.e: Small Sonbai was absorbed into Dutch administration around Kupang, and Great Sonbai kept its independence in the interior until the Dutch campaign of 1906 captured its last ruler, Sobe Sonbai III, who died in exile. The name survives as a symbol of Timorese resistance.

kingdom-of-sai.t: One of the three kingdoms carved from the Qin heartland in 206 BCE, held by the former Qin officer Sima Xin, which fell to Liu Bang within months.
kingdom-of-sai.o: Sima Xin had been chief clerk under the Qin general Zhang Han and surrendered with him to Xiang Yu in 207 BCE. Xiang Yu divided the Guanzhong region among three former Qin commanders to block Liu Bang, giving Sima Xin the kingdom of Sai east of Xianyang, with its capital at Yueyang.
kingdom-of-sai.r: Sai's population resented its new king, since Xiang Yu had massacred some 200,000 surrendered Qin soldiers at Xin'an while sparing their commanders. The kingdom had no time to develop any administration of its own.
kingdom-of-sai.e: When Liu Bang broke out of Hanzhong in 206 BCE, Sima Xin surrendered and his land became Han territory. He later fled back to Xiang Yu and killed himself after a Chu defeat at Chenggao in 203 BCE.

kantora.t: Mandinka kingdom of the upper Gambia river, whose riverside market was the furthest point reached by Portuguese ships in the 15th century.
kantora.o: Kantora was one of the Mandinka states established along the Gambia as the Mali Empire extended its influence west. It occupied the south bank of the upper river around present-day Fatoto and Basse. The Portuguese explorer Diogo Gomes reached its market, which he called Cantor, around 1456.
kantora.r: Kantora's rulers controlled the highest navigable point on the river, where caravans from the upper Niger and Bambuk brought gold, ivory and slaves to trade for salt, cloth and European goods. It later fell within the orbit of the Kaabu Empire, and Muslim traders settled in its towns.
kantora.e: In the 1860s and 1870s Kantora was conquered by the Fula leader Alfa Molo and his son Musa Molo, becoming part of Fuladu. The area was divided between British Gambia and French Senegal by the boundary of 1889.

kingdom-of-yong.t: The kingdom of Zhang Han, the Qin general turned king, who guarded the western Wei valley against Liu Bang until his capital was flooded in 205 BCE.
kingdom-of-yong.o: Zhang Han was the Qin general who crushed Chen Sheng's rising, then surrendered to Xiang Yu after the defeat of Qin forces at Julu. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Yong, ruling the western Guanzhong region from Feiqiu, west of Xianyang, as the main barrier against Liu Bang in Hanzhong.
kingdom-of-yong.r: Yong was one of the Three Qins, with the Kingdom of Sai and the Kingdom of Di (206 BC). Like them, it lacked local loyalty because Xiang Yu had slaughtered the Qin soldiers Zhang Han had led.
kingdom-of-yong.e: Later in 206 BCE Liu Bang's general Han Xin crossed the mountains by the Chencang route and defeated Zhang Han. Besieged in Feiqiu, Zhang held out until 205 BCE, when the Han army flooded the city and he killed himself.

khanate-of-ardabil.t: One of the semi-independent khanates of Azerbaijan after Nader Shah's death, ruled by Shahsevan chiefs from the Safavid holy city of Ardabil.
khanate-of-ardabil.o: When Nader Shah was assassinated in 1747, the Afsharid Empire broke apart and local khans took power across the Caucasus and Azerbaijan. In Ardabil, home of the shrine of Sheikh Safi al-Din, ancestor of the Safavids, chiefs of the Shahsevan tribal confederation established a khanate.
khanate-of-ardabil.r: The khans relied on Shahsevan nomadic cavalry from the Moghan steppe and the Sabalan mountains. Nazar Ali Khan Shahsevan was the leading figure of the later 18th century. The khanate was drawn into the conflicts of its neighbours, notably the Quba khanate, the Talysh Khanate and the Karabakh Khanate, and was briefly occupied by Fath Ali Khan of Quba.
khanate-of-ardabil.e: Agha Mohammad Khan's Qajar Iran imposed control over Azerbaijan in the 1790s, and by 1808 the khanate had been fully absorbed into the Qajar state as a governorate.

kutai-kartanegara-sultanate.t: A Malay-Dayak sultanate on the Mahakam River in East Kalimantan, which absorbed ancient Kutai Martadipura and ruled until 1960.
kutai-kartanegara-sultanate.o: According to the Salasilah Kutai chronicle, the kingdom was founded around 1300 at Kutai Lama near the mouth of the Mahakam River by Aji Batara Agung Dewa Sakti. It was at first a Hindu state that looked to Majapahit, while upriver lay the old Kingdom of Kutai, known as Martadipura.
kutai-kartanegara-sultanate.r: Islam was adopted around 1575. In 1635 Aji Pangeran Sinum Panji Mendapa conquered Martadipura and joined the two names. The sultans traded rattan, gold and birds' nests from the interior with Bugis merchants, and in 1782 moved their capital upriver to Tenggarong. In the colonial era coal and oil brought new wealth.
kutai-kartanegara-sultanate.e: After a clash with British adventurer James Erskine Murray, the sultan accepted Dutch overlordship in 1844. The sultanate became part of Indonesia and was abolished in 1960 under Sultan Aji Muhammad Parikesit. It was revived as a cultural institution in 2001, and its palace is now a museum.

khorezm-peoples-soviet-republic.t: The short-lived Soviet-backed republic that replaced the Khanate of Khiva in 1920 before being divided among the new national republics.
khorezm-peoples-soviet-republic.o: In early 1920 the Red Army and the reformist Young Khivans overthrew the Khanate of Khiva, then dominated by the Turkmen warlord Junaid Khan. In April 1920 the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic was proclaimed, with Khiva as capital.
khorezm-peoples-soviet-republic.r: Officially independent and allied with Soviet Russia, it was governed by Young Khivans and later communists, under strong influence from Moscow. It nationalised the khan's estates, opened schools and fought Junaid Khan's Turkmen forces. Purges in 1921 and 1922 removed many of the original leaders, and it became the Khorezm Soviet Socialist Republic in 1923.
khorezm-peoples-soviet-republic.e: In the national delimitation of 1924 the republic was divided among the Uzbek SSR, the Turkmen SSR and the new Karakalpak Autonomous Oblast, later Karakalpakstan. Khiva's walled inner town, Itchan Kala, survived and is now a World Heritage Site.

kingdom-of-jimma.t: The richest of the Oromo kingdoms of the Gibe region, famous for its coffee and markets, which kept autonomy within Ethiopia until 1932.
kingdom-of-jimma.o: Jimma, also called Jimma Abba Jifar, emerged around 1790 when Oromo groups in the Gibe valley, who had settled there during the migrations of earlier centuries, formed a monarchy under Abba Magal. It grew by absorbing neighbours, and under Abba Jifar I (r. 1830 to 1855) the dynasty adopted Islam.
kingdom-of-jimma.r: The king ruled through appointed governors and officials, a departure from the egalitarian Oromo gadaa system. Jimma's markets, especially at Hirmata near the capital Jiren, traded coffee, ivory, civet, gold and slaves. Abba Jifar II (r. 1878 to 1932) submitted to Menelik II in 1882 and paid tribute in return for internal autonomy.
kingdom-of-jimma.e: After Abba Jifar II's death in 1932 Haile Selassie ended Jimma's autonomy and made it a province of the Ethiopian Empire. Abba Jifar's palace at Jiren is preserved, and Jimma is now one of Ethiopia's main coffee towns.

kingdom-of-ankole.t: A cattle kingdom of south-western Uganda, famous for its long-horned Ankole cattle, which grew by absorbing its neighbours in the colonial era.
kingdom-of-ankole.o: Traditions trace Nkore, later Ankole, to the Hinda dynasty, founded by Ruhinda, who is said to have inherited part of the Empire of Kitara around the 15th century. For centuries it was a small state east of Lake Edward, often raided by Bunyoro and Rwanda, which expanded under rulers such as Ntare IV in the 18th century.
kingdom-of-ankole.r: The mugabe (king) presided over a society divided between the cattle-owning Bahima and the farming Bairu, with power and prestige tied to herds of long-horned cattle. The royal drum Bagyendanwa embodied the kingship. Rule was loose, relying on chiefs and the king's cattle camps. Under Ntare V in the late 19th century Ankole extended its influence over neighbouring states.
kingdom-of-ankole.e: The Ankole Agreement of 1901 made it a kingdom of the Uganda Protectorate and added the Kingdom of Mpororo, the Kingdom of Igara and the Kingdom of Buhweju to its territory. The monarchy was abolished in 1967 and, unlike its neighbours, was not restored in the 1990s.

kassite-babylonia.t: The longest-ruling dynasty in Babylonian history: Kassite kings from the Zagros who reunited Babylonia and made it a great power of the Amarna age.
kassite-babylonia.o: The Kassites, a people from the Zagros with their own language and gods, had settled in Mesopotamia in the 18th century BCE. After the Hittite king Mursili I sacked Babylon in 1595 BCE, Kassite rulers, notably Agum II, took over the city, and around 1460 BCE Ulamburiash conquered the Sealand dynasty, uniting all Babylonia, called Karduniash.
kassite-babylonia.r: The Kassite kings adopted Babylonian language, religion and court culture, promoting Marduk of Babylon. Kurigalzu I built a new royal city, Dur-Kurigalzu, with a ziggurat. In the 14th century kings such as Kadashman-Enlil I and Burna-Buriash II exchanged letters, gold and princesses with Egypt in the Amarna correspondence. Land grants were recorded on carved boundary stones (kudurrus), horses and chariots were prized, and scribes standardised literary works such as the Epic of Gilgamesh.
kassite-babylonia.e: Tukulti-Ninurta I of the Assyrian Empire sacked Babylon around 1225 BCE. In 1158 BCE the Elamite Shutruk-Nahhunte invaded, and around 1155 BCE the last Kassite king, Enlil-nadin-ahi, was carried off, after which the Second Dynasty of Isin took power.

kingdom-of-powys.t: Kingdom of mid and north-east Wales and the Marches that long faced Mercia across Offa's Dyke, until it split into two lordships after 1160.
kingdom-of-powys.o: Powys arose in the territory of the Cornovii after Roman rule ended around 410, its name perhaps from the Latin pagenses, country people. Its early kings claimed descent from Cadell Ddyrnllug and, according to the Pillar of Eliseg, from Vortigern and Magnus Maximus. Its first centre may have been at Wroxeter or Pengwern before the English advance pushed it westward.
kingdom-of-powys.r: Powys bordered the Mercians and suffered heavily from their expansion; Selyf ap Cynan fell at the battle of Chester around 615, and Offa built his dyke along the frontier in the 8th century. Cyngen ap Cadell raised the Pillar of Eliseg near Llangollen to honour an ancestor who won back land from the English. Later kings ruled from Mathrafal, and its society rested on cattle and kin-based law.
kingdom-of-powys.e: Cyngen died on pilgrimage to Rome in 854, and Powys passed to Rhodri the Great of the Kingdom of Gwynedd. A native dynasty returned under Bleddyn ap Cynfyn in the 1060s, but after Madog ap Maredudd died in 1160 the kingdom split into Powys Fadog and Powys Wenwynwyn.

kingdom-of-commagene.t: Commagene, a small kingdom on the upper Euphrates whose king Antiochus I built the colossal god-statues on the summit of Nemrut Dağı.
kingdom-of-commagene.o: Commagene, the former Kummuh, lay between the Taurus mountains and the Euphrates. Its governor Ptolemaeus broke away from the Seleucid Empire c. 163 BCE. His successor Mithridates I Callinicus married a Seleucid princess, uniting Persian and Macedonian royal lines.
kingdom-of-commagene.r: Antiochus I Theos ruled from Samosata and devised a royal cult in which Greek and Persian gods were merged. On Nemrut Dağı he built a burial mound flanked by giant statues of himself with Zeus-Oromasdes, Apollo-Mithras and Heracles-Artagnes. Commagene grew rich from its fertile valleys and river crossings.
kingdom-of-commagene.e: Rome annexed Commagene in 17 CE, restored it to Antiochus IV in 38 CE, and finally absorbed it into the province of Syria in 72 CE under Vespasian.
