kingdom-of-tungning.t: The Ming loyalist kingdom of Koxinga and his heirs on Taiwan, which drove out the Dutch and became the first Han Chinese state on the island.
kingdom-of-tungning.o: Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong), son of the merchant-admiral Zheng Zhilong, led Ming loyalist forces on the Fujian coast after 1646. After a failed attack on Nanjing in 1659 he sought a new base, invaded Dutch Formosa in 1661 and took Fort Zeelandia in 1662, but died a few months later.
kingdom-of-tungning.r: His son Zheng Jing and the minister Chen Yonghua built a Chinese-style administration at Tungning (Tainan), founded the first Confucian temple and schools on Taiwan in 1666, settled soldiers on farmland and traded with Japan, South-east Asia and the English East India Company. Zheng Jing joined the Revolt of the Three Feudatories in 1674 and occupied coastal Fujian for a time.
kingdom-of-tungning.e: After Zheng Jing's death in 1681, court factions placed his young son Zheng Keshuang on the throne. In 1683 the Qing admiral Shi Lang destroyed the Zheng fleet at Penghu, and Zheng Keshuang surrendered. Taiwan became a prefecture of Fujian under the Qing Empire.

kingdom-of-the-swedes.t: Early kingdom of the Svear around Lake Mälaren and Uppsala, whose kings ruled the trading town of Birka and later united the Swedish lands.
kingdom-of-the-swedes.o: Tacitus wrote of the Suiones in the 1st century, and by the 6th century the Svear had a power centre at Old Uppsala, where great royal mounds were raised. Rich boat graves at Vendel and Valsgärde show a wealthy warrior elite. Later sagas trace the kings to the legendary Yngling dynasty.
kingdom-of-the-swedes.r: Kingship was tied to the pagan cult at Uppsala, described by Adam of Bremen, and to assemblies of free men at the thing. Birka, founded in the 8th century on Lake Mälaren, linked the kingdom to trade routes east to Rus' and the Byzantine and Abbasid worlds. Rimbert's life of Ansgar records kings Björn and Anund receiving the Frankish missionary around 830 and 850.
kingdom-of-the-swedes.e: Eric the Victorious, who defeated a rival at Fýrisvellir in the 980s, and his son Olof Skötkonung extended Svear rule over the Geats. This union of the Svear and Götar is regarded as the start of the medieval Kingdom of Sweden, and the Uppsala kingship gave Sweden its name.

kingdom-of-the-gepids.t: East Germanic kingdom in the Tisza plain and Transylvania that rose after Attila's empire collapsed and was destroyed by Lombards and Avars in 567.
kingdom-of-the-gepids.o: The Gepids, a Gothic-related people, were subjects of Attila's Huns. In 454 their king Ardaric led the revolt that crushed Attila's sons at the River Nedao, and the Gepids took over the lands east of the Danube in the Tisza plain and Transylvania.
kingdom-of-the-gepids.r: Gepid kings ruled a mixed population of Germanic, Sarmatian and local peoples, and adopted Arian Christianity. Rich princely graves such as those at Apahida show their wealth. They seized Sirmium (Sremska Mitrovica) on the Sava, a key city, and competed with the Ostrogoths, Byzantium and the Lombards for the middle Danube. Kings Thurisind and Cunimund fought the Lombards in the 550s and 560s.
kingdom-of-the-gepids.e: In 567 the Lombards under Alboin, allied with the newly arrived Avars, destroyed the kingdom; Cunimund was killed and Alboin made his skull into a drinking cup. The Gepid lands passed to the Avar Khaganate.

kingdom-of-lithuania.t: The only crowned kingdom in Lithuanian history, created when Mindaugas accepted Catholic baptism and a royal crown from the Pope.
kingdom-of-lithuania.o: Mindaugas had united the Lithuanian lands by the 1240s but faced a coalition of rivals backed by the Livonian Order. To split his enemies he accepted baptism in 1251, and Pope Innocent IV authorised his coronation, which took place in July 1253, probably in Vilnius.
kingdom-of-lithuania.r: As king, Mindaugas ruled a mainly pagan land with a small Catholic church and a bishop appointed for Lithuania. He granted lands, including parts of Samogitia, to the Livonian Order in return for its support. The kingdom brought Lithuania into the diplomatic world of Latin Europe while Mindaugas extended his power over Black Ruthenia.
kingdom-of-lithuania.e: After the Samogitians crushed the Livonian Order at Durbe in 1260, Mindaugas broke with the order and seems to have abandoned Christianity. He was murdered in 1263 by his nephew Treniota and Daumantas, and the royal title lapsed. The state continued as the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; his coronation is marked by a Lithuanian national holiday.

kadambas-of-goa.t: A Kadamba dynasty that ruled Goa for nearly four centuries, made rich by Arab trade through the port of Gopakapattana.
kadambas-of-goa.o: The Goa Kadambas claimed descent from the earlier Kadamba dynasty of Banavasi. Shashthadeva I established them in the Goa region around 960, at first as feudatories of the Western Chalukya Empire, with the capital at Chandrapura, modern Chandor.
kadambas-of-goa.r: Jayakeshi I moved the capital to the port of Gopakapattana on the Zuari river, modern Goa Velha, which became a busy harbour trading with Arabia, East Africa and Gujarat; the Kadambas welcomed Arab merchants and allowed a mosque to be built. They issued gold coins and fought the Silaharas of North Konkan. The Mahadeva temple at Tambdi Surla, built of basalt, survives from their period.
kadambas-of-goa.e: In the 13th century the Kadambas came under the Yadavas, and in the 14th century Goa was raided by the armies of the Delhi Sultanate. Around 1345 their rule collapsed, and Goa later passed to the Vijayanagara Empire and the Bahmani Sultanate.

kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.t: A tiny Jutish kingdom on the Isle of Wight, the last part of England to accept Christianity, ended by the violent conquest of Caedwalla in 686.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.o: Bede reports that the Isle of Wight, like Kent and part of Hampshire, was settled by Jutes. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle claims that Cerdic and Cynric took the island in 530 and gave it to their kinsmen Stuf and Wihtgar, but the story is largely legendary.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.r: The Wihtwara lived from farming and the sea under their own kings, sometimes dependents of greater neighbours. In 661 Wulfhere of the Kingdom of Mercia gave the island to the South Saxon king Aethelwealh. The island was still pagan in the 680s.
kingdom-of-the-isle-of-wight.e: In 686 Caedwalla of the Kingdom of Wessex conquered the island, killed King Arwald and had his two young brothers executed after baptism, as Bede recounts. The island became part of Wessex and was converted by Wilfrid's clergy.

kwantung-oblast.t: Russia's leased territory at the tip of the Liaodong peninsula, home of the Port Arthur naval base, lost to Japan in the Russo-Japanese War.
kwantung-oblast.o: After the Triple Intervention forced Japan to give up the Liaodong peninsula in 1895, the Russian Empire obtained a twenty-five-year lease of its southern tip from the Qing Empire in 1898. Russia fortified Port Arthur as an ice-free Pacific naval base and built a commercial port at Dalny.
kwantung-oblast.r: The territory was linked to Harbin by the southern branch of the Chinese Eastern Railway. It was governed by military officers, and in 1903 Admiral Yevgeny Alekseyev, based at Port Arthur, became viceroy of the Russian Far East. Russian advance in Manchuria alarmed Japan and Britain and led directly to war.
kwantung-oblast.e: Japan attacked Port Arthur in February 1904. After a costly siege, the fortress commander Anatoly Stessel surrendered in January 1905. The Treaty of Portsmouth transferred the lease to Japan, which renamed it the Kwantung Leased Territory.

kingdom-of-tambora.t: Small kingdom on the slopes of Mount Tambora in Sumbawa, wiped out by the largest volcanic eruption in recorded history.
kingdom-of-tambora.o: Little is known of its origins. Tambora was one of several small realms on Sumbawa, alongside the Bima Sultanate, Dompu, Sanggar and the Sumbawa Sultanate, and from the 17th century it came under Makassarese and then Dutch East India Company influence through treaties with Sumbawan rulers.
kingdom-of-tambora.r: Its people grew rice and traded horses, honey, sappanwood and sandalwood. Tambora was ruled by a Muslim raja. Its language, recorded in a short wordlist gathered for Thomas Stamford Raffles, appears unrelated to the Austronesian languages around it and may have been a non-Austronesian isolate.
kingdom-of-tambora.e: The eruption of Mount Tambora in April 1815 buried the kingdom and neighbouring Pekat under ash and pyroclastic flows, killing nearly all its inhabitants. The ensuing global cooling caused the Year Without a Summer in 1816. Excavations since 2004 have uncovered houses, pottery and remains, earning Tambora the name the Pompeii of the East.

kingdom-of-araucania-and-patagonia.t: A kingdom proclaimed among the Mapuche by a French adventurer in 1860, which never won recognition but survives as a claim of French pretenders.
kingdom-of-araucania-and-patagonia.o: Orélie-Antoine de Tounens, a lawyer from the Dordogne in France, travelled to Chile in 1858 and went to Araucanía, the independent Mapuche lands south of the Biobío. In November 1860 he proclaimed himself King Orélie-Antoine I of Araucanía and, days later, added Patagonia, claiming support from Mapuche chiefs.
kingdom-of-araucania-and-patagonia.r: The kingdom existed largely on paper. Orélie-Antoine issued a constitution, a flag and decrees, and some Mapuche leaders, such as Quilapán, seem to have seen him as a potential ally against Chilean expansion. He had no army, administration or international recognition, and Chile regarded the scheme as a threat to its sovereignty.
kingdom-of-araucania-and-patagonia.e: Chilean authorities arrested him in January 1862, declared him insane and deported him to France. He returned several times without success and died in France in 1878. Chile carried out the Occupation of Araucanía by 1883. French claimants still use his title.

kingdom-of-ndongo.t: The Mbundu kingdom of the Ngola, whose title gave Angola its name and whose queen Njinga fought the Portuguese for decades.
kingdom-of-ndongo.o: Ndongo was formed by Mbundu chiefdoms between the Kwanza and Lukala rivers in the late 15th century under a ruler titled the Ngola. Initially a tributary of the Kingdom of Kongo, it asserted independence in the 1550s, and a Portuguese embassy reached its capital Kabasa in 1560.
kingdom-of-ndongo.r: The Ngola ruled through regional lords (sobas) who paid tribute in cattle, salt, cloth and slaves. From 1575, when Paulo Dias de Novais founded Luanda, Ndongo faced constant war with Portuguese Angola and its Imbangala allies, who sought slaves for the Atlantic trade. Njinga Mbande, who became ruler in 1624, negotiated, converted, fought and allied with the Dutch, later ruling from the Kingdom of Matamba.
kingdom-of-ndongo.e: Ndongo was split between Njinga's party and a Portuguese-backed puppet king, Ngola Hari. When his successor rebelled, the Portuguese stormed the fortress of Pungo Andongo in 1671, ending the kingdom. The Ngola title gave Angola its name, and Njinga is a national heroine.

kingdom-of-greece.t: The Greek monarchy from 1832 to 1973, which more than doubled Greece's territory and lived through the National Schism, occupation, civil war and dictatorship.
kingdom-of-greece.o: Under the London Conference of 1832, Britain, France and Russia made Otto of Bavaria king of independent Greece, replacing the First Hellenic Republic. He arrived at Nauplia in 1833 with Bavarian regents, and Athens became the capital in 1834. A revolt in September 1843 forced him to grant a constitution.
kingdom-of-greece.r: Otto was deposed in 1862 and replaced by George I, whose long reign added the Ionian Islands (1864), Thessaly (1881) and, through the Balkan Wars, Macedonia, Epirus and Crete. Politics were shaped by the Great Idea of uniting Greeks and by the clash between Eleftherios Venizelos and King Constantine I. Defeat in Asia Minor in 1922 brought a population exchange with Turkey.
kingdom-of-greece.e: The monarchy was replaced by the Second Hellenic Republic in 1924 and restored in 1935, followed by the Metaxas dictatorship, Axis occupation and civil war. After the 1967 coup, Constantine II went into exile; the junta abolished the monarchy in 1973, confirmed by referendum in 1974.

kingdom-of-yugoslavia.t: First united state of the South Slavs, a monarchy torn by rivalry between Serbs and Croats and destroyed by the Axis invasion of 1941.
kingdom-of-yugoslavia.o: As Austria-Hungary collapsed, the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs joined the Kingdom of Serbia and Montenegro to form the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, proclaimed in Belgrade on 1 December 1918 under the Karađorđević dynasty. Its borders, confirmed by the post-war treaties, joined lands with very different histories, faiths and economies.
kingdom-of-yugoslavia.r: The centralist Vidovdan Constitution of 1921 favoured Serbian dominance and was opposed by Stjepan Radić's Croatian Peasant Party. After Radić was shot in parliament in 1928, King Alexander imposed a dictatorship in 1929 and renamed the country Yugoslavia. He was assassinated in Marseille in 1934, and Prince Paul's regency created the Banovina of Croatia in 1939.
kingdom-of-yugoslavia.e: In March 1941 the government signed the Tripartite Pact, but officers overthrew it two days later. Germany and its allies invaded on 6 April 1941 and the army capitulated within eleven days. King Peter II went into exile, and the country was partitioned among the Independent State of Croatia and occupying powers.
kingdom-of-yugoslavia.re: Serbian Orthodox and Catholic Christianity, Sunni Islam

kingdom-of-gajaaga.t: Soninke kingdom of the upper Senegal river, called Galam by the French, a hub of the gum, gold and slave trades.
kingdom-of-gajaaga.o: Gajaaga was founded by the Bacili clan of Soninke on the upper Senegal around the junction with the Faleme river, an area rich in gold from nearby Bambuk. It emerged as an independent kingdom in the 17th century as larger Sahel empires declined.
kingdom-of-gajaaga.r: The ruler, the Tunka, was chosen from the Bacili lineages and ruled from Maxanna and other river towns. The French built Fort Saint-Joseph nearby around 1700 and later Bakel, and Gajaaga traded slaves, gum arabic, gold and grain down the river to Saint-Louis. Soninke merchants and clerics were active traders across the region.
kingdom-of-gajaaga.e: Civil war in the 1830s split Gajaaga into two parts, Goye and Kammera. The French extended their control and placed the area under a protectorate in 1858, and it became part of French Senegal.

keos.t: Cycladic island state of four small cities nearest to Attica, home of the poets Simonides and Bacchylides.
keos.o: Keos lies off the tip of Attica and had a major Bronze Age town at Ayia Irini. In the early Iron Age Ionian Greeks settled it, and the island was organised as a tetrapolis of four cities, Ioulis, Karthaia, Koressia and Poiessa, which sometimes acted together as one state.
keos.r: Keos was famous for its poets: Simonides and his nephew Bacchylides, both from Ioulis, wrote for patrons across Greece in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. Strabo records a Keian law said to require citizens over sixty to drink hemlock. The island exported ruddle, a red earth pigment, and paid tribute in the Delian League.
keos.e: Keos joined the Second Athenian League but revolted in the 360s BCE and was subdued. In the 3rd century BCE Koressia became a Ptolemaic naval base renamed Arsinoe. The island passed under Roman control by 146 BCE.

kingdom-of-nri.t: Igbo sacred kingdom whose priest-king, the Eze Nri, held ritual rather than military authority over a wide area of south-eastern Nigeria for nearly a thousand years.
kingdom-of-nri.o: Nri traditions trace the kingdom to Eri, a culture hero said to have come down from the sky near the Anambra river, and to his descendant Ifikuanim, remembered as the first Eze Nri. The traditional founding date of 948 rests on genealogical reckoning. The famous 9th and 10th century bronzes from nearby Igbo-Ukwu are often linked to Nri ritual culture.
kingdom-of-nri.r: The Eze Nri was a ritual ruler chosen after an interregnum and secluded in his palace. Nri did not rule by force: its titled priests, marked with ichi facial scars, travelled across Igboland to cleanse abominations, crown local title-holders, settle disputes and proclaim peace. The Ozo title system and a network of yam and agricultural rites spread from Nri.
kingdom-of-nri.e: Nri's influence waned from the 18th century as the Aro Confederacy and slave trading reshaped Igboland. In 1911 British colonial officials forced the Eze Nri to renounce his ritual powers. The title survives as a traditional office in Anambra State, and Nri is remembered as a cradle of Igbo culture.

kingdom-of-bamum.t: Grassfields kingdom of western Cameroon whose king Ibrahim Njoya invented a script, a religion and a palace culture still admired today.
kingdom-of-bamum.o: Bamum tradition traces the dynasty to Nchare Yen, a Tikar prince who conquered the area around Foumban and became its first Mfon, traditionally in 1394. The kingdom remained small until the late 18th or early 19th century, when Mbuembue expanded it greatly and fortified the capital with a deep ditch.
kingdom-of-bamum.r: The Mfon ruled from a large palace at Foumban with titled palace servants and councils of nobles. Bamum was famous for brass casting, beadwork and carved thrones. King Ibrahim Njoya, who reigned from around 1889, created the Bamum script, a printing press, maps and a syncretic religion blending Islam, Christianity and local belief.
kingdom-of-bamum.e: Bamum came under German Kamerun around 1902 and then French Cameroon after the First World War. The French curtailed Njoya's power in the 1920s and exiled him in 1931. The dynasty survives as a sultanate at Foumban, whose palace houses a renowned museum.

kadi-burhan-al-din-state.t: The sultanate of a judge and poet who seized the Eretnid throne and held central Anatolia against the Ottomans, Mamluks and Turkmen.
kadi-burhan-al-din-state.o: Kadi Burhan al-Din Ahmad was a jurist from Kayseri who served the Eretnids as judge and vizier. As the dynasty weakened he became the real power, and in 1381, after the death of Ala al-Din Ali, he declared himself sultan in Sivas.
kadi-burhan-al-din-state.r: He spent his reign fighting: against the Ottomans, whom he defeated at Kirkdilim in 1392, against the Mamluks, the Aq Qoyunlu, Mutahharten of Erzincan and the beys of Amasya. He was also a poet whose divan of Turkish verse is one of the earliest in Anatolia, and his court historian Astarabadi wrote the Bazm u Razm, a chronicle of his reign in Persian.
kadi-burhan-al-din-state.e: In 1398 he was killed by the Aq Qoyunlu chief Qara Yuluk Osman. Sivas surrendered to Bayezid I, but Timur destroyed it in 1400.

kingdom-of-gumma.t: A Gibe Oromo kingdom of south-western Ethiopia, known for its fervent Islam and for resisting incorporation into Menelik's empire.
kingdom-of-gumma.o: Gumma emerged around 1810 west of the Didessa, as Oromo groups of the region formed hereditary monarchies. It was one of five Gibe kingdoms, alongside the Kingdom of Jimma, Limmu-Ennarea, the Kingdom of Gomma and the Kingdom of Gera.
kingdom-of-gumma.r: Gumma's kings governed through appointed officials and drew revenue from farming and trade in coffee, ivory and slaves. The kingdom became known as a centre of militant Islam, and its rulers waged campaigns against non-Muslim neighbours. Little else is recorded in detail.
kingdom-of-gumma.e: Gumma was subjected to the Ethiopian Empire in the 1880s, and after a revolt it was finally conquered and annexed in 1902.

kingdom-of-lydia.t: Lydia, the western Anatolian kingdom of Sardis, where the first coins were struck and Croesus became a byword for wealth.
kingdom-of-lydia.o: Greek tradition traced a Heraclid dynasty in Lydia, then called Maeonia, back to c. 1200 BCE, but the kingdom becomes historical with Gyges, who seized the throne c. 680 BCE and founded the Mermnad dynasty. He fought the Cimmerians and sent gifts to Delphi.
kingdom-of-lydia.r: From Sardis the Mermnad kings ruled the Hermus valley and subdued most Greek cities of Ionia. Electrum from the river Pactolus underpinned the first coinage in the late 7th century BCE, and Croesus introduced separate gold and silver coins. The huge burial mound of Alyattes stands at Bin Tepe.
kingdom-of-lydia.e: After a war with the Median Empire ended by the eclipse of 585 BCE, Croesus attacked Persia and was defeated by Cyrus, who took Sardis c. 546 BCE. Lydia became a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire, and Sardis its western capital.

kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.t: The short-lived sea realm of Somerled, who seized the southern Hebrides from the kings of Man and founded the dynasty of the Lords of the Isles.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.o: Somerled, a Norse-Gaelic warlord of Argyll married to a daughter of Olaf I of Man, challenged his brother-in-law Godred of the Kingdom of the Isles. After a sea battle in 1156 the Hebrides were divided, and in 1158 Somerled drove Godred from Man, ruling Argyll, Kintyre and the southern isles.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.r: Somerled's power rested on galley fleets and the loyalty of Gaelic and Norse-Gaelic kindreds. He acted as an independent ruler, sometimes allied with and sometimes against the Scottish king, and is linked with the founding of Saddell Abbey in Kintyre.
kingdom-of-argyll-and-the-isles.e: Somerled was killed in 1164 at Renfrew while invading the Kingdom of Scotland. His realm was divided among his sons, ancestors of the MacDougalls, MacDonalds and MacRuairis, whose descendants later formed the Lordship of the Isles.

kingdom-of-nso.t: The largest kingdom of Cameroon's Bamenda Grassfields, ruled by the Fon of Nso from Kumbo.
kingdom-of-nso.o: Nso tradition names Ngonnso, a Tikar princess who left her home with followers, as the founder of the kingdom, traditionally around the late 14th century. The early capital moved several times before settling at Kumbo, and Nso expanded by absorbing neighbouring chiefdoms in the 18th and 19th centuries.
kingdom-of-nso.r: The Fon ruled as a sacred king with regulatory societies, the Ngwerong and Ngiri, which enforced his decisions, kept royal rituals and managed succession. Lineage heads held land and titles. Nso fought long wars with the Kingdom of Bamum, and craftsmen produced carved masks, stools and beaded regalia.
kingdom-of-nso.e: German forces occupied Kumbo in the first years of the 20th century, and Nso became part of German Kamerun and later British Cameroons. The Fon of Nso still reigns. In 2022 a statue of Ngonnso taken by a German officer was returned from Berlin.

kingdom-of-magadha.t: The kingdom of south Bihar that conquered its rivals one by one and became the core of the Nanda and Maurya empires.
kingdom-of-magadha.o: Magadha lay south of the Ganges in modern Bihar, around the hill-ringed capital of Rajagriha. Vedic texts regarded it as a land on the edge of orthodox society. Its rise began in the mid-6th century BCE under Bimbisara of the Haryanka dynasty, who conquered the Kingdom of Anga and won Kashi territory by marriage alliance.
kingdom-of-magadha.r: Magadha's kings built a strong army and a salaried administration, helped by fertile rice land, iron ore from the hills and forests that supplied war elephants. Bimbisara and his son Ajatashatru were patrons of the Buddha and Mahavira, and the First Buddhist Council met at Rajagriha. Ajatashatru conquered the Vajji league and Kosala, his successor Udayin founded Pataliputra, and the Shishunaga dynasty later conquered Avanti.
kingdom-of-magadha.e: Around 345 BCE Mahapadma Nanda overthrew the last Shishunaga king and founded the Nanda Empire, which ruled from Pataliputra over most of the Ganges valley. Magadha remained the heart of the Maurya Empire and, centuries later, of the Gupta Empire.

keraite-khanate.t: A powerful Christian steppe khanate in central Mongolia, whose ruler Toghrul was Genghis Khan's patron and rival, and later the model for legends of Prester John.
keraite-khanate.o: The Keraites were a large tribal union living along the Orkhon and Tuul rivers in central Mongolia, probably of Mongolic speech with strong Turkic influences. Syriac sources record that their ruler converted to the Church of the East around 1007, together with many of his people.
keraite-khanate.r: The khanate was a confederation of clans under a ruling family, with Christian priests and Nestorian practices alongside steppe customs. Its rulers, among them Marghuz Buyruk, fought the Tatars, Naimans and Merkits. Toghrul, sworn brother of Temüjin's father, became the most powerful khan of central Mongolia and received the title Ong Khan from the Jin dynasty (1115-1234) in 1196 after the campaign against the Tatars.
keraite-khanate.e: Toghrul helped the young Temüjin rise but turned against him; in 1203 Temüjin defeated the Keraites, and Toghrul was killed by Naimans while fleeing. The Keraites joined the Mongol Empire; the Keraite princess Sorghaghtani Beki was mother of Möngke, Kublai and Hülegü.

kingdom-of-italy-medieval.t: The medieval Kingdom of Italy, contested by Italian magnates after 888 and then held by the German emperors, whose authority waned as the cities grew.
kingdom-of-italy-medieval.o: When the Carolingian Empire broke up in 888, Italian nobles elected Berengar of Friuli as King of Italy. For seventy years rival magnates and outsiders, among them Guy and Lambert of Spoleto, Louis of Provence, Rudolf of Burgundy and Hugh of Arles, fought for the crown, which was traditionally received at Pavia.
kingdom-of-italy-medieval.r: In 951 Otto I of Germany took the title, and from his imperial coronation in 962 the crown was tied to the German emperors, often crowned with the Iron Crown of Lombardy. Arduin of Ivrea was the last native king (1002–1014). Imperial rule relied on bishops and counts, but the communes grew independent; the Lombard League defeated Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176, and the Peace of Constance in 1183 recognised their self-government.
kingdom-of-italy-medieval.e: After the 13th century the kingdom survived mainly as a legal framework of imperial fiefs. Charles V was the last emperor crowned King of Italy, at Bologna in 1530. Imperial claims in Italy ended with the French Revolutionary Wars and the Treaty of Lunéville in 1801.

kingdom-of-baol.t: Wolof and Serer kingdom of central Senegal, often united with Cayor, where Amadou Bamba later founded the holy city of Touba.
kingdom-of-baol.o: Baol was a province of the Jolof Empire that broke away in the mid-16th century, following Cayor's victory at Danki in 1549. Its ruler, the Teigne, was chosen from royal lineages with ties to both Wolof and Serer families, and the capital was at Lambaye.
kingdom-of-baol.r: The Teigne ruled with titled chiefs and a slave soldiery over a mixed population of Wolof and Serer farmers growing millet and later groundnuts. Baol was frequently united with Cayor under one ruler; Lat Sukaabe Fall held both thrones around 1700. Baol's coastal towns traded with the French and Portuguese.
kingdom-of-baol.e: France established control over Baol in the 1880s and 1890s and absorbed it into French Senegal. In 1887 the Sufi leader Amadou Bamba founded Touba in Baol, and the region became the heartland of the Mouride brotherhood.

kara-khanid-khanate.t: The first Turkic dynasty to adopt Islam as a state religion, which brought Transoxiana under Turkic rule and produced classic works of Turkic literature.
kara-khanid-khanate.o: The Kara-Khanid dynasty emerged in the mid-9th century among the Karluk Yabgu, Chigil and Yagma tribes after the fall of the Uyghur Khaganate, with centres at Balasagun and Kashgar. Around 934 the ruler Satuq Bughra Khan converted to Islam, and his successors made it the religion of the state.
kara-khanid-khanate.r: The khanate had a dual structure, with a senior khagan and a junior co-ruler, and appanages held by members of the royal clan. In 999 it took Bukhara from the Samanid Empire, bringing Transoxiana under Turkic rule. The Kara-Khanids built mosques and madrasas, and their court produced Yusuf Balasaguni's Kutadgu Bilig and Mahmud al-Kashgari's dictionary of Turkic languages.
kara-khanid-khanate.e: Dynastic rivalry split the khanate around 1042 into the Eastern Kara-Khanid Khanate and the Western Kara-Khanid Khanate, which became vassals of the Seljuks and the Qara Khitai.

kingdom-of-navarre.t: The Basque Pyrenean kingdom of Pamplona, which under Sancho III dominated Christian Spain and survived in part until 1841.
kingdom-of-navarre.o: Around 824, after the Basques defeated a Frankish army at the second Battle of Roncevaux, Íñigo Arista became ruler of Pamplona, allied with his kinsmen the Banu Qasi. In 905 Sancho Garcés I founded the Jimena dynasty and pushed south into the Ebro valley and La Rioja.
kingdom-of-navarre.r: Sancho III the Great, from 1004 to 1035, controlled Aragon, Castile and the Pyrenean counties, the dominant power of Christian Iberia. After a period of partition between 1076 and 1134, the kingdom revived. Sancho VII fought at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. French dynasties ruled from 1234, and Charles III the Noble built the palace of Olite. Basque, Romance and Latin were spoken, and the kingdom kept its own fueros and cortes.
kingdom-of-navarre.e: In 1512 Ferdinand the Catholic conquered Upper Navarre, joined to Castile in 1515, while Lower Navarre north of the Pyrenees remained with the Albret family. Its kings became kings of France in 1589. Spanish Navarre kept its own institutions until the law of 1841 made it a province.

khanate-of-kokand.t: An Uzbek khanate of the Ferghana valley that grew to rule Tashkent and the Kyrgyz and Kazakh steppes before Russia annexed it in 1876.
khanate-of-kokand.o: Around 1709 Shahrukh Bi, leader of the Ming Uzbek tribe, broke away from the Khanate of Bukhara and established a separate state in the eastern Ferghana valley. His successors built Kokand as their capital, and Narbuta Bi strengthened the state in the late 18th century.
khanate-of-kokand.r: Alim Khan, who took the title khan around 1800, created a standing army and conquered Tashkent in 1809. His brother and successor Umar Khan was a patron of poetry whose wife Nodira was a celebrated poet. The khanate controlled the trade routes to Kashgar and dominated Kyrgyz and Kazakh nomads, building forts such as Ak-Mechet on the Syr Darya. Rivalry between settled Sarts and nomadic Kipchaks caused civil wars.
khanate-of-kokand.e: Russia took Ak-Mechet in 1853 and Tashkent in 1865. After a revolt against the pro-Russian Khudayar Khan in 1875, General Skobelev crushed resistance and Russia annexed the khanate in 1876 as the Ferghana Oblast of the Turkestan Governorate-General.

kingdom-of-ui-failge.t: Irish midland kingdom of the O'Connor Faly, which resisted English expansion from its bogland strongholds until the plantation of Offaly in 1556.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.o: The Uí Failge, 'descendants of Failge', claimed descent from Rus Failge, a son of the legendary Leinster king Cathair Mór. From the early medieval period they held a kingdom in the north-west of the Kingdom of Leinster, in what is now County Offaly, which takes its name from them. From the 11th century their rulers were the Ua Conchobair Failge, O'Connor Faly.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.r: Their territory of bog, esker and woodland was hard for invaders to penetrate. After the Anglo-Norman invasion the FitzGeralds of Kildare took their eastern lands, but the O'Connors Faly held the rest, raiding the Pale and taking protection payments known as black rent. Their stronghold at Daingean, set among bogs, was their main fortress in the 16th century.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.e: After Brian O'Connor Faly rebelled and surrendered in the 1540s, the English took Daingean. In 1556 the government of Mary I shired the kingdom as King's County, with Daingean renamed Philipstown, and planted it with English settlers, ending the kingdom.
kingdom-of-ui-failge.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102.t: Medieval Croatian kingdom of the Trpimirović dynasty, which reached from the Drava to the Adriatic before passing to the Hungarian crown.
kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102.o: Around 925 Tomislav, ruler of the Duchy of Croatia, also held the Duchy of Pannonian Croatia and was addressed as king in papal letters. He had defeated Hungarian raids and the army of Simeon I of Bulgaria, uniting the Croats in one kingdom.
kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102.r: Kings ruled with a council of nobles and bans, from royal seats such as Knin, Biograd na Moru and Nin. Petar Krešimir IV (1058–1074) brought the Byzantine Dalmatian towns under his control, and Demetrius Zvonimir was crowned by a papal legate in 1076, tying Croatia to the Reformed papacy. The Baška tablet records Zvonimir's gift in Glagolitic script.
kingdom-of-croatia-925-1102.e: After Zvonimir died without heirs, Ladislaus I of Hungary claimed the throne. The last king, Petar Snačić, fell at Gvozd in 1097, and in 1102 Coloman was crowned king of Croatia, beginning the Kingdom of Croatia (1102-1526) in union with Hungary.

kingdom-of-kucha.t: The largest oasis kingdom of the northern Tarim Basin, a Buddhist centre famous for its music, the Kizil caves and the great translator Kumarajiva.
kingdom-of-kucha.o: Kucha, Qiuci in Chinese, was an Indo-European-speaking oasis state between the Tianshan Mountains and the Taklamakan desert, recorded from the 2nd century BCE among the kingdoms of the Western Regions. Its rulers, later known in Chinese by the surname Bai, balanced between the Xiongnu, the Han Dynasty and later steppe powers.
kingdom-of-kucha.r: Kuchean, now called Tocharian B, was written in Brahmi script. Kucha's monasteries, including the painted caves at Kizil, made it a leading centre of Buddhism, and the translator Kumarajiva was born there in 344; in 384 the Former Qin general Lü Guang took the city and carried him east. Kuchean musicians and instruments shaped the court music of the Sui and the Tang Dynasty.
kingdom-of-kucha.e: The Tang conquered Kucha in 648 and made it the seat of the Anxi Protectorate. When Tang control collapsed in the late 8th century, Uyghurs moved in, and after 840 Kucha became part of the Kingdom of Qocho and was gradually Turkicised.

kingdom-of-gododdin.t: British kingdom of Lothian centred on Edinburgh, celebrated in the early Welsh poem Y Gododdin, which fell to Northumbria in the 7th century.
kingdom-of-gododdin.o: Gododdin was the post-Roman kingdom of the Votadini, whose name became Guotodin and then Gododdin in Welsh. Its centre was Din Eidyn, the rock of Edinburgh, and it stretched across Lothian and the eastern Borders. Welsh tradition also linked the district of Manaw Gododdin, around the head of the Forth, with Cunedda, legendary founder of the Kingdom of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-gododdin.r: The kingdom is best known from Y Gododdin, attributed to the poet Aneirin, which mourns a war band feasted for a year by Mynyddog Mwynfawr at Din Eidyn and then slaughtered at Catraeth, usually identified as Catterick, around 600. The poem portrays an aristocratic warrior society bound by loyalty, mead and gifts. Hillforts such as Traprain Law and Edinburgh Castle Rock were key centres.
kingdom-of-gododdin.e: The Anglian kingdom of Bernicia, later Northumbria, expanded northward in the 7th century. Irish annals record the siege of Etin in 638, generally taken as the Northumbrian capture of Edinburgh. Lothian remained English until it passed to the Scottish kings in the 10th and 11th centuries.

kingdom-of-kazembe.t: The eastern Lunda kingdom of the Luapula valley, a wealthy trading state visited by Portuguese explorers and David Livingstone.
kingdom-of-kazembe.o: Around 1740 a Lunda general sent east by the Mwata Yamvo of the Lunda Empire conquered the Luapula valley south of Lake Mweru. His successors, bearing the title Mwata Kazembe, built an independent kingdom that still paid tribute to the Lunda court.
kingdom-of-kazembe.r: The Kazembe ruled from a large capital through Lunda aristocrats who governed local chiefs. The kingdom traded copper from Katanga, ivory and slaves with Portuguese from Tete and Swahili-Arab merchants from the east coast. The Portuguese explorer Francisco de Lacerda died there in 1798, and Livingstone visited in 1867–68. The annual Mutomboko ceremony commemorates the conquest.
kingdom-of-kazembe.e: In the late 19th century Msiri's Yeke state took Katanga and Swahili-Arab traders eroded Kazembe's power. British South Africa Company forces occupied the capital in 1899, and the kingdom was absorbed into Northern Rhodesia. The Mwata Kazembe remains a traditional ruler in Zambia.

kingdom-of-germany.t: The German kingdom at the heart of the Holy Roman Empire, an elective monarchy whose kings claimed the imperial crown for more than eight centuries.
kingdom-of-germany.o: The kingdom grew out of East Francia. Its kings, from Henry the Fowler in 919, were elected by the great nobles. When Otto I was crowned emperor in Rome in 962, the German crown became joined with the imperial title and with kingship of Italy and later Burgundy, a link that defined the Holy Roman Empire.
kingdom-of-germany.r: German kings were elected, from 1356 by the seven prince-electors under the Golden Bull, and crowned at Aachen. Royal power weakened during the Investiture Controversy and after the fall of the Hohenstaufen, while princes, bishops and free cities gained autonomy. From 1438 the Habsburgs held the crown almost without break, governing with the Imperial Diet.
kingdom-of-germany.e: The Reformation and the Thirty Years' War, ended by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, left Germany a federation of nearly sovereign states. Under Napoleonic pressure, Francis II abdicated on 6 August 1806, dissolving the Empire and the German kingdom with it.
kingdom-of-germany.re: Catholic Christianity, Lutheranism and Calvinism after 1517

kingdom-of-hawaii.t: The island kingdom united by Kamehameha I, which became an internationally recognised constitutional monarchy before American businessmen overthrew it in 1893.
kingdom-of-hawaii.o: Hawaii was divided among rival chiefdoms, including the Chiefdom of Hawaii Island, the Chiefdom of Maui and the Chiefdom of Oahu. Kamehameha, a chief from Hawaii Island armed with Western guns and advisers, conquered Maui and won the Battle of Nuʻuanu on Oahu in 1795. Kauaʻi accepted his overlordship peacefully in 1810, completing unification.
kingdom-of-hawaii.r: After Kamehameha's death the kapu system was abolished in 1819, and American Protestant missionaries arrived in 1820. Kamehameha III granted the first constitution in 1840 and the Great Māhele of 1848 created private land ownership, much of it soon held by foreigners. Sandalwood, whaling and then sugar drove the economy, and plantation labour brought Chinese, Japanese and Portuguese migrants. Honolulu became the capital in 1845.
kingdom-of-hawaii.e: Sugar planters forced the Bayonet Constitution on King Kalākaua in 1887. When Queen Liliʻuokalani sought a new constitution, a committee backed by US Marines overthrew her in January 1893 and set up the Provisional Government of Hawaii.

kamakura-shogunate.t: Japan's first warrior government, which ruled from Kamakura alongside the imperial court and twice repelled Mongol invasions.
kamakura-shogunate.o: After victory in the Genpei War, Minamoto no Yoritomo won the right in 1185 to appoint military governors (shugo) and estate stewards (jito) across Japan, creating a warrior administration based at Kamakura. The court named him shogun in 1192.
kamakura-shogunate.r: After Yoritomo's death power passed to the Hojo family, who ruled as regents (shikken) for puppet shoguns. They defeated the retired emperor Go-Toba in the Jokyu War of 1221 and issued the Goseibai shikimoku law code in 1232 for warriors. Under Hojo Tokimune the shogunate resisted Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281. New Buddhist movements of Honen, Shinran, Nichiren and Zen spread widely.
kamakura-shogunate.e: The cost of the Mongol defence left warriors unrewarded and resentful. Emperor Go-Daigo rose against the Hojo, and in 1333 Ashikaga Takauji took Kyoto while Nitta Yoshisada stormed Kamakura, ending the regime and opening the Kenmu Restoration.

kingdom-of-ulaid.t: The ancient over-kingdom of Ulster, linked in legend with Emain Macha and the Ulster Cycle, which shrank to Antrim and Down before the Anglo-Normans.
kingdom-of-ulaid.o: The Ulaid, probably Ptolemy's Voluntii, gave their name to Ulster. Irish tradition remembers them as rulers of the whole north from Emain Macha, Navan Fort near Armagh, the setting of the Ulster Cycle tales of Conchobar mac Nessa and Cú Chulainn. In the 5th century, according to tradition, the Three Collas and the Uí Néill drove them east of the River Bann.
kingdom-of-ulaid.r: In historic times the kingdom was an over-kingship shared between the Dal Fiatach of Down and the Dal nAraidi of Antrim. Kings such as Báetán mac Cairill and Congal Cáech challenged the Uí Néill, but defeat at Mag Rath in 637 ended their hopes of wider supremacy. The kingdom's monasteries, including Bangor, Movilla and Nendrum, were among the great centres of early Irish learning.
kingdom-of-ulaid.e: Viking raids and Uí Néill pressure confined the Ulaid to Antrim and Down. In 1177 John de Courcy captured Downpatrick and defeated Ruaidrí Mac Duinn Sléibe, and the Ulaid lands became the Anglo-Norman Earldom of Ulster.

kingdom-of-kartli.t: The central Georgian kingdom around Tbilisi, a Persian vassal for much of its history, which produced Georgia's first printing press and a famous law code.
kingdom-of-kartli.o: Kartli, the historic core of eastern Georgia, emerged as a separate kingdom during the break-up of the Kingdom of Georgia in the late 15th century. Constantine II, the last king to claim all Georgia, was left by about 1490 with Kartli alone, and his descendants ruled it from Tbilisi.
kingdom-of-kartli.r: Kartli lay on the front line between the Ottoman and Safavid empires and was usually a Safavid vassal; several kings, such as Rostom, converted to Islam to hold the throne. Simon I fought both empires and died an Ottoman captive. Vakhtang VI, regent and king in the early 18th century, compiled a law code, edited the Georgian chronicles and set up a printing press in Tbilisi in 1709.
kingdom-of-kartli.e: After Vakhtang VI sought Russian help and fled to Russia in 1724, the Ottomans occupied Kartli until 1735. Teimuraz II regained the throne in 1744, and on his death in 1762 his son Erekle II united Kartli with Kakheti.

kingdom-of-mercia.t: The great midland kingdom that dominated England in the 8th century under Aethelbald and Offa, whose Dyke still marks the Welsh border.
kingdom-of-mercia.o: Mercia, the 'border people', arose among Angles in the upper Trent valley. Later genealogies place its first kings, Icel and Creoda, in the 6th century, but the first well-attested ruler is the pagan Penda, who fought Northumbria and East Anglia from the 620s to his death at the Winwaed in 655.
kingdom-of-mercia.r: Mercian kings ruled from Tamworth, with a bishopric at Lichfield, and dominated client kingdoms such as the Hwicce and the Magonsaete. Offa took the title king of the English, issued a reformed silver penny, corresponded with Charlemagne and built Offa's Dyke. He briefly created an archbishopric at Lichfield.
kingdom-of-mercia.e: Defeat by Wessex at Ellendun in 825 and the Viking conquests of the 870s split Mercia. Its western half, under Aethelred and Aethelflaed, the Lady of the Mercians, allied with Wessex. After Aethelflaed's death in 918 it was absorbed into the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons.

kingdom-of-finland-1918.t: The short-lived attempt to make independent Finland a monarchy under a German prince, abandoned when Germany lost the First World War.
kingdom-of-finland-1918.o: After the civil war, conservative politicians wanted a strong monarchy tied to Germany, whose troops had helped the Whites win. On 9 October 1918 a rump parliament, without the Social Democrats, elected Prince Frederick Charles of Hesse as king of Finland. Pehr Evind Svinhufvud served as regent.
kingdom-of-finland-1918.r: The kingdom existed largely on paper. Frederick Charles never came to Finland, and no coronation took place. German influence over the army and the economy was strong, and the monarchists hoped the throne would secure German protection against Soviet Russia.
kingdom-of-finland-1918.e: Germany's defeat in November 1918 made a German king impossible. Frederick Charles renounced the throne on 14 December 1918, and Mannerheim replaced Svinhufvud as regent. The constitution of 1919 created the Republic of Finland, and the monarchy project was abandoned.

katsina-emirate.t: The emirate that replaced the Hausa kingdom of Katsina after the jihad, ruled by Fulani emirs while the old dynasty carried on at Maradi.
katsina-emirate.o: In 1807 the Fulani scholar Umaru Dallaji, a follower of Usman dan Fodio, captured Katsina from the Hausa ruler, who fled north and eventually founded the Sultanate of Maradi. Dallaji became the first emir and founded the dynasty that ruled until the colonial period.
katsina-emirate.r: Katsina had been the leading commercial and scholarly city of Hausaland, but war with Maradi and the rise of Kano drew trade away during the 19th century. The emir governed with titled officials, many offices inherited from the Katsina Kingdom, and the emirate remained a frontier power, constantly raided by the Hausa exiles to the north. Islamic scholarship continued in its mosques and schools.
katsina-emirate.e: British forces occupied Katsina in 1903. In 1906 the British deposed the emir and appointed Muhammadu Dikko, founder of the Sullubawa dynasty, which still reigns. The northern part of the old kingdom lies in Niger.

kingdom-of-ouagadougou.t: The leading Mossi kingdom, whose ruler the Mogho Naaba still holds court in the capital of Burkina Faso.
kingdom-of-ouagadougou.o: Mossi tradition credits Oubri, a grandson of Ouedraogo, with founding the kingdom of Ouagadougou around 1495 by subduing the local farming peoples of the White Volta basin. Successive rulers extended its authority, and it became the largest of the Mossi states alongside the Kingdom of Yatenga and the Kingdom of Tenkodogo.
kingdom-of-ouagadougou.r: The Mogho Naaba, 'ruler of the world', governed through ministers, provincial chiefs and a court of pages and royal servants. Mossi cavalry resisted the Mali Empire and the Songhai Empire, whose ruler Askia Muhammad attacked them in 1497. Mossi religion and earth-priests remained strong, and Islam made only limited progress before the 19th century.
kingdom-of-ouagadougou.e: In 1896 French forces took Ouagadougou, and Mogho Naaba Wobgo fled. The kingdom became part of French West Africa, and Ouagadougou the capital of French Upper Volta and later Burkina Faso. The Mogho Naaba still reigns as a respected traditional ruler.

kingdom-of-koki.t: A small kingdom west of Lake Victoria, founded by a prince of Bunyoro and absorbed into Buganda in 1896.
kingdom-of-koki.o: Tradition says Koki was founded around 1740 by Bwohe, a prince of the Kingdom of Bunyoro, who settled in the lands west of Lake Victoria in today's Rakai district. It lay between Buganda, Ankole and the Haya kingdoms.
kingdom-of-koki.r: Koki was a small farming and cattle-keeping kingdom, ruled by a king, or kamuswaga, through chiefs. From around 1800 it paid tribute to the Kingdom of Buganda while keeping its own dynasty, and it took part in the trade in ivory and iron goods around the lake.
kingdom-of-koki.e: In 1896 Koki's ruler agreed to incorporation into Buganda, and it became a county of the kingdom under the Uganda Protectorate, its ruler keeping the title kamuswaga. It remains part of the Buganda region today.

kingdom-of-raiatea.t: The sacred island kingdom of the Society Islands, home of the great marae of Taputapuatea, whose people fought French annexation until 1897.
kingdom-of-raiatea.o: Raiatea, called Havaiʻi in older traditions, was a religious and voyaging centre of eastern Polynesia, and its marae of Taputapuatea at Opoa drew chiefs from across the region. The cult of the war god ʻOro spread from there. By the 18th century the high chiefs of the Tamatoa line ruled Raiatea and neighbouring Tahaʻa, though warriors from Bora Bora conquered the island around the 1760s.
kingdom-of-raiatea.r: Kings ruled through a chiefly hierarchy, with priests of ʻOro wielding great influence. The priest-navigator Tupaia, who sailed with James Cook in 1769, came from Raiatea. Missionaries of the London Missionary Society arrived in 1818, Christianity spread quickly, and the kingdom adopted written law codes. Breadfruit, coconut and fishing sustained the islanders, and Raiatea traded with visiting ships.
kingdom-of-raiatea.e: The Jarnac Convention of 1847 between Britain and France guaranteed the independence of the Leeward Islands. France annexed Raiatea in 1888, but a resistance led by the chief Teraupoʻo lasted until 1897. The island became part of French Polynesia, and Taputapuatea is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

kingdom-of-lindsey.t: A small Anglian kingdom in north Lincolnshire centred on Roman Lincoln, briefly fought over by Northumbria and Mercia before Mercian absorption.
kingdom-of-lindsey.o: Lindsey took its name from the Roman Lindum (Lincoln), and Anglian settlers established a kingdom there in the late 5th or 6th century. A list of its kings survives in a collection of royal genealogies, tracing them to Woden, ending with Aldfrith in the late 8th century.
kingdom-of-lindsey.r: The kingdom lay between the Humber and the Witham, bounded by fen and sea, and was too small to stand alone. Paulinus preached at Lincoln around 628 under Northumbrian protection, building a stone church. A separate bishopric of Lindsey was founded in 678.
kingdom-of-lindsey.e: Northumbria and Mercia contested Lindsey until the Battle of the Trent in 679 left it permanently Mercian. Its kings faded into dependent rulers and disappeared by about 800. The district was later settled by Danes and formed part of Lincolnshire.

khandesh-sultanate.t: A small sultanate of the Tapti valley ruled by the Faruqi dynasty from Burhanpur and the great fortress of Asirgarh.
khandesh-sultanate.o: Malik Raja Faruqi, a noble granted lands in the Tapti valley by Firuz Shah Tughluq of the Delhi Sultanate, became effectively independent around 1382 as Delhi's authority collapsed. His son Nasir Khan took the fortress of Asirgarh and founded the city of Burhanpur, which became the capital of the Faruqi kingdom.
khandesh-sultanate.r: Khandesh was a buffer state between the larger Gujarat Sultanate, Malwa Sultanate and the Deccan sultanates, and its rulers survived by shifting alliances and marriages. Burhanpur grew into a busy centre of cotton textiles and trade on the route between north India and the Deccan. The Faruqis built mosques, including the Jama Masjid of Burhanpur.
khandesh-sultanate.e: Akbar of the Mughal Empire demanded submission, and when Bahadur Shah Faruqi resisted, Mughal armies besieged Asirgarh, which surrendered in 1601. Khandesh became a Mughal province, and Burhanpur served as a base for Mughal campaigns in the Deccan.

kingdom-of-paeonia.t: Ancient kingdom of the Axios (Vardar) valley north of Macedon, whose kings minted fine silver coins before falling under Macedonian control.
kingdom-of-paeonia.o: The Paeonians held the Axios and Strymon valleys from early times; Homer lists them as allies of Troy. In 511 BCE the Persian general Megabazus deported many of them to Asia. A kingdom with its own coinage emerged in the 4th century BCE, centred on Bylazora and Astibos (Štip).
kingdom-of-paeonia.r: Kings such as Lyppeios, Patraos and Audoleon issued silver coins showing Apollo and horsemen, and Audoleon was honoured at Athens. The economy rested on herding, farming and the trade route along the Axios. The Paeonians worshipped the sun and a Dionysus called Dyalos, and were famed riders. Philip II of Macedon forced them into dependency after 358 BCE, and they served in Alexander's army.
kingdom-of-paeonia.e: Celtic invasions in 279 BCE weakened the kingdom. In 217 BCE Philip V of Macedon took Bylazora, ending its independence, and after 168 BCE Paeonia became part of Roman Macedonia.

kingdom-of-hejaz.t: The Hashemite kingdom proclaimed by Sharif Hussein during the Arab Revolt, which held Mecca and Medina until conquered by Ibn Saud.
kingdom-of-hejaz.o: In June 1916 Hussein ibn Ali, head of the Sharifate of Mecca, launched the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire with British support, encouraged by the Hussein-McMahon correspondence. He proclaimed himself King of the Arab Lands; the Allies recognised him as King of the Hejaz. His sons Faisal and Abdullah led Arab forces north.
kingdom-of-hejaz.r: The kingdom controlled the Hejaz, its holy cities, the pilgrimage and the port of Jeddah, financed largely by British subsidies and pilgrim fees. Hussein refused to accept the post-war mandates in Syria, Palestine and Iraq, quarrelled with Britain and declined to sign the Treaty of Versailles. In March 1924, after Turkey abolished the caliphate, he declared himself caliph.
kingdom-of-hejaz.e: Ibn Saud's Ikhwan took Ta'if and then Mecca in late 1924. Hussein abdicated in favour of his son Ali, who surrendered Jeddah in December 1925. The Hejaz became part of the Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd, while Hussein's sons ruled the Kingdom of Iraq and the Emirate of Transjordan.

kingdom-of-kurdistan.t: A short-lived Kurdish kingdom proclaimed at Sulaymaniyah by Sheikh Mahmud Barzanji in defiance of British plans for Iraq.
kingdom-of-kurdistan.o: Sheikh Mahmud Barzanji, a Sufi leader of the Qadiri order and notable of Sulaymaniyah, was appointed governor by the British in 1918. He rebelled in 1919, was defeated and exiled to India. In 1922, with Turkish forces threatening the Mosul region, the British brought him back to restore order, and in November 1922 he proclaimed himself King of Kurdistan.
kingdom-of-kurdistan.r: The kingdom had a cabinet, issued stamps and a newspaper, and claimed authority over the Kurdish districts around Sulaymaniyah, but its administration was rudimentary and depended on tribal support. Mahmud negotiated with Turkey while the British sought to include the region in the new Iraqi state. The Royal Air Force bombed Sulaymaniyah in 1923, one of the first uses of air power to police a colonial territory.
kingdom-of-kurdistan.e: British and Iraqi forces took Sulaymaniyah in 1924, and the region was incorporated into Mandatory Iraq. Sheikh Mahmud led further revolts until 1931 and remains a symbol of Kurdish nationalism.

kingdom-of-hengshan.t: Wu Rui's kingdom in the middle Yangtze, created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, whose ruler switched to Liu Bang and became the first King of Changsha.
kingdom-of-hengshan.o: Wu Rui, a Qin magistrate of Po county who was popular with the Yue peoples, joined the rebellion against the Qin dynasty and sent troops with his son-in-law Ying Bu. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Hengshan, with his capital at Zhu near modern Huanggang in Hubei.
kingdom-of-hengshan.r: Hengshan straddled the Yangtze east of the Kingdom of Linjiang, controlling rice lands and river trade. Wu Rui's support among the Baiyue peoples of the south gave him a following beyond the Chinese population.
kingdom-of-hengshan.e: Wu Rui supported Liu Bang against Xiang Yu, and after the Han victory in 202 BCE he was moved to become King of Changsha. His family held Changsha until 157 BCE, one of the few non-Liu kingdoms to survive under the Han Dynasty.

kingdom-of-cilicia.t: Cilicia, a vassal kingdom of the Syennesis dynasty at Tarsus that kept its own kings under Persia until 401 BCE.
kingdom-of-cilicia.o: After the fall of the Assyrian Empire, local rulers in the Cilician plain and Rough Cilicia formed a kingdom with Tarsus as its capital, drawing on the lands of Que and Hilakku. Babylonian records call part of it Pirindu, and Neriglissar of the Chaldean Empire fought its king Appuashu in 557 BCE.
kingdom-of-cilicia.r: Its kings bore the title or name Syennesis. One Syennesis mediated, with a Babylonian envoy, the peace between Lydia and the Median Empire after the eclipse battle of 585 BCE. Under the Achaemenid Empire the kingdom kept its own rulers, paid tribute in silver and white horses and supplied ships to the Persian fleet.
kingdom-of-cilicia.e: In 401 BCE Syennesis and his wife Epyaxa supported Cyrus the Younger in his revolt. After its failure the Persians abolished the kingship and turned Cilicia into an ordinary satrapy.

kingdom-of-gampola.t: The Sinhalese kingdom of the central hills, under which Buddhist temple architecture flourished and the Alakeshvara family rose to power.
kingdom-of-gampola.o: Bhuvanaikabahu IV moved the royal seat from Kurunegala to Gampola, on the Mahaweli river in the central highlands, around 1341. The move followed the drift of Sinhalese power away from the northern plains after the fall of the Kingdom of Dambadeniya and the pressure of the Jaffna Kingdom.
kingdom-of-gampola.r: The Gampola kings were weak, and real power lay with ministers, above all the Alakeshvara family, who built a fortress at Kotte near Colombo and resisted Jaffna's expansion. The period produced fine Buddhist monuments, notably the Gadaladeniya and Lankatilaka temples, which blend Sinhalese and south Indian styles. Contacts with the Vijayanagara Empire increased.
kingdom-of-gampola.e: In 1411 the Chinese admiral Zheng He fought and captured the ruler Vira Alakeshvara and took him to China. Soon afterwards Parakramabahu VI took power and moved the capital to Kotte, founding the Kingdom of Kotte in 1412.

kingdom-of-castile.t: The medieval kingdom of Castile, which took Toledo, crushed the Almohads at Las Navas de Tolosa and became the dominant power of Christian Iberia.
kingdom-of-castile.o: The County of Castile had been raised to a kingdom by Ferdinand I, who also ruled the Kingdom of León. At his death in 1065 he divided his realms, leaving Castile to his eldest son Sancho II. After Sancho's murder in 1072 his brother Alfonso VI reunited Castile and León.
kingdom-of-castile.r: Castile was a frontier society of free settlers, town councils with their own fueros and mounted warriors, later organised in military orders such as Calatrava and Santiago. Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085. Alfonso VIII, defeated at Alarcos in 1195, led the coalition that destroyed the Almohad army at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. Burgos, on the pilgrim road to Santiago, prospered on trade and wool.
kingdom-of-castile.e: Castile and León were separated again from 1157, but in 1230 Ferdinand III, already king of Castile, inherited León, creating the lasting union known as the Crown of Castile, which absorbed most of al-Andalus within a generation.

karamanli-tripoli.t: The hereditary Karamanli pashas of Tripoli, a corsair dynasty best known for fighting the United States in the First Barbary War.
karamanli-tripoli.o: In 1711 Ahmed Karamanli, a cavalry officer of mixed Turkish and local descent, seized power in Tripoli, massacred his Janissary rivals and founded a dynasty. The Ottoman sultan recognised him as pasha, and Ottoman Tripolitania became a hereditary, largely autonomous state.
karamanli-tripoli.r: The Karamanli pashas lived from corsairing, tribute from European powers and the trans-Saharan trade through the Fezzan, which Yusuf Karamanli annexed in 1812. Yusuf, who ruled from 1795, declared war on the United States in 1801; the frigate Philadelphia was captured, and American forces took Derna in 1805 before a peace treaty.
karamanli-tripoli.e: After European pressure ended corsairing and tribute, debts mounted and civil war broke out in 1832. In 1835 the Ottomans sent a fleet, deposed the last Karamanli and restored direct rule as the Tripolitania Vilayet.

khanate-of-maku.t: The longest-lived of the Azerbaijani khanates: a mountain domain on the Ottoman and Russian borders whose khans kept local power until 1922.
khanate-of-maku.o: Maku, a town built under a cliff in the far north-west of Iran near Mount Ararat, came under the hereditary khans of the Turkic Bayat clan after the death of Nader Shah in 1747. Its strategic position on the routes to the Ottoman Empire and the Caucasus gave it importance beyond its size.
khanate-of-maku.r: Unlike most khanates of Azerbaijan, Maku kept its own khans under Qajar Iran, which treated them as hereditary governors of a frontier district. They controlled tribes, customs posts and border trade. In the early 20th century Morteza Qoli Khan, known as Eqbal al-Saltaneh, was one of the richest and most powerful men in north-western Iran, opposing the constitutionalists of Tabriz.
khanate-of-maku.e: After the First World War, Reza Khan's government reasserted central control, and in 1922 Eqbal al-Saltaneh lost his position; he died in detention soon after. Maku was integrated into the provincial system of Pahlavi Iran.

kingdom-of-palpa.t: A Sen hill kingdom of western Nepal ruled from Tansen, once the most powerful of the Chaubise Rajya before falling to Gorkha.
kingdom-of-palpa.o: The Sen dynasty, claiming Rajput descent, established itself in the hills of Palpa in the late 15th century; Mukunda Sen is the best-known early ruler. He is said to have campaigned as far as the Kathmandu Valley, and his realm, centred on Tansen, was later divided among his sons into Palpa, the Kingdom of Makwanpur and other states.
kingdom-of-palpa.r: Palpa was the leading state of the Chaubise Rajya, the twenty-four hill principalities of central Nepal, and controlled trade routes from the Gangetic plain into the hills. Its kings intermarried with the Gorkha and Tanahun royal families, and the town of Tansen developed Newar trading communities and temples.
kingdom-of-palpa.e: Palpa resisted the Gorkha unification for decades, relying on marriage alliances with the Gorkha court and on its hill fortresses. It was finally annexed by the Kingdom of Nepal in 1806, and its last king, Prithvipal Sen, was killed in Kathmandu.

kyrgyzstan.t: A mountainous Central Asian republic, once called an 'island of democracy', whose politics have been shaped by three popular revolutions.
kyrgyzstan.o: The Kirghiz SSR declared independence on 31 August 1991 under Askar Akayev, a physicist and reformer who had been elected president in 1990. The new state adopted a constitution in 1993 and its own currency, the som.
kyrgyzstan.r: Akayev's early liberal reforms gave way to corruption and family rule. The economy relies on the Kumtor gold mine, agriculture and remittances from migrants in Russia. Divisions between the north and the south around Osh and Jalal-Abad have shaped politics, and in 2010 ethnic violence between Kyrgyz and Uzbeks in Osh killed hundreds. Russia kept an airbase at Kant, while a US base at Manas operated until 2014.
kyrgyzstan.e: Protests overthrew Akayev in the Tulip Revolution of 2005 and his successor Kurmanbek Bakiyev in 2010, after which a parliamentary system was briefly adopted. After unrest in 2020 Sadyr Japarov became president and restored strong presidential rule by referendum in 2021.

katsina-kingdom.t: Hausa kingdom that became the leading commercial and scholarly city of Hausaland in the 17th and 18th centuries.
katsina-kingdom.o: Katsina was one of the Hausa Bakwai, the seven core Hausa states. Tradition says Korau, a wrestler and newcomer, killed Sanau, the last ruler of the earlier Durbawa line, and founded a new dynasty in the 14th century. Under Muhammadu Korau, in the late 15th century, the court adopted Islam.
katsina-kingdom.r: Katsina stood at the southern end of a major trans-Saharan route through Agadez and became a centre of trade in cloth, leather, slaves and kola, and of Islamic learning, with scholars teaching at the Gobarau mosque. It fought long wars with Kano and acknowledged at times the Kanem-Bornu Empire and the Songhai Empire.
katsina-kingdom.e: In 1807 the Fulani jihadist Umaru Dallaji captured the city, and Katsina became the Katsina Emirate within the Sokoto Caliphate. The Hausa royal family withdrew north and founded the Sultanate of Maradi, now in Niger.

kingdom-of-zamfara.t: Hausa kingdom of the north-western plains that rose to power in the 16th and 17th centuries before being destroyed by its rival Gobir.
kingdom-of-zamfara.o: Zamfara was counted among the Banza Bakwai, the 'illegitimate' Hausa states outside the core seven. Its people occupied the fertile valley of the Zamfara river west of Katsina. Tradition dates its first rulers to around 1200, though the kingdom becomes visible in records only in the 16th century.
kingdom-of-zamfara.r: From its capital at Birnin Zamfara the kingdom expanded in the 17th century, raiding as far as Kano and controlling routes between Hausaland and the Niger. Its rulers combined Islam with Hausa royal rites, and the state's power rested on cavalry and slave labour on its farms.
kingdom-of-zamfara.e: In 1762 Gobir under Babari sacked Birnin Zamfara and occupied much of its land. The surviving Zamfara state, based at Anka, was conquered in the Fulani jihad around 1808 and came under the Sokoto Caliphate. Its name lives on in Zamfara State, Nigeria.

kingdom-of-pergamon.t: Hellenistic kingdom of the Attalid dynasty in western Anatolia, a great centre of art and learning that was bequeathed to Rome in 133 BCE.
kingdom-of-pergamon.o: Philetaerus, an officer guarding Lysimachus' treasure of 9,000 talents at the citadel of Pergamon, changed sides to Seleucus I in 282 BCE and kept the fortress and money. His nephew Eumenes I asserted independence from the Seleucids. Attalus I took the title of king around 238 BCE after defeating the Galatians.
kingdom-of-pergamon.r: The Attalids built Pergamon into a showpiece capital of terraces, temples and theatre, with a library second only to Alexandria's, traditionally linked to the development of parchment. The Great Altar of Zeus celebrated victory over the Galatians. Loyal alliance with Rome brought Eumenes II wide lands in Asia Minor after the Peace of Apamea in 188 BCE.
kingdom-of-pergamon.e: Attalus III died in 133 BCE leaving his kingdom to Rome. Aristonicus, claiming to be a royal son, led a revolt that was crushed by 129 BCE, and the kingdom became the Roman province of Asia. The Pergamon Altar is now in Berlin.

kingdom-of-italy-napoleonic.t: Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy, ruled from Milan by his stepson Eugène de Beauharnais, which gave northern Italians a modern state and a common army.
kingdom-of-italy-napoleonic.o: When Napoleon became emperor of the French, the Italian Republic (1802–1805) was turned into a kingdom. On 26 May 1805 Napoleon crowned himself king of Italy in Milan Cathedral with the Iron Crown of Lombardy, and appointed his stepson Eugène de Beauharnais as viceroy.
kingdom-of-italy-napoleonic.r: The kingdom grew to include Venetia in 1806, the Marche in 1808 and South Tyrol in 1810, and for a time Istria and Dalmatia, which passed to the Illyrian Provinces in 1809. It had departments and prefects on the French model, the Napoleonic Code, public schools and an efficient tax system. Its conscript army fought in Spain and Russia, where tens of thousands died in 1812.
kingdom-of-italy-napoleonic.e: After Napoleon's defeats, Eugène signed an armistice in April 1814. A riot in Milan killed the finance minister Giuseppe Prina, and Austrian troops took over; the territory became the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia and other restored states.

kingdom-of-main.t: The Minaean kingdom of al-Jawf, whose merchants ran the incense trade from Yemen to Egypt and even the Greek island of Delos.
kingdom-of-main.o: Ma'in arose in the al-Jawf valley north of Marib, in a region of city-states once subject to the Kingdom of Saba. By the 6th or 5th century BCE it was independent, its kings ruling from Qarnawu with Yathill (Baraqish) as a second major city.
kingdom-of-main.r: Ma'in was above all a trading state. Minaean merchants organised incense caravans to Gaza and Egypt, kept a colony at Dedan in the Hejaz, and left inscriptions as far away as Delos. Inscriptions list Minaean men marrying foreign wives from Gaza and Egypt. The main god was Wadd, and the kings governed with councils drawn from leading families. The language was Minaic.
kingdom-of-main.e: Ma'in depended on caravan trade and lost importance as Ptolemaic and Roman shipping in the Red Sea grew. Around 100 BCE it was absorbed by the Kingdom of Saba. The walls of Baraqish still stand in al-Jawf.

kingdom-of-gyaman.t: An Abron kingdom around the Muslim trading town of Bondoukou, long a reluctant tributary of the Ashanti Empire on the border of modern Ghana and Ivory Coast.
kingdom-of-gyaman.o: Gyaman was founded in the late 17th century by Abron (Bono) migrants under their leader Tan Date, who moved west from the Bono area to escape the rising power of the Ashanti Empire. They settled around Bondoukou, an old town of Dyula Muslim traders on the route between the goldfields and the middle Niger, and ruled the local peoples.
kingdom-of-gyaman.r: Abron kings, chosen from a royal matrilineage on the Akan model, held court at sites near Bondoukou, while Dyula scholars and merchants ran the trade in gold, kola and cloth. Asante armies conquered Gyaman around 1740 and imposed tribute. King Kofi Adinkra revolted and was killed in 1818; Akan tradition links the adinkra cloth symbols to his name.
kingdom-of-gyaman.e: Gyaman regained autonomy after Ashanti defeats in the 1870s, but in the 1890s Britain and France divided it, and Samori Toure occupied it in 1895-1897. Its western part went to the French Ivory Coast and the east to the Gold Coast.
kingdom-of-gyaman.re: Akan traditional religion, Sunni Islam among traders

khasa-malla-kingdom.t: A Himalayan kingdom of the Khasa people that ruled western Nepal and parts of western Tibet from Sinja, with a court that patronised both Buddhism and Hinduism.
khasa-malla-kingdom.o: The Khasa Mallas emerged in the Karnali basin of western Nepal around the 12th century. Under Nagaraja they made Sinja, in the Jumla valley, their capital and expanded north into the Guge and Purang regions of western Tibet and south and east across the western Himalayan foothills.
khasa-malla-kingdom.r: Inscriptions and stone pillars, some in early Nepali written in Devanagari, record the kings and their donations. Ripumalla and Prithvimalla, among the most powerful rulers, left inscriptions at Lumbini and elsewhere. The court supported Buddhist monasteries in Tibet and Hindu shrines in Nepal, and the kingdom grew rich on trans-Himalayan trade in salt, wool and grain. The Dullu inscription of Prithvimalla is a key source for its history.
khasa-malla-kingdom.e: By the late 14th century the kingdom fragmented into small principalities later known as the Baise Rajya, the twenty-two kingdoms of the Karnali region, among them the Kingdom of Jumla and the Kingdom of Doti. The language of its inscriptions is an ancestor of modern Nepali.

kingdom-of-saba.t: Biblical Sheba: the incense kingdom of Marib whose great dam, temples and caravans made it the leading power of ancient south Arabia.
kingdom-of-saba.o: Sabaean inscriptions begin around the 8th century BCE, when rulers titled mukarrib governed from Marib in the Yemeni desert margin. The early Marib Dam captured seasonal floods to irrigate two vast oases. In the 7th century BCE Karib'il Watar conquered the Kingdom of Awsan and imposed Sabaean supremacy over much of south-western Arabia.
kingdom-of-saba.r: Saba grew rich on frankincense and myrrh carried north along the caravan routes to Gaza and Mesopotamia. Society was organised in tribes and communes bound to the king; the national god Almaqah was worshipped at the Awwam temple near Marib. Sabaic, written in the Ancient South Arabian script, became the region's prestige language. Its fame gave rise to the story of the Queen of Sheba.
kingdom-of-saba.e: From the 1st century BCE Saba lost ground as sea trade bypassed the caravans and the Himyarite Kingdom rose in the highlands. After centuries of rivalry, Shammar Yahrish of Himyar absorbed Saba around 275 CE, keeping the title King of Saba and Dhu Raydan. The Marib Dam finally failed in the 6th century.

kingdom-of-mataram-lombok.t: Balinese Hindu kingdom that ruled the Muslim Sasak people of Lombok until the bloody Dutch intervention of 1894.
kingdom-of-mataram-lombok.o: Princes from the Kingdom of Karangasem had established Balinese rule in western Lombok by the late 17th century, displacing Makassarese influence. Several rival Balinese courts emerged on the island, and around 1740 Mataram became the leading one; in 1838 to 1839 it defeated its rivals, uniting Lombok under a single Balinese dynasty based at Mataram and Cakranegara.
kingdom-of-mataram-lombok.r: A Hindu Balinese elite ruled a majority of Muslim Sasak farmers, taxing their rice and controlling their aristocrats. The kingdom grew rich exporting rice and became powerful enough to rule Karangasem on Bali after 1849. Its kings built the Pura Meru temple and the Mayura water palace in Cakranegara.
kingdom-of-mataram-lombok.e: Sasak nobles rebelled and appealed to the Dutch, who sent an expedition in 1894. After a surprise night attack destroyed part of the Dutch force, reinforcements stormed Cakranegara, and the royal family died in a puputan. The Lombok Treasure was taken to the Netherlands, and the island joined the Dutch East Indies.

kingdom-of-munster.t: Southern Irish over-kingdom ruled from the Rock of Cashel by the Eóganachta and later by the Dál Cais of Brian Bóruma, until it split in two in 1118.
kingdom-of-munster.o: Munster, Mumu in Irish, was one of the ancient provinces of Ireland. From around the 5th century the Eóganachta dynasties, tracing descent from Conall Corc, the legendary founder of Cashel, established an over-kingship over the province, displacing earlier Érainn peoples such as the Corcu Loigde.
kingdom-of-munster.r: Kings ruled from Cashel through a confederation of Eóganacht branches, collecting tribute from many subject peoples. Several were also churchmen or patrons of learning, such as Feidlimid mac Crimthainn, king and abbot, who died in 847. Cathal mac Finguine, who died in 742, challenged the Uí Néill for supremacy. In the 10th century the Dál Cais of Thomond took the kingship, and Brian Bóruma, king of Munster from 978, became High King of Ireland in 1002.
kingdom-of-munster.e: In 1101 Muirchertach Ua Briain gave the Rock of Cashel to the Church. In 1118 Toirdelbach Ua Conchobair of the Kingdom of Connacht divided Munster by the Treaty of Glanmire into Desmond, under the MacCarthys, and Thomond, under the O'Briens.

kingdom-of-manyika.t: A Shona kingdom of the eastern highlands, ruled by the Mutasa, whose goldfields drew Portuguese traders and later British and Portuguese rivals.
kingdom-of-manyika.o: Manyika emerged around 1490 in the highlands that now straddle the Zimbabwe–Mozambique border, as a tributary state on the edge of the Mutapa realm. Its rulers, who bore the title Mutasa, soon became effectively independent, controlling the alluvial gold of the region and the routes to the coast.
kingdom-of-manyika.r: The Mutasa ruled through a network of chiefs and kin, and rainmaking and ancestral spirit mediums supported royal authority. Gold was traded at Portuguese fairs such as Masekesa, and the kingdom was a frequent target of Portuguese, Barwe and Uteve ambitions. In the 19th century it suffered raids from the Gaza Nguni.
kingdom-of-manyika.e: In 1890 Mutasa signed an agreement with the British South Africa Company, which clashed with the Portuguese claim. Fighting at Macequece in 1891 and the Anglo-Portuguese treaty that year split Manyika between Southern Rhodesia and Portuguese Mozambique. Manyika remains a Shona dialect and regional identity.

kummuh.t: Kummuh, a Neo-Hittite kingdom on the upper Euphrates around Samosata, forerunner of later Commagene.
kummuh.o: Kummuh arose after the Hittite collapse c. 1180 BCE in the land on the right bank of the upper Euphrates around Samosata, modern Samsat. Assyrian texts mention it from the time of Tiglath-Pileser I, c. 1100 BCE, when it was a target of raids.
kummuh.r: Its kings ruled a farming land of river valleys and wrote inscriptions in Luwian hieroglyphs. Placed between the Assyrian Empire and the Kingdom of Urartu, they usually paid tribute to Assyria; Kushtashpi joined an Urartian alliance against Tiglath-Pileser III and then submitted again.
kummuh.e: In 708 BCE Sargon II deposed King Muwatalli for conspiring with Urartu, deported its people and made Kummuh an Assyrian province. The name survived as Commagene, later the Kingdom of Commagene.

kingdom-of-mysore-1399-1799.t: The south Indian kingdom of the Wodeyars that became a formidable military power under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan.
kingdom-of-mysore-1399-1799.o: According to tradition Yaduraya founded the Wodeyar line at Mysore in 1399. The kingdom was a small vassal of the Vijayanagara Empire until Raja Wodeyar I seized Srirangapatna in 1610 after Vijayanagara's decline, making it his capital and the base of an expanding state in southern Karnataka.
kingdom-of-mysore-1399-1799.r: Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar built a centralised administration with regular revenue departments in the late 17th century. From 1761 the commander Hyder Ali took real power, and his son Tipu Sultan ruled as sultan from 1782. They built a modern army with French help, used iron-cased rockets, promoted sericulture and trade, and fought four wars against the British East India Company.
kingdom-of-mysore-1399-1799.e: Tipu Sultan was killed when British forces stormed Srirangapatna in 1799, ending the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War. The British restored a child Wodeyar, Krishnaraja Wodeyar III, as ruler of a reduced princely state of Mysore, which joined the Dominion of India in 1947.
kingdom-of-mysore-1399-1799.re: Hinduism; Islam under Hyder Ali and Tipu
