koga-kubo.t: A branch of the Ashikaga that ruled from Koga in the Kanto for over a century, fighting the Uesugi and later becoming clients of the Later Hojo.
koga-kubo.o: Ashikaga Shigeuji, the restored Kamakura kubo, killed the Kanto deputy Uesugi Noritada in 1454, starting the long Kyotoku War. In 1455 he lost Kamakura and moved his base to Koga in Shimousa province, from which his line took its name. The shogun sent a rival, Ashikaga Masatomo, who became the Horigoe kubo.
koga-kubo.r: The Koga kubo claimed authority over the eastern provinces and relied on alliances with local warrior families of the northern and eastern Kanto. Shigeuji fought the Uesugi for nearly thirty years. Later kubo, Masauji, Takamoto and Haruuji, were drawn into family feuds and the rise of the Later Hojo, who married into the line and controlled it.
koga-kubo.e: The last kubo, Ashikaga Yoshiuji, was a Hojo puppet; on his death in 1583 the line ended. Toyotomi Hideyoshi later gave his daughter's family a small estate as the Kitsuregawa.

kingdom-of-isandra.t: A Betsileo kingdom of the southern Malagasy highlands, a strong regional power before its absorption by the Merina early in the 19th century.
kingdom-of-isandra.o: Isandra emerged in the 18th century as one of the four main Betsileo kingdoms of the southern highlands of Madagascar, west of the Kingdom of Lalangina. Its dynasty, like other Betsileo houses, claimed descent from noble immigrants, and much of its history survives only in oral tradition.
kingdom-of-isandra.r: Isandra's kings ruled through local lords over rice-farming communities in highland valleys and drew prestige from ancestral tombs and royal rituals. The kingdom was considered among the strongest of the Betsileo states and fought its neighbours for land, cattle and captives.
kingdom-of-isandra.e: Around 1811 the Merina Kingdom absorbed Isandra together with the other Betsileo kingdoms, partly through alliances with local nobles. Its territory became part of the Merina province of Betsileo.

kingdom-of-burundi.t: A Great Lakes kingdom ruled by the Ganwa princes for nearly three centuries, which reached independence as a monarchy before being overthrown in 1966.
kingdom-of-burundi.o: Tradition names Ntare I Rushatsi as founder of Burundi's royal line in the late 17th century, uniting chiefdoms in the hills east of Lake Tanganyika. The kingdom expanded greatly under Ntare IV Rugamba in the early 19th century, absorbing parts of the Kingdom of Bugesera and other neighbours.
kingdom-of-burundi.r: The mwami (king) was a sacred ruler, but much power lay with the ganwa, princes of royal blood who governed provinces and often fought each other. Society included Hutu farmers, Tutsi herders and Twa, with royal rituals such as the annual muganuro sorghum festival. Mwezi IV Gisabo resisted German forces until the Treaty of Kiganda in 1903.
kingdom-of-burundi.e: Burundi became part of German East Africa and then Belgian Ruanda-Urundi. It gained independence in 1962 as a kingdom under Mwambutsa IV, but political violence followed, and in 1966 Michel Micombero deposed Ntare V and proclaimed the Republic of Burundi.

kingdom-of-leinster.t: Province-kingdom of south-east Ireland, whose exiled king Diarmait Mac Murchada invited the Anglo-Normans in and so opened eight centuries of English involvement.
kingdom-of-leinster.o: The Laigin, the people of Leinster, appear in the earliest Irish traditions as a major power whose kings once held the midlands and Tara. From the 5th century the rising Uí Néill drove them south, and Leinster settled into an over-kingdom covering most of the south-east, contested between dynasties such as the Uí Dúnlainge in the north and the Ui Chennselaig in the south.
kingdom-of-leinster.r: Kings ruled through tribute and alliances with subject peoples, and great monasteries such as Kildare, Glendalough and Ferns flourished. Brandub mac Echach defeated the high king at Dún Bolg in 598. Viking Dublin lay within Leinster, and from the 11th century its kings sought to control it; Diarmait mac Máel na mBó, who died in 1072, ruled Dublin and nearly became high king.
kingdom-of-leinster.e: In 1166 Diarmait Mac Murchada was expelled and sought help from Henry II. Anglo-Norman knights led by Strongbow, who married Diarmait's daughter Aoife, took Wexford, Waterford and Dublin. On Diarmait's death in 1171 Strongbow claimed Leinster, and Henry II's arrival brought it under the English crown.

kingdom-of-kanongesha.t: The Ndembu Lunda chiefdom of the upper Zambezi watershed, an outpost of Lunda kingship later made famous by anthropological studies of its rituals.
kingdom-of-kanongesha.o: The Kanongesha title was established in the 18th century by Lunda nobles who moved south-west from the court of the Lunda Empire into the headwaters of the Zambezi and Kabompo rivers. They settled among local peoples who became known as the Ndembu or Southern Lunda.
kingdom-of-kanongesha.r: The Kanongesha held senior rank over Ndembu sub-chiefs, but his power was limited and largely ritual, rooted in Lunda titles, perpetual kinship between offices, and ties to the Mwata Yamvo. Villages farmed cassava and hunted, and in the 19th century the area supplied slaves, ivory and beeswax to Ovimbundu and Chokwe traders.
kingdom-of-kanongesha.e: Colonial boundaries drawn in the early 20th century divided the Ndembu between Northern Rhodesia, Portuguese Angola and the Belgian Congo. The chieftaincy continues in Zambia, and Victor Turner's studies of Ndembu ritual in the 1950s made it well known.

kuwana-domain.t: A domain on the Tokaido road in Ise, guarding the sea crossing to Atsuta, whose last lord fought to the end for the shogunate.
kuwana-domain.o: After Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu gave Kuwana to his famous general Honda Tadakatsu in 1601 with 100,000 koku. Tadakatsu rebuilt the castle and laid out the town at the mouth of the Ibi and Kiso rivers.
kuwana-domain.r: Kuwana was the landing point of the Shichiri no watashi, the ferry across Ise Bay on the Tokaido, making it a busy post town. The domain was held by trusted Tokugawa vassal and related families, which were moved in and out; from 1823 it was ruled by the Hisamatsu-Matsudaira. Its last lord, Matsudaira Sadaaki, served as Kyoto deputy alongside his brother Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu.
kuwana-domain.e: Kuwana troops fought at Toba-Fushimi in 1868, and Sadaaki continued the struggle in the north and Hakodate while the domain surrendered. After abolition in 1871 it became part of Mie Prefecture.

korea-under-japanese-rule.t: Korea's thirty-five years as a Japanese colony, a period of harsh rule, forced assimilation and uneven modernisation that still shapes relations in East Asia.
korea-under-japanese-rule.o: After making the Korean Empire a protectorate in 1905, Japan formally annexed Korea by treaty in August 1910. A Government-General headed by a governor-general, always a senior army or navy officer, was established at Keijo, the Japanese name for Seoul.
korea-under-japanese-rule.r: Early rule relied on military police; a land survey transferred much land to the colonial state and Japanese companies. The nationwide March First Movement of 1919 was suppressed, but Governor-General Saito Makoto then allowed limited press and associations. Railways, ports and northern heavy industry grew to serve Japan. From the late 1930s Koreans were forced to worship at Shinto shrines and adopt Japanese names, and many were conscripted for labour, military service and sexual slavery.
korea-under-japanese-rule.e: Japan's surrender on 15 August 1945 ended colonial rule. Korea was divided at the 38th parallel between Soviet and American occupation, leading to two Korean states in 1948.

kashmir-sultanate.t: The Muslim sultanate of the Kashmir valley founded by Shah Mir, under which the region became predominantly Muslim.
kashmir-sultanate.o: Shah Mir, a migrant from the north-west, rose to prominence at the court of the last Hindu rulers of Kashmir. After the death of Queen Kota Rani, he seized the throne in 1339, taking the title Shams al-Din, and founded the Shah Mir dynasty at Srinagar.
kashmir-sultanate.r: Under the Shah Miris Islam spread widely, encouraged by Sufi missionaries such as Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani, who brought Persian crafts including shawl-weaving and papier-mache. Sultan Sikandar is remembered for destroying temples, while Zain al-Abidin, known as Budshah, the great king, restored tolerance, recalled Hindu Pandits, had Sanskrit works translated into Persian and built canals and bridges.
kashmir-sultanate.e: After Zain al-Abidin the dynasty declined amid noble factions. The Mughal commander Mirza Haidar Dughlat ruled Kashmir from 1540 to 1551, and in 1561 the Chak dynasty took the throne, ending Shah Mir rule. The Mughal Empire annexed Kashmir in 1586.

kingdom-of-aboh.t: An Igbo river kingdom near the head of the Niger Delta whose canoe fleets controlled trade on the lower Niger in the era of palm oil.
kingdom-of-aboh.o: Aboh was founded, according to tradition, in the 17th or early 18th century by migrants from the area of the Benin Empire, who settled at the point where the Niger divides into the creeks of the delta. Ruled by an Obi in a style influenced by Benin, it grew into the strongest power on the lower river.
kingdom-of-aboh.r: The Obi ruled with titled chiefs, and the kingdom commanded fleets of large war and trading canoes. Aboh was a middleman between the hinterland and the coastal states such as the Bonny Kingdom, carrying slaves and later palm oil downstream. Obi Ossai received the explorers Richard and John Lander in 1830 and negotiated with the British Niger Expedition of 1841.
kingdom-of-aboh.e: British and company steamers in the late 19th century broke the river middlemen, and the Royal Niger Company dominated trade. Aboh was absorbed into the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria by 1900, and the Obi of Aboh continues as a traditional ruler in Delta State.

kingdom-of-kangaba.t: The small Mandinka kingdom on the upper Niger from which Sundiata Keita built the Mali Empire.
kingdom-of-kangaba.o: Kangaba was one of several Malinke chiefdoms of the Manden, the upland country along the upper Niger near today's border of Mali and Guinea. By the 11th century the Keita clan ruled there, and it lay within the orbit of the Ghana Empire, supplying gold from the nearby Bure fields.
kingdom-of-kangaba.r: Its kings were hunters' and warriors' chiefs with a council of clan heads, and griots kept their genealogies. Tradition names Maghan Kon Fatta as the father of Sundiata. Around 1200 the Manden fell under the Sosso kingdom of Sumanguru Kante, who killed or scattered the Keita princes.
kingdom-of-kangaba.e: Sundiata Keita returned from exile, united the Mande clans and defeated Sumanguru at Kirina around 1235, founding the Mali Empire. Kangaba remained the Keita heartland, and its Kamabolon sanctuary is still re-roofed every seven years in a ceremony recognised by UNESCO.

kingdom-of-vaspurakan.t: An Armenian kingdom around Lake Van ruled by the Artsruni dynasty, best known for the sculpted Church of the Holy Cross on Aghtamar island.
kingdom-of-vaspurakan.o: The Artsruni family had long held the lands south and east of Lake Van. In 908 the Sajid emir Yusuf crowned Gagik Artsruni king as a rival to Smbat I of Bagratid Armenia, creating a separate kingdom under Sajid Emirate overlordship.
kingdom-of-vaspurakan.r: Gagik I built a palace and the Church of the Holy Cross on Aghtamar island between 915 and 921, its walls carved with biblical scenes, vines and royal portraits. The kingdom was rich in farmland, fish and trade, and kept a lively literary culture; the History of the House of Artsruni was written there. Its kings alternated between rivalry and alliance with the Bagratids.
kingdom-of-vaspurakan.e: Facing Seljuk raids, King Senekerim-Hovhannes ceded Vaspurakan to the Byzantine Empire in 1021 in exchange for estates around Sebasteia, and many Armenians followed him west. The Aghtamar church survives, restored in 2007, as the kingdom's most celebrated monument.

kenya-colony.t: The British settler colony in Kenya, shaped by land alienation in the White Highlands and shaken by the Mau Mau uprising.
kenya-colony.o: In 1920 Britain annexed the interior of the East Africa Protectorate as Kenya Colony, while the coastal strip, still nominally under the Sultanate of Zanzibar, became the Kenya Protectorate. Annexation gave the white settler community, concentrated in the central highlands, more political weight. Nairobi remained the capital.
kenya-colony.r: Europeans held the best farmland and dominated the legislative council, while Africans faced taxes, pass laws and restrictions on growing coffee. Indians campaigned for equal rights. African political protest began with Harry Thuku in 1921 and grew through Kikuyu associations. The Mau Mau uprising from 1952 led to a state of emergency under Governor Evelyn Baring and mass detention.
kenya-colony.e: The emergency ended in 1960, and the Lancaster House conferences opened the way to majority rule. Kenya became independent on 12 December 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta, who had been imprisoned during the emergency.

kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.t: The kingdom of Provence founded by Boso in 879, the first realm in the Carolingian West to elect a king from outside the Carolingian family.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.o: In 879, after the death of Louis the Stammerer, bishops and nobles meeting at Mantaille elected Boso, a brother-in-law of Charles the Bald, as king of the lands around Vienne, Lyon and Provence. The Carolingian kings besieged Vienne in 880–882, but Boso's family kept control of the Rhône valley.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.r: The kingdom was a loose union of counties along the Rhône and in Provence, governed from Vienne with strong support from the bishops. Boso's son Louis the Blind was crowned emperor in Rome in 901 but was captured and blinded by Berengar of Italy in 905. Afterwards real power lay with his kinsman Hugh of Arles.
kingdom-of-lower-burgundy.e: Hugh of Arles, busy with his ambitions as king of Italy, gave up his claims to Rudolf II of Upper Burgundy around 933. The two Burgundian kingdoms were then united as the Kingdom of Arles, which later passed to the Holy Roman Empire.

kingdom-of-awsan.t: A short-lived south Arabian kingdom in Wadi Markha whose power over the coast was broken by Saba in the 7th century BCE.
kingdom-of-awsan.o: Awsan lay in Wadi Markha, south-west of the incense valleys, with its capital at Hagar Yahirr. Known mainly from Sabaean inscriptions, it seems to have risen in the 8th century BCE and controlled territory towards the Gulf of Aden coast and its harbours.
kingdom-of-awsan.r: Very little is known of its internal life. Its wealth probably came from coastal trade and the routes linking the Arabian Sea with the inland incense kingdoms. Later Awsanite inscriptions show kings who were honoured as gods after death, an unusual practice in south Arabia.
kingdom-of-awsan.e: The Sabaean ruler Karib'il Watar destroyed Awsan in the 7th century BCE, according to his great inscription at Sirwah, killing thousands and handing its lands to the Kingdom of Saba and its allies. A smaller Awsan reappeared later, and the Greek name of the Ausanitic coast of East Africa recalls it.

kalachuris-of-kalyani.t: A short-lived dynasty that seized the Western Chalukya capital of Kalyani, remembered for the rise of the Lingayat movement under Basava.
kalachuris-of-kalyani.o: The Kalachuris were feudatories of the Chalukyas of Kalyani holding territory in the northern Deccan. As Chalukya power weakened, their chief Bijjala II, a commander and minister of the Chalukya king Taila III, took control of the capital Kalyani around 1156 and by 1162 proclaimed himself emperor.
kalachuris-of-kalyani.r: The dynasty ruled much of the former Chalukya realm in northern Karnataka. Its reign coincided with the career of Basava, a minister at Bijjala's court, who led the Virashaiva or Lingayat reform movement, rejecting caste hierarchy and temple ritual and promoting vachana poetry in Kannada. Tensions between the movement and orthodox society led to unrest in Kalyani.
kalachuris-of-kalyani.e: Bijjala was killed around 1167, and his sons ruled weakly amid revolts. In 1184 the Chalukya prince Someshvara IV recovered Kalyani, ending Kalachuri rule. The region soon passed to the Hoysalas and the Seuna Yadava dynasty, while the Lingayat tradition endured.

kingdom-of-tahiti.t: A Polynesian kingdom built by the Pōmare dynasty with European guns and missionary support, which became a French protectorate and then a colony.
kingdom-of-tahiti.o: Tahiti was divided among rival chiefdoms when European ships arrived from 1767. The chief Tu, later Pōmare I, used muskets obtained from visiting ships and the services of Bounty mutineers to dominate the island from about 1788. His son Pōmare II, after defeat and exile on Moorea, won the Battle of Fei Pi in 1815 and secured rule over Tahiti.
kingdom-of-tahiti.r: Pōmare II converted to Christianity under the London Missionary Society and issued a written legal code in 1819. Protestant missionaries shaped law, schooling and the use of written Tahitian. The kingdom traded pork, coconut oil and pearl shell. Under Queen Pōmare IV, who reigned for fifty years, conflict between British Protestant missionaries and French Catholic priests drew France in.
kingdom-of-tahiti.e: In 1842 Admiral Dupetit-Thouars imposed a French protectorate, and the Franco-Tahitian War followed from 1844 to 1847. The protectorate was administered within the French Establishments in Oceania, and in 1880 Pōmare V ceded the kingdom to France.

kingdom-of-romania.t: Romanian monarchy that doubled its territory after the First World War as Greater Romania, then fell to dictatorship, war and a communist takeover.
kingdom-of-romania.o: Romania won independence at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, and in 1881 Prince Carol of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was crowned king. The kingdom inherited the constitution of 1866 and the territory of the United Principalities, with Northern Dobruja added in 1878. It gained Southern Dobruja from Bulgaria in the Second Balkan War of 1913.
kingdom-of-romania.r: Before 1914 Romania was a constitutional monarchy run by landowners, exporting grain and oil from Ploiești, and a great peasant revolt in 1907 was harshly put down. In 1918 Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transylvania joined, creating Greater Romania. Land reform and the 1923 constitution followed, but the interwar years saw the fascist Iron Guard and Carol II's royal dictatorship from 1938.
kingdom-of-romania.e: In 1940 Romania lost Bessarabia and northern Bukovina to the Soviet Union and northern Transylvania to Hungary. Ion Antonescu led it into war as an Axis ally until King Michael's coup of August 1944. Under Soviet pressure the communists took power, and Michael was forced to abdicate on 30 December 1947.

khamag-mongol.t: The 12th-century confederation of Mongol clans in the Onon and Kherlen valleys, out of which Temüjin built the Mongol Empire.
khamag-mongol.o: Mongol clans of the Onon and Kherlen river valleys in north-eastern Mongolia united in the early 12th century under Khabul Khan, an ancestor of Genghis Khan, who is said to have defied the Jin dynasty (1115-1234). The name means 'All the Mongols'.
khamag-mongol.r: The confederation was a loose alliance of Borjigin, Tayichiud and other clans, choosing khans at assemblies. Its second khan, Ambaghai, was handed over by the Tatars to the Jin and executed; his successor Hotula Khan fought the Tatars, but after him the khanship lapsed and clans feuded, as with Yesügei, father of Temüjin, and the Tayichiud.
khamag-mongol.e: Temüjin gathered followers in the 1180s and was acclaimed khan of the Mongols, then defeated the Tatars, Keraites and Naimans. In 1206 an assembly on the Onon proclaimed him Genghis Khan, turning the confederation into the Mongol Empire.

koya-temne-kingdom.t: Temne kingdom of the Sierra Leone peninsula whose rulers granted the land on which the Freetown settlement was founded.
koya-temne-kingdom.o: The Temne kingdom of Koya lay on the north and south shores of the Sierra Leone estuary. It took shape by the early 17th century, when Temne groups extended their rule over the peninsula, and Portuguese and later English traders bought slaves and timber from its chiefs.
koya-temne-kingdom.r: Koya's king, the Bai, was installed by the Poro society and senior chiefs, and ruled with subordinate headmen such as King Tom on the peninsula. In 1787 King Tom and King Naimbana granted land to British abolitionists for the Province of Freedom, which grew into Freetown, though disputes over the terms led to conflict.
koya-temne-kingdom.e: Koya steadily lost land to the Sierra Leone Colony and Protectorate, which annexed parts of it in the 19th century and declared a protectorate over the interior in 1896. The Hut Tax War of 1898 followed. Koya is now a chiefdom in Sierra Leone.

kingdom-of-bunyoro.t: Once the dominant power of the Great Lakes, Bunyoro-Kitara resisted British conquest under King Kabalega and survives as a cultural kingdom.
kingdom-of-bunyoro.o: Around 1500 Luo-speaking Babito rulers from the north established a dynasty over the lands of the earlier Empire of Kitara in western Uganda. Their kingdom claimed Kitara's heritage and in the 16th and 17th centuries raided and dominated neighbours, including Buganda, Ankole and Rwanda.
kingdom-of-bunyoro.r: The omukama (king) ruled through chiefs and a court that kept regalia and rituals inherited from the Chwezi tradition. Its wealth came from cattle, iron working and the salt of Kibiro on Lake Albert. From the 18th century it lost ground to Buganda and the Kingdom of Toro broke away. Omukama Kabalega (r. 1870 to 1899) rebuilt the army with firearms.
kingdom-of-bunyoro.e: Kabalega fought the British and their Ganda allies until his capture in 1899. Bunyoro was absorbed into the Uganda Protectorate and lost its 'lost counties' to Buganda, an issue settled by a 1964 referendum. The monarchy was abolished in 1967 and restored as a cultural institution in 1993.

kalhora-dynasty.t: A Sindhi dynasty of Sufi descent that ruled the Indus valley in the 18th century and dug many of Sindh's irrigation canals.
kalhora-dynasty.o: The Kalhoras were a family of hereditary Sufi leaders in northern Sindh whose followers formed an armed movement. Mian Yar Muhammad Kalhoro was recognised by the Mughal Empire as governor of parts of Sindh around 1701, and his successors extended their rule over the whole of the lower Indus valley.
kalhora-dynasty.r: Mian Nur Muhammad Kalhoro, the most powerful ruler, governed Sindh as a vassal of Nadir Shah of Persia and later of the Durrani Empire, paying heavy tribute. The Kalhoras built canals and founded towns, including Khudabad and Hyderabad. The great Sindhi Sufi poet Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai lived under their rule.
kalhora-dynasty.e: Rivalry between the Kalhora rulers and their Baloch Talpur commanders led to civil war after a Talpur leader was murdered. The Talpurs defeated the last Kalhora ruler, Abdul Nabi, at the Battle of Halani in 1783 and founded the Talpur dynasty.

kingdom-of-the-aures.t: A Berber mountain kingdom in the Aurès that defied Vandals and Byzantines and ended with Queen Dihya's resistance to the Arabs.
kingdom-of-the-aures.o: The Berbers of the Aurès mountains broke away from the Vandal Kingdom around 484. An inscription at Arris records a ruler, Masties, who called himself duke for 67 years and emperor for ten, and claimed never to have broken faith with either Romans or Moors.
kingdom-of-the-aures.r: The kingdom drew on Roman titles and Christian faith while resting on Berber clans of the mountains. In the 530s Iaudas (Iabdas) raided Byzantine Numidia and resisted the general Solomon, who finally stormed his strongholds in 539. Little is known of the following century. In the 690s the Jerawa tribal leader Dihya, called al-Kahina by Arab writers, led Berber resistance and defeated Hassan ibn al-Numan.
kingdom-of-the-aures.e: Hassan returned, and Dihya was killed around 701 to 703. The Umayyad Caliphate absorbed the region, and many of her followers converted to Islam and joined the Arab armies. Dihya became a lasting symbol of Berber resistance.

kuba-kingdom.t: A Bushong-led kingdom of the Kasai, famous for its royal portrait statues, raffia velvet textiles and long oral history of kings.
kuba-kingdom.o: Bushong tradition credits Shyaam a Mbul a Ngoong with founding the kingdom around 1625, uniting chiefdoms between the Kasai and Sankuru rivers. He is remembered as a culture hero who brought new crops, including maize, tobacco and cassava, from the west, together with new political institutions.
kuba-kingdom.r: The king (nyimi) ruled from the capital Nsheng with an elaborate council of titled officials, and the court sponsored an exceptional art tradition: wooden ndop statues commemorating each king, carved cups, masks and embroidered raffia cloth. Agriculture and trade in raffia and camwood supported dense villages. Kuba oral history was studied in detail by the historian Jan Vansina.
kuba-kingdom.e: In 1899 Zappo Zap raiders working for the Congo Free State sacked Nsheng, and Belgian administration followed, though the kingship continued under colonial rule. The Kuba remain known worldwide for their art, and the nyimi is still a traditional ruler in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

karnat-dynasty.t: A dynasty of Karnataka origin that ruled Mithila from Simraungadh for two centuries and briefly held the Kathmandu Valley.
karnat-dynasty.o: Nanyadeva, a chief of Karnata descent who probably came north with the armies of the Chalukyas of Kalyani, established himself in the Tirhut plain around 1097. He made Simraungadh, near the modern India and Nepal border, his capital and ruled the region of Mithila between the Ganges and the Himalayan foothills.
karnat-dynasty.r: The Karnat court was a centre of Sanskrit and Maithili learning. Harisimhadeva, the last king, sponsored the codification of Maithil Brahmin genealogies (the panji system) and his minister Jyotirishvara wrote the Varna Ratnakara, one of the earliest prose works in Maithili. The kings also intervened in the politics of the Kathmandu Valley, where some Karnat rulers were recognised as overlords.
karnat-dynasty.e: In 1324 Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq of the Delhi Sultanate invaded Tirhut and took Simraungadh. Harisimhadeva fled into the hills of Nepal. Mithila soon passed to the Oiniwar dynasty, ruling as vassals of Delhi, while Karnat traditions persisted in Nepalese court culture.

kingdom-of-badung.t: South Balinese kingdom centred on Denpasar, whose royal family marched to their deaths in the puputan of 1906.
kingdom-of-badung.o: Badung emerged in southern Bali in the 18th century under the Pemecutan dynasty, part of the Arya noble lineages. Around 1788 a new palace was established at Denpasar, which became the leading court of the kingdom while the Pemecutan branch kept its own seat nearby.
kingdom-of-badung.r: Badung controlled rice lands and the harbour of Kuta, through which slaves, rice and other goods were traded. In the mid 19th century the Danish trader Mads Lange ran a large trading post at Kuta under royal protection. Royal power was shared among the Denpasar, Pemecutan and Kesiman houses.
kingdom-of-badung.e: A dispute over the plunder of a wrecked Chinese ship in 1904 gave the Dutch a pretext. On 20 September 1906 their troops reached Denpasar, where the raja and his court, dressed in white, advanced into the guns in a puputan. Badung was annexed, and Denpasar later became the capital of Bali.

kumharsain-state.t: A small Rajput hill state north of Shimla, one of the Simla Hill States restored under British protection after the Gurkha wars.
kumharsain-state.o: Tradition holds that the ruling family descended from a Rajput named Kirti Singh who came from the plains around 1000 and settled in the hills north of the Sutlej-Giri watershed.
kumharsain-state.r: Kumharsain was a small mountain state of terraced farms and forest, ruled by a Rana and at times a tributary of Bashahr State. Little is recorded of its internal history before the 19th century. Gurkha forces of the Kingdom of Nepal occupied it in the early 1800s.
kumharsain-state.e: After the Anglo-Nepalese War the British issued a sanad in 1815 restoring the Rana as one of the Simla Hill States. Kumharsain merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now part of Shimla district.

kingdom-of-sicily.t: Southern Italy's Norman kingdom, famed for its Arab-Byzantine-Latin court culture, which after 1282 continued as the island realm of Sicily until 1816.
kingdom-of-sicily.o: Roger II, ruler of the County of Sicily and the Duchy of Apulia and Calabria, obtained a royal title from Antipope Anacletus II and was crowned in Palermo on Christmas Day 1130. The kingdom united Sicily and the Italian south, including the former principalities of Capua and Bari.
kingdom-of-sicily.r: The Norman kings ran a centralised state with Arabic, Greek and Latin chanceries, and built the Palatine Chapel, Cefalù and Monreale. Through marriage it passed to the Hohenstaufen: Frederick II issued the Constitutions of Melfi in 1231. Charles of Anjou took it in 1266, but the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 brought Peter III of Aragon to the island, leaving the mainland as the Kingdom of Naples.
kingdom-of-sicily.e: The island kingdom passed to Aragon and Habsburg Spain under viceroys, then briefly to Savoy in 1713, to Austria in 1720 and to the Bourbons in 1735. In 1816 Ferdinand merged it with Naples to form the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

kingdom-of-opobo.t: The trading state founded by Jaja, a former slave who broke away from Bonny and dominated the palm oil trade of the eastern Niger Delta until his deportation in 1887.
kingdom-of-opobo.o: Jaja, born in Igboland and sold as a boy to Bonny, rose to head the Anna Pepple trading house of the Bonny Kingdom. After a civil war between rival houses, he left Bonny in 1869 with his followers and in 1870 founded Opobo on the Imo river, placing himself between Bonny and the interior palm oil markets.
kingdom-of-opobo.r: Opobo was a city-state built around trading houses, each with its own canoe fleet and dependants. Jaja controlled access to the Igbo producers of palm oil, dealt directly with British firms and even shipped oil to Liverpool on his own account. Britain recognised him as king in 1873. He kept missionaries out and maintained traditional religion while sending his children to be educated abroad.
kingdom-of-opobo.e: Jaja refused to let British traders bypass him. In 1887 the British consul Harry Johnston lured him aboard a ship and deported him; he died in 1891. Opobo was absorbed into the Oil Rivers Protectorate, and its king remains a traditional ruler.

kaithal-state.t: A Sikh chiefship ruled by the Bhai family, which lapsed to the British in 1843 when its last chief died without an heir.
kaithal-state.o: The Bhais of Kaithal descended from Bhai Bhagtu, a Sikh devotee honoured by the Gurus. Desu Singh, of that family, seized Kaithal around 1767 in the Sikh expansion across the former Mughal province of Sirhind.
kaithal-state.r: Kaithal was one of the larger Cis-Sutlej chiefships and accepted British protection in 1809. Its chiefs were known by the title Bhai. The state is thinly documented beyond its succession disputes.
kaithal-state.e: When Bhai Udai Singh died childless in 1843, the British annexed most of Kaithal, and resistance by local supporters was put down. The town became a British district headquarters and is now a district of Haryana.

kushalgarh-state.t: A Rathore Rajput chiefship in southern Rajasthan, long a dependency of Banswara with a mostly Bhil population.
kushalgarh-state.o: Kushalgarh was held by a branch of Rathore Rajputs who settled in the hills of Vagad. The register dates it to 1671. Its chiefs held their land as feudatories of Banswara.
kushalgarh-state.r: The Rao ruled a territory of hills and forest with a large Bhil population, practising subsistence farming. In the British period it was treated as a chiefship under Banswara, supervised through the Rajputana Agency, rather than as a fully separate salute state.
kushalgarh-state.e: Kushalgarh joined the United State of Rajasthan in 1948. It is now a town in Banswara district.

kingdom-of-doti.t: A hill kingdom of far-western Nepal ruled by the Raika kings, one of the successor states of the Khasa Malla realm.
kingdom-of-doti.o: Doti emerged from the break-up of the Khasa Malla kingdom in the late 14th century, in the hills between the Karnali and Mahakali rivers. Its rulers, the Raika dynasty, are traditionally said to descend from the Katyuri kings of Kumaon and established themselves at Dipayal and nearby seats.
kingdom-of-doti.r: Doti was one of the larger of the Baise Rajya, the twenty-two hill kingdoms of the Karnali region. Its kings ruled through local chiefs and Brahmin advisers, and fought their neighbours the Kumaon Kingdom and the Kingdom of Jumla. Inscriptions and temple grants are the main sources, and the Doteli dialect of Nepali takes its name from the kingdom.
kingdom-of-doti.e: The expanding Gorkha armies of the Kingdom of Nepal conquered Doti around 1790, defeating its last Raika king. Doti became a district of Nepal, and the name survives in Doti district and the Doteli language.

kamerun.t: The German colony in Central Africa, founded through treaties with the Duala in 1884, which expanded deep into the interior before Allied forces conquered it in 1916.
kamerun.o: On 12 July 1884 the Duala kings Bell and Akwa signed a treaty with German agents, and Gustav Nachtigal raised the German flag at the Duala kingdoms days later. From the coast German forces pushed inland over the next twenty years, defeating resistance from peoples such as the Bulu and from Fulbe lamidates like Ngaoundere, until the colony reached Lake Chad.
kamerun.r: German rule depended on concession companies and plantations on the slopes of Mount Cameroon, worked by forced and recruited labour; the governor Jesko von Puttkamer (1895-1907) was notorious for abuses. The seat of government moved between Duala and Buea, on the cooler slopes of Mount Cameroon. After the Agadir crisis of 1911 France ceded large territories, called Neukamerun, from French Equatorial Africa.
kamerun.e: In 1914 the Germans hanged Rudolf Duala Manga Bell for resisting land expropriation. British and French forces conquered Kamerun in 1914-1916, and it was divided into French Cameroon and the British Cameroons.

kingdom-of-bafut.t: One of the largest kingdoms of the Cameroon Grassfields, whose Fon resisted German conquest and whose palace at Bafut is among the best preserved in the region.
kingdom-of-bafut.o: Bafut was founded by groups said to have migrated from the Tikar area in the north-east, probably in the 18th century, and settled north of what is now Bamenda. Its rulers, the Fons, gradually conquered and absorbed neighbouring villages, building one of the larger chiefdoms of the Grassfields.
kingdom-of-bafut.r: The Fon was a sacred king, supported by palace societies, notables and a regulatory society, the Kwifon, that enforced his decisions and ritual law. The royal compound with its shrine house, the Achum, was the political and religious centre. Bafut farmed, raised livestock and took part in trade in palm oil, kola and slaves across the Grassfields.
kingdom-of-bafut.e: Fon Abumbi I fought German troops in 1901 and 1907 before submitting, and Bafut was absorbed into Kamerun. After 1916 it fell under British Cameroons. The Fon still reigns; Achirimbi II became widely known through Gerald Durrell's book The Bafut Beagles.

kirghiz-assr.t: The autonomous Soviet republic that gave the Kyrgyz their first modern territorial state, the forerunner of today's Kyrgyzstan.
kirghiz-assr.o: In the national delimitation of 1924 the Kyrgyz lands of the Turkestan ASSR were made the Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. In 1925 it was renamed the Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast and in 1926 raised to an Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, with its capital at Pishpek, renamed Frunze.
kirghiz-assr.r: The republic introduced Soviet administration, schools and a written Kyrgyz language, first in Arabic and then Latin script. Collectivisation and settlement of nomadic herders from 1929 brought hardship and revolt, and many fled to China. Leading Kyrgyz communists such as Yusup Abdrakhmanov were purged in the 1930s.
kirghiz-assr.e: Under the 1936 Soviet constitution the republic became a union republic, the Kirghiz SSR. Its borders, drawn in 1924, left large Uzbek and Tajik communities inside the republic and Kyrgyz communities outside it.

kedah-sultanate.t: One of the oldest continuous monarchies in the world, a Malay sultanate that converted to Islam in the 12th century and survives as a state of Malaysia.
kedah-sultanate.o: According to the Kedah annals, the ruler of Old Kedah, Phra Ong Mahawangsa, accepted Islam in 1136 and took the name Sultan Mudzaffar Shah, founding a line that continues today. The date is traditional. The sultans later moved their seat to Alor Setar on the rice plains of the Kedah River.
kedah-sultanate.r: Kedah was the rice bowl of the peninsula, exporting grain, tin and elephants. Its rulers sent the bunga mas, golden flowers, to Siam as a sign of tribute while seeking other allies. In 1786 Sultan Abdullah Mukarram Shah allowed Francis Light of the British East India Company to occupy Penang, hoping for protection that never came.
kedah-sultanate.e: Siam invaded in 1821 and ruled directly until 1842. By the Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909 Kedah passed to British protection as one of the Unfederated Malay States, and it joined the Federation of Malaya in 1948. Its royal house still reigns, and Tunku Abdul Rahman, Malaysia's first prime minister, was a Kedah prince.

kediri-kingdom.t: The East Javanese kingdom ruled from Daha, whose 12th-century court produced classics of Old Javanese poetry and grew rich on the spice trade.
kediri-kingdom.o: Kediri, also called Panjalu, was the western half of the realm Airlangga divided around 1045, with its capital at Daha on the Brantas River. For decades it is poorly documented, but by the 1130s it had absorbed Janggala, and King Jayabaya proclaimed 'Panjalu jayati', Panjalu is victorious.
kediri-kingdom.r: Kediri controlled the rice lands of the Brantas valley and the ports that shipped Moluccan cloves and nutmeg westward; Chinese writers such as Zhou Qufei counted Java among the richest lands overseas. Its court poets wrote the Kakawin Bharatayuddha, completed in 1157 under Jayabaya, and the Smaradahana. Jayabaya is also remembered in Javanese prophecy.
kediri-kingdom.e: The last king, Kertajaya, quarrelled with the clergy, who sided with Ken Arok of Tumapel. Ken Arok defeated him at Ganter in 1222 and founded Singhasari. Kediri revived briefly as Gelang-gelang under Jayakatwang in 1292.

kingdom-of-andarig.t: One of the small kingdoms of the Sinjar plain that rose after Shamshi-Adad's death and played the great powers against each other in the Mari letters.
kingdom-of-andarig.o: Andarig lay in the plain south of Jebel Sinjar in northern Iraq; its site is uncertain. When the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia collapsed around 1776 BCE, local rulers took power there, among them Qarni-Lim, an ally of Zimri-Lim of Mari.
kingdom-of-andarig.r: The Mari archives show Andarig as a regional power competing with Karana, Kurda and Ekallatum for control of the Sinjar plain. Its kings bound themselves by oath to Mari, Eshnunna or Elam as interests shifted. After Qarni-Lim was killed, Atamrum, a ruler from Allahad backed first by Elam and then by Mari, took the throne and became one of the leading kings of the region, with troops and treaties recorded in letters.
kingdom-of-andarig.e: After Hammurabi of Babylon destroyed Mari in 1761 BCE, he imposed his authority on the Sinjar kingdoms, and Andarig vanishes from the sources, absorbed into Babylonian and later local northern powers.

kano-emirate.t: The richest emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate, centred on the walled city of Kano, the great manufacturing and trading hub of the central Sudan.
kano-emirate.o: In 1805 Fulani jihadists loyal to Usman dan Fodio overthrew the last Hausa ruler of the Kingdom of Kano, Muhammad Alwali. The scholar Sulaimanu became the first emir, and in 1819 he was succeeded by Ibrahim Dabo, whose descendants, the Dabo dynasty, have provided Kano's emirs ever since.
kano-emirate.r: The emir governed through a council of titled officials, many inherited from Hausa Kano, with district heads collecting taxes from farms and crafts. Kano produced indigo-dyed cloth and leather goods sold across the Sahara and the Sudan, and its market drew caravans from Tripoli, Bornu and the forest. The explorer Heinrich Barth described it in 1851 as the commercial centre of the region.
kano-emirate.e: A civil war over the succession in 1893-1895 weakened the emirate. British forces took Kano in February 1903, and Emir Aliyu Babba was deposed. Kano became the centrepiece of indirect rule in Northern Nigeria, and the emirate continues today.

kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.t: The realm created by Alfred the Great and his son Edward, joining Wessex and English Mercia into the direct ancestor of the Kingdom of England.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.o: In 886 Alfred occupied London and, according to the Chronicle, all the English not under the Danes submitted to him. His charters began to use the title king of the Anglo-Saxons, uniting the Kingdom of Wessex with western Mercia under Aethelred, Lord of the Mercians, who married Alfred's daughter Aethelflaed.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.r: The kingdom was defended by burhs and a reorganised army. Alfred issued a law code and sponsored translations of Latin works into English. Edward the Elder and Aethelflaed reconquered the southern Danelaw, including the Five Boroughs and Danish East Anglia, between 910 and 920.
kingdom-of-the-anglo-saxons.e: After Aethelflaed's death Edward absorbed Mercia in 918. In 927 his son Aethelstan took York and received the submission of northern rulers, becoming the first king of the Kingdom of England.

kingdom-of-yin-206-bc.t: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, held by the Zhao general Sima Ang until he surrendered to Liu Bang a year later.
kingdom-of-yin-206-bc.o: After the fall of the Qin dynasty, Xiang Yu divided the empire into eighteen kingdoms in 206 BCE. Sima Ang, a general of the revived state of Zhao who had captured the Henei region, was made King of Yin, ruling from Zhaoge in northern Henan, the old Shang capital area.
kingdom-of-yin-206-bc.r: The kingdom was a military holding with no time to develop institutions of its own. It covered the Henei commandery north of the Yellow River and served as a buffer between the kingdoms around Luoyang and those of Zhao.
kingdom-of-yin-206-bc.e: In 205 BCE, as Liu Bang advanced east from the Kingdom of Han (206 BC), Sima Ang was captured or surrendered, and his realm became the Henei commandery of Han. Sima Ang was later claimed as an ancestor of the Sima family who founded the Western Jin.

kingdom-of-prilep.t: Western Macedonian realm of King Vukašin and his son Marko, whose life as an Ottoman vassal inspired the hero of South Slav epic poetry.
kingdom-of-prilep.o: Vukašin Mrnjavčević, a Serbian noble, was crowned king in 1365 as co-ruler with Emperor Uroš V of the Serbian Empire, ruling lands in western Macedonia from Prilep. With his brother Jovan Uglješa of the Despotate of Serres he led the campaign against the Ottomans in 1371.
kingdom-of-prilep.r: After Vukašin was killed at the Maritsa in 1371, his son Marko inherited the royal title and a much smaller realm around Prilep, Ohrid and the Pelagonian plain. Marko became an Ottoman vassal, minted coins and founded the Marko's Monastery near Skopje. His neighbours took Ohrid and other lands.
kingdom-of-prilep.e: Marko died fighting for the Ottomans against Mircea the Elder of Wallachia at Rovine in 1395, and his lands were annexed by the Ottomans. As Kraljević Marko, he became the best-loved hero of Serbian, Macedonian and Bulgarian folk epic.

khalji-dynasty-of-bengal.t: The first Muslim regime in Bengal, founded by Bakhtiyar Khalji's conquest of the Sena capital and ruled from Lakhnauti.
khalji-dynasty-of-bengal.o: Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji, a Turkic-Afghan commander serving the Ghurids, raided Bihar and then, around 1204, surprised the Sena king Lakshmana Sena at Nadia. He established a capital at Lakhnauti (Gaur) and ruled northern and western Bengal with his Khalji officers, nominally under the Ghurid sultans.
khalji-dynasty-of-bengal.r: The Khalji chiefs governed as a military aristocracy, dividing land among commanders and founding mosques and madrasas. Bakhtiyar died after a disastrous expedition towards Tibet around 1206. Iwaz Khalji, who took the title Ghiyath al-Din, was the most effective ruler: he built roads and embankments, created a river fleet and struck coins in his own name.
khalji-dynasty-of-bengal.e: Iltutmish of the Delhi Sultanate sent his son Nasir al-Din Mahmud against Iwaz, who was defeated and killed in 1227. Bengal became a province of Delhi, governed from Lakhnauti, until independent sultans arose again, leading eventually to the Bengal Sultanate.

kos.t: Dorian island state off Anatolia, birthplace of Hippocrates and home of the famous healing sanctuary of Asclepius.
kos.o: Kos, an island off the Carian coast near Halicarnassus, was settled from the Bronze Age, with Mycenaean remains. Dorian Greeks occupied it in the early Iron Age, and it joined the Dorian Hexapolis with Knidos, Halicarnassus and the Rhodian cities. Its first chief town was Astypalaia in the south-west.
kos.r: Kos was known for wine and fine translucent silk cloth. Hippocrates was born there c. 460 BCE and the Coan school of medicine bears his name. After Persian rule the island joined the Delian League. In 366 BCE the Coans founded a new capital on the north-east tip, and the Asclepieion was later built nearby.
kos.e: Kos was a favoured base of the Ptolemaic Empire, where Ptolemy II was born and the poet Philitas taught. It later allied with Rome and became part of the province of Asia in 129 BCE, remaining a free city prized for its sanctuary.

kingdom-of-zimbabwe.t: The builders of Great Zimbabwe, whose dry-stone city controlled the gold trade of the southern African plateau for over two centuries.
kingdom-of-zimbabwe.o: After the decline of the Kingdom of Mapungubwe in the early 13th century, a Shona-speaking elite on the Zimbabwe plateau took over the routes carrying gold and ivory to the coast. Building at Great Zimbabwe began with walls on the Hill Complex and grew into the largest stone-built settlement in sub-Saharan Africa south of Ethiopia.
kingdom-of-zimbabwe.r: Kings ruled from the Hill Complex, while the Great Enclosure, with its conical tower and walls up to 11 metres high, probably served royal or ritual purposes. The economy rested on cattle, farming and gold mined across the plateau and sent via Sofala to Kilwa. Finds include soapstone bird carvings, Chinese porcelain, Persian pottery and a Kilwa copper coin. The city may have held 10,000 to 18,000 people.
kingdom-of-zimbabwe.e: Great Zimbabwe declined from the mid-15th century, perhaps through overgrazing, exhausted resources and a northward shift of the gold trade. Its heirs were the Mutapa state in the north and the Kingdom of Butua at Khami in the south-west. The ruins gave modern Zimbabwe its name and its national emblem, the Zimbabwe bird.

kimek-khanate.t: A confederation of Turkic tribes on the Irtysh whose western Kipchak wing became the Cumans, masters of the western steppe.
kimek-khanate.o: The Kimek confederation formed in the mid-8th century on the Irtysh River from tribes, including the Imek and Kipchaks, who left the Mongolian steppe as the Uyghur Khaganate rose. By the 9th century their ruler held the title khagan.
kimek-khanate.r: Arab and Persian geographers such as Gardizi and the Hudud al-Alam describe the Kimek as a confederation of seven tribes, pastoral but with towns along the Irtysh, with Imakiya as the ruler's seat. They traded furs and slaves south to the Samanid Empire and the Oghuz. Religion included Tengrism and Manichaean and Buddhist influences, and they burned their dead.
kimek-khanate.e: In the early 11th century the confederation broke up as the Kipchaks, its western component, moved west across the steppe. Pressure from the Qai and other peoples of the east also played a part. The Kipchaks became the Cumans, who dominated the Pontic steppe until the Mongol conquest.

kingdom-of-pontus.t: Pontus, a Hellenistic kingdom on the Black Sea whose king Mithridates VI fought Rome in three wars and nearly drove it from Asia.
kingdom-of-pontus.o: Mithridates I Ktistes, a noble of Persian descent, fled the wars of Alexander's successors and seized lands in north-eastern Anatolia. He took the title king in 281 BCE, with his capital at Amaseia, where royal tombs are cut into the cliffs. Pharnaces I captured Sinope in 183 BCE and made it the capital.
kingdom-of-pontus.r: The kings combined Persian court traditions with Greek city culture, ruling over Greek ports and rural temple estates. Pontus was rich in metals, timber and grain. Mithridates VI extended his rule around the Black Sea and in 88 BCE ordered the massacre of Romans and Italians in Asia.
kingdom-of-pontus.e: Mithridates VI fought Sulla, Lucullus and Pompey in three wars. Defeated, he died at Panticapaeum in 63 BCE, and Pompey divided Pontus between Roman provinces and client kings, later including Polemonid Pontus.

kingdom-of-tambapanni.t: The first kingdom of Sri Lanka in the island's chronicles, founded by the legendary prince Vijaya on the north-west coast.
kingdom-of-tambapanni.o: The Mahavamsa and Dipavamsa chronicles tell how Prince Vijaya, exiled from northern India, landed with 700 followers on the day of the Buddha's death, traditionally 543 BCE. He married Kuveni, a local woman of the Yakkha people, and founded a settlement called Tambapanni, probably near Mannar or Puttalam. The account is legendary, though it may reflect the arrival of Indo-Aryan speakers.
kingdom-of-tambapanni.r: Nothing is known of the kingdom from contemporary sources. The chronicles say Vijaya later sent Kuveni away and married a princess from the Pandya country, and that his followers founded villages across the north of the island. Archaeology shows early iron-using settlements in the region, notably at Anuradhapura, that predate the chronicles' kings.
kingdom-of-tambapanni.e: According to the chronicles, Vijaya's nephew Panduvasudeva moved the seat of rule to Upatissa Gama, and his grandson Pandukabhaya founded Anuradhapura around 437 BCE, beginning the Anuradhapura Kingdom. The Greek name for Sri Lanka, Taprobane, derives from Tambapanni.

kingdom-of-hermopolis.t: A short-lived Middle Egyptian kingdom whose king Nimlot defied, then surrendered to, the Kushite conqueror Piye.
kingdom-of-hermopolis.o: As the Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt fragmented in the 8th century BCE, Hermopolis, the cult centre of the god Thoth, became the seat of an independent local king. Its ruler Nimlot (Namart), probably of Libyan descent, held the region of Middle Egypt around the city by about 750 BCE.
kingdom-of-hermopolis.r: Almost all that is known comes from the Victory Stela of Piye. Nimlot first acknowledged Kushite overlordship, then joined the coalition of Tefnakht of Sais, which brought on a Kushite siege. After months of siege his queen pleaded with Piye's women, and Nimlot surrendered his treasures and horses; Piye, a lover of horses, was angered to find them starving.
kingdom-of-hermopolis.e: Nimlot was allowed to keep his throne as a vassal of the Kushite Empire after about 728 BCE, but the kingdom vanishes from the record soon after.

kingdom-of-paris.t: Merovingian kingdom centred on Paris, created when Clovis' realm was divided among his sons in 511.
kingdom-of-paris.o: On the death of Clovis in 511 the Kingdom of the Franks was shared among his four sons. Childebert I received the lands around Paris, together with the Channel coast and later parts of Aquitaine and Burgundy.
kingdom-of-paris.r: Childebert ruled for nearly fifty years, campaigning against the Kingdom of the Burgundians and the Visigoths in Spain, from where he brought back relics of Saint Vincent. For them he founded the abbey later called Saint-Germain-des-Prés. He joined his brother Chlothar I in murdering their nephews, the sons of Chlodomer of Orléans.
kingdom-of-paris.e: Childebert died without sons in 558, and Chlothar I briefly reunited the Frankish lands. In 561 Paris passed to Chlothar's son Charibert I, and after Charibert's death in 567 his kingdom was divided among his brothers, with Paris shared between them.

kingdom-of-portugal.t: One of Europe's oldest kingdoms, which fixed its borders by 1249, led the age of oceanic exploration and lasted until the revolution of 1910.
kingdom-of-portugal.o: The County of Portugal, a fief of León, passed to Afonso Henriques, who styled himself king after his victory at Ourique in 1139. León recognised him at Zamora in 1143 and the papacy in 1179. With crusader help he took Lisbon in 1147, and Afonso III completed the conquest of the Algarve in 1249.
kingdom-of-portugal.r: Portugal was a Catholic monarchy with Cortes, military orders and a strong maritime economy. After the victory of Aljubarrota in 1385, John I founded the Aviz dynasty, whose princes launched the voyages that created the Portuguese Empire. Pepper, Brazilian sugar and gold financed the crown. Manuel I ruled at the peak of the spice trade.
kingdom-of-portugal.e: The kingdom fell under Spanish kings in the Iberian Union from 1580 to 1640, then revived under the Braganzas. After the 1908 assassination of Carlos I, a revolution on 5 October 1910 ended the monarchy and created the First Portuguese Republic.

cr.a: Tonyjeff, based on ancient national symbol.

kingdom-of-toro.t: A kingdom of western Uganda that broke away from Bunyoro in the 1830s, was restored by the British, and survives as a cultural monarchy.
kingdom-of-toro.o: Around 1830 Prince Kaboyo Olimi I, a son of the omukama of the Kingdom of Bunyoro, rebelled and set up an independent kingdom in the fertile lands around the Rwenzori Mountains. Bunyoro's king Kabalega reconquered Toro in 1876, but in 1891 Frederick Lugard of the Imperial British East Africa Company restored the Toro dynasty under Kasagama.
kingdom-of-toro.r: The omukama ruled through chiefs over a population of farmers and herders, with royal regalia and rituals taken from Bunyoro. Under Kasagama Kyebambe IV the court adopted Anglicanism, and the Toro Agreement of 1900 defined the kingdom's place in the Uganda Protectorate, with its capital at Fort Portal.
kingdom-of-toro.e: The kingdom was abolished with Uganda's other monarchies in 1967 and restored as a cultural institution in 1993. In 1995 Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV was crowned at the age of three.

kingdom-of-judah.t: The southern Kingdom of Judah, ruled from Jerusalem by the House of David, whose fall and exile shaped the Hebrew Bible.
kingdom-of-judah.o: Judah emerged as a separate kingdom c. 930 BCE when Solomon's son Rehoboam kept only the southern tribes after the split of the United Kingdom of Israel. It remained smaller and poorer than the Kingdom of Israel, but its capital Jerusalem held the temple of Yahweh.
kingdom-of-judah.r: Kings of the line of David ruled throughout. Hezekiah dug the Siloam tunnel and survived Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BCE, though Lachish fell. Josiah centralised worship in Jerusalem. Prophets such as Isaiah and Jeremiah were active, and inscriptions such as the Lachish letters reveal daily administration.
kingdom-of-judah.e: Judah became a vassal of the Chaldean Empire. After revolts, Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 587 BCE and deported King Zedekiah and the elite to Babylon. The exile shaped Judaism, and later Yehud Medinata arose under Persian rule.

kingdom-of-klungkung.t: Senior royal house of Bali, heir to Gelgel, whose Dewa Agung was recognised as paramount king of the island until the puputan of 1908.
kingdom-of-klungkung.o: After a revolt destroyed the court of Gelgel, the Dewa Agung Jambe re-established the main Balinese dynasty at Klungkung (Semarapura) in 1686. Though other kingdoms such as Karangasem, Buleleng and Badung became stronger, they still acknowledged the Dewa Agung as first among the rajas of Bali, the heir of the Majapahit-descended kings.
kingdom-of-klungkung.r: Klungkung was small, but its ruler held ritual primacy and presided over Balinese law and ceremonial. The court built the Kertha Gosa hall of justice, whose painted ceilings in the Kamasan style survive. In 1849 the Dewa Agung Istri Kanya, a woman ruler, led resistance at Kusamba, where the Dutch commander Andreas Michiels was killed.
kingdom-of-klungkung.e: When the Dutch invaded in April 1908, the Dewa Agung Jambe II led his family and followers into a puputan, a ritual suicidal march into rifle fire. Klungkung was annexed into the Dutch East Indies, and later restored as a regency under the descendants of the royal house.

kamakura-fu.t: The Ashikaga branch government that ruled eastern Japan from Kamakura and repeatedly challenged the shoguns in Kyoto.
kamakura-fu.o: To control the Kanto, the Ashikaga shogunate created a regional government in Kamakura. In 1349 Ashikaga Takauji sent his son Motouji there as Kamakura kubo, assisted by a deputy, the Kanto kanrei, an office soon held by the Uesugi family.
kamakura-fu.r: The kubo governed the eight Kanto provinces and later Mutsu and Dewa, with their own vassals and courts, and acted almost as rival shoguns. Successors Ujimitsu, Mitsukane and Mochiuji resented Kyoto's authority, and tension with the Uesugi deputies led to the Uesugi Zenshu revolt of 1416.
kamakura-fu.e: Ashikaga Mochiuji openly defied Shogun Yoshinori; in the Eikyo Rebellion he was defeated and forced to kill himself in 1439. The office was revived in 1449 for his son Shigeuji, who after fighting the Uesugi moved to Koga in 1455 as the Koga kubo.

kingdom-of-ui-maine.t: Kingdom of the O'Kellys in east Galway and south Roscommon, one of the largest subject kingdoms of Connacht, which lasted until the Composition of 1585.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.o: The Uí Maine claimed descent from Maine Mór, said to have won lands west of the Shannon in the 5th century. By the early medieval period they held a large kingdom in what is now east County Galway and south Roscommon, within the over-kingdom of the Kingdom of Connacht, with privileges of their own.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.r: Their kings, from the 10th century the Ua Cellaig, O'Kelly, served the kings of Connacht in war and sometimes contested the kingship. Tadhg Mór Ua Cellaig fell fighting for Brian Bóruma at Clontarf in 1014. The O'Kellys were famous patrons of learning: Uilliam Buidhe Ó Ceallaigh held a great Christmas feast for the poets of Ireland in 1351, and the Book of Uí Maine was compiled for the family.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.e: Anglo-Norman lords, especially the de Burghs, took part of Uí Maine in the 13th century, but the O'Kellys kept much of it. Under the Composition of Connacht in 1585 their lordship was converted into crown tenure, ending the kingdom's independent status.
kingdom-of-ui-maine.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-kutai.t: The earliest documented kingdom in Indonesia, known from King Mulavarman's Sanskrit pillar inscriptions of around 400 at Muara Kaman in East Kalimantan.
kingdom-of-kutai.o: Seven stone yupa, sacrificial posts inscribed in Sanskrit with Pallava script, were found at Muara Kaman on the Mahakam River. They name Kudungga, his son Asvavarman, called the founder of the dynasty, and grandson Mulavarman. Kudungga's name is not Sanskrit, suggesting a local chief whose descendants adopted Indian kingship and ritual.
kingdom-of-kutai.r: The inscriptions praise Mulavarman for giving thousands of cattle to Brahmins and for performing Vedic sacrifices, showing a court shaped by Hindu ideas of kingship. Its position on the Mahakam allowed it to gather forest products and gold from the interior. After the inscriptions almost nothing is recorded for centuries.
kingdom-of-kutai.e: The later history of Kutai Martadipura is known mainly from the chronicles of its rival, the Kutai Kartanegara Sultanate, which conquered it in 1635 and merged the two under the name Kutai Kartanegara ing Martadipura. The yupa inscriptions are held in the National Museum in Jakarta.

kingdom-of-ife.t: The sacred city of the Yoruba, cradle of their royal dynasties and home of some of Africa's finest naturalistic bronze and terracotta sculpture.
kingdom-of-ife.o: Ile-Ife was a substantial town by the end of the first millennium. Yoruba tradition makes it the place where the world was created and where Oduduwa, ancestor of the Yoruba kings, established the first throne; his descendants are said to have founded the other Yoruba kingdoms and the Oba dynasty of the Benin Empire.
kingdom-of-ife.r: The Ooni of Ife ruled as a sacred king. Between the 12th and 15th centuries Ife artists cast copper-alloy heads and modelled terracottas of striking realism, and the city made glass beads that were traded widely. Streets and courtyards were paved with potsherds. Ife's authority was chiefly religious, conferring legitimacy on other Yoruba rulers.
kingdom-of-ife.e: Political power passed to the Oyo Empire and other states, and in the 19th century Ife was devastated in the Yoruba civil wars and long conflict with neighbouring Modakeke. It came under British rule around 1900. The Ooni still reigns in Ile-Ife, one of Nigeria's most senior traditional rulers.

kingdom-of-tenkodogo.t: Mossi kingdom of south-eastern Burkina Faso, held by tradition to be the oldest of the Mossi states.
kingdom-of-tenkodogo.o: Mossi tradition tells that Yennenga, a princess of Mamprugu, rode north and bore a son, Ouedraogo, to a hunter named Riale. Ouedraogo and his descendants founded the Mossi kingdoms, and Tenkodogo, 'the old land', is regarded as the first of them, established around the 15th century in the White Volta basin.
kingdom-of-tenkodogo.r: The Naaba of Tenkodogo ruled through chiefs descended from the royal house over farming villages, whose earth-priests (tengsoba) kept rites of the land. The Mossi system combined mounted aristocracies with local religious authority. Tenkodogo later became less powerful than the Kingdom of Ouagadougou and the Kingdom of Yatenga.
kingdom-of-tenkodogo.e: French forces brought Tenkodogo under colonial control in 1897, and it became part of French West Africa, later French Upper Volta. The Naaba of Tenkodogo remains a recognised traditional ruler in Burkina Faso.

kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385.t: The Piast kingdom of Poland, which fragmented into rival duchies, was reunited in 1320 and flourished under Casimir the Great.
kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385.o: Boleslaw I the Brave was crowned king in 1025, turning the Duchy of Poland into a kingdom. His son Mieszko II faced invasion and revolt, and in the 1030s a pagan uprising and a Bohemian raid devastated Greater Poland. Casimir I the Restorer rebuilt the state and made Krakow its main seat.
kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385.r: Under the testament of Boleslaw III in 1138 the realm was divided among his sons, with the senior duke ruling Krakow. For almost two centuries Poland was a patchwork of duchies, settled by German colonists and towns under German law and hit by the Mongols in 1241. The church, with the archbishopric of Gniezno, held it together.
kingdom-of-poland-1025-1385.e: Wladyslaw I the Elbow-high reunited much of the country and was crowned in 1320. His son Casimir III the Great codified law, founded the University of Krakow in 1364 and added Red Ruthenia. After Louis of Hungary, his daughter Jadwiga married Jogaila of Lithuania under the Union of Krewo of 1385, beginning the Kingdom of Poland (1385-1569).

kingdom-of-niumi.t: Mandinka kingdom at the mouth of the Gambia river, whose rulers taxed European ships and traders for four centuries.
kingdom-of-niumi.o: Niumi, called Barra by Europeans, was one of the Mandinka kingdoms founded along the Gambia river as Mali Empire influence spread westward, probably by the 15th century. It occupied the north bank at the river mouth, including the villages of Juffure and Albreda, opposite James Island.
kingdom-of-niumi.r: The mansa was chosen in rotation from royal lineages of the Sonko, Manneh and Jammeh families, with the town of Essau as royal seat. Niumi collected customs from European ships entering the river and supplied food, water and slaves. English and French posts on James Island and at Albreda depended on its goodwill.
kingdom-of-niumi.e: In 1826 Niumi ceded a strip of land, the Ceded Mile, to Britain, and in 1831 the Barra War between Niumi and the British ended in its defeat. It was made part of the Gambia Colony and Protectorate in the 1890s and is now a district of the Gambia.
kingdom-of-niumi.re: Sunni Islam and Mandinka traditional religion

kingdom-of-cyrene-under-magas.t: The breakaway Hellenistic kingdom of Magas, stepson of Ptolemy I, who ruled Cyrenaica independently of Egypt.
kingdom-of-cyrene-under-magas.o: Magas, son of Ptolemy I's queen Berenice I by an earlier marriage, became governor of Cyrene around 300 BCE after a revolt there was suppressed. On the death of his stepfather he grew restive and around 276 BCE proclaimed himself king, breaking away from the Ptolemaic Empire.
kingdom-of-cyrene-under-magas.r: Magas married Apama, daughter of the Seleucid king Antiochus I, and in alliance with the Seleucids marched on Egypt in the mid-270s BCE, but was forced back by a Libyan revolt. He ruled Cyrene and the Pentapolis for decades, minting his own coins. Later he made peace with his half-brother Ptolemy II and betrothed his daughter Berenice to the heir, the future Ptolemy III.
kingdom-of-cyrene-under-magas.e: After Magas died around 250 BCE, Apama invited Demetrius the Fair to marry Berenice and rule, but Berenice had him killed. She then married Ptolemy III in 246 BCE, reuniting Cyrene with Egypt, and became the queen Berenice II.

kholodny-yar-republic.t: A partisan self-governing district in the forests of central Ukraine, which held out against Whites and Bolsheviks from 1919 to 1922.
kholodny-yar-republic.o: Kholodny Yar is a forested ravine area near Chyhyryn, rich in memories of the Cossack Hetmanate and the 18th-century haidamaka rebels. In 1919 villagers around the Motronynskyi Monastery formed a self-defence force under Vasyl Chuchupak, which took control of some twenty villages and declared loyalty to the Ukrainian People's Republic.
kholodny-yar-republic.r: The district was governed by village councils and its partisan otamans, with the monastery as headquarters. The insurgents fought Denikin's Whites and then the Red Army, raiding railways and Soviet detachments, and kept contact with the exiled government of the Ukrainian People's Republic. Its forces numbered from a few hundred to several thousand fighters.
kholodny-yar-republic.e: Vasyl Chuchupak was killed in 1920, and Soviet campaigns slowly broke the resistance. In 1922 the Cheka lured several leading otamans to a fake meeting and arrested them, ending organised resistance. The story was later told in Yuri Horlis-Horsky's memoir Kholodny Yar.

kingdom-of-mengwi.t: Powerful 18th-century kingdom of southern Bali, builder of the moated royal temple of Taman Ayun, destroyed by its neighbours in 1891.
kingdom-of-mengwi.o: Mengwi was founded around 1700 by I Gusti Agung Putu, a noble who broke away from the declining Gelgel order and built a new realm in the rice lands of south-central Bali. Through war and marriage alliances it became one of the strongest Balinese states of the 18th century.
kingdom-of-mengwi.r: The rulers dominated an extensive network of irrigation societies and temple congregations, and their state temple, Pura Taman Ayun, surrounded by moats, expressed royal claims to fertility and order. In the 18th century Mengwi also held Blambangan in eastern Java for a time. Power depended on shifting loyalties of vassal lords.
kingdom-of-mengwi.e: Rivalries with neighbouring courts wore the kingdom down, and in 1891 a coalition of the Kingdom of Badung, Kingdom of Tabanan and Kingdom of Gianyar conquered Mengwi and divided its lands. Taman Ayun is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape.

kingdom-of-dalmatia.t: Austrian crown land along the Adriatic coast, where Croatian and Italian national movements competed for a century before it joined Yugoslavia.
kingdom-of-dalmatia.o: Austria had taken Venetian Dalmatia in 1797 but lost it to Napoleon. After the Congress of Vienna it recovered the coast, now including the former Republic of Ragusa and the Bay of Kotor, and organised it in 1815 as the Kingdom of Dalmatia, a crown land of the Austrian Empire governed from Zara.
kingdom-of-dalmatia.r: Dalmatia was poor and rural, living from wine, olive oil, fishing and seafaring, and many emigrated to the Americas. Its diet, created in 1861, was at first dominated by the Italian-speaking Autonomist Party, but the Croatian People's Party won control in 1870. Croats sought union with Croatia-Slavonia, which Vienna refused. The Austrian navy defeated Italy off Lissa in 1866.
kingdom-of-dalmatia.e: In October 1918 Dalmatia joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, and then the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. Zara and some islands passed to Italy under the Treaty of Rapallo in 1920, returning to Yugoslavia after 1945.

khanate-of-maragheh.t: A local khanate of the Muqaddam tribe around Maragheh, the old Ilkhanid capital, in the decades between the Afsharids and the Qajars.
khanate-of-maragheh.o: After Nader Shah's death in 1747, the town of Maragheh, south of Tabriz, and its fertile district came under the hereditary control of khans of the Muqaddam tribe. Maragheh had been the first capital of the Ilkhanate and site of Nasir al-Din al-Tusi's observatory.
khanate-of-maragheh.r: The Muqaddam khans ruled a small agricultural region of orchards and vineyards near Lake Urmia, maintaining their own troops and paying tribute to the dominant power of the moment, including Karim Khan of the Zand Empire. Ahmad Khan Muqaddam is the best-known ruler. They were in frequent conflict with the khans of Tabriz and Urmia.
khanate-of-maragheh.e: Agha Mohammad Khan's Qajar Iran subdued the Azerbaijani khanates in the 1790s, and around 1800 Maragheh was absorbed, its Muqaddam khans continuing as governors under the Qajars.

kingdom-of-benin-restored.t: The monarchy of Benin, restored by the British in 1914 after the sack of 1897, whose Oba remains a central figure of Edo culture in Nigeria.
kingdom-of-benin-restored.o: After the British expedition of 1897 sacked Benin City and ended the Benin Empire, Oba Ovonramwen was exiled to Calabar. When he died in 1914, the British allowed his son to succeed as Oba Eweka II, restoring the monarchy within Colonial Nigeria as the head of the Benin Native Authority.
kingdom-of-benin-restored.r: Eweka II rebuilt the royal palace and revived court ceremonies and the royal guilds, including the bronze casters of Igun Street, who continue to make brass works. The Oba had a recognised role in local government under indirect rule, though real authority lay with British officials. Oba Akenzua II (1933-1978) took part in Nigerian politics in the late colonial period.
kingdom-of-benin-restored.e: After Nigerian independence the Oba remained a traditional ruler, today in Edo State, with ceremonial and religious authority. Erediauwa reigned from 1979 and Ewuare II from 2016, amid campaigns that have brought the return of some Benin Bronzes looted in 1897.

kumaon-kingdom.t: The Himalayan hill kingdom of the Chand rajas, who ruled Kumaon for centuries from Champawat and later Almora until the Gorkha conquest.
kumaon-kingdom.o: According to tradition the Chand dynasty was founded by Som Chand, a Rajput prince from the plains, who established himself at Champawat in eastern Kumaon. The early chronology is legendary, but by the 15th and 16th centuries the Chands had subdued rival hill chiefs, and Kalyan Chand moved the capital to Almora around 1563.
kumaon-kingdom.r: The rajas ruled a society of farming villages on terraced slopes, administered through local headmen and land grants to temples and Brahmins. They warred with the neighbouring Garhwal Kingdom and with the Rohilla State in the plains. Baz Bahadur Chand, a contemporary of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, extended the kingdom to the Tibetan border and built temples, including at Jageshwar.
kumaon-kingdom.e: Weakened by court intrigue in the 18th century, Kumaon was conquered by the Gorkha army of the Kingdom of Nepal, which took Almora in 1790. After the Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814 to 1816 the region passed to British control and is now part of Uttarakhand.

kingdom-of-khwarazm.t: The ancient oasis kingdom of the lower Amu Darya, a land of canals and fortified towns that kept its own kings and Iranian culture for eight centuries.
kingdom-of-khwarazm.o: Khwarazm, or Chorasmia, grew from irrigation farming on the Amu Darya delta south of the Aral Sea. It appears as a province of the Achaemenid Empire under Darius I and seems to have regained independence by the 4th century BCE, when its king Pharasmanes offered alliance to Alexander the Great in 328 BCE.
kingdom-of-khwarazm.r: Its economy rested on a dense canal network feeding wheat, cotton, vines and orchards, protected by walled settlements and fortresses such as Toprak-Kala, Koy-Krylgan-Kala and Ayaz-Kala. Kings issued their own silver coinage, and later Khwarazmian tradition traced their line to the hero Siyavush. Zoroastrian practice included bone burial in ossuaries, and the Khwarazmian language had its own Aramaic-derived script.
kingdom-of-khwarazm.e: In the early 4th century CE the ancient royal house gave way to the Afrighid Khwarazm dynasty, which al-Biruni dates to 305. The Kushan Empire and Sasanians may have held loose overlordship at times. Khwarazm's distinct language and calendar survived until the Mongol era.

kingdom-of-kurda.t: A small kingdom of the Sinjar region known from the Mari letters, one of the rival states that filled the gap left by Shamshi-Adad's empire.
kingdom-of-kurda.o: Kurda lay in the Sinjar plain of northern Iraq, probably near Andarig and Karana; its site is not identified. It emerged as an independent kingdom when the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia dissolved around 1776 BCE.
kingdom-of-kurda.r: The Mari letters name a king Simah-ilane and later a Hammurabi of Kurda, not to be confused with his famous namesake of Babylon. Kurda's rulers concluded and broke oaths with Mari, Andarig, Eshnunna and Babylon, and their envoys appear at the courts of greater kings. Nothing is known of its institutions beyond this diplomatic record.
kingdom-of-kurda.e: After Hammurabi of Babylon conquered Mari in 1761 BCE, the Sinjar kingdoms fell under Babylonian control, and Kurda drops out of the record.

kosrae-paramount-chiefdom.t: The island-wide chiefdom of Kosrae in Micronesia, ruled from the basalt-walled royal town of Leluh, a sister site to Pohnpei's Nan Madol.
kosrae-paramount-chiefdom.o: By about 1250 the chiefdoms of Kosrae, the easternmost of the Caroline Islands, had been unified under a single paramount ruler, the Tokosra. The capital was built on Leluh, a small island off the east coast that was enlarged with coral fill and covered with walled compounds of stacked basalt columns over the following centuries.
kosrae-paramount-chiefdom.r: Kosrae was among the most centralised societies in Micronesia. The Tokosra held ultimate title to land, and high chiefs living at Leluh administered the island's districts, drawing food from commoners who farmed breadfruit, taro and bananas on the main island. Royal tombs stood inside high walls, and canals ran through the town. Pohnpeian tradition makes Kosrae the homeland of Isokelekel, who overthrew the Saudeleur dynasty.
kosrae-paramount-chiefdom.e: Whalers, beginning in the 1830s, brought epidemics that reduced the population to a few hundred by the 1870s. American Protestant missionaries arrived in 1852, and the old kingship lost its authority. Kosrae passed to Spain in 1885, Germany in 1899 and Japan in 1914, and is now a state of the Federated States of Micronesia.

kingdom-of-rarotonga.t: A chiefly kingdom on the main island of the Cook Islands, led by the Makea line, which sought British protection and became the core of the Cook Islands Federation.
kingdom-of-rarotonga.o: Rarotonga was divided among tribes led by hereditary ariki, including the Makea, Pa, Kainuku and Tinomana titles. After the London Missionary Society brought Christianity from 1823, through the Tahitian teacher Papeiha and John Williams, the ariki governed with mission backing, and the Makea title holders of Avarua came to be regarded by outsiders as monarchs of the island.
kingdom-of-rarotonga.r: The ariki ruled through chiefly councils and mission-inspired law codes enforced by church judges. The island traded fruit, copra and cotton with Tahiti and New Zealand. Makea Takau Ariki, who held her title from 1871, was treated by visiting ships and governments as queen. Details of the kingdom's formal institutions before the 1880s are thinly documented.
kingdom-of-rarotonga.e: Fearing French annexation, the ariki requested British protection, and a protectorate was proclaimed in 1888. The British Resident Frederick Moss set up a federal parliament, and Rarotonga became part of the Cook Islands Federation in 1893.
