kotawaringin-sultanate.t: Malay sultanate of south-western Borneo founded by a prince of Banjarmasin, long the main power on the Lamandau and Arut rivers.
kotawaringin-sultanate.o: Kotawaringin was founded in the early 17th century by Pangeran Dipati Anta-Kasuma, a son of Sultan Mustain Billah of the Banjar Sultanate, who was given the western lands of Banjar to rule. Its court was first at Kotawaringin Lama on the Lamandau river and moved to Pangkalan Bun in the early 19th century.
kotawaringin-sultanate.r: The sultans ruled a Malay Muslim riverine elite that collected tribute from inland Dayak communities, trading forest goods such as rattan, resin, gold and birds nests to Banjarmasin and Java. The court preserved Banjar customs and titles, and Islam spread among coastal settlers while most of the interior remained Dayak.
kotawaringin-sultanate.e: The Dutch brought Kotawaringin under contract in the 19th century as a self-governing domain of the Dutch East Indies. The sultanate continued under colonial supervision and was absorbed into the Republic of Indonesia around 1948 to 1950. The royal palace in Pangkalan Bun still stands.

kingdom-of-persis.t: The local kings of Fars, heartland of the Persians, who kept Achaemenid memory alive under Greek and Parthian overlords until one of them founded the Sasanian Empire.
kingdom-of-persis.o: After Alexander's conquest Persis became part of the Seleucid Empire, but in the 3rd century BCE local dynasts called frataraka ('governor' or 'leader') began issuing their own coins from Istakhr and Persepolis. Bagadates is often seen as the first independent frataraka, and his successors broke away from Seleucid control.
kingdom-of-persis.r: The frataraka coins show the ruler before a fire altar or Achaemenid-style monuments, with Aramaic legends, signalling continuity with the Persian past and Zoroastrian worship. From the mid-2nd century BCE Persis became a vassal of the Parthian Empire, and its rulers took the title king (shah). Kings such as Darayan and Manchihr bore names drawn from Iranian epic. The land lived from agriculture in the valleys of the Kur and Pulvar rivers.
kingdom-of-persis.e: Around 205 CE Pabag, a local lord at Istakhr, seized power, and his son Ardashir made himself king of Persis. In 224 CE Ardashir defeated the Parthian king Artabanus IV and founded the Sasanian Empire.

kingdom-of-paphos.t: Ancient Cypriot kingdom centred on the great sanctuary of Aphrodite, whose kings served as the goddess's high priests for some eight centuries.
kingdom-of-paphos.o: Paphos grew at Palaepaphos, modern Kouklia, a Late Bronze Age town in south-west Cyprus. In the 12th and 11th centuries BCE Aegean settlers arrived, and Greek legend credited Agapenor of Tegea with founding the city after the Trojan War. An inscription of the 11th century BCE shows Greek already written there.
kingdom-of-paphos.r: Its kings combined royal power with the priesthood of the Paphian goddess, later identified with Aphrodite, whose open-air sanctuary with a conical stone drew pilgrims from across the Mediterranean. Paphos used the Cypriot syllabary for Greek and struck its own coins. It paid tribute to Assyria and later to the Achaemenid Empire, and joined the revolt against Persia in 498 BCE.
kingdom-of-paphos.e: The last king, Nicocles, founded the harbour city of Nea Paphos, which became the capital of Ptolemaic and Roman Cyprus. The kingdom was abolished when Ptolemy I took the island, by c. 306 BCE, but the sanctuary of Aphrodite flourished into late antiquity.

kingdom-of-champasak.t: The southern Lao kingdom on the Mekong around Wat Phu, founded in 1713, whose princes later led the southern Lao nobility in modern Laos.
kingdom-of-champasak.o: In 1713 Soysisamouth, a grandson of Sourigna Vongsa, was installed as king at Champasak in southern Laos with the support of the monk Phra Khu Phonsamek, separating the south from the Kingdom of Vientiane. The region contained the ancient Khmer temple of Wat Phu.
kingdom-of-champasak.r: Champasak ruled the Mekong plains of the south and upland areas with Mon-Khmer peoples, trading forest products, cardamom and slaves. From 1778 it became a vassal of Siam, which later governed much of its territory directly. The kingdom's capital moved several times along the river near Bassac.
kingdom-of-champasak.e: After the Franco-Siamese treaties of 1893 and 1904, Champasak's lands west of the Mekong stayed with Siam while the rest passed to French Laos. Prince Boun Oum of Champasak renounced his dynastic claim in 1946 so that Laos could be unified as the Kingdom of Laos.

kirata-dynasty.t: The ancient Kirata kings of the Kathmandu Valley, remembered in Nepalese chronicles as the rulers who came before the Licchavis.
kirata-dynasty.o: The Kirata dynasty is known only from later Nepalese chronicles, above all the 14th-century Gopalarajavamshavali. They say the Kiratas, a people of the eastern Himalaya, took the Kathmandu Valley from earlier cowherd dynasties, the Gopalas and Mahishapalas, and were ruled by a line of some 28 or 29 kings.
kirata-dynasty.r: No inscriptions or coins of the Kirata kings survive, so their government and society are unknown. The name links them to the Kiranti peoples of eastern Nepal, such as the Rai and Limbu, who regard the dynasty as their ancestors. Indian epics and the Greek geographer Ptolemy mention Kiratas as a Himalayan people, and non-Sanskrit place names in early inscriptions may preserve their language.
kirata-dynasty.e: The chronicles say Kirata rule ended when kings from the south, followed by the Licchavis, took the valley. The Licchavi Kingdom of Nepal was established by the 5th century, when the first datable inscriptions of Nepal appear.

kingdom-of-bangli.t: Landlocked kingdom of the Balinese highlands, home of the Kehen temple and the lands around Lake Batur.
kingdom-of-bangli.o: Bangli was the only Balinese kingdom without a coastline. Its ruling house was a branch of the noble lineages tied to the Kingdom of Klungkung, and it emerged as a separate kingdom by about 1800. Its documented history is thin compared with the coastal courts.
kingdom-of-bangli.r: The kingdom stretched from the rice terraces of central Bali up to Kintamani and Lake Batur, where Bali Aga villages kept older customs. Its state temple, Pura Kehen, is one of the oldest on the island. Bangli was often at war with Gianyar and Klungkung, and allied itself with whichever court served its interests.
kingdom-of-bangli.e: In 1909, after the conquests of Badung, Tabanan and Klungkung, Bangli accepted Dutch protection, with its ruler kept on as regent within the Dutch East Indies. It is now a regency of Bali province.

kingdom-of-alashiya.t: Late Bronze Age kingdom on Cyprus whose rulers traded copper with Egypt, the Hittites and Ugarit, as revealed by the Amarna letters.
kingdom-of-alashiya.o: Alashiya appears in Near Eastern texts from the 18th century BCE as a source of copper, and most scholars identify it with Cyprus or part of it. Cyprus developed urban centres in the Late Cypriot period from c. 1650 BCE, including Enkomi on the east coast, Kalavasos and Alassa, though which was the royal seat is uncertain.
kingdom-of-alashiya.r: The king of Alashiya corresponded with Pharaoh Akhenaten as a 'brother' in the Amarna letters, sending copper ingots in return for silver, oil and luxury goods. Clay analysis shows these letters were made on Cyprus. Enkomi had copper workshops and ashlar buildings, and the island used the Cypro-Minoan script. The Hittite Empire claimed overlordship in the 13th century BCE.
kingdom-of-alashiya.e: Letters from Ugarit describe enemy ships threatening Alashiya c. 1200 BCE, and Suppiluliuma II fought naval battles off its coast. In the following century Cypriot towns declined or moved, Aegean settlers arrived, and the island reorganised into the Iron Age kingdoms such as Salamis, Paphos and Kition.

khanate-of-urmia.t: A khanate of the Afshar tribe on the western shore of Lake Urmia, whose khan Fath Ali Khan Afshar contended for power in Iran after Nader Shah's death.
khanate-of-urmia.o: Urmia was home to a branch of the Turkic Afshar tribe, kin of Nader Shah. After Nader's assassination in 1747 and the break-up of the Afsharid Empire, Afshar chiefs held Urmia and its plain as a khanate.
khanate-of-urmia.r: Fath Ali Khan Afshar, the most ambitious of the khans, fought Azad Khan Afghan and Karim Khan Zand for control of north-western Iran. Karim Khan besieged and took Urmia in 1763, and Fath Ali Khan was later killed. The khanate continued under other Afshar khans as Zand vassals. Its population included Azerbaijani Turks, Kurds and Assyrian Christians, and the plain produced grain, fruit and tobacco.
khanate-of-urmia.e: Agha Mohammad Khan's Qajar Iran took Urmia in the 1790s, and by 1797 the khanate was incorporated into the Qajar province of Azerbaijan.

khilchipur-state.t: A small Khichi Chauhan Rajput state in the Malwa region of central India, one of the minor states of the Bhopal Agency.
khilchipur-state.o: The ruling family belonged to the Khichi branch of the Chauhan Rajputs, and tradition dates the founding of the state to 1544. Little is reliably known of its early rulers.
khilchipur-state.r: Khilchipur was a small agricultural state on the Malwa plateau. It paid tribute to the Sindhia rulers of Gwalior State and came under British protection in the early 19th century. Its history is poorly recorded.
khilchipur-state.e: Khilchipur merged into Madhya Bharat in 1948, which became part of Madhya Pradesh in 1956. It is now in Rajgarh district.

kangju.t: A long-lived nomad kingdom of the middle Syr Darya, a rival of the Wusun and Dayuan that dominated the steppe north of Sogdiana for six centuries.
kangju.o: Kangju first appears in the account of the Han envoy Zhang Qian, who passed through around 128 BCE and reported a nomadic state north-west of Dayuan with perhaps 120,000 archers. Its people were Iranian-speaking pastoralists on the middle Syr Darya and the Talas and Chu valleys, part of the wider Saka world.
kangju.r: The king ruled from a winter seat called Beitian and summered in the steppe, with five lesser kings beneath him, according to the Han histories. Kangju controlled routes between the steppe, Sogdiana and the Kingdom of Dayuan, and at times held Sogdian towns as dependencies. In 36 BCE it sheltered the Xiongnu chanyu Zhizhi, whom a Han army killed there.
kangju.e: Kangju is linked by archaeologists to the Kaunchi and Otrar-Karatau cultures. It weakened under pressure from the Kidarite Kingdom, Hephthalites and Rouran, and by the 5th century its name passed to Sogdiana itself, 'Kang' being the later Chinese name for Samarkand.

kingdom-of-tanahun.t: A Sen hill kingdom of central Nepal and one of the Chaubise Rajya, a neighbour and rival of Gorkha and Lamjung.
kingdom-of-tanahun.o: Tanahun was founded by a branch of the Sen dynasty of Palpa in the early 16th century, after the realm of Mukunda Sen was divided among his heirs. It held hill country along the Marsyangdi and Seti rivers, east of the Kingdom of Palpa and south of the Kingdom of Lamjung.
kingdom-of-tanahun.r: As one of the Chaubise Rajya, the twenty-four principalities of the central hills, Tanahun was ruled by Sen kings who were linked by marriage to other hill dynasties. Little is recorded of its administration. In the 18th century its ruler Trivikram Sen tried to resist Gorkha expansion through alliances with Lamjung and Palpa.
kingdom-of-tanahun.e: The Gorkha forces of the Kingdom of Nepal annexed Tanahun in 1782 during the unification of Nepal under the regent Bahadur Shah. It is now Tanahun district.

kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.t: A northern kingdom of the Chu-Han war, first the place of exile for the Zhao king Zhao Xie and then the fief of Chen Yu, overrun by Han Xin.
kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.o: In 206 BCE Xiang Yu moved Zhao Xie, the restored king of Zhao, north to the frontier region of Dai, with its capital at Dai near modern Yuxian, Hebei, so that Zhang Er could rule the Zhao heartland as the Kingdom of Changshan.
kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.r: In 205 BCE Chen Yu drove out Zhang Er and brought Zhao Xie back to Zhao; in thanks, Zhao Xie made Chen Yu King of Dai. Chen Yu stayed in Zhao as chief minister and governed Dai through his deputy Xia Yue. The kingdom was a frontier zone of herding and farming facing the Xiongnu.
kingdom-of-dai-206-bc.e: In 205 BCE Han Xin defeated and captured Xia Yue, and in 204 BCE he destroyed the Zhao army at Jingxing, where Chen Yu was killed. Dai passed to the Han Dynasty and later became a Han kingdom held by Liu Bang's son, the future Emperor Wen.

kathiwara-state.t: A small Rajput chiefship in the hills of western Malwa, under British supervision through the Bhopawar Agency.
kathiwara-state.o: Kathiwara was a small estate in the hills of western Malwa near Jhabua, held by a Rajput family from around 1600. Its founding is not well documented.
kathiwara-state.r: Its chief ruled hilly, forested country with a largely Bhil population, paying tribute to more powerful neighbours. In the British period it was a minor state in the Bhopawar Agency of Central India. Little else is recorded.
kathiwara-state.e: Kathiwara joined Madhya Bharat in 1948, which became part of Madhya Pradesh in 1956.

kingdom-of-hazor.t: Hazor, the largest Canaanite city, which traded with Mari and Babylon and which the Bible calls the head of all those kingdoms.
kingdom-of-hazor.o: Hazor grew north of the Sea of Galilee on the road from Egypt to Syria. In the 18th century BCE a huge lower city was added to the old mound, creating a city of some 80 hectares. It is the only Canaanite city named in the Mari letters, which mention tin sent to its king.
kingdom-of-hazor.r: Its kings ruled from a palace on the upper city with basalt orthostats and temples in Syrian style, and controlled much of northern Canaan. In the Amarna age King Abdi-Tirshi was a vassal of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom, though neighbours accused him of disloyalty. Excavations by Yigael Yadin and Amnon Ben-Tor uncovered statues and cuneiform tablets.
kingdom-of-hazor.e: In the 13th century BCE the Canaanite city was destroyed by fire, and its statues deliberately defaced. The Book of Joshua credits its destruction to the Israelites; scholars still debate who was responsible. A smaller fortified town later belonged to the Kingdom of Israel.

kingdom-of-desmond.t: The MacCarthy kingdom of South Munster, created when Munster was split in 1118 and surviving in parts until the end of the 16th century.
kingdom-of-desmond.o: The Treaty of Glanmire in 1118 divided Munster, giving the south, Deasmumu, to the MacCarthys, heirs of the Eoganacht kings of Cashel. Cormac MacCarthy ruled from Cork and built Cormac's Chapel on the Rock of Cashel, consecrated in 1134.
kingdom-of-desmond.r: Desmond's kings lost much of Cork to the Normans after 1177, but Finghin MacCarthy's victory at Callann in 1261 halted the colonists. The MacCarthy Mor branch then ruled from Pallis in Kerry, with cadet lines in Carbery and Muskerry. The kingdom was an overlordship of Gaelic lords such as the O'Sullivans and O'Donoghues.
kingdom-of-desmond.e: Donal MacCarthy Mor became Earl of Clancare in 1565 under the Kingdom of Ireland. His death without a legitimate male heir in 1596 ended the senior line, and its lands passed into English plantations.

khanate-of-khoy.t: A khanate of the Kurdish Donboli family in north-western Iran whose last khan resisted the Qajars and ended his days ruling a khanate under Russia.
khanate-of-khoy.o: The Donboli, a Kurdish family long settled around Khoy, held hereditary authority there under the Safavids. After Nader Shah's death in 1747 they ruled Khoy and Salmas as a khanate. Ahmad Khan Donboli (r. 1763 to 1786) was the most powerful of the line, extending his influence over Tabriz.
khanate-of-khoy.r: Khoy lay on the main route between Tabriz and the Ottoman frontier and was a prosperous trading town. The Donboli khans kept tribal cavalry and patronised building in the town. Ahmad Khan was murdered in 1786, and his son Jafar Qoli Khan Donboli opposed the rising power of Agha Mohammad Khan.
khanate-of-khoy.e: Agha Mohammad Khan's Qajar Iran took control of the region in the 1790s; Jafar Qoli Khan fled north in 1799 and was later installed by Russia as khan of Sheki. Khoy became part of Qajar Azerbaijan.

kingdom-of-mpororo.t: A short-lived pastoral kingdom between Uganda and Rwanda whose breakup left a patchwork of small chiefdoms later absorbed by Ankole.
kingdom-of-mpororo.o: Mpororo arose in the mid-17th century in the grasslands of south-western Uganda and northern Rwanda, ruled by the Bashambo clan. Traditions connect its founding with the decline of the Kingdom of Ndorwa and the rivalries of the Kingdom of Rwanda and the Kingdom of Ankole.
kingdom-of-mpororo.r: It was a cattle-keeping kingdom with a court and royal drums like its neighbours. Its power seems to have rested on the king's herds and on alliances with pastoral clans. Only fragments of its history survive in oral tradition.
kingdom-of-mpororo.e: In the mid-18th century Mpororo split into several small principalities, among them Rujumbura and Kajara. Under the Ankole Agreement of 1901 most of these were merged into the Kingdom of Ankole, while others went to Kigezi district.

kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.t: Croatian kingdom in personal union with Hungary, governed by bans and a noble diet, until the disaster of Mohács led it to the Habsburgs.
kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.o: After the Trpimirović line ended and the last king fell at Gvozd in 1097, Coloman of Hungary was crowned king of Croatia and Dalmatia at Biograd in 1102. Later tradition held that a pact (Pacta conventa) with Croatian nobles guaranteed their rights, though its authenticity is disputed.
kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.r: The kingdom kept its own institutions: a ban governed for the king, and the Sabor (diet) of nobles met separately. Great families such as the Šubići of Bribir and the Frankopans held vast lands; Ban Paul I Šubić was almost independent around 1300. Venice and Hungary fought over Dalmatia for centuries, and in 1409 Ladislaus of Naples sold his Dalmatian claims to Venice. Ottoman raids grew after 1463, with a heavy defeat at Krbava Field in 1493.
kingdom-of-croatia-1102-1526.e: After Louis II died at Mohács in 1526, the Croatian nobles meeting at Cetin in 1527 elected Ferdinand of Habsburg as king, beginning centuries of Habsburg rule.

kingdom-of-urartu.t: Urartu, a mountain kingdom around Lake Van, Assyria's great northern rival, famed for its fortresses, canals and bronze work.
kingdom-of-urartu.o: Urartu formed in the 9th century BCE when the chiefdoms of Nairi united under pressure from the Assyrian Empire. Sarduri I built the fortress of Van, called Tushpa, on a rock above Lake Van c. 840 BCE, and his successors pushed the kingdom into Transcaucasia and north-western Iran.
kingdom-of-urartu.r: Kings governed through fortified centres with storerooms for grain and wine, linked by roads. Menua built a canal over 50 km long that still waters Van, and Argishti I founded Erebuni in 782 BCE, origin of Yerevan. The god Haldi headed the pantheon; his temple at Musasir was famous for its treasures.
kingdom-of-urartu.e: Sargon II of the Assyrian Empire defeated Rusa I and sacked Musasir in 714 BCE. Urartu recovered under Rusa II but collapsed in the early 6th century BCE, probably under attacks by the Median Empire and Scythians. Armenians later occupied its lands.

kingdom-of-anshan.t: The small Persian kingdom in Fars ruled by the ancestors of Cyrus the Great, the springboard for the Achaemenid Empire.
kingdom-of-anshan.o: After Ashurbanipal crushed the Neo-Elamite kingdom in the mid-7th century BCE, Persian rulers took control of Anshan, the old Elamite highland capital at Tall-i Malyan in Fars. Assyrian texts mention Kurash of Parsumash, often identified with Cyrus I, sending his son as hostage to Ashurbanipal around 640 BCE.
kingdom-of-anshan.r: The Cyrus Cylinder gives the line of Teispes, Cyrus I and Cambyses I, all 'king of Anshan'. The dynasty, called Teispid by historians, ruled a mixed Persian and Elamite society; a seal of Cyrus I follows Elamite style and Elamite remained a written language of administration. The kingdom was probably a vassal first of Assyria and then of the Median Empire, and Herodotus says Cambyses I married a Median princess.
kingdom-of-anshan.e: In 550 BCE Cyrus II, king of Anshan, defeated the Median king Astyages and took Ecbatana, then went on to found the Achaemenid Empire. Anshan's royal tradition lived on in the titles of Persian kings.

kahat.t: Kahat, a small kingdom of the upper Khabur plains in the age of Mari, one of many rival city-states of the region known as Ida-Maras.
kahat.o: Kahat grew at Tell Barri on the Jaghjagh river in north-eastern Syria, a site inhabited since the 4th millennium BCE. By the 18th century BCE it was one of the minor kingdoms of the Ida-Maras district, between the larger powers of Mari, Ashnakkum and Shubat-Enlil.
kahat.r: Known mainly from the Mari letters, its kings swore alliances with Zimri-Lim and switched sides as the balance of power shifted. Kahat was also a religious centre of the storm god, honoured in later Hurrian and Assyrian sources. Italian excavations since 1980 have explored the town.
kahat.e: The kingdom lost its independence when Hammurabi's Babylonian Empire and later the Mitanni Empire reshaped northern Mesopotamia. Kahat survived as a town under Mitanni and the Assyrian Empire.

kingdom-of-kasanje.t: An Imbangala kingdom on the Kwango whose fair channelled captives from the Lunda interior to Portuguese Luanda for two centuries.
kingdom-of-kasanje.o: Kasanje was founded around 1620 by an Imbangala warband, formerly allied with Portuguese Angola, which settled in the Baixa de Kasanje, the fertile Kwango valley. Its leader, Kasanje, and his successors combined Imbangala military traditions with Mbundu lineage institutions to build a stable kingdom.
kingdom-of-kasanje.r: The king, titled the Jaga Kasanje, ruled through officials drawn from different lineages, and Imbangala rituals shaped kingship. The kingdom's wealth came from its position as middleman: captives and ivory from the Lunda Empire passed through the Kasanje market to Portuguese traders, who kept a resident agent there. Kasanje jealously blocked direct contact between the coast and the interior.
kingdom-of-kasanje.e: The end of the slave trade undermined Kasanje's economy, and wars with the Portuguese in the 1850s weakened it. Portuguese forces finally occupied the region in 1912, absorbing it into Portuguese Angola.

kingdom-of-eile.t: Irish kingdom of the O'Carrolls around Birr, on the border of Munster and Leinster, which survived as Ely O'Carroll until the 16th century.
kingdom-of-eile.o: Éile was the territory of an early medieval people of the Irish midlands, in what is now south Offaly and north Tipperary, counted as part of the Kingdom of Munster. Its ruling family claimed descent from the Eóganachta's kin, and from the 11th century the Ua Cerbaill, O'Carroll, became the dominant line, giving the region its later name of Ely O'Carroll.
kingdom-of-eile.r: The kingdom lay on the boundary between Munster and Leinster, which gave it strategic value and exposed it to raids. The monastery of Birr, founded by St Brendan of Birr in the 6th century, produced the Book of MacRegol, an illuminated gospel book of about 800. The O'Carrolls ruled from strongholds such as Leap Castle and Birr.
kingdom-of-eile.e: Anglo-Norman settlers took part of the territory in the 13th century, but the O'Carrolls recovered much of it. In 1552 their chief Tadhg O'Carroll surrendered his lands to the crown and was created Baron of Ely, and the region was later divided between King's County and Tipperary.
kingdom-of-eile.la: Old Irish, later Middle and Early Modern Irish

kingdom-of-cusco.t: The small highland kingdom around Cusco from which the Incas rose to build the largest empire of the pre-Columbian Americas.
kingdom-of-cusco.o: Inca tradition says the founder Manco Capac emerged from Lake Titicaca or the cave of Pacaritambo and led his people to the valley of Cusco, founding the city around 1200. Archaeology shows the Killke culture in the valley from about 1000, which developed into the early Inca polity.
kingdom-of-cusco.r: The early Inca kingdom was one of several competing lordships in the region, led by a ruler called the Sapa Inca and by royal lineages called panacas. Cusco was organised in two halves, Hanan and Hurin. Successive rulers such as Sinchi Roca, Mayta Capac and Viracocha Inca fought and allied with neighbours such as the Ayarmaca. The economy depended on maize terraces and herding.
kingdom-of-cusco.e: According to Inca tradition, around 1438 Cusi Yupanqui repelled the Chanka Confederation, deposed his father Viracocha Inca and took the name Pachacuti. He rebuilt Cusco and began the conquests that created the Inca Empire.

karkiya-dynasty.t: A Shia dynasty of eastern Gilan, centred on Lahijan, that sheltered the boy who became Shah Ismail I, founder of the Safavid state.
karkiya-dynasty.o: Sayyid Ali Kiya, a Zaydi sayyid supported by the Mar'ashi dynasty of Mazandaran, took Lahijan and eastern Gilan (Biyapish) around 1370. His descendants, the Kar-Kiya, ruled this part of Gilan east of the Sefidrud.
karkiya-dynasty.r: The Karkiya combined religious authority as sayyids with princely rule over a wet, forested land of rice, silk and fishing. They long followed Zaydi Shia Islam, later adopting Twelver Shi'ism, and fought the Sunni Ishaqid dynasty of western Gilan. Sultan Ali Mirza Karkiya gave refuge at Lahijan from 1494 to 1499 to the young Ismail, heir of the Safavid order, who left from there to found the Safavid Empire.
karkiya-dynasty.e: Khan Ahmad Khan, the last ruler, quarrelled with Shah Abbas I, who conquered Gilan in 1592; Khan Ahmad fled to the Ottoman Empire.

khyrim-state.t: A Khasi state of the Meghalaya plateau with its seat at Smit, home of the annual Nongkrem dance held by its Syiem.
khyrim-state.o: Hima Khyrim emerged as one of the Khasi chiefdoms of the Shillong plateau; its origins are known from oral tradition, and the register's start date is approximate.
khyrim-state.r: Khyrim was headed by a Syiem chosen from a royal clan, with succession through the female line, and ruled with clan elders in a dorbar. The Syiem also had ritual duties: the annual Shad Nongkrem, a dance and thanksgiving at Smit, is held by the Syiem and the high priestess (Syiem Sad) of Khyrim.
khyrim-state.e: Khyrim came under British supervision in the 19th century and acceded to India in 1948, joining Assam. It is now part of Meghalaya, where the Nongkrem festival continues.

kalachuris-of-ratanpur.t: A Kalachuri branch that ruled Chhattisgarh from Ratanpur for over seven centuries, from the 11th century until the Maratha conquest.
kalachuris-of-ratanpur.o: Around 1000 Kalingaraja, a member of the Kalachuris of Tripuri, conquered the region of Dakshina Kosala, in modern Chhattisgarh, and settled at Tummana. His grandson Ratnaraja I founded Ratanpur, which became the capital, and the family gradually became independent of the Tripuri line.
kalachuris-of-ratanpur.r: Jajalladeva I and Prithvideva II extended the kingdom and fought the Eastern Ganga dynasty and other neighbours. The kings, Shaivas, built temples and tanks at Ratanpur and Malhar, and inscriptions show a structured administration with ministers and district chiefs. In later centuries the kingdom split into the Ratanpur and Raipur branches, and it is often linked with the name Chhattisgarh, thirty-six forts.
kalachuris-of-ratanpur.e: The Haihaya rajas survived as a regional power, acknowledging the Mughals in name. In 1741 the Maratha Bhonsles of Nagpur, under their general Bhaskar Pant, conquered Ratanpur, and the last raja was pensioned off.

kenedougou-kingdom.t: A Senufo and Dyula kingdom ruled from walled Sikasso, which held off Samori Toure and fell to the French only after a bloody siege in 1898.
kenedougou-kingdom.o: Kenedougou formed among Senufo farming communities in what is now southern Mali and western Burkina Faso, where Dyula traders of the Traore clan established a ruling dynasty, traditionally from the late 17th century. For long it was a loose chiefdom; it became a strong kingdom only in the 19th century, when Tieba Traore expanded it and moved the capital to Sikasso.
kenedougou-kingdom.r: Its kings ruled through a court of warriors, Senufo village chiefs and a Muslim Dyula merchant class, while most subjects kept Senufo traditional religion. Sikasso was ringed by a massive earthen tata wall several kilometres long. Kenedougou drew wealth from kola, cattle and the trade between the savanna and the forest, and bought firearms through the Atlantic trade.
kenedougou-kingdom.e: Samori Toure besieged Sikasso in 1887 and 1888 without success, and Tieba allied with the French. His brother Babemba Traore refused French demands, and on 1 May 1898 a French column stormed the city; Babemba died rather than surrender. The land became part of French Sudan.
kenedougou-kingdom.re: Senufo traditional religion and Sunni Islam

kingdom-of-dayuan.t: The ancient kingdom of the Ferghana valley, famed in China for its 'heavenly horses', which provoked the Han dynasty's longest-range war.
kingdom-of-dayuan.o: Dayuan, the Chinese name for the farming people of the Ferghana valley, was described by the envoy Zhang Qian around 128 BCE as a land of over 70 walled towns and several hundred thousand people. Its population may have included descendants of Greek settlers from Alexander's era, though this is debated.
kingdom-of-dayuan.r: The people grew rice, wheat and grapes, made wine and bred tall, fast horses that the Han court prized as 'blood-sweating' heavenly horses. A king ruled with nobles from the capital Ershi. In 104 BCE Dayuan refused to supply horses, and Emperor Wu sent the general Li Guangli, who after two campaigns besieged Ershi in 102 BCE, forcing the nobles to kill their king Wugua and hand over horses.
kingdom-of-dayuan.e: Dayuan remained a tributary of the Han for a time and appears in Chinese records into the 3rd century CE. Thereafter Ferghana was ruled by local dynasties that became the later Principality of Ferghana, still noted for its horses.

kingdom-of-the-regni.t: Client kingdom of Togidubnus in Sussex and Hampshire, a loyal ally of Rome after the conquest whose seat may have been the palace at Fishbourne.
kingdom-of-the-regni.o: After the Roman invasion of 43, much of the former realm of the Atrebates (Britain) was entrusted to Togidubnus, a British noble loyal to Rome. Tacitus says that certain states were given to him and that he remained faithful down to his own day, and the region became a base for Roman operations along the south coast.
kingdom-of-the-regni.r: An inscription from Chichester dedicating a temple to Neptune and Minerva names Tiberius Claudius Togidubnus as great king in Britain, showing that he held Roman citizenship and royal status. His capital, Noviomagus Reginorum, grew into a Roman-style town, and the lavish villa at Fishbourne, with mosaics and formal gardens, has often been linked to him. The kingdom provided Rome with a stable and Romanised territory.
kingdom-of-the-regni.e: When Togidubnus died, probably around 80, the client kingdom was absorbed into the province of Roman Britain. Its lands were divided into civitates, the Regni around Chichester and probably the Belgae (Britain) around Winchester. Chichester remains the main town of the region.

kingdom-of-the-heruli.t: A short-lived East Germanic kingdom on the middle Danube, briefly dominant over the Lombards before a crushing defeat around 508.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.o: The Heruli had been in the Black Sea region and under Hunnic rule; after the Huns' collapse following the Battle of Nedao in 454, one group settled near the middle Danube, probably in southern Moravia, western Slovakia and Lower Austria. By about 490 they had a strong kingdom that took tribute from the Lombards.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.r: Procopius describes the Heruli as fierce warriors who kept old pagan customs, including the sacrifice of elderly people and the suicide of widows. Their king Rodulf allied with Theodoric the Great, who adopted him as a 'son in arms' around 507. The kingdom rested on warrior power and tribute rather than settled institutions.
kingdom-of-the-heruli.e: Around 508 Rodulf attacked the Lombards under Tato and was killed in a heavy defeat. The Heruli scattered: some moved into Roman territory and became federates in Illyricum, others went to Scandinavia according to Procopius. Herul soldiers later fought for Justinian in Italy and Persia.

kingdom-of-bavaria.t: Wittelsbach kingdom created by Napoleon, the largest German state after Prussia and home of the fairy-tale castles of Ludwig II.
kingdom-of-bavaria.o: Elector Maximilian IV Joseph, allied with Napoleon, was proclaimed King Maximilian I of Bavaria on 1 January 1806. Napoleon's settlements added Franconia, Swabian lands and imperial cities, creating a state of mixed religion and identity.
kingdom-of-bavaria.r: Minister Montgelas modernised the administration, and the constitution of 1818 established a parliament. Ludwig I turned Munich into a city of classical architecture and museums before abdicating in 1848 over the Lola Montez affair. Ludwig II, patron of Wagner, built Neuschwanstein and Linderhof and was deposed in 1886; his uncle Luitpold ruled as regent. Bavaria kept its own army and railway in the German Empire.
kingdom-of-bavaria.e: Bavaria sided with Austria in 1866 but joined the German Empire in 1871. In November 1918 Kurt Eisner proclaimed a republic in Munich and Ludwig III fled, ending the monarchy; the state became the Free State of Bavaria.

kii-domain.t: One of the three Tokugawa branch houses, ruling from Wakayama, which gave Japan two shoguns, Yoshimune and Iemochi.
kii-domain.o: In 1619 the shogunate moved Tokugawa Yorinobu, the tenth son of Tokugawa Ieyasu, to Wakayama, giving him Kii province and part of Ise with about 555,000 koku. Kii became one of the three Gosanke houses entitled to supply a shogun.
kii-domain.r: The domain controlled the Kii peninsula, with forests of the Kumano region, mandarin orange orchards, fisheries and the soy sauce makers of Yuasa. When the main line of shoguns ended in 1716, the Kii lord Tokugawa Yoshimune became the eighth shogun and launched the Kyoho reforms. In 1858 another Kii lord, Yoshitomi, became Shogun Tokugawa Iemochi.
kii-domain.e: Kii submitted to the new government in 1868 and carried out military reforms. After abolition in 1871 it became Wakayama Prefecture; the diplomat Mutsu Munemitsu came from Kii.

kuru-kingdom.t: The leading kingdom of the Middle Vedic period, where the Vedic hymns were collected and the ritual order of early Hinduism took shape.
kuru-kingdom.o: The Kuru tribe formed in the upper Ganges-Yamuna Doab around 1200 BCE, when the Bharata and Puru clans merged into a single polity. Under kings remembered in the Atharvaveda and the Brahmanas, notably Parikshit and his son Janamejaya, it became the dominant power of northern India, with centres at Asandivat and Hastinapura. Many historians regard it as the first state-level society in South Asia.
kuru-kingdom.r: Kuru kings patronised Brahmin priests, who arranged the hymns of the Rigveda into collections and developed the Samaveda and Yajurveda. Royal consecration rites such as the Rajasuya and the horse sacrifice reinforced kingship, and society was ordered into the four varnas. The economy rested on cattle herding, barley and rice farming, and the early use of iron. Memories of the kingdom later formed the backdrop of the Mahabharata.
kuru-kingdom.e: Tradition says a flood of the Ganges drove the court from Hastinapura to Kaushambi. By the 6th century BCE the Kurus were a minor mahajanapada, partly ruled as a sangha, overshadowed by Kosala and Magadha. Their territory was absorbed by the Nanda Empire in the 4th century BCE.

kingdom-of-cottius.t: Alpine client kingdom around Susa whose ruler Cottius allied with Augustus and gave his name to the Cottian Alps.
kingdom-of-cottius.o: In the 1st century BCE the Segusini and neighbouring Alpine peoples around the Mont Genèvre pass were ruled by a king named Donnus, who appears in Caesar's time. His son, Marcus Julius Cottius, chose to make peace with Augustus rather than resist the Roman conquest of the Alps.
kingdom-of-cottius.r: Cottius governed fourteen Alpine communities as a Roman prefect while keeping royal status locally. He built and maintained the road over the Mont Genèvre pass, a key route between Italy and Gaul. In 9–8 BCE he erected the Arch of Augustus at Segusio (Susa), whose inscription lists his peoples. The kingdom combined Celtic traditions with Roman administration.
kingdom-of-cottius.e: Claudius restored the royal title to Cottius's son, Marcus Julius Cottius II, in 44 CE. When he died without an heir around 63 CE, Nero annexed the kingdom as the province of the Alpes Cottiae. The name survives in the Cottian Alps.

kingdom-of-moylurg.t: A Gaelic lordship of north Roscommon ruled by the MacDermots from their island fortress on Lough Key.
kingdom-of-moylurg.o: Magh Luirg was the territory of a branch of the Sil Muiredaig, the ruling kindred of Connacht. In the 12th century the MacDermot family, descended from Diarmait mac Taidg, emerged as its rulers and as marshals of the O'Connor kings of Connacht.
kingdom-of-moylurg.r: The MacDermots ruled from the Rock of Lough Ce, an island fortress on Lough Key, and patronised the abbey of Boyle and the learned families who compiled the Annals of Loch Ce. Their lordship was based on cattle, clients and armed retainers, and they served as kingmakers in Connacht politics.
kingdom-of-moylurg.e: The Composition of Connacht in 1585 brought the lordship under English land law. The MacDermots kept part of their lands and their title, the MacDermot, Prince of Coolavin, has been recognised into modern times.

kievan-rus.t: The first great East Slavic state, ruled by the Rurikid princes from Kiev, which brought Orthodox Christianity to the lands of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.
kievan-rus.o: In 882, according to the Primary Chronicle, Oleg of Novgorod seized Kiev and joined the northern and southern ends of the river route from the Varangians to the Greeks. His successors Igor, Olga and Sviatoslav I forced the East Slavic tribes into tribute, destroyed the Khazar Khaganate and raided Byzantium.
kievan-rus.r: The state was a family enterprise of the Rurikid princes, who shared out towns among themselves, with Kiev as the senior seat. Vladimir the Great accepted Christianity from Byzantium in 988, bringing churches, Church Slavonic writing and Byzantine art. Yaroslav the Wise issued the law code known as the Russkaya Pravda and built the Cathedral of Saint Sophia.
kievan-rus.e: After Vladimir Monomakh and his son Mstislav, who died in 1132, Rus' broke into rival principalities such as Chernigov, Vladimir-Suzdal and the Novgorod Republic. The Mongol invasion ended it, sacking Kiev in 1240. Ukraine, Belarus and Russia all trace their history to Rus'.

khanate-of-qaradagh.t: A mountain khanate north of Tabriz, centred on Ahar, that emerged after Nader Shah's death and was gradually absorbed by the Qajars.
khanate-of-qaradagh.o: Qaradagh, the 'Black Mountain' country between Tabriz and the Aras river, became a separate khanate after the assassination of Nader Shah in 1747 broke up the Afsharid Empire. Local tribal chiefs ruled from Ahar, a town known for the shrine of the Sufi Sheikh Shihab al-Din.
khanate-of-qaradagh.r: The khanate was a land of mountain villages and pastoral tribes, with copper and other mineral resources. Its khans, of whom Kazem Khan Qaradaghi is among the best known, competed with the neighbouring Tabriz and Karabakh khanates and paid tribute to whichever power dominated Azerbaijan. Records of its internal government are sparse.
khanate-of-qaradagh.e: Agha Mohammad Khan's Qajar Iran brought Qaradagh under its control in the 1790s. After the Russo-Persian War ended with the Treaty of Turkmenchay in 1828, the Aras became the border, and Qaradagh remained within Iran as a governorate.

kingdom-of-karagwe.t: A kingdom west of Lake Victoria whose ruler Rumanyika welcomed the explorers Speke and Grant on their way to the source of the Nile.
kingdom-of-karagwe.o: Karagwe emerged around the 15th or 16th century, ruled by the Hinda dynasty that also ruled Ankole and other states of the region. It lay in the hills of north-western Tanzania, between Lake Victoria and the Kagera river, and traced its royal line to the legendary Ruhinda.
kingdom-of-karagwe.r: The mukama (king) ruled with chiefs over pastoral Bahima and farming Bairu. Karagwe grew rich in the 19th century as a staging post on the caravan routes linking Buganda with Zanzibar traders, trading ivory for cloth and firearms. King Rumanyika I hosted John Hanning Speke and James Grant in 1861, and their accounts made Karagwe known in Europe.
kingdom-of-karagwe.e: Succession wars and disease weakened the kingdom in the late 19th century, and it was absorbed into German East Africa and then Tanganyika Territory as a native authority. The chiefdom was abolished by the government of independent Tanganyika in 1963.

kingdom-of-lapethos.t: North Cypriot kingdom where Phoenician kings ruled a Greek population in the Classical age, until Ptolemy I deposed the last king in 312 BCE.
kingdom-of-lapethos.o: Lapethos lay on the north coast of Cyprus near modern Lambousa, facing Anatolia. Greek tradition said it was founded by Praxandros from Laconia after the Trojan War. A city-kingdom by the 7th century BCE, it had close ties with the Phoenician coast.
kingdom-of-lapethos.r: In the 5th and 4th centuries BCE Lapethos was ruled by a dynasty with Phoenician names, such as Sidqmelek, who issued coins with Phoenician legends; Phoenician inscriptions from the town honour Melqart and other gods. The economy rested on farming, fishing and trade, and the city had a good harbour.
kingdom-of-lapethos.e: Its last king, Praxippos, supported Antigonus against Ptolemy I, who removed him in 312 BCE and annexed the kingdom. Lapethos continued as a Ptolemaic and Roman town, later called Lambousa, abandoned after Arab raids in the 7th century CE.

kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.t: Self-governing Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary, a time of rapid growth and Budapest's rise, and of tension with the kingdom's many nationalities.
kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.o: Austria's defeat by Prussia in 1866 forced Franz Joseph to settle with the Hungarian leaders Ferenc Deák and Gyula Andrássy. The Compromise of 1867 restored Hungary's constitution and parliament, with the emperor crowned king, and created Austria-Hungary, sharing only the monarch, foreign policy, the army and common finances. The Croatian-Hungarian Settlement of 1868 gave Croatia-Slavonia autonomy within it.
kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.r: Parliament was dominated by the landed nobility and gentry under a narrow franchise, led by premiers such as Kálmán Tisza and István Tisza. Pest, Buda and Óbuda merged into Budapest in 1873, which grew into a major industrial city, celebrated in the Millennium of 1896. Policies of Magyarisation, such as the Apponyi school laws of 1907, angered Slovaks, Romanians and Serbs.
kingdom-of-hungary-1867-1918.e: Defeat in the First World War brought the Aster Revolution of October 1918, and the Hungarian Democratic Republic was proclaimed in November. The Treaty of Trianon in 1920 transferred two-thirds of the former kingdom to its neighbours.

kingdom-of-damot.t: A powerful non-Christian kingdom of the southwestern Ethiopian highlands that rivalled Shewa and the Muslim sultanates in the 13th century.
kingdom-of-damot.o: Damot is known mainly from Ethiopian Christian traditions and hagiographies. In the 13th century it was a strong kingdom south of the Abay (Blue Nile), and tradition says its ruler, remembered under the title Motalami, forced Muslim and Christian neighbours in Shewa to pay tribute.
kingdom-of-damot.r: Little is known of its government or society. Its people followed traditional religions, and saints' lives describe the missionary Tekle Haymanot, founder of Debre Libanos, preaching there. Damot lay on routes that brought gold and slaves from the southwest to the highland and coastal markets.
kingdom-of-damot.e: The Solomonic emperor Amda Seyon conquered Damot around 1316 and made it a province of the Ethiopian Empire. The name lived on as a province, and from the 16th century Oromo migrations transformed the region.

kingdom-of-kashi.t: The ancient kingdom of Varanasi on the Ganges, an early centre of Vedic learning and a prize fought over by Kosala and Magadha.
kingdom-of-kashi.o: Kashi grew around Varanasi, where the Varuna meets the Ganges, in the Later Vedic period. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad names a learned king, Ajatashatru of Kashi, who taught the Brahmin Gargya about the nature of the self. By the 6th century BCE it was listed among the sixteen mahajanapadas of Buddhist texts.
kingdom-of-kashi.r: Its wealth came from river trade, fine textiles and its sacred standing, for Varanasi was already a place of pilgrimage and teaching. The Jataka tales set many stories in the reigns of kings called Brahmadatta of Varanasi, and Jain tradition makes the 23rd tirthankara, Parshvanatha, the son of a Kashi king. The Buddha gave his first sermon at nearby Sarnath.
kingdom-of-kashi.e: Kashi lost a long rivalry with its neighbour, the Kingdom of Kosala, in the 6th century BCE. Revenue from a Kashi village formed the dowry of a Kosalan princess who married Bimbisara of Magadha, and the quarrel over it led to war; the territory passed to Magadha under Ajatashatru. Varanasi remains Hinduism's holiest city.

kingdom-of-kosala.t: A great kingdom of the middle Ganges plain, ruled from Shravasti, where the Buddha spent much of his teaching life before Magadha swallowed it.
kingdom-of-kosala.o: Kosala appears in Later Vedic texts as a kingdom east of Panchala, between the Gomti and the Sarayu rivers, with early centres at Ayodhya and Saketa. Its kings claimed descent from the solar Ikshvaku line, the lineage of Rama in the Ramayana. By the 7th and 6th centuries BCE it had become one of the strongest of the sixteen mahajanapadas, with its capital at Shravasti.
kingdom-of-kosala.r: King Mahakosala annexed the Kingdom of Kashi and held the Shakya and Koliya republics as dependants. His son Prasenajit was a lay follower of the Buddha, and the merchant Anathapindika gave the Jetavana grove at Shravasti, where the Buddha spent many rainy seasons. Shravasti and Saketa were wealthy trading cities on the northern route. Kosala's rivalry with Magadha was eased for a time by royal marriages.
kingdom-of-kosala.e: Prasenajit was overthrown by his son Vidudabha, who destroyed the Shakyas around the time of the Buddha's death. Soon after, Kosala was absorbed by the Kingdom of Magadha under Ajatashatru or his successors in the 5th century BCE. Ayodhya's place in the Ramayana kept the name Kosala alive in Indian tradition.

kingdom-of-pylos.t: Mycenaean kingdom of Messenia whose burnt palace preserved more than a thousand Linear B tablets, the fullest record of a Bronze Age Greek state.
kingdom-of-pylos.o: Pylos grew on the Englianos ridge in western Messenia, where rich shaft and tholos tombs show an emerging elite by c. 1650 BCE, including the Griffin Warrior burial found in 2015. By the 14th and 13th centuries BCE its rulers had unified Messenia into a single kingdom divided into two provinces.
kingdom-of-pylos.r: The palace, linked by Homer with King Nestor, was headed by a wanax with a lawagetas below him. Its Linear B archive records taxation of some 16 districts, landholding, bronze-smiths, flax and perfumed oil production, rowers for the fleet and offerings to Poseidon, Zeus, Hera and the Potnia. Frescoes and a well-preserved throne room survive.
kingdom-of-pylos.e: The palace was destroyed by fire c. 1180 BCE, apparently while preparing coastal defences, and the region largely depopulated. Its tablets, baked by the fire, were found by Carl Blegen in 1939 and helped Michael Ventris show in 1952 that Linear B was Greek.

kingdom-of-egypt.t: Egypt's constitutional monarchy under Fuad I and Farouk, independent in name but under British influence, overthrown by the Free Officers.
kingdom-of-egypt.o: Britain's declaration of February 1922 ended the Sultanate of Egypt, recognising Egypt as independent while reserving defence, communications, foreign interests and Sudan. Fuad I took the title of king, and a constitution followed in 1923.
kingdom-of-egypt.r: Parliamentary politics were dominated by the struggle between the popular Wafd party, the palace and the British. The Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936 kept British troops in the Canal Zone. In 1942 British tanks surrounded Abdeen Palace to force Farouk to appoint a Wafd government, and the Axis advance was halted at El Alamein. Defeat in the 1948 war against Israel discredited the regime.
kingdom-of-egypt.e: After the Cairo riots of January 1952, the Free Officers led by Muhammad Naguib and Gamal Abdel Nasser seized power in July. Farouk abdicated for his infant son Fuad II, and the monarchy was abolished in June 1953, creating the Republic of Egypt.

kingdom-of-baguirmi.t: Sultanate of the lower Chari river in Chad, a slave-raiding state caught between the larger powers of Bornu and Wadai.
kingdom-of-baguirmi.o: Baguirmi was founded in the early 16th century, traditionally in 1522, by a dynasty that established its capital at Massenya, south-east of Lake Chad. Its rulers took the title mbang. Islam was adopted at court under Mbang Abdullah, who reigned in the late 16th century.
kingdom-of-baguirmi.r: The mbang ruled with a court of officials, many of them eunuchs, and a cavalry force that raided the peoples to the south for slaves, who were traded north and used on Baguirmi farms. The kingdom paid tribute at times to the Kanem-Bornu Empire and later to the Wadai Empire.
kingdom-of-baguirmi.e: In 1871 Wadai sacked Massenya, and in the 1890s Rabih az-Zubayr devastated the country. Mbang Gaourang II accepted a French protectorate in 1897, and Baguirmi became part of French colonial Chad. The sultanate survives as a traditional office.

kingdom-of-circinn.t: A Pictish kingdom or province in the area of Angus and the Mearns, named in early Irish annals and in the legend of the seven sons of Cruithne.
kingdom-of-circinn.o: Circinn appears as one of the seven Pictish provinces in the origin legend that named them after the sons of Cruithne, and in Irish annals, which record a battle of Circinn in 598. It is usually placed in Angus and the Mearns, south of the Mounth.
kingdom-of-circinn.r: Almost nothing is known of its government. It was probably one of the regional lordships within the Pictish kingdom, and the fertile lowlands of Angus held important church sites such as Aberlemno and later Brechin, with their carved Pictish stones.
kingdom-of-circinn.e: Circinn's identity merged into the Kingdom of Scotland when Pictland became Alba in the 9th and 10th centuries. The later earldoms of Angus and the Mearns may continue its territory.

kingdom-of-kullu.t: An ancient kingdom of the upper Beas valley, whose 17th-century Raja Jagat Singh founded the Dussehra festival that still draws gods from across the valley to Kullu.
kingdom-of-kullu.o: Kullu appears in early Indian texts as Kuluta, and local tradition traces its Pal dynasty to a founder called Behangamani Pal. The early capital was at Jagatsukh and later Naggar. Firm history begins only in the 16th and 17th centuries, when the Rajas took the name Singh and expanded across the surrounding valleys.
kingdom-of-kullu.r: Raja Jagat Singh (r. 1637–1672) moved the capital to Sultanpur, now Kullu town, and installed the image of Raghunath, making him the kingdom's divine sovereign. The annual Dussehra, at which village deities are carried to Raghunath's presence, dates from his reign. Kullu controlled trade routes to Lahaul, Spiti and Ladakh, and under Man Singh it reached its greatest extent.
kingdom-of-kullu.e: Weakened by succession quarrels, Kullu fell under the Sikh Empire, which took direct control in 1840. After the First Anglo-Sikh War it passed to the British in 1846 and became part of Kangra district; the royal family kept only the jagir of Rupi. Kullu is now a district of Himachal Pradesh.

kingdom-of-mycenae.t: The leading Bronze Age Greek kingdom in the Argolid, whose shaft graves, Lion Gate and tholos tombs gave its name to the Mycenaean civilisation.
kingdom-of-mycenae.o: Mycenae occupies a hill in the north-east Argolid controlling routes to Corinth. Its rise is shown by Grave Circles A and B, used c. 1650 to 1500 BCE, with gold masks and weapons. In the 14th and 13th centuries BCE a palace, Cyclopean walls and great tholos tombs such as the Treasury of Atreus were built.
kingdom-of-mycenae.r: Mycenae was ruled by a wanax from a palace with a central megaron and frescoes, and was probably the most powerful of several Argolid centres including Tiryns. Linear B tablets record perfumed oil and other goods. Its pottery spread across the Mediterranean, and some scholars link it to the Ahhiyawa known from Hittite texts. The Lion Gate dates to c. 1250 BCE.
kingdom-of-mycenae.e: The citadel suffered destructions c. 1200 BCE and the palace system collapsed, though occupation continued until c. 1100 BCE. Later the small town was destroyed by Argos c. 468 BCE. Homer made it the seat of Agamemnon, and Schliemann's excavations from 1876 made it famous.

kingdom-of-norway.t: One of Europe's oldest kingdoms, forged by Harald Fairhair in the Viking Age and, after five centuries of union with its neighbours, independent again since 1905.
kingdom-of-norway.o: Norway grew out of the petty kingdoms of the Viking Age. Harald Fairhair of Vestfold united much of the coast, traditionally after the Battle of Hafrsfjord around 872. Olaf Tryggvason and Olaf Haraldsson imposed Christianity; Olaf fell at Stiklestad in 1030 and, as Saint Olaf, became the kingdom's patron and eternal king.
kingdom-of-norway.r: After a century of civil wars, Haakon IV restored strong monarchy, and Magnus the Lawmender issued a national law code in 1274. Medieval Norway ruled Iceland, Greenland, the Faroes and the Northern Isles, and lived from fishing, especially the stockfish trade through Bergen, dominated by the Hanseatic League. The Black Death of 1349 severely weakened it.
kingdom-of-norway.e: From 1380 Norway shared its kings with Denmark, in the Kalmar Union and then Denmark-Norway until 1814, when it adopted a constitution at Eidsvoll but was joined to Sweden as Sweden-Norway. Full independence came in 1905 under Haakon VII. Occupied by Germany in 1940-1945, it became a wealthy oil-producing constitutional monarchy.

kingdom-of-cologne.t: Kingdom of the Rhineland Franks at Cologne, absorbed by Clovis through murder around 509.
kingdom-of-cologne.o: The Franks of the middle Rhine, later called Ripuarian Franks, took over Cologne in the mid 5th century as Roman power collapsed. By the late 5th century they had their own king, Sigibert, who ruled from the former Roman capital of Germania Inferior.
kingdom-of-cologne.r: Sigibert, called the Lame from a wound received fighting the Alemanni at Zülpich, was an ally of Clovis and sent his son Chloderic to fight the Visigoths at Vouillé in 507. The Ripuarian Franks kept their own law, the Lex Ripuaria, written down in the 7th century.
kingdom-of-cologne.e: Gregory of Tours relates that Clovis incited Chloderic to murder his father, then had Chloderic killed and was raised on a shield as king by the people of Cologne, around 509. The realm became part of the Kingdom of the Franks and later of Austrasia.

kedatuan-of-dapitan.t: A Visayan polity on Bohol whose people, after a raid from Ternate around 1563, moved to northern Mindanao and gave their name to Dapitan.
kedatuan-of-dapitan.o: Dapitan is known from Spanish accounts, especially the Jesuit historian Francisco Combes, and from Boholano tradition. It was a settlement of the Bohol coast, probably on Panglao Island, ruled by datus and trading with other Visayan and Mindanao ports. Its founding date is unknown.
kedatuan-of-dapitan.r: Spanish sources describe a prosperous community of seafarers, traders and boat builders, led by datus over freemen and dependants, with indigenous religion and ties to Butuan and Cebu.
kedatuan-of-dapitan.e: Around 1563 raiders from Ternate, perhaps with Portuguese help, attacked Bohol. Datu Pagbuaya led many of the survivors to the north coast of Mindanao, where they founded Dapitan, in today's Zamboanga del Norte. Pagbuaya later helped the Spanish, and Dapitan became an early mission centre.

kingdom-of-maynila.t: The Muslim Tagalog kingdom on the south bank of the Pasig River, closely tied to Brunei, whose capture in 1571 gave Spain its Philippine capital.
kingdom-of-maynila.o: Maynila grew on the southern side of the Pasig River mouth, across from Tondo. Tradition holds that around 1500 Sultan Bolkiah of Brunei conquered it and set up a ruling family allied to Brunei, beginning with Rajah Salalila. By the 16th century its elite was Muslim and spoke of the Bruneian court as kin.
kingdom-of-maynila.r: Maynila was a fortified port with a palisade and bronze cannon, trading with Chinese, Bornean and Japanese merchants. Power was shared between Rajah Matanda and his nephew Rajah Sulayman, who led a nobility of datus over freemen and dependants.
kingdom-of-maynila.e: In 1570 a Spanish force under Martin de Goiti burned the town after a clash with Sulayman. In 1571 Miguel Lopez de Legazpi occupied the site and founded Spanish Manila. Sulayman was killed in the Battle of Bangkusay that year, and Manila became the capital of the Captaincy General of the Philippines.

kingdom-of-vatsa.t: The kingdom of Kaushambi on the Yamuna, ruled by the romantic hero Udayana and one of the four great powers of the Buddha's age.
kingdom-of-vatsa.o: Vatsa lay along the Yamuna south-west of modern Prayagraj, with its capital at Kaushambi. Tradition says the Kuru royal house moved there after Hastinapura was destroyed by a flood, and the Vatsa kings claimed that descent. By the 6th century BCE it was one of the four leading kingdoms, alongside Magadha, Kosala and Avanti.
kingdom-of-vatsa.r: Kaushambi was a large walled city on the trade routes between the Ganges plain and the west. Its best-known king, Udayana, a contemporary of the Buddha, became the hero of later Sanskrit plays such as Bhasa's Svapnavasavadatta, which tells of his marriage to Vasavadatta, daughter of Chanda Pradyota of Avanti. Kaushambi had important Buddhist monasteries, including the Ghositarama.
kingdom-of-vatsa.e: After Udayana the kingdom declined. It appears to have passed under the Kingdom of Avanti and then, with Avanti, under the Kingdom of Magadha by the 4th century BCE. Kaushambi stayed an important city under the Mauryas and Shungas.

kingdom-of-singapura.t: The 14th-century Malay port kingdom on Singapore island, founded according to legend by Sang Nila Utama and ancestor of the Malacca Sultanate.
kingdom-of-singapura.o: The Malay Annals tell how Sang Nila Utama, a prince of Palembang, landed on the island of Temasek, saw a beast he took for a lion and named the place Singapura, lion city. The register follows the traditional date of 1299. Chinese traveller Wang Dayuan described Danmaxi, Temasek, around 1330, with a settlement on a hill and pirates in the strait.
kingdom-of-singapura.r: Excavations on Fort Canning Hill and along the Singapore River have uncovered Chinese ceramics, gold ornaments and workshops, confirming a busy 14th-century port. Its rulers, called raja, presided over a Malay court and trade in forest goods, tin and textiles, under pressure from both Majapahit and Siam.
kingdom-of-singapura.e: Around 1398 the kingdom fell to an attack, attributed by the Malay Annals to Majapahit and by Portuguese sources to Siam. The last ruler, Iskandar Shah, also known as Parameswara, fled north and founded the Malacca Sultanate. Singapore was refounded as a British port in 1819.

kingdom-of-kent.t: The first English kingdom to accept Christianity, under Æthelberht in 597, and the home of the earliest laws written in English.
kingdom-of-kent.o: Bede says Kent was settled by Jutes led by Hengest and Horsa, who came as mercenaries of Vortigern around 449 and then turned against the Britons. The story is legendary, but archaeology shows strong links with Jutland and Frankish Gaul by the 6th century. The kingdom took its name from the British Cantiaci, and its centre was Canterbury.
kingdom-of-kent.r: Æthelberht, king from about 589 to 616, married the Frankish Christian princess Bertha and in 597 received Augustine's mission from Pope Gregory, making Canterbury the seat of the English Church. His law code is the earliest document in English. Kent was rich from trade with Francia, producing fine garnet jewellery and gold coinage, and later kings such as Wihtred issued further laws.
kingdom-of-kent.e: From the 760s Kent fell under Offa of Mercia; a revolt by Eadberht Præn was crushed in 798. In 825 Egbert of Wessex took Kent, which was ruled as a sub-kingdom by West Saxon princes until it was merged into Wessex in the 860s, later becoming an English shire.

kingdom-of-norway-1814.t: The brief independent Norway of 1814, which adopted the Eidsvoll constitution, still in force, before entering union with Sweden.
kingdom-of-norway-1814.o: When the Treaty of Kiel in January 1814 transferred Norway from Denmark to Sweden, the Danish prince Christian Frederik, governor in Norway, led resistance. A constituent assembly at Eidsvoll adopted a liberal constitution on 17 May 1814 and elected him king.
kingdom-of-norway-1814.r: The constitution, inspired by the American and French revolutions, divided power between king, an elected parliament, the Storting, and independent courts, and gave the vote to a relatively broad group of men. The new state had little time to govern: the great powers backed Sweden's claim, and the country was blockaded.
kingdom-of-norway-1814.e: Sweden invaded in July 1814, and after a short war the Convention of Moss on 14 August preserved the constitution in return for union. Christian Frederik abdicated in October, and on 4 November the Storting elected Charles XIII king, beginning Sweden-Norway. 17 May remains Norway's national day.

kingdom-of-deheubarth.t: The kingdom of south-west Wales, founded by Hywel Dda and later led by the Lord Rhys, a centre of Welsh law, poetry and resistance to Norman conquest.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.o: Deheubarth, 'the southern part', was formed around 920 when Hywel Dda united his inheritance of the Kingdom of Seisyllwg with Dyfed. Hywel later also ruled Gwynedd and Powys, and became the only Welsh king to issue coins.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.r: Hywel was credited with codifying Welsh law, the Cyfraith Hywel, which governed inheritance, compensation and status. The kingdom's centre was Dinefwr in the Tywi valley. Norman lords overran much of it after 1093, but Rhys ap Gruffydd, the Lord Rhys, rebuilt its power, held the first recorded eisteddfod at Cardigan in 1176 and patronised Strata Florida Abbey.
kingdom-of-deheubarth.e: After the Lord Rhys died in 1197, his sons divided Deheubarth in bitter feuds. Its remnants came under Gwynedd's Principality of Wales, and its lands were absorbed by the English crown after 1283.

kingdom-of-gelgel.t: The Balinese kingdom founded after Majapahit's conquest, whose 16th-century court shaped classical Balinese Hindu culture.
kingdom-of-gelgel.o: After Majapahit's conquest of the Bedulu Kingdom in 1343, Javanese rulers of the Kepakisan line were installed at Samprangan. By the late 14th century the court moved to Gelgel, near Klungkung in southeast Bali, which became the island's royal centre.
kingdom-of-gelgel.r: Under Dalem Waturenggong in the 16th century Gelgel ruled Bali, Lombok, Blambangan in Java and parts of Sumbawa. The Javanese priest Dang Hyang Nirartha, who came to Bali in that era, reshaped Balinese Hinduism and founded temples such as Tanah Lot and Uluwatu. Many Javanese nobles and priests fled to Gelgel as Islam spread in Java. Dutch sailors under Cornelis de Houtman visited in 1597.
kingdom-of-gelgel.e: In the 17th century Gelgel lost its overseas lands and faced revolts, including that of Gusti Agung Maruti around 1651. In 1686 Dewa Agung Jambe moved the court to Klungkung, and Bali divided into several kingdoms, among which Klungkung kept the senior title.

kingdom-of-kars.t: A small Armenian kingdom centred on the fortress city of Kars, ruled by a junior Bagratid line until it was handed to Byzantium.
kingdom-of-kars.o: In 963 Ashot III of Bagratid Armenia gave the district of Vanand, with the fortress of Kars, to his brother Mushegh, who took the title king. The kingdom remained linked to the senior line at Ani while governing its own affairs.
kingdom-of-kars.r: Kars was a strong fortress town on the route from Anatolia to the Caucasus, and its Cathedral of the Holy Apostles, built by King Abas in the 930s-40s when Kars was still the Bagratid capital, dominated the city. The kings ruled local nobles and peasants and acted as allies and rivals of the kings at Ani.
kingdom-of-kars.e: After Byzantium annexed Ani in 1045 and the Seljuks sacked it in 1064, King Gagik-Abas surrendered Kars to the Byzantine Empire in 1065 for lands in Cappadocia. The Seljuks took the city soon after.

kingdom-of-lori.t: An Armenian Bagratid kingdom in the gorges of northern Armenia, known for the monasteries of Haghpat and Sanahin.
kingdom-of-lori.o: Around 979 Gurgen, son of Ashot III of Bagratid Armenia, was given the northern provinces of Tashir and Dzoraget and took the title king, founding the Kyurikian line, named after his Georgian-style name Kyurike. The kingdom straddled the borderlands between Armenia and Georgia.
kingdom-of-lori.r: Kings ruled from fortresses such as Samshvilde and later Lori, controlling routes between Armenia and Georgia. The royal family endowed the monasteries of Sanahin and Haghpat, founded by Queen Khosrovanuysh in the 960s and 970s, which became major centres of learning and manuscript copying. The kingdom survived the fall of Ani in 1045 by allying with neighbours.
kingdom-of-lori.e: Seljuk attacks reduced the kingdom to Lori and its gorges, and it paid tribute to the Seljuk Empire. In 1118 David IV of the Kingdom of Georgia took Lori; the Kyurikians later held Tavush and Matsnaberd in the north-east.

kingdom-of-sabe.t: Yoruba kingdom in central Benin, on the north-western edge of the Yoruba world, ruled by the Onisabe.
kingdom-of-sabe.o: Known mainly from local tradition. Sabe, or Save, was founded by Yoruba-speakers who traced their kings to Ile-Ife, and took shape by the 16th century in the hilly country west of the Oyo lands.
kingdom-of-sabe.r: The Onisabe ruled with town chiefs and religious societies. Sabe traded with the Oyo Empire, Borgu and the coast, and was exposed to raids from the Kingdom of Dahomey and the Bariba of Borgu. It was a small state that survived by shifting alliances.
kingdom-of-sabe.e: Sabe came under French control after the conquest of Dahomey and was included in French Dahomey in 1894. The Onisabe remains a traditional ruler in the town of Save in Benin.

kingdom-of-laos.t: The constitutional monarchy of Laos from 1947 to 1975, independent from 1953 and torn apart by civil war between royalists and the Pathet Lao.
kingdom-of-laos.o: In 1946 France and King Sisavang Vong agreed to unite Luang Phrabang, Vientiane, Champasak and other Lao provinces into a single kingdom, with Prince Boun Oum of Champasak renouncing his claims. A constitution of 1947 made Laos a constitutional monarchy within the French Union, and full independence came in 1953.
kingdom-of-laos.r: The royal capital was Luang Prabang and the administrative capital Vientiane. Neutralist, rightist and communist factions competed, and the Geneva conference of 1962 created a coalition under Souvanna Phouma. The communist Pathet Lao, backed by North Vietnam, controlled the east, through which the Ho Chi Minh Trail ran, and the United States waged a massive secret bombing campaign.
kingdom-of-laos.e: After the Paris accords of 1973 a new coalition government formed, but in 1975 the Pathet Lao took power as communist forces won in Vietnam and Cambodia. King Savang Vatthana abdicated on 2 December 1975, and the Lao People's Democratic Republic was proclaimed.

kingdom-of-sweden.t: Scandinavian kingdom formed by uniting the Svear and Geats, which became a 17th-century great power and later a model of neutrality and welfare.
kingdom-of-sweden.o: The medieval kingdom emerged when Eric the Victorious and his son Olof Skötkonung, the first Christian king, ruled both the Svear around Uppsala and the Geats of Götaland, around 1000. Christianity and royal power spread slowly, and in the 13th century Birger Jarl strengthened the crown, founded Stockholm and conquered Tavastia.
kingdom-of-sweden.r: Sweden joined the Kalmar Union in 1397 but broke away when Gustav Vasa was elected king in 1523 and introduced the Lutheran Reformation. Gustav II Adolf made Sweden a great power in the Thirty Years' War, and its empire ringed the Baltic, from Finland and Livonia to Pomerania. Copper and iron mining at Falun and Bergslagen funded the state, and the Riksdag shared power with the crown.
kingdom-of-sweden.e: Defeat by Russia under Charles XII in the Great Northern War ended the empire in 1721, and Finland was lost in 1809. The Bernadotte dynasty took the throne in 1818, and Sweden ruled Norway in union until 1905. It stayed neutral in both world wars, built an extensive welfare state, joined the EU in 1995 and NATO in 2024.

kingdom-of-wukari.t: The Jukun kingdom of Wukari in the Benue valley, ruled by a sacred king, the Aku Uka, and heir to the older power known as Kwararafa.
kingdom-of-wukari.o: Wukari emerged as the main Jukun centre as the older Jukun power, Kwararafa, declined in the 18th century. Jukun tradition holds that the royal line moved south from earlier capitals such as Kororofa and Puje, and by about 1800 Wukari, south of the Benue river, was the seat of the paramount Jukun ruler.
kingdom-of-wukari.r: The Aku Uka was a sacred king, surrounded by taboos and ritual, whose well-being was believed to govern the harvest and the rains; Jukun ritual kingship became a classic case in anthropology. Real administration lay with officials and the heads of related Jukun communities. The economy rested on farming, salt from the Benue valley and regional trade.
kingdom-of-wukari.e: In the 19th century Wukari was hemmed in by the Muri Emirate and Fulani raids. It came under British control in the early 1900s within the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria, and the Aku Uka remains a traditional ruler in Taraba State.

kingdom-of-kaarta.t: A Bambara kingdom north of the upper Senegal, ruled by the Massasi branch of the Kulibali, rival of Segou until its conquest by Umar Tall in 1854.
kingdom-of-kaarta.o: Kaarta was founded by the Massasi, a branch of the Kulibali dynasty that lost a struggle for power at Segou and moved north-west. Around 1753 their leader Sebamana established a kingdom in the Sahel country north of the Senegal river, among Soninke and Fulbe communities, eventually with its capital at Nioro.
kingdom-of-kaarta.r: Kaarta was a warrior state like the Bamana Empire, with an army of slave soldiers and Bambara warriors and a mostly non-Muslim ruling class over Muslim Soninke and Fulbe subjects. It raided and fought Segou, Khasso, Bundu and the Moors to the north, and controlled routes linking the Sahara salt trade with the upper Senegal. Under Desse Koro around 1800 it reached the peak of its power.
kingdom-of-kaarta.e: In 1854 Umar Tall conquered Kaarta and killed its king Mamadi Kandia. Nioro became an important garrison and religious centre of the Toucouleur Empire, and the region later passed into French Sudan.

kingdom-of-makwanpur.t: A Sen kingdom on the southern approaches to the Kathmandu Valley, whose fall in 1762 opened the way for the Gorkha conquest of the valley.
kingdom-of-makwanpur.o: Makwanpur was formed in the early 16th century when the Sen realm of Mukunda Sen of Palpa was divided among his heirs. One branch took the hill fort of Makwanpur and the adjacent lowlands of the Terai, controlling the main route from Bihar to the Kathmandu Valley.
kingdom-of-makwanpur.r: The Makwanpur Sens ruled hill and Terai territory with a mixed population of Magars, Tharus and Hindu settlers, drawing revenue from agriculture and trade with Bihar. They maintained ties with the Nawabate of Bengal and its governors in Bihar, from whom they at times sought help.
kingdom-of-makwanpur.e: Prithvi Narayan Shah of the Gorkha Kingdom captured Makwanpur in 1762. In 1763 he defeated an army sent by Mir Qasim, Nawab of Bengal, to restore its king. The conquest cut the Kathmandu Valley's southern supply lines.

kingdom-of-the-burgundians.t: East Germanic kingdom of the Rhône and Saône valleys, whose destruction on the Rhine inspired the Nibelungenlied and whose laws shaped Burgundy.
kingdom-of-the-burgundians.o: The Burgundians crossed the Rhine in the early 5th century, and in 411 their king Gundahar set up a realm around Worms as Roman allies. In 436 the general Aetius had them crushed by Hunnic troops, a disaster remembered in the Nibelungenlied. In 443 the survivors were resettled in Sapaudia, around Geneva.
kingdom-of-the-burgundians.r: From there they spread across the Rhône and Saône valleys, ruling from Lyon and Geneva. King Gundobad issued a law code for his Burgundian subjects and another for Romans, and Burgundians and Gallo-Romans shared land. The kings were Arians, but Sigismund converted to Catholic Christianity.
kingdom-of-the-burgundians.e: Clovis' sons attacked them in 523, killing Sigismund. After a final defeat in 534 King Godomar disappeared and the land became part of the Kingdom of the Franks, later the Frankish Kingdom of Burgundy. The name Burgundy has endured for fifteen centuries.

kingdom-of-iceland.t: Sovereign Iceland in personal union with Denmark from 1918, until Icelanders voted to become a republic in 1944.
kingdom-of-iceland.o: After a century of national struggle led by figures such as Jón Sigurðsson, Iceland won home rule in 1904. The Danish-Icelandic Act of Union, effective 1 December 1918, recognised Iceland as a sovereign kingdom sharing a king, Christian X, with Denmark, with the right to end the union after 25 years.
kingdom-of-iceland.r: Iceland governed itself through the Althing and its own cabinet, while Denmark handled foreign affairs and fisheries protection on its behalf. A Supreme Court was set up in 1920, and in 1930 the Althing celebrated its millennium at Þingvellir. The economy depended on fishing, and the Depression hit hard.
kingdom-of-iceland.e: When Germany occupied Denmark in 1940, Iceland took over its own foreign affairs and Britain, then the United States, occupied the island. Sveinn Björnsson became regent in 1941. In a 1944 referendum Icelanders voted overwhelmingly to end the union, and the Republic of Iceland was proclaimed on 17 June 1944.
