kalabari-kingdom.t: Ijaw trading state of the eastern Niger delta whose 'canoe houses' dealt in slaves and later palm oil with European ships.
kalabari-kingdom.o: Kalabari tradition tells of migrants from the central delta who settled on an island in the eastern delta and founded Elem Kalabari, known to Europeans as New Calabar. Fishing and salt making gave way to trade with the hinterland by the 15th century, and Portuguese ships arrived soon afterward.
kalabari-kingdom.r: The Amanyanabo, or king, ruled with the heads of wari, the trading houses that owned war canoes and absorbed slaves as members who could rise to lead them. Under King Amakiri, in the 18th century, Kalabari became a major slave port. After abolition it turned to palm oil. The Ekine masquerade society governed much of public ritual.
kalabari-kingdom.e: Rivalry with the Bonny Kingdom and a civil war led to Elem Kalabari's abandonment in the early 1880s, the people regrouping at Buguma, Abonnema and Bakana. Kalabari signed a British protection treaty in 1884 and became part of the Oil Rivers Protectorate. The Amanyanabo still reigns at Buguma.

kittur-state.t: A Lingayat chiefdom in northern Karnataka whose queen, Rani Chennamma, led one of the earliest armed revolts against the East India Company.
kittur-state.o: Kittur was founded in the late 16th century by a family of Lingayat chiefs who served the Adil Shahi sultans of Bijapur and held the title Desai. The territory lay between Belgaum and Dharwad in the fertile black-soil country of northern Karnataka.
kittur-state.r: The Desais ruled from the fort of Kittur, paying tribute successively to Bijapur, the Mughals, the Marathas and Mysore. Mallasarja, who died in 1816, was its best-known ruler. The state was predominantly Lingayat and Kannada-speaking, with an economy based on cotton and grain.
kittur-state.e: When Shivalingarudra Sarja died in 1824 the Company refused to recognise his adopted heir. Rani Chennamma resisted, and her forces killed the collector St John Thackeray, but Kittur was captured in December 1824 and annexed. She is honoured today as a pioneer of Indian resistance.

kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.t: The Austrian-ruled kingdom of Lombardy and Venetia, centre of Habsburg power in Italy and target of the wars of Italian independence.
kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.o: In 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave Lombardy and the former Republic of Venice to the Austrian Empire, which joined them as a kingdom with the emperor as king, governed by a viceroy, at first Archduke Rainer.
kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.r: Lombardy-Venetia had an efficient administration, good schools and a prosperous economy, but censorship and police repression made Austria unpopular; the patriot Silvio Pellico described his imprisonment in the Spielberg fortress. In 1848 the Five Days of Milan and the Republic of San Marco drove out the Austrians, but Marshal Radetzky reconquered both. Archduke Maximilian tried liberal reforms as governor-general in 1857–1859.
kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia.e: Defeat by France and the Kingdom of Sardinia at Solferino in 1859 cost Austria Lombardy. After the war of 1866, Venetia passed to the Kingdom of Italy.

kaga-ikko-ikki.t: A province of Japan ruled for almost a century by leagues of Jodo Shinshu Buddhist believers after they overthrew its governor in 1488.
kaga-ikko-ikki.o: The preaching of Rennyo spread the True Pure Land, or Ikko, sect among farmers, local warriors and townspeople of the Hokuriku region. In 1488 a league of believers rose against the governor Togashi Masachika, besieged his castle and drove him to suicide.
kaga-ikko-ikki.r: A Togashi relative remained nominal governor, but real power lay with leagues of local warriors and village communities organised around temples of the Hongan-ji, whose head priests in Yamashina and later Ishiyama directed affairs. In 1546 the Oyama Gobo temple was founded at the site of modern Kanazawa as the regional centre. Contemporaries called Kaga a province held by peasants.
kaga-ikko-ikki.e: Oda Nobunaga fought the Ikko leagues for years. After the Ishiyama Hongan-ji surrendered in 1580, his general Shibata Katsuie captured the Oyama Gobo and crushed resistance. Kaga later became the domain of the Maeda.

kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301.t: Christian kingdom of the Árpád dynasty in the Carpathian basin, founded by Stephen I, which survived the Mongol invasion and united with Croatia.
kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301.o: Stephen I, son of Grand Prince Géza of the Principality of Hungary, was crowned in 1000 or 1001. He defeated rival chiefs, annexed the Realm of the Gyulas and the Duchy of Ahtum, and built a Latin church with archbishoprics at Esztergom and Kalocsa.
kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301.r: Royal counties centred on castles organised the realm, and the king owned vast estates. Ladislaus I and Coloman extended rule to Croatia, crowned in 1102. Germans settled in Transylvania and the towns, and the Golden Bull of 1222 under Andrew II limited royal power. The Mongols devastated the country in 1241–1242; Béla IV rebuilt it with stone castles and new towns.
kingdom-of-hungary-1000-1301.e: Royal power weakened as barons such as Matthew Csák built regional domains. With the death of Andrew III in 1301 the Árpád male line ended, and the throne was contested, leading to the Angevin Kingdom of Hungary (1301-1526).

kingdom-of-luang-phrabang.t: The northern successor of Lan Xang, whose royal house survived Siamese and French overlordship to become the monarchy of modern Laos.
kingdom-of-luang-phrabang.o: During the succession conflicts after Sourigna Vongsa's death, his grandson Kingkitsarath, with backing from Sipsongpanna, established himself at Luang Prabang in 1707 as king, separate from the court of the Kingdom of Vientiane. Lan Xang was thereby formally divided.
kingdom-of-luang-phrabang.r: The kingdom ruled the northern Lao highlands, with Lao, Khmu and Hmong subjects, and was frequently threatened by Burma, Vientiane and Siam. From 1779 it was a vassal of Siam. Its capital, with temples such as Wat Xieng Thong and the Phra Bang image, was the religious heart of Lao kingship.
kingdom-of-luang-phrabang.e: After Chinese Haw raiders sacked Luang Prabang in 1887, the French consul Auguste Pavie rescued King Oun Kham, and the kingdom came under the French protectorate of Laos in 1893. Its king Sisavang Vong became monarch of the unified Kingdom of Laos in 1946 to 1947.

kingdom-of-linjiang.t: The middle Yangtze kingdom of Gong Ao and his son, the last ally of Xiang Yu to hold out, conquered by Han forces in 202 BCE.
kingdom-of-linjiang.o: Gong Ao had served as Pillar of State to King Huai of Chu, the figurehead of the rebellion against the Qin dynasty, and led an army into the Nanjun region. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Linjiang, with his capital at Jiangling in Hubei, the former heartland of the State of Chu.
kingdom-of-linjiang.r: Linjiang controlled the rich Jianghan plain and the river routes to the south. Gong Ao died in 204 BCE and was succeeded by his son Gong Wei, who remained loyal to Xiang Yu when other kings defected.
kingdom-of-linjiang.e: After Xiang Yu's death in 202 BCE, Liu Bang sent Lu Wan and Liu Jia to attack Linjiang. Gong Wei was captured and executed, and his lands became part of the Han Dynasty.

kingdom-of-dedan.t: An oasis kingdom at al-Ula in the Hejaz, a key stop on the incense road and precursor of the Lihyanite kings.
kingdom-of-dedan.o: Dedan, the ancient name of the oasis at al-Ula, is mentioned in the Hebrew Bible as a trading people. A local monarchy is attested in Dadanitic inscriptions from around the 7th century BCE. The oasis grew rich supplying water and provisions to caravans moving between south Arabia and the Levant.
kingdom-of-dedan.r: Kings of Dedan are known by name from short inscriptions, and the town had sanctuaries of the god Dhu Ghabat. In the mid-6th century BCE the Babylonian king Nabonidus campaigned in the Hejaz and listed Dedan among the oases he took while residing at Tayma. A colony of Minaean merchants from the Kingdom of Ma'in was later based there.
kingdom-of-dedan.e: After the Babylonian interlude the oasis came under the Lihyanite dynasty, and the Kingdom of Lihyan ruled from the same site. The ruins at al-Khuraybah near al-Ula, with their temple and lion tombs, are now excavated.

kingdom-of-syrmia.t: Realm of the former Serbian king Stefan Dragutin on the Sava and Danube, held as a Hungarian fief and rival to his brother's Serbia.
kingdom-of-syrmia.o: In 1282 Stefan Dragutin, king of Serbia, gave up the throne to his brother Milutin after a riding accident, keeping some Serbian lands. Through his wife Catherine, daughter of Stephen V of Hungary, he received from Ladislaus IV in 1284 the Banate of Macsó, Belgrade, Usora and Soli.
kingdom-of-syrmia.r: Dragutin, styled king, ruled from Debrc near Belgrade, supporting the Catholic Church in his lands as well as Orthodox monasteries. He joined Milutin against the Bulgarian lords of Braničevo, but from about 1301 the brothers fought for years over the Serbian succession.
kingdom-of-syrmia.e: After Dragutin's death in 1316 Milutin seized most of his lands, imprisoning Dragutin's son Vladislav II. Hungary soon retook Mačva and Belgrade, restoring the Banate of Macsó.

kingdom-of-dunoding.t: Small early kingdom of north-west Wales, named in legend after a son of Cunedda, which became the cantrefi of Eifionydd and Ardudwy in Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-dunoding.o: According to Welsh genealogical tradition, Dunoding was named after Dunod, a son of Cunedda, who received the land as his share when Cunedda's family settled north Wales in the 5th century. Historians treat the Cunedda story as a later origin legend, but Dunoding existed as a distinct territory on the coast south of Snowdonia.
kingdom-of-dunoding.r: Little is recorded of its rulers or government. The kingdom comprised two districts, Eifionydd around Criccieth and Ardudwy around Harlech, a land of coastal farmland backed by mountains, rich in prehistoric monuments. It seems to have been ruled by a local branch of the dynasty of the Kingdom of Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-dunoding.e: Dunoding was absorbed into the Kingdom of Gwynedd as two cantrefi, probably by the 10th century. Eifionydd and Ardudwy remained administrative districts, later guarded by the castles of Criccieth and Harlech after the English conquest of 1283.

kontagora-emirate.t: A late emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate in western Nigeria, built by a grandson of Usman dan Fodio and notorious for large-scale slave raiding.
kontagora-emirate.o: Kontagora was founded around 1859 by Umaru Nagwamatse, a son of the Sokoto caliph Abubakar Atiku and grandson of Usman dan Fodio. Leaving Sokoto, he gathered followers and conquered lands among the Kamuku, Gbagyi and other peoples between the Niger and Kaduna rivers, establishing his capital at Kontagora.
kontagora-emirate.r: Nagwamatse styled himself Sarkin Sudan, and his emirate lived largely by war. Its armies raided surrounding communities for captives, who were sold or settled on estates, and much of the region was depopulated. The emirate's rulers owed allegiance to Sokoto but acted with considerable independence. Under his son Ibrahim Nagwamatse, from 1880, the raiding reached its peak.
kontagora-emirate.e: British forces under Frederick Lugard attacked Kontagora in 1901, and Ibrahim was captured in 1902 and later restored. The emirate became part of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria, and its emir still reigns in Niger State.

kadamba-dynasty.t: The first native dynasty of Karnataka, founded by a Brahmin turned warrior, whose reign produced the earliest known Kannada inscription.
kadamba-dynasty.o: According to the Talagunda inscription, Mayurasharma, a Brahmin scholar, was insulted by a Pallava guard while studying at Kanchipuram. He took up arms, gathered forest chiefs and forced the Pallava dynasty to recognise him as ruler of the region around Banavasi in the mid-4th century.
kadamba-dynasty.r: Mayurasharma's descendants took the warrior title varma and ruled from Banavasi, with a branch at Triparvata. Kakusthavarma made marriage alliances with the Gupta Empire and the Vakataka dynasty. The Halmidi inscription, from around 450, is the oldest known inscription in Kannada, though Sanskrit remained the main court language. The kings patronised Brahmins and Jains, and their temple style influenced later Karnataka architecture.
kadamba-dynasty.e: Weakened by divisions between branches, the Kadambas were conquered around 540 by Pulakeshin I of the Chalukyas of Badami. Later families claiming Kadamba descent ruled smaller states, notably the Kadambas of Goa and the Kadambas of Hangal.

kingdom-of-adiabene.t: A Parthian vassal kingdom centred on Arbela (Erbil) whose royal family converted to Judaism in the 1st century CE.
kingdom-of-adiabene.o: Adiabene lay between the Great and Lesser Zab rivers east of the Tigris, the heartland of ancient Assyria. After Seleucid control weakened in the 2nd century BCE, a local dynasty emerged at Arbela, becoming a client of the Parthian Empire and at times of Armenia.
kingdom-of-adiabene.r: Josephus tells how Queen Helena and her son King Izates II adopted Judaism in the 1st century CE; Helena sent food to Jerusalem during a famine and was buried in the so-called Tomb of the Kings there, and Adiabenian princes fought for the Jews against Rome in 66 to 70 CE. The population spoke Aramaic and practised a mix of Iranian, Mesopotamian, Jewish and, from early on, Christian faiths. Adiabene played a role in Parthian succession struggles.
kingdom-of-adiabene.e: Trajan briefly occupied Adiabene in 116 CE. Under the Sasanian Empire it became a dependent kingdom and then a province, ending in the 4th century; Arbela became a major centre of the Church of the East.

kingdom-of-cyprus.t: Crusader kingdom of the Lusignan dynasty that ruled Cyprus for three centuries, the last Latin outpost in the Levant after the fall of Acre.
kingdom-of-cyprus.o: In 1192 Richard I sold Cyprus, recently taken from Isaac Komnenos and returned by the Templars, to Guy of Lusignan, the deposed king of Jerusalem. Guy settled Frankish knights on the island. His brother Aimery obtained a crown from the Emperor Henry VI and was crowned king in 1197.
kingdom-of-cyprus.r: A French-speaking Catholic nobility ruled a mostly Greek Orthodox population, using the laws of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and a High Court of barons. The Orthodox church was subordinated to Latin bishops. After the fall of Acre in 1291 Famagusta became a great entrepot for Italian merchants. Gothic cathedrals in Nicosia and Famagusta and the abbey of Bellapais survive. Peter I led a crusade that sacked Alexandria in 1365.
kingdom-of-cyprus.e: Genoa seized Famagusta in 1373, and a Mamluk invasion in 1426 captured King Janus and made the kingdom tributary to Egypt. James II married the Venetian Catherine Cornaro; after his death she ruled as queen until Venice forced her to abdicate in 1489, creating Venetian Cyprus.

kubota-domain.t: The Satake domain of northern Dewa, rich in timber and mines, which broke with its northern neighbours to side with the imperial government in 1868.
kubota-domain.o: Tokugawa Ieyasu punished Satake Yoshinobu for his neutrality at Sekigahara by moving him in 1602 from Hitachi to Dewa, with about 205,800 koku. Yoshinobu built Kubota castle in 1604 at the site of modern Akita city.
kubota-domain.r: The domain drew income from Akita cedar forests and from the Innai silver mine and Ani copper mine, among the most productive in Japan. In the 18th century Satake Yoshiatsu, known as Shozan, and his retainer Odano Naotake developed the Akita school of Western-style painting under the influence of Hiraga Gennai.
kubota-domain.e: In 1868 Kubota left the Ouetsu Reppan Domei and fought for the imperial side, suffering invasion by Shonai and other neighbours. After abolition in 1871 it became Akita Prefecture.

kokand-autonomy.t: A short-lived Muslim autonomous government in Turkestan, set up by Jadid reformers in 1917 and crushed by Soviet forces months later.
kokand-autonomy.o: After the October Revolution, the Tashkent Soviet, dominated by Russian settlers, excluded Muslims from power. In November 1917 the Fourth Extraordinary Regional Muslim Congress met in Kokand and proclaimed the Turkestan Autonomy within a future democratic Russian federation.
kokand-autonomy.r: The government, led first by Muhammadjan Tynyshbaev and then by Mustafa Chokay, included Jadid reformers and some Russian members. It planned a constituent assembly and a militia, but lacked money and troops and depended on the support of the Kokand population and local strongmen.
kokand-autonomy.e: In February 1918 Red Guards and Armenian Dashnak units from Tashkent stormed Kokand, killing thousands and burning much of the city. The government collapsed, and Chokay fled into exile. Its destruction helped spark the Basmachi resistance against Soviet rule.

kingdom-of-alania.t: The medieval Christian kingdom of the Alans in the North Caucasus, a Byzantine ally and Georgian partner until the Mongols destroyed it in 1239.
kingdom-of-alania.o: The Alans who stayed in the North Caucasus after the Hunnic invasions came under the Khazar Khaganate. As Khazar power declined in the 10th century, Alanian rulers formed a kingdom along the upper Kuban and Terek rivers, and around 916 they accepted Christianity from a Byzantine mission sent by Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos.
kingdom-of-alania.r: Kings ruled a land of fortified towns and hill forts, controlling the Darial Pass and trade with the Black Sea and the steppe. The Alanian church had its own metropolitan, and stone churches survive in the Zelenchuk valley. Royal marriages linked the Alans to the Kingdom of Georgia and Byzantium; Queen Tamar's husband David Soslan was an Alanian prince.
kingdom-of-alania.e: The Mongols defeated the Alans in 1222, and in 1239 they stormed the capital Maghas. Survivors withdrew into the mountains, where their descendants became the Ossetians. Others fled to Hungary, the Crimea and Mongol service in China, and the name of Alania survives in the official title of North Ossetia.

kingdom-of-idalion.t: Inland Cypriot kingdom famous for the Idalion Tablet, a bronze contract recording how the city paid a doctor to treat the wounded during a siege.
kingdom-of-idalion.o: Idalion grew on the hills of central Cyprus, near the copper-bearing foothills of Troodos, in the early Iron Age. By the 7th century BCE it was a city-kingdom listed among Cypriot states paying tribute to the Assyrian king Esarhaddon. Its acropolis held sanctuaries of the goddesses later called Athena and Aphrodite.
kingdom-of-idalion.r: Idalion controlled copper production and fertile land. The Idalion Tablet, a bronze plaque of the early 5th century BCE written in the Cypriot syllabary, records that King Stasicypros and the city granted land to the physician Onasilos and his brothers for treating those wounded when 'the Medes and the Kitians' besieged the town.
kingdom-of-idalion.e: Idalion was conquered by the Phoenician Kingdom of Kition c. 450 BCE and lost its independence, Kition then ruling it with Phoenician administration. The town continued under Ptolemaic and Roman rule but declined.

kingdom-of-macedon.t: The Argead kingdom of northern Greece that Philip II turned into the dominant power of the Greek world, launching the conquests of his son Alexander.
kingdom-of-macedon.o: The Argead kings, who claimed descent from Temenos of Argos, built a kingdom in the plains of Lower Macedonia around Aigai, modern Vergina. Herodotus names Perdiccas I as founder in the 7th century BCE; later writers added an earlier Caranus, traditionally dated 808 BCE. The kingdom expanded over the Haliacmon and Axios plains.
kingdom-of-macedon.r: Macedon was a monarchy whose king ruled with a warrior aristocracy of Companions. It was a vassal of the Achaemenid Empire c. 512 to 479 BCE; Alexander I then courted Greek opinion. Archelaus I moved the capital to Pella c. 400 BCE and hosted Euripides. Timber, silver and horses supported it. Philip II, from 359 BCE, built a professional army with the long sarissa pike.
kingdom-of-macedon.e: Philip II took Amphipolis and the Chalcidice, defeated Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE and founded the League of Corinth. His murder at Aigai in 336 BCE brought Alexander to the throne, opening the age of the Macedonian Empire.

khairpur-state.t: The Talpur Mirs' state in upper Sindh, the one Talpur principality to survive the British conquest of Sindh in 1843.
khairpur-state.o: The Talpurs, a Baloch clan, overthrew the Kalhora rulers of Sindh at the Battle of Halani in 1783. The victors divided Sindh, and Mir Sohrab Khan Talpur took the northern share with his capital at Khairpur.
khairpur-state.r: When the British conquered Sindh in 1843 after the Battle of Miani, Mir Ali Murad Khan of Khairpur had sided with them and kept his state, though he later lost land after being accused of forging a treaty. Khairpur was a Shia-ruled state with a 15-gun salute, a Sindhi-speaking population and an economy of dates, grain and cotton. The fort of Kot Diji guarded it.
khairpur-state.e: Mir George Ali Murad Khan acceded to Pakistan in October 1947. Khairpur was merged into West Pakistan in 1955 and is now a district of Sindh.

kingdom-of-montenegro.t: Montenegro's brief kingdom under Nikola I, which fought in the Balkan Wars and the First World War before being merged into Yugoslavia.
kingdom-of-montenegro.o: On the fiftieth anniversary of his reign, on 28 August 1910, Prince Nikola I of the Principality of Montenegro proclaimed himself king, with the agreement of the Great Powers. The new kingdom kept its capital at Cetinje and its constitution of 1905.
kingdom-of-montenegro.r: Nikola continued to rule as a patriarchal monarch, clashing with opponents who favoured union with Serbia. In the First Balkan War Montenegro besieged and took Scutari in 1913, but the powers forced it to hand the town to the new Albania; it did gain much of the Sandžak and Metohija, including Peć and Đakovica.
kingdom-of-montenegro.e: Montenegro joined Serbia in the First World War but was occupied by Austria-Hungary in January 1916, and Nikola went into exile. In November 1918 the Podgorica Assembly deposed him and voted for union with Serbia, provoking the Christmas Uprising of 1919. Montenegro became part of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.

kingdom-of-the-suebi.t: A Germanic kingdom that ruled Gallaecia from Braga for over 170 years, one of the first barbarian realms in the former Roman West.
kingdom-of-the-suebi.o: The Suebi crossed the Rhine in 406 with the Vandals and Alans and entered Hispania in 409. In 411 they received lands in Gallaecia under their king Hermeric. After the Vandals left for Africa in 429, Rechila expanded south, taking Emerita Augusta in 439 and Seville in 441.
kingdom-of-the-suebi.r: The kingdom was centred on Bracara Augusta and ruled a Hispano-Roman majority through bishops and local elites. Rechiar became the first Catholic Germanic king around 448 and minted silver coins, but was defeated and killed by the Visigoth Theodoric II in 456. The Suebi later turned Arian, then returned to Catholicism under Martin of Braga's influence around 560. The Councils of Braga of 561 and 572 organised the church.
kingdom-of-the-suebi.e: King Miro was drawn into Visigothic conflicts and died in 583. In 585 the Visigothic king Leovigild overthrew the usurper Andeca and annexed the kingdom, ending Suebic rule. Its territory shaped the later Kingdom of Galicia.

kingdom-of-dacia.t: Kingdom of the Dacians in the Carpathian basin, united by Burebista and defended by Decebalus against Trajan, whose conquest created Roman Dacia.
kingdom-of-dacia.o: About 82 BCE Burebista united the Getae and Dacian tribes, aided by the high priest Deceneus. He built a realm from the middle Danube to the Black Sea, defeating the Boii and Scordisci and taking Greek coastal cities such as Olbia and Apollonia.
kingdom-of-dacia.r: The heart of the kingdom lay in the Orăștie Mountains, where fortresses and sanctuaries ringed the capital, Sarmizegetusa Regia. Kings ruled with a priestly elite devoted to Zalmoxis. Gold and silver mining, iron working and trade with Rome supported the state. After Burebista's murder in 44 BCE the realm split, but Decebalus reunited it and defeated a Roman army at Tapae.
kingdom-of-dacia.e: Trajan's two Dacian Wars (101–102 and 105–106 CE) destroyed the kingdom; Sarmizegetusa fell and Decebalus killed himself in 106 CE. Most of the land became the province of Dacia, commemorated on Trajan's Column, and Dacian identity later became central to Romanian national history.

kengtung-state.t: The largest of the Shan states, in Myanmar's far east near China, Laos and Thailand, with close cultural ties to Lan Na.
kengtung-state.o: Kengtung, Tai Khun Chiang Tung, was settled by Tai Khun people and, according to tradition, brought under Mangrai of Lan Na in the 13th century, who installed a governor there. Its ruling house dates from this period, and the city stands by Naung Tung lake.
kengtung-state.r: Kengtung's Khun culture, script and Buddhism were closely related to Lan Na and Chiang Hung, and its rulers balanced between Lan Na, Burmese kings and China. From the 16th century it was a tributary of the First Toungoo Empire and later Konbaung, while trading tea, horses and opium across the borderlands.
kengtung-state.e: Kengtung came under British protection in 1890 and joined the Federated Shan States. The saopha's powers ended in 1959, and the Burmese military demolished his palace in 1991. Kengtung remains the main town of eastern Shan State.

kroraina.t: The kingdom of Loulan, later Shanshan, on the shores of Lop Nur, whose desert-preserved documents give an unusually detailed view of Silk Road life.
kroraina.o: Kroraina, called Loulan in Chinese, was an oasis state on the north-western shore of Lop Nur in the eastern Tarim Basin, the first stop for travellers leaving China westward. It appears in a Xiongnu letter to the Han of 176 BCE. In 77 BCE the Han envoy Fu Jiezi assassinated its pro-Xiongnu king, and the Han installed Weituqi, renaming the kingdom Shanshan and moving its centre south to Yuni.
kroraina.r: In the 3rd and 4th centuries Shanshan used Gandhari Prakrit in Kharoshthi script for government; hundreds of wooden tablets found at Niya record taxes, lawsuits, camels and slaves. Buddhism flourished, and its monasteries and paintings show Indian and Hellenistic influence. Chinese garrisons were stationed at Loulan, and its kings balanced between China and the steppe.
kroraina.e: Weakened by the drying of Lop Nur and wars with its neighbours, Shanshan was conquered by the Northern Wei in 445. The ruins of Loulan and Niya were rediscovered by Sven Hedin and Aurel Stein around 1900.

kingdom-of-wolaita.t: A long-lived kingdom of southern Ethiopia whose last king, Kawo Tona, fought a costly war against Menelik II's expanding empire.
kingdom-of-wolaita.o: Wolaita traditions describe a first royal dynasty, the Wolaita Malla, which ruled from about the 13th century, followed by the Tigre dynasty, founded according to tradition by a northerner who settled in the region and seized power in the 17th century. The kingdom lay between the Omo river and the Rift Valley lakes, south of the Gurage and Hadiya lands.
kingdom-of-wolaita.r: The king, or kawo, ruled from fortified residences such as Dalbo with a court of officials and a council of clan leaders, and the kingdom was defended by ditches and walls. Farming of ensete (false banana), cereals and cattle supported a dense population. Wolaita traded cloth, cotton and slaves and absorbed neighbouring peoples. Traditional religion coexisted with older Christian traces.
kingdom-of-wolaita.e: In 1894 Menelik II invaded with a large army, and after fierce resistance Kawo Tona Gaga was wounded and captured. Tens of thousands died or were enslaved, and Wolaita was annexed to the Ethiopian Empire. Its memory remains strong in the Wolaita Zone today.

kingdom-of-the-algarve.t: Portugal's southern coast, held as a nominally separate kingdom by the Portuguese crown from its conquest until 1910.
kingdom-of-the-algarve.o: Afonso III of Portugal completed the conquest of the Algarve by taking Faro in 1249. Castile disputed the territory until the Treaty of Badajoz of 1267, after which Portuguese kings styled themselves Kings of Portugal and the Algarve.
kingdom-of-the-algarve.r: The Algarve had no separate institutions: it was governed from Lisbon as part of the Kingdom of Portugal, though its title and arms were kept as a mark of conquest. Its ports, especially Lagos, served as bases for Henry the Navigator's voyages to Africa. Fishing, salt, figs and almonds sustained its economy.
kingdom-of-the-algarve.e: The title was later expanded under Manuel I to cover territories in Africa. The Kingdom of the Algarve ended in law with the Portuguese monarchy in the revolution of 1910 and became a region of the First Portuguese Republic.

kingdom-of-viguera.t: A short-lived sub-kingdom in La Rioja, carved out of Pamplona for a royal younger son and soon folded back into the realm of Navarre.
kingdom-of-viguera.o: Around 970 King Sancho II Garcés of Pamplona, following the will of his father García Sánchez I, granted the Rioja lands around Viguera to his younger brother Ramiro Garcés with the title of king. The territory, recently won from the Muslims, guarded the upper Ebro and the approaches to Nájera.
kingdom-of-viguera.r: Viguera was an appanage rather than a fully independent state: its kings acknowledged the senior line in Pamplona and fought alongside it against the Caliphate of Córdoba. Ramiro is said to have died at the Battle of Torrevicente in 981. Charters show his sons Sancho Ramírez and García Ramírez styled as kings, though little else is recorded.
kingdom-of-viguera.e: After the line of Ramiro faded out in the early 11th century, Viguera was reabsorbed into the Kingdom of Navarre, by then under Sancho III the Great. It survives chiefly as a case study in how Iberian kings provided for younger sons with subordinate royal titles.

kadana-state.t: A small Rajput state on the upper Mahi river in eastern Gujarat, in the forested borderland with Rajasthan.
kadana-state.o: Kadana was held by a Rajput family in the hilly country of the upper Mahi, on the border of Gujarat and Rajasthan. The estate emerged around 1600, though its founding is known mainly from local tradition.
kadana-state.r: The ruler governed forested hills with a sizeable Bhil population. In the British period Kadana was a minor state of the Rewa Kantha Agency. Few details of its rulers are widely recorded.
kadana-state.e: Kadana was merged into Bombay Province in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960. The Kadana dam on the Mahi now stands in its former territory.

kingdom-of-ondonga.t: An Ovambo kingdom of northern Namibia and the first to welcome Finnish Lutheran missionaries, whose influence reshaped its society.
kingdom-of-ondonga.o: Ondonga was one of the Ovambo kingdoms on the floodplains south of the Kunene river, formed by the 17th century under rulers drawn from a royal matriclan. Its people farmed millet, kept cattle and traded salt from the Etosha pan and copper with neighbours.
kingdom-of-ondonga.r: The king held wide powers over land and justice and governed through district headmen. Finnish Lutheran missionaries arrived in 1870, and Martti Rautanen worked at Olukonda, translating the Bible into Oshindonga. In 1904 Nehale lyaMpingana, ruler of eastern Ondonga, attacked the German fort at Namutoni. King Martin Elifas, baptised in 1912, made Ondonga largely Christian.
kingdom-of-ondonga.e: German colonial claims reached Ovamboland but had little effect until South Africa occupied South West Africa in 1915, after which the kingdom came under South African administration. Ondonga's kingship survives as a traditional authority in independent Namibia.

kingdom-of-amurru.t: Amurru, a kingdom on the Syrian-Lebanese coast built by adventurers in the Amarna age, which changed sides between Egypt and the Hittites.
kingdom-of-amurru.o: Amurru was the mountainous land behind the coast between Byblos and Ugarit, home to fugitives and landless groups. In the 14th century BCE Abdi-Ashirta united them into a kingdom at the expense of Egyptian vassals, and his son Aziru captured Simyra and made it his capital, despite angry letters from Rib-Hadda of Byblos.
kingdom-of-amurru.r: Aziru defected from the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom to the Hittite Empire and signed a treaty with Suppiluliuma I. His successors ruled as Hittite vassals with family ties to the Hittite court; a treaty with Shaushgamuwa ordered him to stop Ahhiyawan ships from trading with Assyria.
kingdom-of-amurru.e: Bentesina was deposed for siding with Egypt after Kadesh but restored by Hattusili III. Around 1190 BCE Amurru was overrun in the attacks by the Sea Peoples recorded at Medinet Habu, and the kingdom disappeared.

kart-dynasty.t: A Tajik dynasty of maliks who rebuilt Herat after the Mongol destruction and ruled it for more than a century.
kart-dynasty.o: Shams al-Din Muhammad Kart, of a family linked to the Ghurid Sultanate, was appointed ruler of Herat by the Mongols around 1245. The Mongol khan Möngke confirmed him, and he and his successors became vassals of the Ilkhanate.
kart-dynasty.r: The Karts rebuilt Herat, which had been devastated by the Mongols in 1221, restoring its walls, mosques and irrigation. They ruled over Herat, Ghor and parts of Khurasan as maliks, balancing Ilkhanid and Chagatai pressures. After the Ilkhanate collapsed in 1335, Mu'izz al-Din Husayn Kart ruled as an independent sovereign, patronising Persian scholarship and Sunni learning.
kart-dynasty.e: In 1381 Timur took Herat and deposed Ghiyath al-Din Pir Ali. After a revolt in 1383 the dynasty was exterminated. Herat later became the brilliant Timurid capital.

kingdom-of-jumla.t: The leading kingdom of the Karnali basin in western Nepal, heir to the Khasa Malla realm and head of the Baise Rajya confederation.
kingdom-of-jumla.o: After the Khasa Malla kingdom broke up in the late 14th century, a Kalyal dynasty established itself in Jumla, the former Khasa heartland near Sinja, around 1400. Its rulers claimed the prestige of the earlier Malla kings and became the most powerful of the hill states of the Karnali region.
kingdom-of-jumla.r: Jumla was regarded as the senior state of the Baise Rajya, the twenty-two kingdoms of western Nepal, and at its height received tribute from neighbouring rajas and from the Kingdom of Mustang. Its economy rested on farming in high valleys and on the trade of salt and wool from Tibet for grain. Hindu temples and the Khas language marked its culture.
kingdom-of-jumla.e: The Gorkha army of the Kingdom of Nepal conquered Jumla in 1789 after hard fighting, and its royal family fled to Tibet. Jumla became a district of Nepal.

kingdom-of-rwanda.t: A centralised kingdom of the Great Lakes ruled by the Nyiginya dynasty, whose colonial-era transformation shaped the tragic politics of modern Rwanda.
kingdom-of-rwanda.o: Rwanda's kingdom grew from a small state near Lake Muhazi in the 16th or 17th century, though court traditions push its origins earlier. The Nyiginya dynasty expanded through conquest of neighbouring states such as the Kingdom of Bugesera, the Kingdom of Gisaka and the Kingdom of Ndorwa. Ruganzu II Ndori is remembered as a refounder of the kingdom in the 17th century.
kingdom-of-rwanda.r: The mwami (king) was a sacred ruler with ritual specialists, army chiefs and land and cattle chiefs. Cattle clientage, ubuhake, bound clients to patrons, and the political divide between the largely Tutsi elite and Hutu farmers hardened under Kigeli IV Rwabugiri (r. 1853 to 1895), who centralised power and campaigned widely. Kinyarwanda was shared by all.
kingdom-of-rwanda.e: Rwanda became part of German East Africa in 1897 and of Belgian Ruanda-Urundi from 1916, where colonial rule rigidified ethnic categories. Mutara III Rudahigwa died in 1959, the Hutu revolution followed, and the monarchy was abolished in 1961, confirmed by referendum before the independence of Rwanda.

khaniadhana-state.t: A small Bundela Rajput principality in Bundelkhand, an offshoot of the ruling house of Orchha.
khaniadhana-state.o: Khaniadhana was founded in the early 18th century by a branch of the Bundela Rajputs of Orchha, one of several small holdings created as the Bundela kingdoms divided among heirs.
khaniadhana-state.r: Little is recorded of its internal history. Under British paramountcy it was a minor state of the Bundelkhand Agency, ruled by a Raja over a few dozen villages, without a gun salute.
khaniadhana-state.e: Khaniadhana acceded to India after 1947 and was absorbed in 1948. Its former territory lies in Shivpuri district of Madhya Pradesh.

kingdom-of-manipur.t: The Meitei kingdom of the Imphal valley, one of the longest-lived monarchies of South Asia, which kept its own royal chronicle for nearly two thousand years of claimed history.
kingdom-of-manipur.o: The royal chronicle, the Cheitharol Kumbaba, traditionally dates the founding to 33 CE, when Nongda Lairen Pakhangba became ruler of the Ningthouja clan. Over the following centuries the Ningthouja kings absorbed the other Meitei clans of the Imphal valley into a single kingdom known to its people as Kangleipak.
kingdom-of-manipur.r: Kings ruled through the lallup system, under which adult men owed periodic labour and military service to the state. In the early 18th century Pamheiba, known as Garib Niwaz, made Gaudiya Vaishnavism the court religion, though the older Sanamahi faith survived. Manipuri cavalry and polo were famous, and the kingdom fought repeated wars with the Burmese kingdoms to the east.
kingdom-of-manipur.e: Burmese occupation from 1819 was ended in 1826 by Gambhir Singh with British help. After the Anglo-Manipur War of 1891 Manipur became a princely state under British control. Maharaja Bodhachandra Singh signed a merger agreement with the Dominion of India in 1949, and Manipur became a full state of the Republic of India in 1972.

kingdom-of-hungary-1301-1526.t: Late medieval Hungary under the Angevins, Sigismund and Matthias Corvinus, a gold-rich central European power that fell at Mohács in 1526.
kingdom-of-hungary-1301-1526.o: When the Árpád line ended in 1301, rival claimants fought for the crown. Charles Robert of Anjou, grandson of a Hungarian princess, won out, was crowned in 1310 and broke the power of oligarchs such as Matthew Csák by 1321.
kingdom-of-hungary-1301-1526.r: Charles I reformed finances, and gold from Kremnica and Transylvania made the Hungarian florin a standard coin. Louis I also became king of Poland in 1370. Sigismund, later Holy Roman Emperor, led the crusade crushed at Nicopolis in 1396. John Hunyadi held off the Ottomans, saving Belgrade in 1456, and his son Matthias Corvinus built the Black Army, a famous Renaissance library, and took Vienna in 1485.
kingdom-of-hungary-1301-1526.e: Under the Jagiellonian kings royal power weakened, and the Dózsa peasant revolt of 1514 was brutally suppressed. In 1526 Suleiman the Magnificent destroyed the Hungarian army at Mohács, killing Louis II; the kingdom was then divided between the Habsburgs, John Zápolya and the Ottomans.

kuban-black-sea-soviet-republic.t: A Soviet republic formed in May 1918 by merging the Kuban and Black Sea soviets during the Russian Civil War.
kuban-black-sea-soviet-republic.o: On 28 May 1918 the Bolsheviks united the Kuban Soviet Republic, centred on Yekaterinodar, and the Black Sea Soviet Republic, based in Novorossiysk, into a single Kuban-Black Sea Soviet Republic, as an autonomous part of the Russian SFSR. The merger reflected the threat posed by the Volunteer Army and by German forces advancing from Ukraine.
kuban-black-sea-soviet-republic.r: The republic was governed by a council of commissars and fought both the Volunteer Army and the Kuban Cossack government. In June 1918, on Lenin's orders, much of the Black Sea Fleet was scuttled in the bay of Novorossiysk to prevent its capture by Germany. The republic struggled with grain requisitions and Cossack resistance.
kuban-black-sea-soviet-republic.e: In July 1918 it was merged with the Terek and Stavropol soviet republics into the North Caucasian Soviet Republic, which the White armies overran by the end of the year.

kingdom-of-georgia.t: The united medieval Georgian monarchy, which under David the Builder and Queen Tamar became the leading power of the Caucasus and the setting of a golden age.
kingdom-of-georgia.o: Bagrat III, heir to both the Kingdom of Abkhazia and the Bagratid lands of the Kingdom of the Iberians, united western and eastern Georgia in 1008. The young kingdom first faced Byzantine pressure and then the Seljuk invasions, paying tribute to the Seljuk Empire from the 1080s.
kingdom-of-georgia.r: David IV the Builder reformed the army, settled Kipchak warriors, won the Battle of Didgori in 1121 and took Tbilisi. Under Queen Tamar, who ruled from 1184, Georgia dominated Shirvan and Armenia, the Zakarids governed Ani, and culture flourished: Rustaveli's poem The Knight in the Panther's Skin, the cave monastery of Vardzia and the Gelati academy. The church and great nobles balanced royal power.
kingdom-of-georgia.e: Mongol conquest in the 1230s made Georgia a vassal of the Ilkhanate; George V the Brilliant restored unity after 1327, but Timur's invasions devastated the country. After 1490 it split into the Kingdom of Kartli, the Kingdom of Kakheti, the Kingdom of Imereti and the Principality of Samtskhe.

kingdom-of-brazil.t: The kingdom created when Brazil was raised to equal status with Portugal, with Rio de Janeiro as the capital of the whole Portuguese monarchy.
kingdom-of-brazil.o: The Portuguese royal court had moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1808 to escape Napoleon. On 16 December 1815 the Prince Regent John raised Brazil to a kingdom within the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves, ending colonial status for the State of Brazil. He was acclaimed King John VI in Rio in 1818.
kingdom-of-brazil.r: Rio grew into a royal capital with the Bank of Brazil, a royal library, a botanical garden and a French artistic mission. Brazil's ports had been open to friendly nations since 1808. The crown crushed the Republic of Pernambuco in 1817 and annexed the Banda Oriental as Cisplatina. Slavery and the slave trade continued to expand.
kingdom-of-brazil.e: The liberal revolution in Porto in 1820 forced John VI to return to Lisbon in 1821, leaving his son Pedro as regent. When the Portuguese Cortes sought to reduce Brazil's status, Pedro declared independence on 7 September 1822 and founded the Empire of Brazil.

kingdom-of-yatenga.t: Northern Mossi kingdom of Burkina Faso, a long-standing rival of Ouagadougou, ruled from Ouahigouya.
kingdom-of-yatenga.o: Mossi tradition says Yatenga was founded around 1540 by Yadega, a prince who left the Kingdom of Ouagadougou after a succession dispute and carried off part of the royal regalia. He and his successors conquered the northern lands of the White Volta basin from earlier inhabitants.
kingdom-of-yatenga.r: The Yatenga Naaba ruled with ministers and provincial chiefs, while earth-priests kept their role in rites of the land. Under Naaba Kango, who reigned in the late 18th century, the kingdom was reorganised and the capital fixed at Ouahigouya. Yatenga traded with Timbuktu and the Niger bend and fought the Kingdom of Ouagadougou and neighbouring peoples.
kingdom-of-yatenga.e: Weakened by civil wars in the late 19th century, Yatenga accepted French protection in 1895 and became part of French West Africa and later Burkina Faso. The Yatenga Naaba remains a traditional ruler at Ouahigouya.

kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria.t: The Habsburg crown land carved from partitioned Poland, a poor but politically lively province that shaped modern Polish and Ukrainian identity.
kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria.o: In the First Partition of Poland in 1772 the Habsburg Monarchy took the lands around Lviv and south of the Vistula. It justified the annexation through old Hungarian claims to the medieval principalities of Halych and Volodymyr, hence the name Galicia and Lodomeria. Krakow was added in 1846.
kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria.r: Lviv, called Lemberg, was the capital. After 1867 the province gained wide autonomy within the Austro-Hungarian Empire, run by Polish nobles through a Diet, with Polish schools and universities in Krakow and Lviv. It was a land of Poles, Ukrainians and a large Jewish population, known for rural poverty and mass emigration, but also for oil wells at Boryslav and a flourishing Ukrainian national movement.
kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria.e: Galicia was a major battlefield in the First World War. When the empire collapsed in 1918, Ukrainians in Lviv proclaimed the West Ukrainian People's Republic, and the Second Polish Republic won the war that followed, taking all of Galicia by 1919.
kingdom-of-galicia-and-lodomeria.re: Catholic and Greek Catholic Christianity, Judaism

kharan-state.t: A Baloch chiefdom of the deserts of western Balochistan, ruled by the Nausherwani family and long a feudatory of Kalat.
kharan-state.o: Kharan was ruled by the Nausherwani Baloch, who claimed descent from Persian nobles. The register dates its founding to 1697. Through much of its history it acknowledged the Khanate of Kalat, while contending for independence.
kharan-state.r: The chiefs ruled a vast, arid territory of sand desert and scattered oases, with a small nomadic and farming population. The British treated Kharan as a feudatory of Kalat but dealt with its chiefs directly.
kharan-state.e: Kharan acceded to Pakistan in 1948, joined the Baluchistan States Union in 1952 and was absorbed into West Pakistan in 1955. It is now a district of Balochistan.

kamarina.t: Syracusan colony on Sicily's south coast, destroyed and refounded several times, whose restless history became a Greek proverb.
kamarina.o: Syracuse founded Kamarina around 598 BCE near the mouth of the Hipparis river, on the south-east coast of Sicily, to extend its reach towards the territory of Gela. The settlers laid out a regular town on a coastal hill beside a marsh.
kamarina.r: Kamarina repeatedly defied its mother city: it revolted around 553 BCE and was destroyed, was refounded by Hippocrates of Gela around 492 BCE, emptied again by Gelon in 484 BCE and refounded from Gela in 461 BCE. Pindar wrote odes for its Olympic victor Psaumis. The Greek proverb 'do not move Camarina', said to come from a disastrous draining of the marsh, warned against stirring up trouble.
kamarina.e: Its people evacuated before the Carthaginians in 405 BCE, and Timoleon resettled it in the 4th century. In 258 BCE, during the First Punic War, the Romans captured it and sold most inhabitants into slavery. The site, near Santa Croce Camerina, was excavated from the 19th century.

kadesh.t: Kadesh, a fortified Syrian city on the Orontes that led resistance to Egypt and gave its name to the great chariot battle of 1274 BCE.
kadesh.o: Kadesh, at Tell Nebi Mend south of Homs, controlled the route through the Homs gap between the coast and inner Syria. In the 15th century BCE its king, backed by the Mitanni Empire, led the Canaanite and Syrian coalition that Thutmose III of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom defeated at Megiddo.
kadesh.r: Its kings governed a compact territory of the upper Orontes and were courted by every great power. In the Amarna age King Aitakkama went over to the Hittite Empire and raided Egyptian vassals, and the Hittites kept Kadesh as a vassal kingdom.
kadesh.e: In 1274 BCE Ramesses II fought Muwatalli II outside the city in the Battle of Kadesh, after which the city stayed in Hittite hands. Kadesh was destroyed around 1200 BCE in the end of the Late Bronze Age and survived only as a village.

kingdom-of-gwynedd.t: The most enduring Welsh kingdom, ruled from Aberffraw on Anglesey, whose princes led Welsh resistance until Edward I's conquest in 1283.
kingdom-of-gwynedd.o: Gwynedd arose in north-west Wales after Roman rule ended. Its dynasty traced descent from Cunedda, said to have come from Manaw Gododdin in the 5th century. By the 6th century it was a leading power under Maelgwn Gwynedd, whom Gildas denounced as Maglocunus, the dragon of the island, and its core lay in Snowdonia and the grain lands of Anglesey.
kingdom-of-gwynedd.r: Kings ruled from llysoedd, royal courts, with Aberffraw as the chief seat, governing through cantrefi and kin-based Welsh law. Cadwallon ap Cadfan killed Edwin of Northumbria in 633. Rhodri the Great, who died in 878, joined the Kingdom of Powys and Seisyllwg to Gwynedd. Later princes such as Owain Gwynedd and Llywelyn the Great built castles and charters, and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd won recognition as Prince of Wales by the Treaty of Montgomery in 1267.
kingdom-of-gwynedd.e: Edward I invaded in 1277 and again in 1282. Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed at Cilmeri in 1282, and his brother Dafydd was executed in 1283. The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 turned Gwynedd into English shires, guarded by castles such as Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech.

kingdom-of-sedang.t: A self-proclaimed kingdom in the Central Highlands of Vietnam created by the French adventurer Charles-Marie David de Mayrena, which lasted barely two years.
kingdom-of-sedang.o: In 1888 Charles-Marie David de Mayrena, a French adventurer and former soldier, travelled to the Kon Tum highlands, nominally to explore for the colonial administration. With the support of local Catholic missionaries he persuaded Sedang, Bahnar and Rengao chiefs to accept him as king, and he proclaimed himself Marie I.
kingdom-of-sedang.r: Marie I issued a constitution, created orders of chivalry, designed a flag and printed postage stamps, which he sold to collectors. He made Catholicism the state religion and set up his court at Kon Gung. Real authority among the highland villages remained with local chiefs, and the kingdom existed mostly on paper.
kingdom-of-sedang.e: French officials refused to recognise the kingdom and blocked Mayrena's return when he went to Europe seeking backers in 1889. The area was absorbed into French Annam, and Mayrena died on the island of Tioman in 1890.

kingdom-of-sitawaka.t: A short-lived Sinhalese kingdom that led the fight against the Portuguese, reaching its height under Rajasinha I.
kingdom-of-sitawaka.o: In 1521 the Kingdom of Kotte was divided after the Vijayabahu Kollaya, a palace revolt in which three princes killed their father. Mayadunne received Sitawaka, an inland district east of Colombo, and became the bitter rival of his brother Bhuvanaikabahu VII of Kotte, who relied on Portuguese support.
kingdom-of-sitawaka.r: Mayadunne waged almost continuous war on Kotte and its Portuguese allies. His son Rajasinha I conquered most of the west and central highlands, besieged Colombo in 1587 to 1588 and converted to Shaivism, which alienated the Buddhist clergy. The kingdom relied on a large peasant army and control of cinnamon lands.
kingdom-of-sitawaka.e: After Rajasinha I died in 1593 the kingdom quickly collapsed; the Portuguese occupied Sitawaka by 1594, and much of its territory went to Portuguese Ceylon while the hill country passed to the Kingdom of Kandy.

kamboja.t: A warlike people of the Hindu Kush borderlands, counted among the sixteen mahajanapadas and famous across ancient India for their horses.
kamboja.o: The Kambojas are named by the grammarian Panini and in Buddhist lists of the sixteen great states. They lived north-west of Gandhara, probably in north-eastern Afghanistan and the hills of north-western Pakistan. The Vedic etymologist Yaska noted that they used an Iranian word for to go, and many scholars see them as an Iranian-speaking people.
kamboja.r: Kautilya's Arthashastra describes the Kambojas as a sangha whose members lived by trade and arms, suggesting rule by a warrior aristocracy rather than a king. Indian literature praised Kamboja horses and cavalry, and the epics place Kamboja horsemen on the battlefield. Little else is known of their society or religion.
kamboja.e: Their lands fell under Achaemenid rule and were overrun by Alexander's army around 327 BCE; some scholars identify the Aspasioi and Assakenoi he fought as Kamboja groups. The Maurya Empire later absorbed them, and Ashoka's edicts name the Kambojas among the frontier peoples of his realm.

kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.t: The O'Neill kingdom of mid-Ulster, the most powerful Gaelic lordship of late medieval Ireland, whose last ruler led the Nine Years' War.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.o: Tir Eoghain, 'Eogan's land', descends from the Cenel nEogain, the northern Ui Neill kindred traced to Eogan, son of Niall of the Nine Hostages. After the decline of the Mac Lochlainn line in the late 12th century, the O'Neills emerged as kings, ruling from Dungannon with inaugurations at Tullyhogue.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.r: The O'Neills dominated Ulster, taking tribute from lesser lords such as the O'Cahans and Maguires. Their power rested on cattle, a large army including Scottish gallowglasses, and a court of poets and lawyers. Conn Bacach O'Neill became Earl of Tyrone in 1542, but conflict with the crown continued under Shane O'Neill.
kingdom-of-tir-eoghain.e: Hugh O'Neill led the Nine Years' War against England, but defeat at Kinsale in 1601 forced his submission. He left in the Flight of the Earls in 1607, and Tyrone was confiscated for the Plantation of Ulster in the Kingdom of Ireland.

kingdom-of-karana.t: A northern Mesopotamian kingdom of the Mari age, centred on Tell al-Rimah, whose queen Iltani left a remarkable archive of letters.
kingdom-of-karana.o: Karana lay south of Jebel Sinjar in northern Iraq. The site of Tell al-Rimah, excavated by David Oates in the 1960s, is usually identified as Karana or its twin city Qattara. After the death of Shamshi-Adad around 1776 BCE, Karana became an independent kingdom under Samu-Addu and later Asqur-Addu.
kingdom-of-karana.r: Karana's kings competed with Andarig and Kurda and swore alliances with Zimri-Lim of Mari and other powers. The temple and palace at Tell al-Rimah contained tablets of Queen Iltani, wife of King Aqba-hammu, who managed textile production, grain and personnel and corresponded with her family, a rare view of a royal woman's administration. The kingdom rested on dry-farmed barley and sheep.
kingdom-of-karana.e: Aqba-hammu became a vassal of Hammurabi of Babylon after the fall of Mari in 1761 BCE, and Karana lost its independence. Tell al-Rimah continued to be occupied in later periods.

kurundwad-junior.t: The junior of two Patwardhan Brahmin states at Kurundwad, formed by the division of 1855.
kurundwad-junior.o: The Patwardhan holding of Kurundwad, created in the family partition of 1811, was divided in 1855 between two branches, and the Junior branch received its own scattered villages.
kurundwad-junior.r: Kurundwad Junior was a small state of the Southern Maratha Country, later the Deccan States Agency, sharing the town of Kurundwad with Kurundwad Senior. Little else of its history is recorded.
kurundwad-junior.e: After accession to India Kurundwad Junior was merged into Bombay State in 1948 and has been part of Maharashtra since 1960, in Kolhapur district.

kingdom-of-jolof.t: The Wolof heartland kingdom left after the break-up of the Jolof Empire, whose last king Alboury Ndiaye resisted French conquest.
kingdom-of-jolof.o: Until the mid-16th century the Buurba Jolof ruled an empire over all the Wolof states. In 1549 Amari Ngoone Sobel Fall of Cayor defeated and killed the Buurba at the battle of Danki, and the coastal provinces broke away. What remained was an inland kingdom centred on Yang-Yang, cut off from direct trade with European ships.
kingdom-of-jolof.r: The Buurba was chosen by electors from royal lineages and ruled over Wolof farmers and Fulani herders of the dry interior. Without access to the coast, Jolof was poorer than Cayor or Waalo and was often drawn into their wars. Islam spread steadily during the 18th and 19th centuries.
kingdom-of-jolof.e: Alboury Ndiaye, who became Buurba in 1875, built alliances against the French but was forced out in 1890 and fled east, dying in exile around 1901. Jolof was absorbed into French Senegal, and its name is still used for the region of Linguere.

kingdom-of-scotland.t: The medieval and early modern kingdom of the Scots, forged from Pictland and Dal Riata, which kept its independence until the Union with England in 1707.
kingdom-of-scotland.o: Tradition dates the kingdom to Kenneth MacAlpin, who ruled the Picts from about 843. The Pictish and Gaelic realms merged into the kingdom of Alba by around 900, centred on Scone and Dunkeld. It expanded over Lothian, Strathclyde, and in 1266 the Western Isles from Norway.
kingdom-of-scotland.r: Scotland developed royal burghs, feudal lordship and a church of its own under David I. The Wars of Independence, with William Wallace and Robert the Bruce's victory at Bannockburn in 1314, secured independence. The Stewart monarchy followed in 1371, Edinburgh became the capital, and the Reformation of 1560 created a Presbyterian church.
kingdom-of-scotland.e: In 1603 James VI inherited England, joining the crowns. The Acts of Union of 1707 merged the Scottish and English parliaments into the Kingdom of Great Britain, though Scotland kept its own law, church and education.

kingdom-of-kition.t: Phoenician kingdom on Cyprus, founded by Tyre, that conquered its Greek neighbours Idalion and Tamassos and was the birthplace of Zeno the Stoic.
kingdom-of-kition.o: Kition, at modern Larnaca, was a Late Bronze Age copper-working town. In the 9th century BCE Phoenicians from Tyre settled there and built a great temple of Astarte on the ruins of an earlier sanctuary. Kition probably began as a Tyrian dependency, and in 707 BCE Sargon II of Assyria set up a stele there recording Cypriot submission.
kingdom-of-kition.r: From the early 5th century BCE an independent Phoenician dynasty ruled Kition, beginning with Baalmelek I, and it was loyal to the Achaemenid Empire. Kition conquered Idalion c. 450 BCE, its kings then styling themselves rulers of both, and Pumiyaton later bought Tamassos. Its harbour served Persian fleets, and its kings issued coins showing Heracles-Melqart.
kingdom-of-kition.e: Ptolemy I executed Pumiyaton and annexed the kingdom in 312 BCE. Kition continued as a Ptolemaic and Roman city; its most famous son, Zeno, founded Stoic philosophy at Athens.
kingdom-of-kition.re: Phoenician religion; cults of Astarte and Melqart

kingdom-of-onitsha.t: An Igbo kingdom on the east bank of the Niger, ruled by an Obi in a court style borrowed from Benin and later a gateway for missions and British trade.
kingdom-of-onitsha.o: According to tradition, Onitsha was founded in the 17th century by migrants from the west of the Niger, led by Eze Chima, who left the area of the Benin Empire after a dispute and crossed the river. They settled among existing Igbo communities on the east bank and created a kingdom unusual in a region where most Igbo lived in small, chiefless village groups.
kingdom-of-onitsha.r: The Obi ruled with the Ndichie, a council of titled chiefs ranked in grades, and the ozo title system gave wealthy men a route into public life. Royal ceremony, such as the annual Ofala festival, echoed the court of Benin. The town lived from river trade in yams, palm oil and slaves. Anglican missionaries under Samuel Ajayi Crowther arrived in 1857.
kingdom-of-onitsha.e: From the 1870s British traders and the Royal Niger Company made Onitsha a commercial base, and a British gunboat shelled the town in 1879. It was absorbed into the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria around 1900. The Obi survives as a traditional ruler and Onitsha became one of Nigeria's largest market towns.

kingdom-of-osraige.t: Irish kingdom between Leinster and Munster, centred on Kilkenny, whose Mac Giolla Phádraig rulers survived as lords until the Tudor surrender of 1541.
kingdom-of-osraige.o: Osraige emerged in early medieval Ireland as the kingdom of a people living in the valleys of the Nore and its tributaries, in modern County Kilkenny and south Laois. Its kings traced descent from ancestors distinct from both the Laigin and the Eóganachta, and the kingdom stood between the Kingdom of Leinster and the Kingdom of Munster, usually as a tributary of Munster.
kingdom-of-osraige.r: The monasteries of Saighir, linked with St Ciarán, and later Aghaboe and Kilkenny, where St Canice is honoured, were centres of learning and gave their names to the diocese of Ossory. Cerball mac Dúnlainge, who died in 888, made Osraige a major power by fighting and allying with Viking leaders. His descendants, the Mac Giolla Phádraig, briefly held the kingship of Leinster under Donnchad mac Gilla Pátraic in the 1030s.
kingdom-of-osraige.e: After the Anglo-Norman invasion of 1169, Kilkenny became the seat of English lords, and the Mac Giolla Phádraig held only Upper Ossory. In 1541 their chief, Brian, surrendered his lands to Henry VIII and received them back as Baron of Upper Ossory, ending the kingdom.

kingdom-of-france.t: The monarchy that grew from the Capetians' small domain around Paris into Europe's most populous and centralised state, ending with the Revolution.
kingdom-of-france.o: In 987 the magnates elected Hugh Capet, duke of the Franks, as king after the last Carolingian died. The early Capetians directly controlled only the Île-de-France and Orléans, while dukes and counts of Normandy, Aquitaine, Burgundy and Flanders were in practice independent.
kingdom-of-france.r: Kings slowly extended the royal domain by war, marriage and law: Philip II took Normandy in 1204, Louis IX became a model of Christian kingship, and the Valois survived the Hundred Years' War. After the Wars of Religion, Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598. Louis XIV built absolute rule at Versailles, and French language and culture dominated Europe.
kingdom-of-france.e: Debt and political crisis led Louis XVI to call the Estates-General in 1789, beginning the Revolution. The monarchy became constitutional in 1791 and was abolished in September 1792, replaced by the French First Republic; Louis XVI was executed in 1793.

kingdom-of-igara.t: A small kingdom of western Uganda, merged into the Kingdom of Ankole under British rule in 1901.
kingdom-of-igara.o: Igara lay in the hills west of today's Bushenyi, between Buhweju and the Kingdom of Ankole. It emerged as a separate state in the 18th century, with a royal line remembered in local tradition. Little is reliably known of its early history.
kingdom-of-igara.r: Igara was a farming and cattle-keeping kingdom, governed by a king with clan heads and drums of office in the manner of its neighbours. It was often drawn into the wars between Ankole and Bunyoro.
kingdom-of-igara.e: The Ankole Agreement of 1901 merged Igara into the Kingdom of Ankole as one of its counties. It is now part of western Uganda's Bushenyi area.

kaska.t: The Kaska, tribal peoples of the Pontic mountains who for three centuries raided the Hittite heartland and once burned Hattusa.
kaska.o: The Kaska lived in the wooded mountains between the Hittite heartland and the Black Sea. They appear in Hittite texts from the 15th century BCE, when they overran the holy city of Nerik and pushed into central Anatolia.
kaska.r: They were not a state but groups of villages under local chiefs, living from herding and farming and raiding Hittite lands. Hittite kings made short-lived treaties with individual groups. Mursili II wrote that one chief, Pihhuniya, ruled not in the Kaska way but like a king.
kaska.e: Kaska raiders sacked Hattusa in the 14th century BCE, and Hattusili III only recovered Nerik in the 13th. After the Hittite collapse they moved south-east, where Tiglath-Pileser I of the Assyrian Empire fought them c. 1100 BCE; then they vanish.

kingdom-of-hatra.t: A fortified caravan city in the desert of northern Iraq, ruled by 'kings of the Arabs', that twice beat off Roman emperors before falling to the Sasanians.
kingdom-of-hatra.o: Hatra grew in the Jazira steppe west of the Tigris as a religious and caravan centre in the 1st century BCE under Parthian protection. Its rulers at first bore the title 'lord' (mry'), and from the mid-2nd century CE, under Sanatruq I, they styled themselves 'king of the Arabs'.
kingdom-of-hatra.r: At its centre stood a vast temple precinct to the sun god Shamash, called Maran ('our lord'), with shrines to Allat, Baalshamin and other deities. Hundreds of inscriptions in Hatran Aramaic and statues of kings, nobles and priests reveal a society blending Arab, Aramaean, Mesopotamian and Parthian traditions. Its round double walls withstood sieges by Trajan in 117 CE and Septimius Severus in 198 to 199.
kingdom-of-hatra.e: Hatra allied with Rome against the new Sasanian Empire but was captured by Shapur I around 240 to 241 and abandoned. Its ruins, a World Heritage Site, were damaged by Islamic State fighters in 2015.

kingdom-of-agona.t: Akan kingdom of the central Gold Coast, known in 17th century European reports for being ruled by queens.
kingdom-of-agona.o: Agona was a small Akan state on the coast and hinterland between the Fante lands and Accra. It existed by the 16th century, with its political centre inland at Nyakrom and coastal towns that traded with European ships.
kingdom-of-agona.r: European visitors in the 17th century recorded female rulers of Agona, reflecting the importance of royal women in Akan politics. The Dutch built Fort Patience at Apam on its coast in the 1690s. Agona traded gold, slaves and food with European companies, but was often subject to stronger neighbours such as Akwamu.
kingdom-of-agona.e: In the 18th century Agona was drawn into the Fante sphere and the wars against the Ashanti Empire. It came under British rule with the Gold Coast Colony in 1874, and survives as a traditional area in Ghana's Central Region.

kingdom-of-dublin.t: The Norse kingdom founded around Dublin's harbour, a hub of the Viking trade network that linked Ireland to Scandinavia, Britain and the slave markets.
kingdom-of-dublin.o: Vikings built a fortified base, the longphort, at Dublin in 841. From 853 the annals record Amlaib and later Imar, ancestors of a dynasty of kings who ruled both Dublin and, at times, the Kingdom of York. Expelled by the Irish in 902, they returned in 917.
kingdom-of-dublin.r: Dublin was a trading town of streets, houses and workshops, revealed by excavations at Wood Quay, dealing in slaves, silver, furs and craft goods. It minted coins from about 997. Its rulers converted to Christianity in the 10th century and Sitric Silkbeard founded Christ Church Cathedral around 1030. Irish kings often controlled it as a valuable prize.
kingdom-of-dublin.e: After defeat at Clontarf in 1014, Dublin was dominated by Irish overkings. In 1170 Strongbow and Diarmait Mac Murchada captured it, and in 1171 Henry II made it the capital of the Lordship of Ireland.
kingdom-of-dublin.re: Norse paganism; Christianity from the 10th century

kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.t: The Alpine kingdom of the Welf dynasty, founded at Saint-Maurice in 888, which later absorbed Provence to form the Kingdom of Arles.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.o: After the deposition of Emperor Charles the Fat in 888, the Welf noble Rudolf, margrave of Transjurane Burgundy, had himself crowned king at the abbey of Saint-Maurice d'Agaune. His kingdom covered western Switzerland, the Jura and parts of Franche-Comté, and he held it against the East Frankish king Arnulf.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.r: The kings controlled the Great St Bernard pass and relied on rich abbeys such as Saint-Maurice and on alliances with local bishops at Lausanne, Geneva and Sion. Rudolf II was defeated by Swabia at Winterthur in 919, then reached for the Italian crown in the 920s before trading those claims for Provence.
kingdom-of-upper-burgundy.e: Around 933 Rudolf II obtained Lower Burgundy from Hugh of Arles, merging the two realms into the Kingdom of Arles. His son Conrad the Peaceful ruled the united kingdom under strong Ottonian influence, and in 1032 it passed to the Holy Roman Empire.

kingdom-of-leon.t: The Christian kingdom that succeeded Asturias in 910, claimed Visigothic heritage and held the first European parliament with townsmen in 1188.
kingdom-of-leon.o: In 910 the sons of Alfonso III of Asturias divided his realm, García I taking León. In 914 Ordoño II made the city of León the royal seat, and the kingdom took its name from it, incorporating Asturias and Galicia and the newly resettled lands of the Douro plain.
kingdom-of-leon.r: The Leonese kings claimed to restore the Visigothic monarchy, some styling themselves emperor. Ramiro II beat Abd al-Rahman III at Simancas in 939, though Almanzor later sacked León and Santiago. Alfonso V's fuero of 1017 regulated the city, and Alfonso VI took Toledo in 1085. Alfonso IX summoned the Cortes of León in 1188, with representatives of towns alongside nobles and clergy.
kingdom-of-leon.e: León was united with Castile under Ferdinand I and his successors, separated again from 1157, and definitively joined with Castile in 1230 under Ferdinand III, forming the Crown of Castile.

kidarite-kingdom.t: The first of the Hunnic dynasties to rule Bactria and Gandhara, named after its founder Kidara and long locked in war with Sasanian Persia.
kidarite-kingdom.o: The Kidarites emerged in Bactria in the 4th century, probably from among the Chionites who invaded the lands of the Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom. Their eponymous leader Kidara issued coins in the Kushan style and claimed the old Kushan title, ruling from Balkh and later spreading into Gandhara.
kidarite-kingdom.r: They governed a mixed population of Bactrians and Indians, issuing gold coins modelled on Kushan and Sasanian types, some with Brahmi legends naming Kidara. They fought repeated wars with Sasanian kings such as Yazdegerd II and Peroz I, and probably clashed with the Gupta Empire in northern India.
kidarite-kingdom.e: Around 467 the Sasanians under Peroz I drove them from Bactria, and the Hephthalite Empire soon took over their northern lands. Remnant Kidarite principalities held out in Gandhara and Kashmir until the Alchon Huns absorbed them in the late 5th century.

kingdom-of-ugarit.t: Ugarit, a rich Late Bronze Age port-kingdom on the Syrian coast whose scribes invented an alphabetic cuneiform and recorded the myths of Baal.
kingdom-of-ugarit.o: Ugarit, at Ras Shamra north of Latakia, was settled from the Neolithic. In the early 2nd millennium BCE it became the capital of a coastal kingdom with an outlet at Minet el-Beida, and it appears in the Mari letters when Zimri-Lim travelled there. A farmer's discovery of a tomb in 1928 led to excavations by Claude Schaeffer.
kingdom-of-ugarit.r: Its kings ruled a cosmopolitan trading state linking Egypt, Cyprus, the Aegean and Mesopotamia. Scribes wrote in Akkadian, Hurrian, Hittite, Egyptian and the local Ugaritic, using a 30-sign cuneiform alphabet. Temple libraries preserved the Baal cycle and the epics of Kirta and Aqhat, close relatives of later Hebrew poetry.
kingdom-of-ugarit.e: Ugarit was a vassal first of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom and then, from Niqmaddu II, of the Hittite Empire. Around 1185 BCE seaborne raiders destroyed it; letters of its last king Ammurapi describe enemy ships. The city was never rebuilt.

kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.t: The largest pre-unification Italian state, the Bourbon kingdom of Naples and Sicily, overthrown by Garibaldi's Thousand in 1860.
kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.o: After the Congress of Vienna restored him, Ferdinand IV of Naples and III of Sicily merged the Kingdom of Naples and the Kingdom of Sicily in December 1816, becoming Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies, with Naples as capital.
kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.r: The kingdom was an absolute monarchy that put down revolts in 1820 and 1848; Sicilians resented losing their autonomy. Ferdinand II opened Italy's first railway, from Naples to Portici, in 1839 and built a strong navy, but his harsh repression earned him the nickname King Bomba. The south remained largely rural, with powerful landowners and widespread poverty.
kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies.e: In 1860 Giuseppe Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand conquered Sicily and Naples. Francis II held out at Gaeta until February 1861, and the kingdom was annexed to the new Kingdom of Italy.
