kingdom-of-croatia-habsburg.t: Croatian kingdom under the Habsburgs, reduced by Ottoman conquest to the 'remnants of the remnants' and later a centre of the Croatian national revival.
kingdom-of-croatia-habsburg.o: On 1 January 1527 the Croatian nobles assembled at Cetin elected Ferdinand of Habsburg as king, in return for his help against the Ottomans. By the late 16th century Ottoman conquests had reduced Croatia to a narrow band around Zagreb, Karlovac and the coast, the reliquiae reliquiarum of the old kingdom.
kingdom-of-croatia-habsburg.r: Croatia was governed by a ban and its own Sabor, within the Lands of the Hungarian Crown, while much of its territory was detached into the Military Frontier under Vienna. The victory at Sisak in 1593 halted the Ottoman advance. Nobility, Catholic Church and Latin dominated public life until the Illyrian movement of Ljudevit Gaj revived Croatian in the 1830s.
kingdom-of-croatia-habsburg.e: In 1848 Ban Josip Jelačić led Croatian forces against the Hungarian revolution. The Croatian-Hungarian Settlement of 1868 joined the kingdom with Slavonia as the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia, an autonomous part of the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary.

katagum-emirate.t: An emirate of the Sokoto Caliphate on the western frontier of Bornu, founded by Fulani fighters who once sacked the Bornu capital.
katagum-emirate.o: Katagum was founded by Ibrahim Zaki, a Fulani scholar and commander who took up the jihad in the western borderlands of the Kanem-Bornu Empire. In 1808 he joined other Fulani leaders in capturing the Bornu capital, Birni Ngazargamu, and in about 1807-1809 he founded the town of Katagum as the seat of his emirate.
katagum-emirate.r: Katagum remained a frontier state facing Bornu, which recovered under al-Kanemi and pushed back the Fulani. The emir ruled through titled officials and district heads on the Sokoto model, and the emirate's economy rested on farming, cattle and trade in grain and natron. It had rivalries with neighbouring Hadejia.
katagum-emirate.e: British forces occupied Katagum in 1903 and it became part of the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria. The emirate's seat later moved to Azare, where the Emir of Katagum still reigns in Bauchi State.

kingdom-of-lar.t: A long-lived local kingdom in southern Iran on the trade road to Hormuz, whose silver 'larin' coins circulated across the Indian Ocean.
kingdom-of-lar.o: The rulers of Lar, often called the Miladi dynasty, claimed descent from Gurgin son of Milad, a hero of the Shahnameh. They are attested from the 12th century in Laristan, the arid region of southern Fars between Shiraz and the Gulf, with their capital at Lar.
kingdom-of-lar.r: Lar prospered from its position on the caravan route between Shiraz and the port of Hormuz, through which Indian, Arabian and Persian goods passed. The kingdom was famous for the larin, a strip of silver wire bent into a hook and stamped, which became a common currency in the Gulf, India and the Maldives in the 16th century. Its rulers accepted the overlordship of the Ilkhanate, the Timurid Empire and the Safavid Empire while keeping local autonomy. The population remained largely Sunni.
kingdom-of-lar.e: In 1601 to 1602 the Safavid general Allahverdi Khan conquered Lar for Shah Abbas I and deposed its last ruler, Ibrahim Khan, and Laristan became a Safavid province.

kingdom-of-akure.t: Yoruba city-kingdom of the Ekiti uplands, ruled by the Deji of Akure and long a borderland between Yoruba and Benin influence.
kingdom-of-akure.o: Akure traditions trace the dynasty to Omoremilekun Asodeboyede, a descendant of Oduduwa who is said to have left Ile-Ife and settled with his followers in the forest east of Ife. The kingdom is traditionally dated to the 12th century, though its early history is known mainly from oral tradition.
kingdom-of-akure.r: The Deji ruled with councils of senior chiefs and town quarters, over farmers of yams, cocoyams and later cocoa. Lying close to the Benin Empire, Akure was for long periods subject to Benin, whose influence shows in its titles and court customs. In the 19th century it joined the Ekiti Parapo alliance against Ibadan.
kingdom-of-akure.e: Akure came under British control in the 1890s and was incorporated into the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria. The city is now the capital of Ondo State, and the Deji of Akure remains its traditional ruler.

kingdom-of-the-picts.t: Early medieval kingdom of northern and eastern Scotland, known for its carved symbol stones, which merged with the Gaels to form the kingdom of Alba.
kingdom-of-the-picts.o: The Picts are first named in a Roman panegyric of 297 as enemies of Britain alongside the Irish. The name, Latin for 'painted people', was applied to the peoples north of the Forth, descendants of the Caledonii, Maeatae and other Iron Age groups. Over the following centuries their many districts were drawn together under powerful over-kings.
kingdom-of-the-picts.r: The Picts left few written records but carved distinctive symbol stones with combs, mirrors, crescents and animals, later combined with Christian crosses. Kings such as Bridei son of Maelchon, visited by Columba in the 560s, ruled through regional lords. Bridei son of Beli defeated the Northumbrians at Dun Nechtain in 685, and Óengus son of Fergus dominated northern Britain in the 8th century. Christianity spread from Iona and Northumbria.
kingdom-of-the-picts.e: Viking attacks in the 9th century devastated the Pictish elite, notably in a great defeat in 839. Cináed mac Ailpín, a king of Gaelic descent, took power around 843, and by about 900 Pictland had become the Gaelic-speaking kingdom of Alba, the core of medieval Scotland.
kingdom-of-the-picts.re: Celtic polytheism; Christianity from the 6th century

kingdom-of-maroboduus.t: The first large Germanic kingdom known by name, built in Bohemia by Maroboduus, who drilled an army on Roman lines and alarmed Augustus.
kingdom-of-maroboduus.o: Maroboduus, a Marcomannic noble who had spent his youth in Rome, led his people from the Main region into Bohemia around 9 BCE to escape Roman offensives. There he subjected neighbouring peoples, including the Quadi, Lugii, Semnones and Langobardi, building a realm that stretched from the Danube to the Elbe and beyond.
kingdom-of-maroboduus.r: Velleius Paterculus describes a centralised monarchy with a standing army of about 70,000 foot and 4,000 horse trained in Roman fashion, and a royal seat called Marobudum. Roman merchants lived there. Augustus planned to crush him in 6 CE with twelve legions, but the Pannonian revolt forced a treaty recognising Maroboduus as a friend of Rome.
kingdom-of-maroboduus.e: Maroboduus stayed neutral when Arminius destroyed Varus' legions in 9, and in 17 Arminius defeated him; the Semnones and Langobardi deserted. In 19 the Gothic exile Catualda seized his capital, and Maroboduus fled to Roman territory, dying in Ravenna in 37. Rome then created the client Kingdom of Vannius.

kingdom-of-kakheti-hereti.t: An eastern Georgian kingdom that resisted absorption into the united Georgian monarchy for nearly a century before David the Builder conquered it.
kingdom-of-kakheti-hereti.o: Around 1010 Kvirike III, chorepiscopus of the Principality of Kakheti, which had already absorbed the Principality of Hereti, took the title king of the Kakhs and Rans. His realm, centred on Telavi, emerged just as Bagrat III was uniting the rest of Georgia and fought off his attempts to take it.
kingdom-of-kakheti-hereti.r: Kvirike III, called the Great, was a strong ruler and builder who allied with neighbours against the Georgian kings. The kingdom lived from the vineyards and pastures of the Alazani valley and controlled routes towards Shirvan. Aghsartan I submitted to the Seljuk sultan Alp Arslan in 1068 and outwardly converted to Islam to keep his throne.
kingdom-of-kakheti-hereti.e: Seljuk overlordship weakened the kingdom, and in 1104 nobles of Hereti handed King Aghsartan II to David IV, who annexed it to the Kingdom of Georgia. Kakheti re-emerged as a separate kingdom in 1465.

kingdom-of-essex.t: The kingdom of the East Saxons north of the Thames, which controlled London for long periods and had a dynasty with unusual 'S' names.
kingdom-of-essex.o: The East Saxons settled Essex, Middlesex and parts of Hertfordshire. Their royal genealogy traces kings to Aescwine, traditionally placed in 527, and later kings bore names beginning with S, such as Saeberht, Sigeberht and Swithred.
kingdom-of-essex.r: Essex held London, which Bede called a market of many peoples. Saeberht accepted Christianity around 604 and Mellitus became bishop of London, but the kingdom reverted to paganism after his death until Cedd's mission in the 650s. Several kings often ruled jointly. Essex usually stood under the overlordship of Kent or Mercia.
kingdom-of-essex.e: After 825 Essex submitted to Ecgberht of the Kingdom of Wessex, and later fell within the Danelaw. In the 10th century it was absorbed into the Kingdom of England as a shire, which survives as the county of Essex.

khanate-of-bukhara.t: The Uzbek khanate of Transoxiana under the Shaybanid and Janid dynasties, whose capital Bukhara was a leading centre of Islamic learning.
khanate-of-bukhara.o: In 1500 Muhammad Shaybani, grandson of Abu'l-Khayr of the Uzbek Khanate, took Samarkand from the Timurids and soon conquered Transoxiana and Khurasan. After he was killed by the Safavid Shah Ismail at Merv in 1510, his kinsmen restored Shaybanid rule in Transoxiana, with Bukhara becoming the capital in the mid-16th century.
khanate-of-bukhara.r: The Shaybanids ruled through appanages held by members of the dynasty and Uzbek tribal chiefs. Abdullah Khan II reunited the realm in the late 16th century, building caravanserais, bridges and madrasas. In 1599 the Janids, or Ashtarkhanids, a branch of the Astrakhan Khanate's Jochid line, took over. Trade with India, Russia and Persia continued, and Naqshbandi Sufi orders were influential.
khanate-of-bukhara.e: Janid power declined, and in 1740 Nader Shah of Persia made Bukhara a vassal. The Manghit atalik Muhammad Rahim took effective power, and in 1785 his relative Shah Murad formally founded the Emirate of Bukhara.

kingdom-of-dyfed.t: South-west Welsh kingdom ruled by a dynasty of Irish descent, home of St Davids, which became the core of Deheubarth under Hywel Dda.
kingdom-of-dyfed.o: Dyfed grew from the Roman civitas of the Demetae after Roman rule ended around 410. Irish settlers crossed to the region in the 4th and 5th centuries, and its royal line traced descent from the Déisi of Ireland, a link supported by the many ogham-inscribed stones of the area.
kingdom-of-dyfed.r: In the 6th century Gildas denounced its king Vortiporius as tyrant of the Demetae, and a memorial stone at Castell Dwyran bearing his name in Latin and ogham may be his. The monastery of St Davids, founded by Dewi Sant, became the leading church of Wales. Asser records that its king Hyfaidd ap Bleddri submitted to Alfred of Wessex in the 880s to escape pressure from Gwynedd.
kingdom-of-dyfed.e: After Llywarch ap Hyfaidd died around 904, his daughter Elen married Hywel Dda of Seisyllwg, who took over Dyfed. Hywel joined the two realms to form the kingdom of Deheubarth, and Dyfed survived as a region and, much later, as a county name.

kussara.t: Kussara, the Anatolian kingdom of Pithana and Anitta, who forged the first large state of central Anatolia and paved the way for the Hittites.
kussara.o: Kussara was a city in central or eastern Anatolia whose site is still unknown. In the 18th century BCE its king Pithana seized Nesa, the city of Kanesh, and made it a second capital, launching the kingdom's rise.
kussara.r: His son Anitta conquered Zalpa, Hattus and the great kingdom of Purushanda, and took the title great king. His deeds are told in the Anitta text, the oldest known text in the Hittite language. Anitta built temples to the storm god and his own god Siusummi and celebrated victories with hunts of wild animals.
kussara.e: The kingdom of Anitta did not last long, but the Hittite royal line traced its origins to Kussara; Hattusili I called himself a man of Kussara. His move to Hattusa c. 1650 BCE marks the start of the Hittite Empire.

kingdom-of-naples.t: The southern Italian kingdom ruled from Naples for five centuries by Angevins, Aragonese, Spanish viceroys and Bourbons.
kingdom-of-naples.o: The Sicilian Vespers of 1282 drove Charles of Anjou from Sicily, leaving him only the mainland part of the Kingdom of Sicily. He and his heirs kept calling themselves kings of Sicily but ruled from Naples, which became the capital of a separate kingdom.
kingdom-of-naples.r: Robert the Wise made Naples a cultural centre, hosting Petrarch and Giotto. Alfonso V of Aragon conquered the kingdom in 1442. After French invasions, Spain ruled it from 1504 through viceroys, making Naples one of Europe's largest cities. A powerful baronage, heavy taxes and the Masaniello revolt of 1647 marked this period. Austria took the kingdom in 1707, and in 1734 Charles of Bourbon made it independent again.
kingdom-of-naples.e: Napoleon's armies drove out the Bourbons in 1806, creating the Kingdom of Naples (1806–1815). Ferdinand IV returned in 1815 and in 1816 united Naples and Sicily as the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

kingdom-of-shewa.t: An Amhara kingdom in central Ethiopia that rose to virtual independence and became the power base of Menelik II, the founder of modern Ethiopia.
kingdom-of-shewa.o: While the Gondar emperors weakened, Negasi Krestos, a Shewan noble claiming Solomonic descent, established an autonomous lordship in northern Shewa around 1682. His successors, at first with the title meridazmach, gradually extended their rule over the surrounding Oromo and Amhara districts, with capitals at Ankober and later Angolalla and Debre Berhan.
kingdom-of-shewa.r: The rulers combined Orthodox Christian kingship with pragmatic alliances with Oromo and Muslim neighbours. Sahle Selassie (r. 1813 to 1847), who took the title negus, built a wealthy state and received British and French missions. Shewa controlled trade routes from the Gibe region and Harar to the coast at Tadjoura and Zeila.
kingdom-of-shewa.e: In 1855 to 1856 Tewodros II conquered Shewa, but Menelik, Sahle Selassie's grandson, escaped from Magdala and restored the kingdom in 1865. When Menelik became emperor in 1889, Shewa merged into the Ethiopian Empire, with its new capital at Addis Ababa.

kingdom-of-bora-bora.t: A warrior kingdom of the Society Islands whose chiefs conquered neighbouring Raiatea and Tahaʻa and remained independent until French annexation in 1888.
kingdom-of-bora-bora.o: Bora Bora, a high island ringed by a wide lagoon in the Leeward Society Islands, was known in tradition as Porapora. Its chiefs were famed warriors, and in the mid-18th century the chief Puni led conquests of Tahaʻa, Raiatea and Maupiti, making Bora Bora the leading power of the Leeward group when Europeans first arrived in the 1760s.
kingdom-of-bora-bora.r: Kings ruled through a hierarchy of chiefs, with the marae of Fare Opu and others serving as ritual centres. The island's warriors and canoes gave it influence over its neighbours, and marriage ties linked its royal family to Raiatea and to the Kingdom of Tahiti. Missionaries of the London Missionary Society arrived in the 1820s, and the island adopted Christianity and written laws.
kingdom-of-bora-bora.e: The Jarnac Convention of 1847 recognised Bora Bora's independence. Its last queen, Teriimaevarua III, reigned from 1873 until France annexed the island in 1888. It became part of French Polynesia and, during the Second World War, a United States supply base.

karluk-yabgu.t: A Turkic confederation that fought beside the Arabs at Talas and seized Suyab, preparing the ground for the Kara-Khanid Khanate.
karluk-yabgu.o: The Karluks lived in the Altai and joined the Uyghurs and Basmyls in overthrowing the Second Turkic Khaganate in 744. Driven west by the Uyghur Khaganate, they moved to the Zhetysu region, and in 751 their defection to the Abbasid side helped decide the Battle of Talas against Tang China.
karluk-yabgu.r: Led by a yabghu, the Karluks took Suyab and the lands of the Turgesh Khaganate by 766, ruling a mix of nomadic tribes and the Sogdian towns of the Chu valley. They controlled Silk Road routes between Transoxiana and the Tarim, and Muslim geographers describe them as rich in livestock and towns. Some groups converted to Islam early.
karluk-yabgu.e: After the Uyghur Khaganate fell in 840, the Karluk leader Bilge Kul Qadir Khan proclaimed himself khagan, an event many historians take as the founding of the Kara-Khanid Khanate, which absorbed the Karluk lands.

kalinyamat.t: The north Javanese state of Ratu Kalinyamat, the warrior queen of Jepara who twice sent fleets against Portuguese Malacca.
kalinyamat.o: Kalinyamat, near the port of Jepara, was ruled by Sultan Hadlirin and his wife, a daughter of Sultan Trenggana of Demak. In 1549, during the Demak succession war, Hadlirin was murdered by agents of Arya Penangsang. His widow became ruler, remembered as Ratu Kalinyamat.
kalinyamat.r: Ratu Kalinyamat helped Hadiwijaya of Pajang defeat Arya Penangsang and made Jepara a leading port and shipbuilding centre. She sent fleets to support attacks on Portuguese Malacca in 1551 and 1574, and Portuguese writers called her the queen of Japara. She also patronised mosques such as the one at Mantingan.
kalinyamat.e: After Ratu Kalinyamat died around 1579, Jepara came under Pajang and then the Mataram Sultanate. She was named a National Hero of Indonesia in 2023.

karkota-dynasty.t: The dynasty that made Kashmir a regional empire under Lalitaditya Muktapida and built the Sun temple at Martand.
karkota-dynasty.o: According to Kalhana's Rajatarangini, Durlabhavardhana founded the dynasty around 625, succeeding the last king of the Gonanda dynasty through marriage. Xuanzang visited Kashmir during his reign and described a powerful kingdom with many Buddhist monasteries.
karkota-dynasty.r: Lalitaditya Muktapida, who ruled in the 8th century, led campaigns into the Punjab, Kannauj and beyond, defeating Yashovarman of the Varman dynasty of Kannauj, and sent envoys to Tang China. He founded the city of Parihaspora and built the Martand Sun temple, whose ruins still dominate the valley. Kashmir became a centre of Sanskrit poetry and philosophy, and Jayapida later patronised scholars and poets at his court. Irrigation and saffron supported the economy.
karkota-dynasty.e: Later Karkota kings were weak and dominated by ministers and court factions. In 855 Avantivarman took the throne, founding the Utpala dynasty.

khanate-of-sibir.t: The Tatar khanate of western Siberia whose defeat by Yermak's Cossacks in 1582 began Russia's conquest of Siberia.
khanate-of-sibir.o: The khanate emerged from the Tyumen Khanate when the local Taibugid dynasty seized power around 1495 and moved the capital to Qashliq (Isker) on the Irtysh. The Shibanid descendants of Jochi later contested the throne with the Taibugids.
khanate-of-sibir.r: Sibir ruled Siberian Tatars and tribute-paying forest peoples such as the Khanty and Mansi, whose fur tribute was its main wealth. The Taibugid ruler Yadegar paid tribute to Ivan IV from 1555, but in 1563 the Shibanid Kuchum seized power, stopped payments and promoted Islam among his subjects with missionaries from Bukhara.
khanate-of-sibir.e: In 1582 the Cossack leader Yermak, employed by the Stroganov merchants, took Qashliq. Kuchum fought on from the steppe until his final defeat on the Ob in 1598, after which the khanate's lands became part of Russia.

kingdom-of-aquitaine.t: Carolingian sub-kingdom of south-western Francia, created by Charlemagne for his son Louis the Pious.
kingdom-of-aquitaine.o: After crushing the last independent dukes of the Early Duchy of Aquitaine, Charlemagne made Aquitaine a kingdom for his three-year-old son Louis, crowned by the pope in Rome in 781. It reached from the Loire to the Pyrenees and was meant to secure the frontier against Al-Andalus.
kingdom-of-aquitaine.r: Louis governed with Frankish counts and advisers, reformed monasteries with Benedict of Aniane and led campaigns into Spain, taking Barcelona in 801. Royal residences included Toulouse, Poitiers and Chasseneuil. After he became emperor in 814 the kingdom passed to his son Pepin I.
kingdom-of-aquitaine.e: After Pepin I died in 838, his son Pepin II fought a long war against his uncle Charles the Bald of West Francia. Charles installed his own sons, Charles the Child and Louis the Stammerer, and when Louis succeeded to West Francia in 877 the kingdom merged into it.

kingdom-of-denmark.t: The world's oldest continuing monarchy, founded by Gorm the Old and Harald Bluetooth, which once ruled England, Norway and much of the Baltic.
kingdom-of-denmark.o: Danish kings are mentioned from the 8th century, but the continuous kingdom is traced to Gorm the Old, who ruled from Jelling around 936. His son Harald Bluetooth raised the Jelling stone, which claims that he won all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian, and built ring fortresses such as Trelleborg.
kingdom-of-denmark.r: Sweyn Forkbeard and Cnut the Great ruled England, and the Valdemar kings of the 12th and 13th centuries expanded into the Baltic. Margaret I united Denmark, Norway and Sweden in the Kalmar Union in 1397. The Lutheran Reformation came in 1536, and Frederick III made the monarchy absolute in 1660. Copenhagen grew rich from the Sound Toll on Baltic shipping.
kingdom-of-denmark.e: Denmark lost Scania to Sweden in 1658, Norway in 1814 and Schleswig and Holstein to Prussia and Austria in 1864. A liberal constitution was adopted in 1849. Occupied by Germany in 1940-1945, Denmark became a welfare state and joined the European Community in 1973; the Faroe Islands and Greenland remain self-governing parts of the realm.

kotda-sangani-state.t: A small Jadeja Rajput state of central Kathiawar, a branch of the Gondal ruling family.
kotda-sangani-state.o: Kotda Sangani was held by a Jadeja Rajput family related to the ruling house of Gondal. It emerged as a separate holding around 1650, though details of its founding are sparse.
kotda-sangani-state.r: The Thakor ruled a small group of farming villages, paying tribute before 1807 and then coming under British supervision in the Kathiawar Agency. Little else is recorded in standard references.
kotda-sangani-state.e: Kotda Sangani merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960, in present Rajkot district.

kingdom-of-samoa.t: A Samoan national government contested by rival chiefly lines and by Germany, Britain and the United States, which ended in the islands' partition in 1899.
kingdom-of-samoa.o: Samoa was divided among districts and great titles such as Malietoa, Tupua Tamasese and Mataʻafa. As the German firm Godeffroy developed plantations near Apia, Samoan chiefs formed a central government at Mulinuʻu in 1873, with a council of chiefs and an assembly. The American adventurer Albert Steinberger acted as premier until British and American consuls had him deported in 1876.
kingdom-of-samoa.r: Kingship, held mostly by Malietoa Laupepa, was repeatedly disputed in civil wars, with each rival courting a foreign power. Germany backed Tamasese against Laupepa in 1887, and a naval confrontation at Apia ended only when a hurricane wrecked the German and American warships in 1889. The Berlin Treaty of 1889 restored Laupepa under a three-power supervision. Robert Louis Stevenson, living at Vailima, wrote against foreign meddling.
kingdom-of-samoa.e: After Laupepa's death in 1898, war between supporters of Mataʻafa Iosefo and Malietoa Tanumafili I drew in foreign navies. The Tripartite Convention of 1899 abolished the kingship and partitioned the islands into German Samoa and American Samoa.

kingdom-of-livonia.t: Puppet kingdom created by Ivan the Terrible for the Danish prince Magnus during the Livonian War, which collapsed within eight years.
kingdom-of-livonia.o: Ivan IV of Russia, seeking to win the Baltic Germans to his side in the Livonian War, proclaimed Magnus of Holstein, brother of Frederick II of Denmark and ruler of Danish Ösel, king of Livonia in 1570. Magnus was to rule all Livonia as the tsar's vassal, and he married Ivan's relative Maria Staritskaya.
kingdom-of-livonia.r: Magnus resided at Oberpahlen (Põltsamaa) in central Estonia. His kingdom depended entirely on Russian troops and never controlled the major towns. A 30-week siege of Reval in 1570-1571 failed, and the Estonian and Livonian nobility largely refused to accept him.
kingdom-of-livonia.e: In 1577 Magnus tried to act independently and was punished by Ivan, who seized his towns. Magnus fled to Polish protection in 1578, renounced his royal title and died at Pilten in 1583. The kingdom disappeared, and its lands were divided among Poland-Lithuania, Sweden and Russia.

kingdom-of-england.t: The medieval and early modern kingdom unified by Aethelstan, transformed by the Norman Conquest and joined with Scotland in 1707.
kingdom-of-england.o: In 927 Aethelstan took York and received the submission of the northern rulers, completing the work of the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons. Viking kings briefly regained York until 954, and Danish kings Cnut and his sons ruled England from 1016 to 1042.
kingdom-of-england.r: Late Anglo-Saxon England had shires, a strong coinage and royal writs. After William the Conqueror's victory at Hastings in 1066, Norman lords, Domesday Book and a French-speaking elite reshaped society. Magna Carta in 1215, the growth of Parliament and common law, the wool trade and the Reformation under Henry VIII defined later centuries.
kingdom-of-england.e: England annexed Wales between 1283 and 1543 and ruled the Lordship of Ireland. James VI of Scotland inherited the crown in 1603, and after the Civil War and the Commonwealth of England, the Acts of Union of 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain.

kingdom-of-the-geats.t: The kingdom or kingdoms of the Geats in southern Sweden's Götaland, the people of Beowulf, later merged with the Svear to form Sweden.
kingdom-of-the-geats.o: Ptolemy and Jordanes mention Gautoi and Gautigoths in southern Scandinavia, and the Old English poem Beowulf makes the Geats and their king Hygelac its heroes. Hygelac's raid on Frisia, recorded by Gregory of Tours around 520, is one of the few datable events. Their heartland lay in Västergötland and Östergötland, around lakes Vänern and Vättern.
kingdom-of-the-geats.r: Whether the Geats formed one kingdom or several regional lordships is uncertain. Each land kept its own assembly and laws, later written down as the Västgötalagen. Society was based on farming, ironworking and a warrior aristocracy, and the region kept close ties with Denmark across the Kattegat.
kingdom-of-the-geats.e: Around 1000 the Geats came under the kings of the Svear, and Olof Skötkonung, traditionally baptised at Husaby in Västergötland, ruled both peoples. Götaland remained a distinct part of the Kingdom of Sweden, with its own lawmen, and its people sometimes elected rival kings into the 12th century.

klein-venedig.t: A short-lived German colony in Venezuela, leased by Emperor Charles V to the Welser banking house of Augsburg to pay off his debts.
klein-venedig.o: In 1528 Charles V granted the Welser family of Augsburg the right to colonise and govern the province of Venezuela in return for loans. The Welsers took over Coro, founded the year before by Juan de Ampíes, and sent the first German governor, Ambrosius Ehinger, in 1529.
klein-venedig.r: The Welser governors used the colony mainly as a base for expeditions into the interior in search of gold and the legendary El Dorado. Ehinger, Nikolaus Federmann, Georg Hohermuth von Speyer and Philipp von Hutten led long marches into the Andes and llanos, often with great brutality towards indigenous peoples. Little permanent settlement or farming developed, and German miners brought to the colony achieved little. Indigenous people were enslaved and sold.
klein-venedig.e: In 1546 the Spaniard Juan de Carvajal killed Philipp von Hutten and Bartholomäus Welser the younger. The Council of the Indies withdrew the Welser lease, confirmed in 1556, and the territory reverted to the Spanish Province of Venezuela.

kingdom-of-dagbon.t: The largest kingdom of northern Ghana, ruled by the Ya Na from Yendi, whose drummers preserve one of Africa's richest oral histories.
kingdom-of-dagbon.o: Dagbon traces its royal house to Na Gbewaa, founder of Mamprugu, through his son Sitobu. Under Na Nyagse, probably in the 15th century, Dagomba horsemen conquered the local peoples of the White Volta basin, killing or displacing their earth-priests and installing princes as chiefs. Later pressure from Gonja pushed the capital east to Yendi.
kingdom-of-dagbon.r: The Ya Na ruled through a hierarchy of chieftaincies held by royal sons and grandsons, who competed to rise toward the paramountcy. Royal drummers, the lunsi, recited genealogies and history at festivals. Islam was adopted at court under Na Zangina in the early 18th century, and Muslim traders linked Dagbon to the kola routes between Hausaland and the forest.
kingdom-of-dagbon.e: In 1744 Dagbon was defeated by the Ashanti Empire and paid an annual tribute of slaves. In 1899 it was divided between the British Gold Coast and German Togoland, separating Yendi from its western lands. The Ya Na still reigns at Yendi in Ghana's Northern Region.

kingdom-of-al-abwab.t: A Christian Nubian kingdom on the Nile south of Makuria, once a province of Alodia, known mainly from Mamluk-era Arabic sources.
kingdom-of-al-abwab.o: Al-Abwab, Arabic for 'the gates', was originally the northern province of Alodia, centred near Kabushiya close to the junction of the Nile and the Atbara. By 1276 it appears as an independent kingdom, apparently having broken away as Alodian power declined.
kingdom-of-al-abwab.r: Almost nothing is known of its internal government. In 1276 its king Adur captured the fugitive Makurian king David, who had fled the Mamluk Sultanate's invasion, and handed him over to Sultan Baybars. Adur later corresponded with Sultan Qalawun, offering alliance against Makuria. Its people were Christian Nubians.
kingdom-of-al-abwab.e: The kingdom fades from the record in the late 14th century, probably absorbed by advancing Arab tribes and the general collapse of Christian Nubia. The area later fell within the sphere of the Abdallab Sheikhdom and the Funj Sultanate.

kenya.t: East Africa's leading economy, independent since 1963, which moved from one-party rule to a multi-party democracy with a new constitution in 2010.
kenya.o: Kenya Colony became independent on 12 December 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta, leader of the Kenya African National Union (KANU), after the Mau Mau emergency and negotiations at Lancaster House. It became a republic a year later, with Kenyatta as president.
kenya.r: Kenyatta built a centralised state, favouring capitalist development, land purchase by Africans and close ties with the West, while tourism, tea and coffee drove growth. Daniel arap Moi, president from 1978, made KANU the sole legal party in 1982. Domestic and foreign pressure restored multi-party politics in 1991, and Mwai Kibaki's victory in 2002 ended KANU's rule.
kenya.e: A disputed election in 2007 led to violence that killed more than 1,000 people, followed by a power-sharing deal and a new constitution in 2010 that devolved power to 47 counties. Kenya remains a republic, with William Ruto president since 2022.

kingdom-of-owo.t: Yoruba kingdom between Ife and Benin, known for its ivory carving, terracotta sculpture and court culture shaped by both neighbours.
kingdom-of-owo.o: Owo traditions trace its royal line, the Olowo, to Ojugbelu, a son or grandson of Oduduwa who left Ile-Ife and settled in the forest to the south-east. The kingdom is usually dated from around the 15th century, though settlement on the site is older.
kingdom-of-owo.r: The Olowo ruled with chiefs organised in grades and with town quarters that kept their own titles. Lying close to the Benin Empire, Owo paid tribute to Benin for long periods and adopted Benin styles of regalia and ritual. Terracotta sculptures excavated at Igbo'Laja, dated to the 15th century, and ivory work made for the court show a distinctive art blending Ife and Benin traditions.
kingdom-of-owo.e: Owo came under British rule in the 1890s and was incorporated into the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria. It is now a town in Ondo State, where the Olowo remains a senior traditional ruler.

kuthar-state.t: A small Rajput hill state in the Shimla hills, part of whose land became the British cantonment of Subathu.
kuthar-state.o: The ruling family claimed Rajput descent and tradition dates the state to around 1500. Its early history is not reliably documented.
kuthar-state.r: Kuthar was a small hill state near the Gambhar river. It was occupied by the Gurkhas of the Kingdom of Nepal in the early 19th century. After the Anglo-Nepalese War the British restored its Rana in 1815 but kept Subathu, which became one of their first hill cantonments.
kuthar-state.e: Kuthar merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now part of Solan district.

kingdom-of-dambadeniya.t: The Sinhalese kingdom that moved the island's capital south-west to Dambadeniya after the fall of Polonnaruwa and restored Buddhist learning.
kingdom-of-dambadeniya.o: After Kalinga Magha's invasion devastated the Polonnaruwa kingdom around 1215, Sinhalese resistance gathered in the south-west. Vijayabahu III established himself at Dambadeniya, a defensible rock fortress in the wet zone, and by the 1230s had founded a new royal line there, recovering the Tooth Relic and the Alms Bowl.
kingdom-of-dambadeniya.r: Parakramabahu II, the dynasty's most celebrated king, drove out Magha's forces from Polonnaruwa, held a coronation there and convened a Buddhist council to reform the monastic order. He was himself an author, and the period produced classic Sinhala prose such as the Pujavaliya and Saddharma Ratnavaliya. The kings faced invasions by the Later Pandyan Empire and the Malay ruler Chandrabhanu.
kingdom-of-dambadeniya.e: Under later kings the capital moved repeatedly, to Yapahuwa and Kurunegala, as the Pandyas raided and carried off the Tooth Relic. Power drifted south-west, and by 1341 the court had settled at Gampola, beginning the Kingdom of Gampola.

kangra-state.t: The kingdom of the Katoch Rajputs, among the oldest ruling families in India, whose court under Sansar Chand gave rise to the Kangra school of painting.
kangra-state.o: The Katoch dynasty claimed descent from the Trigarta kingdom of the Mahabharata, and tradition gives it great antiquity. Its seat was the fort of Nagarkot, or Kangra, with its rich temple of Vajreshwari, which Mahmud of Ghazni plundered in 1009.
kangra-state.r: Kangra fort fell to the Mughals in 1620, and the Katoch Rajas were reduced to vassals until the empire weakened. Sansar Chand Katoch (r. 1775–1823) regained the fort in 1786, dominated the neighbouring hill states and made his courts at Tira Sujanpur and Nadaun centres of the delicate Kangra style of miniature painting, known for its scenes of Krishna.
kangra-state.e: A Gurkha siege from 1806 forced Sansar Chand to call in Ranjit Singh, who took Kangra fort for the Sikh Empire in 1809. In 1828 his son Anirudh Chand fled to British territory and the state was annexed. Kangra passed to the British in 1846 and is now a district of Himachal Pradesh.

kingdom-of-jiaodong.t: A short-lived kingdom on the eastern Shandong peninsula, given to the young Qi king Tian Shi in 206 BCE, whose ruler was killed within months.
kingdom-of-jiaodong.o: Tian Shi had been installed as king of Qi by his uncle Tian Rong during the war against the Qin dynasty. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu demoted him to King of Jiaodong, with his capital at Jimo, giving Linzi to Tian Du.
kingdom-of-jiaodong.r: Tian Rong ordered his nephew to stay in Linzi, but Tian Shi, fearing Xiang Yu, slipped away to Jiaodong. The kingdom existed for only a few months and left no trace of separate government.
kingdom-of-jiaodong.e: Enraged, Tian Rong pursued Tian Shi and killed him at Jimo in 206 BCE, absorbing Jiaodong into Qi (206 BC).

kumamoto-domain.t: The domain of Higo in central Kyushu, ruled from Kumamoto's mighty castle by the Kato and then the Hosokawa family.
kumamoto-domain.o: Kato Kiyomasa, one of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's leading generals, received northern Higo in 1588 and the whole province after supporting Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1600. He completed Kumamoto castle around 1607, one of the strongest fortresses in Japan, and carried out major river and land reclamation works.
kumamoto-domain.r: In 1632 the shogunate removed Kiyomasa's son Tadahiro and gave Higo to Hosokawa Tadatoshi with 540,000 koku; the Hosokawa ruled until 1871. Tadatoshi hosted the swordsman Miyamoto Musashi in his last years. In the 18th century Hosokawa Shigekata reformed finances and administration and founded the Jishukan school and a medical academy.
kumamoto-domain.e: Kumamoto took a cautious line in the Restoration and joined the new government. After abolition in 1871 it became Kumamoto Prefecture, and in 1877 the castle withstood a siege by Saigo Takamori's rebels.

khariar-state.t: A Chauhan chiefship of western Orissa, a branch of the Patna ruling house, transferred from the Central Provinces to Orissa in 1936.
khariar-state.o: Khariar was held by a branch of the Chauhan family of Patna (Patnagarh), one of the dynasties that dominated the hill country of western Orissa from the 14th century. The register dates its separate existence to around 1600.
khariar-state.r: The ruler governed an upland of forest and dry farming. In the 18th century Khariar fell under the Bhonsles of Nagpur, and under British rule it was treated as a large zamindari of Raipur district in the Central Provinces rather than as a full princely state.
khariar-state.e: Khariar was transferred to the new province of Orissa in 1936, and the zamindari was abolished after independence. Its territory lies in today's Nuapada district of Odisha.

khmer-republic.t: The US-backed Cambodian republic of Lon Nol, which deposed Sihanouk in 1970 and fell to the Khmer Rouge in April 1975.
khmer-republic.o: On 18 March 1970 Cambodia's national assembly, led by Prime Minister Lon Nol and Prince Sisowath Sirik Matak, voted to remove Norodom Sihanouk as head of state while he was abroad. The monarchy was abolished and the Khmer Republic proclaimed on 9 October 1970.
khmer-republic.r: Lon Nol, who became president in 1972, sought to expel North Vietnamese forces from Cambodia and received US military aid. The republic was weakened by corruption, an inexperienced army and Lon Nol's ill health. US bombing of the countryside intensified, and the Khmer Rouge, now allied with the exiled Sihanouk, gained recruits. Refugees swelled Phnom Penh to over two million.
khmer-republic.e: Khmer Rouge forces besieged Phnom Penh in early 1975. Lon Nol fled on 1 April, the US evacuated its embassy, and on 17 April 1975 the city fell. The Khmer Rouge emptied the capital and established Democratic Kampuchea.

kingdom-of-cornwall.t: The last surviving British kingdom of the south-west peninsula, which held out against Wessex until the 9th and 10th centuries.
kingdom-of-cornwall.o: Cornwall emerged as a separate British kingdom as the larger kingdom of Dumnonia shrank under West Saxon pressure. By the early 8th century Wessex had taken Devon, and the British realm beyond the Tamar became known as Kernow or Cornwall. Its kings are poorly recorded; Geraint fought Ine of Wessex around 710.
kingdom-of-cornwall.r: Cornwall kept its Brittonic language, saints' cults and links with Wales and Brittany. Tin mining and sea trade continued from Roman times. A defeat of a combined Cornish and Viking army at Hingston Down in 838 shows its kings still resisting the Kingdom of Wessex. The Annales Cambriae record the drowning of King Dungarth in 875.
kingdom-of-cornwall.e: Cornwall was brought under English control by the 9th century, and Aethelstan fixed the Tamar as the boundary around 936. It became part of the Kingdom of England, while the Cornish language survived into the 18th century.

kishangarh-state.t: A Rathore Rajput state of Rajasthan celebrated for the Kishangarh school of painting and its iconic image of Bani Thani.
kishangarh-state.o: Kishangarh was founded in 1611 by Kishan Singh, a son of Raja Udai Singh of Marwar, who received the territory near Ajmer from the Mughal emperor Jahangir. The state took its name from him.
kishangarh-state.r: The Maharajas served as Mughal mansabdars and later accepted British protection in 1818. The court became a centre of Krishna devotion and art: under Raja Sawant Singh, the poet Nagari Das, painters such as Nihal Chand created the elongated, lyrical Kishangarh style, epitomised by the portrait known as Bani Thani. It was a fifteen-gun salute state.
kishangarh-state.e: Kishangarh joined the United State of Rajasthan in 1948. The town, in Ajmer district, is now known for its marble trade and the miniature painting tradition that still bears its name.

kakatiya-dynasty.t: The Telugu dynasty of Warangal that united the Andhra country, built the Thousand Pillar Temple and was famed for its diamonds and tanks.
kakatiya-dynasty.o: The Kakatiyas began as feudatories of the Chalukyas of Kalyani in the Telangana region. As Chalukya power declined, Prola II and then Rudradeva asserted independence; Rudradeva declared sovereignty around 1163, built the Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamkonda and laid out a new capital at Orugallu (Warangal).
kakatiya-dynasty.r: Ganapatideva united most Telugu-speaking lands and encouraged trade through the port of Motupalli. His daughter Rudramadevi ruled as one of the few reigning queens of medieval India, praised by Marco Polo. The kingdom built large irrigation tanks such as Ramappa and Pakhal, and the Ramappa temple is now a World Heritage Site. Nayaka military chiefs held land in return for service.
kakatiya-dynasty.e: The Delhi Sultanate attacked Warangal repeatedly from 1309. In 1323 an army under Ulugh Khan, the future Muhammad bin Tughluq, captured the city and took Prataparudra prisoner. Former Kakatiya Nayakas soon led a revolt, founding the Musunuri Nayaks and Recherla Nayakas.

kalsia-state.t: A Sikh princely state on the Punjab–Haryana border with its capital at Chhachhrauli, founded by a sardar of the Karorsinghia misl.
kalsia-state.o: Gurbakhsh Singh, a Sandhu Jat of the village of Kalsia near Lahore and a member of the Karorsinghia misl, took territory south of the Sutlej around 1760. His son Jodh Singh enlarged the holding, and the family made Chhachhrauli its seat.
kalsia-state.r: Kalsia entered British protection with the other Cis-Sutlej states in 1809. It was a small Sikh-ruled state with a mixed Sikh, Hindu and Muslim population, ruled by a Raja and supervised through the Punjab States Agency.
kalsia-state.e: Ravi Sher Singh acceded to India in 1947, and in 1948 Kalsia was merged into the Patiala and East Punjab States Union. Its former lands are in Yamunanagar district of Haryana.

kingdom-of-kaffa.t: A forested kingdom of south-western Ethiopia, often linked with the origin of coffee, that kept its independence until 1897.
kingdom-of-kaffa.o: According to tradition the Kingdom of Kaffa was founded around 1390 by the Minjo dynasty, which united the Kafa-speaking clans of the highland forests south of the Gojeb river. It later absorbed the remnants of the Kingdom of Ennarea, whose rulers fled south in the 18th century, and expanded over neighbouring peoples.
kingdom-of-kaffa.r: The king, or tato, was a sacred ruler secluded from his subjects and advised by a council of seven great officials. The kingdom was defended by deep ditches and fortified gates. Kaffa exported ivory, civet, coffee, spices and slaves, and its religion blended traditional beliefs with Christian elements. The highland province gave its name, by some accounts, to coffee.
kingdom-of-kaffa.e: In 1897 Menelik II's armies conquered Kaffa after a long resistance, and its last king, Gaki Sherocho, was taken captive. War, famine and slave raiding devastated the population, and the kingdom became a province of the Ethiopian Empire. The Kafa Zone preserves the name.

kingdom-of-bulgaria.t: Bulgarian tsardom that fought on the losing side of three wars in search of Macedonia and Thrace, before its monarchy was abolished under Soviet influence.
kingdom-of-bulgaria.o: On 5 October 1908 Prince Ferdinand of the Principality of Bulgaria proclaimed independence from the Ottoman Empire and took the title of tsar. Bulgaria joined the Balkan League and won the First Balkan War in 1912, but its attack on Serbia and Greece in 1913 led to defeat in the Second Balkan War and loss of most of its gains.
kingdom-of-bulgaria.r: Hoping to win Macedonia, Bulgaria joined the Central Powers in 1915; defeat in 1918 brought Ferdinand's abdication in favour of Boris III and the harsh Treaty of Neuilly. Aleksandar Stamboliyski's agrarian government was overthrown in 1923, and Boris ruled personally from 1935. As an Axis ally from 1941 Bulgaria occupied Yugoslav Macedonia and Thrace; Jews of the old kingdom were saved from deportation in 1943.
kingdom-of-bulgaria.e: After Boris died in 1943, the Soviet army entered Bulgaria in September 1944 and the communist-led Fatherland Front seized power. A referendum in 1946 abolished the monarchy, and the boy king Simeon II went into exile, leading to the People's Republic of Bulgaria.

kingdom-of-lalitpur.t: The Malla kingdom of Patan in the Kathmandu Valley, whose Durbar Square is among the finest groups of Newar temples and palaces.
kingdom-of-lalitpur.o: Patan, an ancient Buddhist city long dominated by its own nobles, was brought under the Kathmandu king Shiva Simha Malla of the Kingdom of Kantipur, who around 1597 placed it under his son Hariharasimha. Hariharasimha's son Siddhi Narasimha Malla ruled it as a fully separate kingdom from about 1620, alongside Kantipur and the Kingdom of Bhaktapur.
kingdom-of-lalitpur.r: Siddhi Narasimha Malla, a devout ruler, built the stone Krishna Mandir. His son Shrinivasa Malla added to the palace complex. Patan was known for Buddhist monasteries and metalwork, and its nobles were powerful, often deposing kings. The city competed with its neighbours for the trade with Tibet.
kingdom-of-lalitpur.e: Prithvi Narayan Shah of the Gorkha Kingdom captured Patan in 1768, shortly after Kathmandu, and its last ruler Tej Narsingh Malla fled to Bhaktapur. Patan became part of the Kingdom of Nepal, and its Durbar Square is a World Heritage Site.

karamanids.t: The most powerful Turkish beylik of Anatolia after the Ottomans, centred on Karaman and Konya and their chief rival for two centuries.
karamanids.o: The Karamanids took their name from Karaman Bey, son of Nure Sufi, a Turkmen leader in the Taurus mountains. Around 1250 they rose against the weakened Sultanate of Rum, and Karaman's son Mehmed Bey briefly occupied Konya in 1277, where he reportedly decreed that Turkish alone be used in government.
karamanids.r: The Karamanids held the old Seljuk heartland, including Larende (Karaman) and later Konya, and saw themselves as heirs of the Seljuks. They allied with Venice, the Mamluks and the Aq Qoyunlu against the Ottomans. Alaeddin Bey was defeated and executed by Bayezid I in 1397, but Timur restored the dynasty in 1402. They built mosques and madrasas, such as the Ak Tekke and Hatuniye in Karaman.
karamanids.e: Mehmed II conquered most of the beylik in 1468, and the last Karamanid claimants were defeated by the 1480s; the region became the Ottoman province of Karaman.

kingdom-of-fermanagh.t: The Maguire lordship around Lough Erne, a Gaelic lordship of islands and churches whose last chief joined the Flight of the Earls.
kingdom-of-fermanagh.o: The Maguires rose in Fermanagh in the 13th century, with Donn Mor Maguire recognised as king in 1264. They displaced earlier rulers and became vassals of the O'Neills of the Kingdom of Tir Eoghain.
kingdom-of-fermanagh.r: Fermanagh was organised around Lough Erne, with islands, crannogs and monasteries such as Devenish. The Maguires built Enniskillen Castle in the 15th century. Their learned families compiled the Annals of Ulster on Belle Isle under Cathal Mac Maghnusa. Their economy rested on cattle and fishing.
kingdom-of-fermanagh.e: Hugh Maguire fought with Hugh O'Neill in the Nine Years' War and died in 1600. His brother Cuchonnacht left with the Flight of the Earls in 1607. Fermanagh was then planted with English and Scottish settlers, and Enniskillen became a Protestant garrison town.

kingdom-of-butua.t: The Torwa kingdom centred on Khami, heir to Great Zimbabwe in the south-west of the plateau and builder of richly decorated stone platforms.
kingdom-of-butua.o: Butua arose in the mid-15th century as the Kingdom of Zimbabwe declined, when the Torwa dynasty took control of the south-western plateau around modern Bulawayo. Its capital at Khami continued the Great Zimbabwe building tradition, and the kingdom controlled gold-bearing lands and rich cattle pastures.
kingdom-of-butua.r: Khami was built on terraced stone platforms faced with chequered and herringbone patterns, a style later seen at Danangombe and Naletale. Kings drew wealth from cattle and gold, trading with the Portuguese and Swahili through the Mutapa lands and the coast. Portuguese sources describe Butua as a rich gold country but give few details of its rulers or government.
kingdom-of-butua.e: In the mid-17th century a succession dispute brought in Portuguese allies and Khami was burnt. In the 1680s Changamire Dombo, a former Mutapa herder-general, overthrew the Torwa and founded the Rozvi state on the same lands.

kenmu-restoration.t: Emperor Go-Daigo's brief attempt to restore direct imperial rule in Japan after the fall of the Kamakura shogunate.
kenmu-restoration.o: Emperor Go-Daigo plotted against the Hojo regents for years and was exiled to the Oki islands, but he escaped. When the warlords Ashikaga Takauji and Nitta Yoshisada turned against the shogunate and destroyed it in 1333, Go-Daigo returned to Kyoto to rule in person, naming his era Kenmu in 1334.
kenmu-restoration.r: Go-Daigo abolished the office of regent and sought to govern through new offices such as the Records Office and a court for rewards. Yet he favoured courtiers over warriors in distributing confiscated lands, and the new regime proved slow and confused, as satirised in the Nijo-gawara lampoons posted in the capital.
kenmu-restoration.e: In 1335 Takauji went east to suppress a Hojo revolt and then broke with the emperor. He defeated Kusunoki Masashige at Minatogawa in 1336, installed a rival emperor and founded the Ashikaga shogunate, while Go-Daigo fled to Yoshino to found the Southern Court.

kingdom-of-lotharingia.t: Northern share of Middle Francia, named after its king Lothair II, whose name survives in Lorraine.
kingdom-of-lotharingia.o: At the Treaty of Prüm in 855 Lothair I left the northern part of Middle Francia, from Frisia through the Low Countries and the Rhineland to the Vosges, to his son Lothair II. The kingdom took its name from him as the realm of Lothair.
kingdom-of-lotharingia.r: It held the old Carolingian heartland around Aachen, Metz, Trier and Cologne, with wealthy abbeys and episcopal cities. Lothair II's reign was dominated by his attempt to divorce his childless wife Teutberga and marry Waldrada, which Pope Nicholas I blocked, leaving him without a legitimate heir.
kingdom-of-lotharingia.e: After Lothair II died in 869 his uncles divided the kingdom at Meerssen in 870, and in 880 all of it passed to East Francia. Arnulf of Carinthia made his son Zwentibold king in 895, but he was killed in 900, and the land became the Duchy of Lotharingia.

kaminaljuyu.t: The great highland centre of the Valley of Guatemala, which controlled obsidian and jade routes and later had close ties with Teotihuacan.
kaminaljuyu.o: Settled by about 800 BCE in what is now Guatemala City, Kaminaljuyu grew rich in the Late Preclassic period from irrigated farming, using canals fed by Lake Miraflores, and from control of the nearby El Chayal obsidian source. By 400 BCE it had hundreds of earthen mounds.
kaminaljuyu.r: Preclassic rulers were buried in elaborate tombs within earthen platforms, and carved monuments show an early writing system related to the southern Maya and Epi-Olmec traditions. In the Early Classic, around 400 CE, buildings in the talud-tablero style and Teotihuacan-style pottery show strong links with Teotihuacan, whether through alliance, trade or settlement.
kaminaljuyu.e: Kaminaljuyu declined in the Late Classic and was largely abandoned by about 900 CE. Most of its mounds have been destroyed by the growth of Guatemala City, but it remains essential for understanding highland Maya origins.

kingdom-of-jiujiang.t: The Huai River kingdom of Ying Bu, the tattooed convict turned general, whose defection from Xiang Yu to Liu Bang in 204 BCE helped decide the Chu-Han war.
kingdom-of-jiujiang.o: Ying Bu, also called Qing Bu after the tattoo that marked him as a convict, led a band of escaped labourers in the rising against the Qin dynasty and became one of Xiang Yu's fiercest generals. In 206 BCE Xiang Yu made him King of Jiujiang, with his capital at Lu (near Lu'an, Anhui).
kingdom-of-jiujiang.r: Jiujiang was Ying Bu's personal military domain on the Huai River, covering the old Jiujiang commandery. When Xiang Yu demanded troops, Ying Bu sent only token forces and became estranged from his overlord.
kingdom-of-jiujiang.e: Persuaded by Liu Bang's envoy Sui He, Ying Bu defected in 204 BCE; Chu troops overran Jiujiang and he fled to Liu Bang. In 203 BCE he was made King of Huainan over much the same land, but he rebelled against the Han Dynasty in 196 BCE and was killed.

kingdom-of-porto-novo.t: A Gun kingdom on the lagoon coast of Benin, rival of Dahomey, whose kings sought French protection and whose capital became the capital of French Dahomey.
kingdom-of-porto-novo.o: Tradition holds that Te Agbanlin, a prince of the Kingdom of Allada, founded the kingdom around 1688 at Hogbonu on the coastal lagoon, among Yoruba communities who called it Ajashe. Portuguese traders named the place Porto-Novo, and the kingdom grew as a port for the Atlantic trade, often under pressure from the Oyo Empire and later the Kingdom of Dahomey.
kingdom-of-porto-novo.r: Kings, chosen in rotation among royal branches, ruled with ministers and nobles in a court shaped by Allada traditions and by Yoruba neighbours. The slave trade was the mainstay until the mid-19th century, when palm oil took over. The population mixed Gun, Yoruba and returning Afro-Brazilians, who brought Catholicism, Islam and Brazilian-style architecture.
kingdom-of-porto-novo.e: King Soji accepted a French protectorate in 1863, and Toffa renewed it in 1882 as protection against Dahomey. Porto-Novo became the capital of French Dahomey, and after Toffa's death in 1908 the French ended the monarchy's political role. It remains the official capital of Benin.

keladi-nayaka-kingdom.t: A Kannada kingdom of the western Ghats ruled from Ikkeri and Bednore, famous for its pepper trade and for Queen Chennamma's defiance of Aurangzeb.
keladi-nayaka-kingdom.o: The Keladi Nayakas began as local chiefs at Keladi in the Malnad hills, serving the Vijayanagara Empire as governors from around 1499. After Vijayanagara's defeat at Talikota in 1565 they became effectively independent, moving their capital to Ikkeri and later, in the 1640s, to Bidanur (Bednore).
keladi-nayaka-kingdom.r: Shivappa Nayaka, the greatest ruler, introduced a celebrated land revenue system, the shist, and expanded the kingdom to the coast of Kanara, driving the Portuguese from several ports. The kingdom profited from pepper and rice exports. Keladi Chennamma, who ruled from 1671, sheltered Shivaji's son Rajaram from the Mughal Empire. The Aghoreshwara temple at Ikkeri shows the dynasty's patronage.
keladi-nayaka-kingdom.e: Hyder Ali of the Kingdom of Mysore conquered Bednore in 1763, seizing its treasury, and renamed it Haidarnagar. The territory remained part of Mysore and later British India.

kara-del.t: A Mongol-ruled oasis kingdom at Hami, gateway between Ming China and Central Asia, which fell under the control of Turfan in the early 16th century.
kara-del.o: After the fall of the Yuan Dynasty, a branch of the Chinggisid family descended from Chagatai held the oasis of Hami (Kumul) at the eastern end of the Tarim routes. Its prince Gunashiri sent tribute to the Ming Empire from the 1380s, and in 1404 the Ming recognised his successor Engke Temür as Prince of Zhongshun and soon set up the Hami Guard.
kara-del.r: Kara Del controlled the road between the Hexi Corridor and Turfan, and its rulers lived by taxing caravans and by the tribute trade with China. Its population included Uyghurs, Mongols and Hui; Buddhism was giving way to Islam. The Ming treated it as the key outpost of its western frontier system.
kara-del.e: From the 1470s the Muslim rulers of Turfan, descendants of the khans of Moghulistan, repeatedly seized Hami, and Ming attempts to restore its princes failed. In 1513 Hami submitted to Mansur Khan of Turfan, and the kingdom ended. Islam became the dominant faith of the oasis.

kingdom-of-chimor.t: The largest kingdom of the Andean coast before the Incas, ruled from the vast adobe city of Chan Chan and stretching some 1,000 km along northern Peru.
kingdom-of-chimor.o: Chimor arose around 900 in the Moche valley, where the Moche had once ruled. According to a legend recorded by the Spanish, its founder Tacaynamo came by sea and established a dynasty at Chan Chan. Later rulers expanded by conquest, and Ñancen Pinco extended the kingdom over neighbouring valleys.
kingdom-of-chimor.r: The Chimú kings ruled from Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas, with walled palace compounds called ciudadelas that each served a ruler in life and as his tomb after death. The state managed extensive irrigation canals, including one linking the Chicama and Moche valleys. Chimú craftsmen excelled in gold and silver work and black burnished pottery. Around 1375 Chimor conquered the lands of the Sicán, and under Minchancaman it reached as far as Tumbes.
kingdom-of-chimor.e: Around 1470 the Incas under Túpac Inca Yupanqui conquered Chimor, captured Minchancaman and moved its craftsmen to Cusco. Chan Chan was later looted for gold by the Spanish. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.

kingdom-of-gisaka.t: An eastern rival of the Kingdom of Rwanda, ruled by its own dynasty until Rwanda annexed it in the mid-19th century.
kingdom-of-gisaka.o: Gisaka occupied the lands of south-eastern Rwanda near the Kagera river. Its rulers belonged to the Bagesera clan, and court traditions present it as one of the older kingdoms of the region, already established when the Nyiginya dynasty of the Kingdom of Rwanda was still small.
kingdom-of-gisaka.r: Gisaka was a cattle-keeping and farming kingdom with sacred kingship, royal drums and rituals similar to those of Rwanda. For generations it fought Rwanda over borderlands and cattle, at times defeating its rival in the 17th and 18th centuries, according to Rwandan court traditions.
kingdom-of-gisaka.e: Rwanda conquered and annexed Gisaka around 1852 under Mwami Mutara II Rwogera. In the colonial period the British briefly claimed the region in 1919 before it returned to Belgian Ruanda-Urundi. Gisaka's identity survived as a region of eastern Rwanda.

kingdom-of-coorg.t: A hill kingdom of the Western Ghats ruled by the Haleri Rajas until the British annexed it in 1834.
kingdom-of-coorg.o: Around 1600 a member of the Haleri family, a Lingayat house related to the Nayakas of Ikkeri (Keladi), established himself in Kodagu, the hilly country at the source of the Kaveri. His successors built a kingdom with its capital at Madikeri (Mercara).
kingdom-of-coorg.r: The Rajas ruled the warrior Kodava landholders through their own officials. Coorg resisted Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan of Mysore, who occupied it in the 1780s. Dodda Vira Rajendra regained the throne and allied with the British in the Anglo-Mysore wars. The economy rested on rice and forest produce; coffee arrived later.
kingdom-of-coorg.e: After Chikka Vira Rajendra quarrelled with the Company, a British force deposed him in 1834 and annexed Coorg. It became a province of British India, then a state of India until 1956, when it joined Mysore State, now Karnataka.

kingdom-of-banda.t: Kingdom of the Nafana people in west-central Ghana, near the old trading town of Begho.
kingdom-of-banda.o: Known mainly from oral tradition. Banda was established by the Nafana people in the hills north-west of the Bono State, close to Begho, a Mande trading town of the gold and kola routes. It took shape around the 17th century.
kingdom-of-banda.r: Banda's ruler governed with clan chiefs over farming villages, while Dyula traders linked the area to the Niger bend. From the 18th century Banda was a tributary of the Ashanti Empire, sending troops and tribute, and it suffered from Ashanti's wars against Gyaman.
kingdom-of-banda.e: In the 1890s Banda was disrupted by the armies of Samori Ture, then came under British rule in the Northern Territories of the Gold Coast. It remains a traditional area in Ghana's Bono Region.

kingdom-of-soloi.t: Cypriot kingdom on Morphou Bay, said to have taken its name from the Athenian lawgiver Solon, who advised its king.
kingdom-of-soloi.o: Soloi lay on the bay of Morphou in north-western Cyprus, near the copper mines of Skouriotissa. Founded in the early Iron Age, it was a city-kingdom by the 7th century BCE. Plutarch tells that King Philocyprus moved the city to a better site on Solon's advice and named it after him.
kingdom-of-soloi.r: Soloi grew rich on copper and farmland. Its king Aristocyprus fell fighting the Persians at Salamis in 497 BCE, after which Soloi endured a five-month siege. The palace of Vouni on a nearby hill, built in the 5th century BCE, may have been used to watch over Soloi. King Pasicrates aided Alexander at Tyre in 332 BCE.
kingdom-of-soloi.e: Its last king, Eunostos, married Eirene, daughter of Ptolemy I, and the kingdom was absorbed into Ptolemaic Cyprus c. 312 BCE. Soloi remained a city into Roman and early Christian times.

kingdom-of-gianyar.t: Central Balinese kingdom that chose Dutch protection in 1900 and whose princes at Ubud fostered Bali's modern arts.
kingdom-of-gianyar.o: Gianyar was founded around 1770 by a branch of the Dewa Manggis family, nobles linked to the senior court of the Kingdom of Klungkung, who established a palace at Gianyar in the fertile valleys between the Ayung and Pakerisan rivers. The kingdom expanded through the 18th and 19th centuries at the expense of its neighbours.
kingdom-of-gianyar.r: Gianyar was densely populated and rich in irrigated rice land, temples and craftsmen. Power was shared with branch lineages such as the princes of Ubud and Peliatan. In the 1880s it was shattered by wars with Klungkung and other courts, and its raja was briefly held captive by Klungkung before the kingdom was restored.
kingdom-of-gianyar.e: Seeking security, Gianyar accepted Dutch protection in 1900, retaining its dynasty as regents. Under colonial rule Ubud became the centre of a famous artistic revival, and Gianyar royals, including Ide Anak Agung Gde Agung, became Indonesian statesmen. It is now a regency of Bali.

komancza-republic.t: A tiny Ukrainian-oriented republic of Lemko villages in the Carpathians, which lasted from November 1918 to January 1919.
komancza-republic.o: When Austro-Hungarian rule collapsed in November 1918, Ukrainian-minded Lemkos in about thirty villages around Komancza, in the eastern Lemko region of Galicia, set up their own commissariat. Unlike the pro-Russian Lemko-Rusyn Republic further west, they aimed to join the West Ukrainian People's Republic.
komancza-republic.r: The republic was a local self-government led by a council and the Greek Catholic priest Pantaleimon Shpylka, with a small militia to keep order and guard against Polish units. It had little territory and no resources of its own, and it existed mainly to hold the area until it could be united with the Ukrainian state.
komancza-republic.e: In January 1919 Polish troops entered the area during the Polish-Ukrainian War and dissolved the republic. Its villages became part of the Second Polish Republic, and their Lemko inhabitants were deported in 1947.

kokura-domain.t: The domain guarding the Kanmon Straits in northern Kyushu, held by the Hosokawa and then by the Ogasawara, and defeated by Choshu in 1866.
kokura-domain.o: After Sekigahara, Hosokawa Tadaoki received Buzen province and built Kokura castle from 1602 on the southern shore of the Kanmon Straits. In 1632 the Hosokawa were moved to Kumamoto, and Ogasawara Tadazane, a relative of the Tokugawa, took over Kokura with 150,000 koku.
kokura-domain.r: The Ogasawara, a hereditary vassal family, ruled until the end of the period with a mission to watch over the outside lords of Kyushu and the sea route between Honshu and Kyushu. Kokura was a stop for Korean embassies and Dutch missions travelling to Edo, and lay on the Nagasaki road.
kokura-domain.e: In the second shogunate expedition against Choshu in 1866, Choshu forces under Takasugi Shinsaku crossed the straits; Kokura burned its castle and withdrew inland to Kawara. After abolition in 1871 the area became part of Fukuoka Prefecture.
