kingdom-of-brega.t: A kingdom of the southern Ui Neill on the fertile plain north of Dublin, home to Tara, Knowth and Newgrange and rival of Mide.
kingdom-of-brega.o: Brega emerged in the 7th century when the Sil nAedo Slaine, descendants of Aed Slaine of the southern Ui Neill, established themselves in the plain between the Liffey and the Boyne. Their rulers made the ancient passage tomb at Knowth into a royal residence.
kingdom-of-brega.r: Brega's kings shared the kingship of Tara with Clann Cholmain of Mide until the 8th century, but later lost out. The kingdom split into northern and southern parts. It contained monasteries such as Slane, Duleek and Monasterboice, and from the 9th century suffered heavy pressure from the Norse of the Kingdom of Dublin.
kingdom-of-brega.e: By the 11th century Brega was fragmented and dominated by Mide, Dublin and Leinster. Its lands passed into the Lordship of Meath granted to Hugh de Lacy in 1172, and its name survives in Irish place-names.

kunihar-state.t: One of the smallest of the Simla Hill States, a Rajput chiefship near Shimla restored under British protection after the Gurkha wars.
kunihar-state.o: Tradition holds that the ruling family came from Akhnoor near Jammu and founded the state around 1154.
kunihar-state.r: Kunihar consisted of a few villages in the hills west of Shimla, ruled by a Thakur or Rana. Like its neighbours it was occupied by the Gurkhas of the Kingdom of Nepal in the early 19th century; little else is recorded of its history.
kunihar-state.e: The British restored the ruler by sanad in 1815. Kunihar merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now in Solan district.

kingdom-of-belgium.t: The kingdom born of the 1830 revolution, an early industrial power and colonial ruler of the Congo, now a federal state and home of the EU's institutions.
kingdom-of-belgium.o: In August 1830 a revolt in Brussels against the United Kingdom of the Netherlands spread across the south. A provisional government declared independence in October, a congress adopted a liberal constitution in 1831, and Leopold of Saxe-Coburg became king. The Netherlands recognised Belgium in the Treaty of London of 1839, which also guaranteed its neutrality.
kingdom-of-belgium.r: Belgium became continental Europe's first industrial nation, with coal, iron and railways in Wallonia. Leopold II ruled the Congo Free State as a personal possession, notorious for forced labour, until Belgium annexed it in 1908. Germany invaded in 1914 and 1940; King Albert I led resistance in the First World War. Tension between French and Dutch speakers grew steadily.
kingdom-of-belgium.e: After 1945 Belgium co-founded Benelux, NATO and the European Communities, and Brussels hosts the EU and NATO headquarters. The Congo became independent in 1960. Language conflicts led to reforms that made Belgium a federal state of regions and communities in 1993.

kingdom-of-nikki.t: The leading Bariba kingdom of Borgu, famed for its cavalry aristocracy and the Gaani festival still celebrated in northern Benin.
kingdom-of-nikki.o: Nikki was founded by Wasangari horsemen who imposed their rule on Bariba farming communities of eastern Borgu, probably in the 16th century. Its kings traced descent from Sunon Sero and through him to the legendary conqueror Kisra. Nikki came to be recognised as the most powerful of the Borgu states, alongside the Kingdom of Bussa.
kingdom-of-nikki.r: The Sina Boko, the king of Nikki, ruled with princes and Wasangari warriors who held provinces and lived from tribute and raiding. Borgu cavalry checked the Oyo Empire and later the Fulani; Sero Kpera of Nikki died fighting the Ilorin forces in the 1830s. The annual Gaani festival renewed loyalty to the king.
kingdom-of-nikki.e: Britain and France raced to sign treaties at Nikki in 1894, and the Anglo-French Convention of 1898 assigned it to France. It became part of French Dahomey, and the king of Nikki remains a respected traditional ruler in Benin.

kingdom-of-tylis.t: Celtic kingdom in eastern Thrace that extorted heavy tribute from Byzantium after the great Celtic invasion of 279 BCE.
kingdom-of-tylis.o: Celts who had invaded the Balkans in 279 BCE, defeating Macedon, settled in eastern Thrace under their leader Comontorius around 277 BCE. They founded a kingdom with its capital at Tylis, whose exact location near the Haemus or Strandzha mountains is still debated.
kingdom-of-tylis.r: The kingdom lived largely from tribute. According to Polybius, Byzantium paid it ever larger sums, rising to 80 talents a year. Celtic warriors ruled over a Thracian population, and coins of the last king, Cavarus, are known. Cavarus was praised as a statesman and mediated in the war between Byzantium and Rhodes in 220 BCE.
kingdom-of-tylis.e: Around 212 BCE the local Thracians rose against Celtic rule and destroyed the kingdom. Thracian dynasts reasserted themselves in the region, which later came under Macedonian and Roman influence.

kingdom-of-northumbria.t: The kingdom of the Angles north of the Humber, home of Bede, Lindisfarne and the Northumbrian Renaissance, later carved up by the Vikings.
kingdom-of-northumbria.o: Northumbria grew out of the union of the Kingdom of Bernicia and the Kingdom of Deira, which became lasting under Oswiu after his victory over Penda at the Winwaed in 655. At its height it stretched from the Humber to the Firth of Forth and west to the Irish Sea.
kingdom-of-northumbria.r: Northumbrian kings were Christian patrons of monasteries such as Lindisfarne, Wearmouth-Jarrow and Whitby, where the Synod of 664 chose Roman over Irish church practice. This produced the Lindisfarne Gospels, the Codex Amiatinus and the works of Bede and Alcuin. The 8th century was marked by frequent royal murders and depositions.
kingdom-of-northumbria.e: Defeat by the Picts at Nechtansmere in 685 checked its northward growth, and Vikings sacked Lindisfarne in 793. In 867 the Great Heathen Army took York, creating the Kingdom of York, while English rulers held out at Bamburgh. The last Viking king, Eric Bloodaxe, was expelled in 954.

kingdom-of-thomond.t: The O'Brien kingdom of North Munster, descendant of Brian Boru's power base, which kept its independence until 1543.
kingdom-of-thomond.o: Thomond arose from the Dal Cais lands in Clare and Limerick. In 1118 the Treaty of Glanmire, imposed by Turlough O'Connor, split Munster, leaving the O'Briens with the north, Tuadmumu. Their capital was Limerick, the former Kingdom of Limerick.
kingdom-of-thomond.r: The O'Brien kings were patrons of churches such as Holy Cross, Killaloe and Limerick's cathedral, founded by Domnall Mor O'Brien. After losing Limerick to the Normans in the 1190s, they ruled from Clonroad near Ennis. In 1318 Muirchertach O'Brien defeated the Normans at Dysert O'Dea, preserving Gaelic rule west of the Shannon.
kingdom-of-thomond.e: In 1543 Murrough O'Brien surrendered his kingship to Henry VIII and became Earl of Thomond under the Kingdom of Ireland. His lands became County Clare in the 1570s.

kasadi-sultanate.t: A dynasty of Yafa'i origin that ruled the Hadrami port of Mukalla until the Qu'aiti sultans took it in 1881.
kasadi-sultanate.o: The Kasadi were a family of the Yafa tribal confederation, whose men served as soldiers across Hadramawt. In the 18th century they established themselves as naqibs, or governors, of the port of Mukalla on the coast of Hadramawt and ruled it as a small independent state.
kasadi-sultanate.r: Mukalla was the main outlet of Hadramawt to the sea, and the Kasadi lived from customs on trade with India, East Africa and the Red Sea, including slaves and dates. Their rule was contested by Kathiri and other Yafa'i rivals and depended on armed retainers. Little is recorded about their internal administration.
kasadi-sultanate.e: In the 19th century the Kasadi came into conflict with the rising Qu'aiti Sultanate. With British support the Qu'aiti took Mukalla in 1881, and the Kasadi naqib went into exile in Zanzibar. Mukalla became the Qu'aiti capital.

kingdom-of-gojjam.t: A royal province of north-western Ethiopia whose rulers, Negus Tekle Haymanot and Ras Hailu, were among the empire's most powerful vassals.
kingdom-of-gojjam.o: In 1881 Emperor Yohannes IV crowned Ras Adal Tessema, the ruler of Gojjam, as Negus Tekle Haymanot of Gojjam and Kaffa, partly to balance the power of Menelik of the Kingdom of Shewa. The two kings soon clashed over the rich lands south of the Abay, and Menelik defeated Tekle Haymanot at the Battle of Embabo in 1882.
kingdom-of-gojjam.r: Gojjam was a highland province of farmers and Orthodox monasteries, with its capital at Debre Markos. Its king kept his own court and army and collected taxes and tribute. Tekle Haymanot fought at the Battle of Adwa in 1896. His son Ras Hailu Tekle Haymanot later ruled Gojjam as one of the empire's wealthiest lords.
kingdom-of-gojjam.e: In 1932 Ras Hailu was arrested for helping the deposed emperor Lij Iyasu escape, and Haile Selassie ended Gojjam's autonomy, placing it under a governor and fully integrating it into the Ethiopian Empire.

kel-adagh.t: The Tuareg confederation of the Adrar des Ifoghas mountains around Kidal, led by the Ifoghas lineage and central to Tuareg politics in Mali.
kel-adagh.o: The Kel Adagh, meaning the people of the mountain, formed in the Adrar des Ifoghas massif of north-eastern Mali. By the 18th century the Ifoghas, a lineage of religious prestige, had become the leading group, providing the confederation's amenokal.
kel-adagh.r: The confederation united noble, vassal and dependent groups of camel and goat herders who moved between wells and pastures in a harsh environment. It traded livestock and salt with the Niger valley and the Sahara, and maintained shifting relations with the Kel Ahaggar and the Iwellemmeden Kel Ataram. Islamic scholarship gave the Ifoghas authority.
kel-adagh.e: French forces occupied the Adrar des Ifoghas around 1908 to 1910 and ruled through the amenokal. The confederation became part of French Sudan, and after independence Kidal was the centre of repeated Tuareg rebellions in Mali.

kingdom-of-adansi.t: Early Akan kingdom of the central forest, remembered as one of the first Akan states before its conquest by Denkyira.
kingdom-of-adansi.o: Adansi lay in the forest south of present-day Kumasi, with its capital at Fomena. Akan tradition regards it as one of the earliest organised Akan states, and its name is linked in tradition with building, as its people were said to be the first to construct houses in the forest.
kingdom-of-adansi.r: Its rulers controlled gold mining and the trade routes from the central forest toward the coast and northern markets. Several Akan clans trace their early migrations through Adansi, and its political forms, including the stool and matrilineal succession, were shared by later states.
kingdom-of-adansi.e: In the 17th century Adansi was conquered by Denkyira and then passed under the Ashanti Empire. Fomena later gave its name to the 1874 treaty that ended the Anglo-Ashanti war, and Adansi remains a traditional area in Ghana.

kingdom-of-derge.t: The leading kingdom of eastern Tibet (Kham), renowned for the Derge printing house and as the cradle of the 19th-century Rime religious movement.
kingdom-of-derge.o: The royal house of Derge claimed descent from Gar Tongtsen, minister of the Tibetan Empire. The family rose in the 15th century around the Sakya monastery of Lhundrup Teng, which became the royal seat, and gradually extended its rule over large parts of the upper Yangtze valley in Kham.
kingdom-of-derge.r: Its kings combined secular and religious authority and ruled through hereditary officials over farming valleys and nomad pastures. King Tenpa Tsering founded the Derge Parkhang printing house in 1729, which carved woodblocks for the Buddhist canon still used today. In the 19th century Derge patronised the non-sectarian Rime movement of teachers such as Jamgön Kongtrul. Derge recognised Qing suzerainty while remaining close to Lhasa.
kingdom-of-derge.e: From 1848 Derge was occupied by the warlord Gönpo Namgyal of Nyarong until Lhasa's troops expelled him in 1865. In 1909 the Qing commander Zhao Erfeng deposed the king and placed Derge under direct Chinese administration.

kingdom-of-kakongo.t: A small Kongo coastal kingdom between Loango and Ngoyo whose port of Malemba was a busy Atlantic slave-trading harbour.
kingdom-of-kakongo.o: Kakongo was one of the Kikongo-speaking kingdoms north of the Congo estuary that recognised the senior Kingdom of Loango in early times. By the mid-16th century it had its own king, ruling from Kinguele, with lands between the coast and the Mayombe forest.
kingdom-of-kakongo.r: Its sacred king was elected by senior lineages and surrounded by ritual restrictions, and regional chiefs controlled much of the land. In the 18th century the port of Malemba became a major market for French and English slavers, and the Abbe Proyart's history of Loango and Kakongo (1776), based on French missionaries' reports, described the court and customs.
kingdom-of-kakongo.e: With the end of the slave trade Kakongo declined into a cluster of chiefdoms. In 1885 its lands were divided between Portuguese Angola, where they formed part of Cabinda, and the Congo Free State.

kingdom-of-italy.t: The united Italian monarchy of the House of Savoy, which completed unification, fought two world wars and fell to a referendum in 1946.
kingdom-of-italy.o: On 17 March 1861 the parliament in Turin proclaimed Victor Emmanuel II of the Kingdom of Sardinia king of Italy, after the annexation of Lombardy, central Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Venetia was added in 1866 and Rome taken from the Papal States in 1870.
kingdom-of-italy.r: The capital moved from Turin to Florence in 1865 and to Rome in 1871. Under the Statuto Albertino, liberal governments led by Agostino Depretis, Francesco Crispi and Giovanni Giolitti industrialised the north while millions emigrated. Italy entered the First World War in 1915. Benito Mussolini took power in 1922, built a Fascist dictatorship, signed the Lateran Treaty in 1929, conquered Ethiopia in 1936 and allied with Nazi Germany.
kingdom-of-italy.e: Defeat led the king to dismiss Mussolini in 1943 and sign an armistice with the Allies. On 2 June 1946 a referendum abolished the monarchy, creating the Italian Republic.

kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.t: Habsburg-ruled Kingdom of Hungary, from the narrow frontier strip of Royal Hungary to the reconquered kingdom that won self-government in 1867.
kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.o: After the death of Louis II at Mohács in 1526, a diet at Pozsony elected Ferdinand of Habsburg king, against the rival John Zápolya. The Ottoman capture of Buda in 1541 left the Habsburgs with only a western and northern strip, Royal Hungary, governed from Pressburg, where diets met and kings were crowned.
kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.r: Hungary kept its own diet, counties and noble privileges while the Habsburgs controlled war and foreign affairs from Vienna. Latin was the official language until 1844. Ottoman wars dominated until the reconquest of Buda in 1686 and the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699. Revolts by Bocskai, Thököly and Rákóczi defended Protestant and noble rights; the Reform Era brought Széchenyi's modernisation.
kingdom-of-hungary-1526-1867.e: The revolution of 1848 and the war of independence were crushed in 1849 with Russian help, followed by direct rule from Vienna. Defeat by Prussia in 1866 forced the Compromise of 1867, which created Austria-Hungary and the self-governing Kingdom of Hungary (1867-1918).

kingdom-of-lagos.t: Yoruba island kingdom under the authority of Benin that became a major 19th century slave port before Britain annexed it in 1861.
kingdom-of-lagos.o: Lagos, known locally as Eko, began as a settlement of Awori Yoruba on the lagoon islands. In the 16th or early 17th century the Benin Empire established a war camp there, and Ashipa, recognised by the Oba of Benin, founded the line of Obas of Lagos.
kingdom-of-lagos.r: The Oba ruled with Yoruba white-cap chiefs and paid tribute to Benin. Lagos grew into a leading slave port in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. A succession struggle between Kosoko and his uncle Akitoye drew in the British, who bombarded Lagos in 1851, deposed Kosoko and installed Akitoye.
kingdom-of-lagos.e: Under pressure from Britain, Oba Dosunmu signed a treaty ceding Lagos in 1861, and it became Lagos Colony. Lagos grew into Nigeria's largest city, and the Oba of Lagos remains its traditional ruler.

kaulonia.t: Achaean Greek city on the Calabrian coast, a dependency of Croton, destroyed by Dionysius I of Syracuse in 389 BCE.
kaulonia.o: Kaulonia was founded in the 7th century BCE on the Ionian coast of Calabria, near modern Monasterace Marina, by Achaean settlers, probably sent out by Croton, to secure its southern border against Locri.
kaulonia.r: Kaulonia remained closely tied to Croton. Its silver coins, showing Apollo carrying a small running figure and a deer, are among the finest of Magna Graecia. Excavations have uncovered a Doric temple, walls and houses, and a large floor mosaic with a dragon of the 3rd century BCE. Little is known of its government.
kaulonia.e: After defeating the Italiote League at the Elleporus river in 389 BCE, Dionysius I took Kaulonia, moved its people to Syracuse and gave its land to Locri. A smaller town revived later but was destroyed during the wars with Pyrrhus and Hannibal, and by the Roman period the site was deserted.

kingdom-of-ladakh.t: A Tibetan Buddhist kingdom high in the western Himalaya that lasted nine centuries, ruled from Leh by the Namgyal kings until the Dogra conquest.
kingdom-of-ladakh.o: After the collapse of the Tibetan Empire, Nyimagon, a descendant of the Tibetan royal line, founded a kingdom in western Tibet around 930. His son received Maryul, the upper Indus valley around Leh, which became the core of Ladakh. Buddhism revived there in the 11th century, when the translator Rinchen Zangpo is credited with founding many temples.
kingdom-of-ladakh.r: The kingdom lived on trade between Kashmir, Tibet and Central Asia, especially in pashmina wool, and on irrigated barley farming. Monasteries such as Alchi, Hemis and Thiksey held great influence. The Namgyal dynasty took power in the 15th century; its greatest king, Sengge Namgyal, built Leh Palace and patronised Hemis. After a war with Tibet, the Treaty of Tingmosgang of 1684 fixed Ladakh's borders, with Mughal help on Ladakh's side.
kingdom-of-ladakh.e: Between 1834 and 1842 the Dogra general Zorawar Singh conquered Ladakh for Gulab Singh, and it became part of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. The Namgyal family kept the palace at Stok, and Ladakh is now a union territory of India.

kingdom-of-akyem-kotoku.t: Akan kingdom of the eastern Gold Coast forest, a partner of Akyem Abuakwa in the wars against Akwamu and Ashanti.
kingdom-of-akyem-kotoku.o: Akyem Kotoku was one of the three Akyem states formed in the Birim and Pra forests by the 17th century, alongside Akyem Abuakwa and Akyem Bosome. Its ruling house traced descent from the Akan clans that migrated south from the region of Adansi.
kingdom-of-akyem-kotoku.r: The Kotokuhene ruled with divisional chiefs, queen mothers and councils in the usual Akan form. The kingdom mined and traded gold. In 1730 it joined Akyem Abuakwa and the Ga in defeating Akwamu, and it fought the Ashanti Empire repeatedly over the following century, at times being driven from its lands.
kingdom-of-akyem-kotoku.e: Akyem Kotoku allied with Britain against Ashanti and came under British rule with the Gold Coast Colony in 1874. Its capital was fixed at Oda in the 19th century, and the Kotokuhene still reigns there.

kingdom-of-abemama.t: A small Gilbertese kingdom whose rulers conquered neighbouring atolls and controlled the copra trade, famed through Robert Louis Stevenson's portrait of Tem Binoka.
kingdom-of-abemama.o: The chiefs of Abemama in the central Gilbert Islands built up their power in the mid-19th century. Tem Baiteke, using firearms obtained from traders, brought the nearby atolls of Aranuka and Kuria under his rule, creating a small island kingdom unlike the council-based societies of the other Gilberts.
kingdom-of-abemama.r: Under Tem Binoka, who succeeded in the 1870s, Abemama was an autocracy: the king controlled land, labour and trade, and he dealt directly with European ships, selling copra and buying goods for himself. Foreign residents were strictly limited. Robert Louis Stevenson, who stayed on the island in 1889, described Binoka in 'In the South Seas' as a shrewd and formidable ruler. Little else is documented in detail.
kingdom-of-abemama.e: Binoka died in 1891, and in 1892 Britain declared a protectorate over the Gilbert Islands, absorbing Abemama into what became the Gilbert and Ellice Islands. Captain Davis of HMS Royalist proclaimed the protectorate there. The atoll is now part of Kiribati.

kingdom-of-ennarea.t: A gold-rich kingdom of south-western Ethiopia beyond the Gibe river that paid tribute to the emperors and briefly adopted Christianity.
kingdom-of-ennarea.o: Ennarea emerged by the 14th century among the Gonga-speaking peoples of the Gibe region, related to the people of the Kingdom of Kaffa. Ethiopian chronicles record it as a tributary land from the 15th century, valued as the main source of the gold and civet that reached the highlands and the Red Sea.
kingdom-of-ennarea.r: Ennarea was ruled by a sacred king who traded gold, ivory, slaves and coffee northward. Its rulers paid tribute in gold to the Ethiopian Empire, and in the late 16th century, under Emperor Sarsa Dengel, its king and court were baptised. Portuguese Jesuits passed through in the early 17th century, describing it as a major market.
kingdom-of-ennarea.e: Cut off from the highlands by the Oromo migrations, Ennarea was gradually overrun, and in the early 18th century its old dynasty fled south to Kaffa. Oromo rulers later founded Limmu-Ennarea on its former territory.

kingdom-of-iraq.t: The Hashemite monarchy that ruled Iraq from 1921 until the revolution of 1958, balancing British influence, Arab nationalism and a divided society.
kingdom-of-iraq.o: Faisal I, son of Sharif Hussein of Mecca and leader of the Arab Revolt, was crowned king of Iraq in August 1921 under the British mandate. The monarchy gained formal independence when Mandatory Iraq ended in 1932.
kingdom-of-iraq.r: Iraq was a constitutional monarchy with a parliament dominated by landowners, tribal sheikhs and ex-Ottoman officers, while Britain kept bases and influence. Faisal I died in 1933 and was followed by Ghazi and the boy king Faisal II, under the regent Abd al-Ilah. The period saw the Simele massacre of Assyrians in 1933, the Arab world's first military coup in 1936, and in 1941 Rashid Ali's pro-Axis coup, the Anglo-Iraqi War and the Farhud pogrom against Baghdad's Jews. Oil revenue funded development, and Nuri al-Said dominated politics.
kingdom-of-iraq.e: In 1955 Iraq joined the Baghdad Pact, and in 1958 it formed the Arab Federation with Jordan. On 14 July 1958 army officers led by Abd al-Karim Qasim overthrew the monarchy; Faisal II and much of the royal family were killed, and the Republic of Iraq was proclaimed.

karakalpakstan.t: The autonomous republic of the Karakalpak people on the lower Amu Darya, now part of Uzbekistan and at the heart of the Aral Sea disaster.
karakalpakstan.o: The Karakalpaks, a Kipchak Turkic people living in the Amu Darya delta under the Khanate of Khiva, received their own Karakalpak Autonomous Oblast in 1925, created from lands of the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic and attached to the Kazakh ASSR. In 1932 it became the Karakalpak ASSR within Russia, and in 1936 it was transferred to the Uzbek SSR.
karakalpakstan.r: Its capital moved from Turtkul to Nukus in 1939. The economy was based on irrigated cotton and rice, along with fishing on the Aral Sea. Massive Soviet irrigation from the Amu Darya caused the sea to shrink from the 1960s, destroying the fishing industry of Moynaq and bringing salt storms, polluted water and high rates of disease. The Savitsky museum in Nukus preserved banned Soviet avant-garde art.
karakalpakstan.e: Karakalpakstan declared sovereignty in 1990 and joined independent Uzbekistan in 1993 as a sovereign republic with a constitutional right to secede. In 2022 proposals to remove that right sparked deadly protests in Nukus, and the plan was withdrawn.

kingdom-of-gobir.t: Warlike northern Hausa kingdom whose clash with the scholar Usman dan Fodio set off the jihad that created the Sokoto Caliphate.
kingdom-of-gobir.o: Gobir, one of the Hausa Bakwai, is believed to have formed further north, near the Air massif, and moved south under Tuareg pressure. Its rulers were known as the frontier guards of Hausaland. By the 15th century it occupied the lands of present-day southern Niger and north-western Nigeria.
kingdom-of-gobir.r: Gobir was a military state relying on cavalry. In 1762 its king Babari sacked Birnin Zamfara and moved Gobir's capital to Alkalawa. Its rulers were Muslim but tolerated older practices, which the Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio, once tutor at the court of Bawa Jan Gwarzo, condemned in his preaching.
kingdom-of-gobir.e: When Sarkin Gobir Yunfa moved against dan Fodio's community in 1804, the scholar declared jihad. Alkalawa fell in 1808 and Yunfa was killed. Gobir loyalists withdrew north and founded the Sultanate of Tsibiri, and the Sokoto Caliphate took over the old Gobir lands.

kingdom-of-rheged.t: A British kingdom of the 'Old North' around the Solway, celebrated in Welsh poetry for King Urien and his battles against the Angles.
kingdom-of-rheged.o: Rheged emerged in the 6th century among the Brittonic kingdoms of northern Britain. Its location is uncertain, but scholars usually place it around Carlisle, Cumbria and Galloway. Its fame rests on poems attributed to Taliesin praising Urien Rheged, and on the Historia Brittonum.
kingdom-of-rheged.r: Urien is remembered as a leader of a coalition of British kings that besieged the Angles of Bernicia on Lindisfarne in the late 6th century, before he was murdered by a rival. Welsh tradition remembers the court as a centre of bardic patronage. Its society and economy are otherwise almost unknown.
kingdom-of-rheged.e: Rheged seems to have passed peacefully to Northumbria, perhaps through the marriage of Oswiu to Rhiainfellt, a descendant of Urien, around 638. Its memory lived on in Welsh poetry and Arthurian romance, where Urien and his son Owain became famous figures.

kingdom-of-tonga.t: The only Pacific island state never formally colonised, a constitutional monarchy founded by George Tupou I that still rules today.
kingdom-of-tonga.o: Tonga had long been ruled through the sacred Tuʻi Tonga Empire and related chiefly lines, but civil wars broke out in the early 19th century. Tāufaʻāhau, a chief from Haʻapai converted by Wesleyan missionaries, united the islands by 1845 and took the name George Tupou I, with Nukuʻalofa as his capital.
kingdom-of-tonga.r: George Tupou I issued codes freeing commoners from chiefly obligations in 1862 and granted a constitution in 1875, assisted by the missionary Shirley Baker; it guaranteed every adult male a plot of land and remains in force in amended form. The Tuʻi Tonga line was ended in 1865. Methodism became the dominant faith. From 1900 to 1970 Tonga was a British protected state, governing itself internally, and Queen Sālote Tupou III became widely admired.
kingdom-of-tonga.e: Tonga regained full independence in 1970 and joined the Commonwealth. Riots in 2006 hastened reforms, and since 2010 most of parliament has been elected by the people. King Tupou VI has reigned since 2012.

kanoman-sultanate.t: Junior branch of the divided Cirebon Sultanate, ruled by the Sultan Anom from a palace in the heart of old Cirebon.
kanoman-sultanate.o: Kanoman was created in 1677 when Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa of the Banten Sultanate partitioned Cirebon among the sons of Panembahan Girilaya, who had died as a hostage of Mataram. The younger son, Pangeran Kartawijaya, became Sultan Anom, the junior sultan, alongside his elder brother in the Kasepuhan Sultanate, and built the Keraton Kanoman as his seat.
kanoman-sultanate.r: The two sultans shared authority over Cirebon, a port and pilgrimage centre around the grave of Sunan Gunung Jati, and rivalry between their houses invited outside arbitration. From 1681 both accepted the protection of the Dutch East India Company, which controlled their trade in rice, sugar, indigo and textiles. A further split in 1807 created the Kacirebonan line.
kanoman-sultanate.e: Reforms under Herman Willem Daendels and the British during British Java removed the sultans political powers by 1815, leaving them pensions and ceremonial roles. The Keraton Kanoman survives, still hosting traditional rites and markets.

kingdom-of-cochin.t: The Kerala kingdom of Kochi, whose early alliance with the Portuguese made its harbour the first European foothold in India and whose rulers reigned until 1949.
kingdom-of-cochin.o: The ruling house, the Perumpadappu Swaroopam, emerged as one of the successor chiefdoms after the Chera Perumals of Makotai collapsed in the early 12th century. In the 14th century, after a flood of the Periyar opened a new harbour, the dynasty made Kochi its centre, and the port grew as older Muziris declined.
kingdom-of-cochin.r: Cochin's rulers were long overshadowed by the Zamorins of the Kingdom of Calicut, so in 1500 they welcomed the Portuguese, who built Fort Manuel at Kochi in 1503. The Dutch replaced them in 1663. Pepper and spices drove the economy, and Kochi was home to Syrian Christians, Jews and Konkani merchants. Sakthan Thampuran (r. 1790–1805) curbed the nobles and rebuilt Thrissur.
kingdom-of-cochin.e: After invasions by Mysore, Cochin became a British subsidiary ally from 1791 and was known for its schools and administration. In 1949 it merged with Travancore to form Travancore-Cochin, which became part of Kerala in 1956.

kingdom-of-kano.t: The largest Hausa kingdom, a walled market city whose dyed cloth and leather were traded across the Sahara and the Sudan.
kingdom-of-kano.o: The Kano Chronicle dates the kingdom to Bagauda, said to have become king in 999 among communities of farmers and ironworkers around Dala hill. Over the following centuries the rulers extended their authority over the surrounding plain and built the earthen walls that enclosed farmland as well as the city, making Kano defensible in long sieges.
kingdom-of-kano.r: Islam was adopted at court under Ali Yaji in the 14th century, brought by Wangara traders from Mali. Muhammad Rumfa, ruling in the late 15th century, built the Gidan Rumfa palace and the Kurmi market and took advice from the scholar al-Maghili on Islamic government. Kano prospered on textiles, indigo dyeing, leather and the caravan trade, at times paying tribute to the Kanem-Bornu Empire.
kingdom-of-kano.e: In 1805 Fulani reformers of Usman dan Fodio's jihad drove out the last Hausa king, Muhammad Alwali II, and Kano became the Kano Emirate within the Sokoto Caliphate. The city remained the commercial heart of northern Nigeria, and its emir still reigns.

kwantung-leased-territory.t: Japan's foothold at the tip of the Liaodong peninsula, base of the South Manchuria Railway and of the Kwantung Army that seized Manchuria in 1931.
kwantung-leased-territory.o: By the Treaty of Portsmouth in 1905 Japan took over Russia's lease of Kwantung Oblast, including Port Arthur (Ryojun) and Dalny (Dairen), together with the railway south of Changchun. A Kwantung Government-General was set up in 1906 under Ōshima Yoshimasa.
kwantung-leased-territory.r: Dairen became one of East Asia's busiest ports and the headquarters of the South Manchuria Railway Company, which ran mines, hotels, research bureaus and towns along its line. The Twenty-One Demands of 1915 extended the lease to ninety-nine years. The garrison, renamed the Kwantung Army in 1919, acted with growing independence and in 1931 staged the Mukden Incident, leading to the creation of Manchukuo.
kwantung-leased-territory.e: Soviet troops occupied the territory in August 1945. The Soviet Union kept a naval base at Port Arthur until 1955, when the area was handed to the People's Republic of China; it is now part of Dalian.
kwantung-leased-territory.re: Chinese folk religion, Buddhism, State Shinto

kingdom-of-iberia.t: The eastern Georgian kingdom of Kartli, centred on Mtskheta, which adopted Christianity in the 4th century and laid the foundations of Georgian statehood and letters.
kingdom-of-iberia.o: Georgian chronicles credit Pharnavaz I with uniting Kartli around 302 BCE after the collapse of Achaemenid power, establishing his seat at Mtskheta and organising the land into duchies. Classical authors knew the kingdom as Iberia, a well-organised state on the Mtkvari river guarding key passes across the Caucasus.
kingdom-of-iberia.r: Kings ruled through regional eristavis, with a priestly and military aristocracy above a farming population. Iberia balanced between Rome and Persia, hosting Pompey's army in 65 BCE and later serving as a Roman client. King Mirian III adopted Christianity in the 330s through the mission of St Nino, and the Georgian alphabet appeared by the 5th century.
kingdom-of-iberia.e: Vakhtang I Gorgasali fought the Persians and founded Tbilisi as a new capital, but Sasanian pressure grew. In 580 the Sasanian Empire abolished the monarchy, and the land passed to local aristocrats who formed the Principality of Iberia.

kingdom-of-valencia.t: A realm of the Crown of Aragon created by James I's conquest, famed for its rice and silk, its 15th-century golden age and its own laws.
kingdom-of-valencia.o: James I of Aragon conquered the Third Taifa of Valencia between 1232 and 1245, taking the city in 1238. He made it a separate kingdom with its own legal code, the Furs of Valencia, rather than attaching it to Aragon or Catalonia.
kingdom-of-valencia.r: Catalan and Aragonese settlers lived alongside a large Muslim population that farmed the irrigated huertas, producing rice, sugar and silk. In the 15th century Valencia was the Crown's largest city, building the Silk Exchange and producing writers such as Ausiàs March and Joanot Martorell. The Germanies revolt of 1519-1523 and the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609 brought upheaval.
kingdom-of-valencia.e: Valencia backed the Habsburg claimant in the War of the Spanish Succession. After the Bourbon victory at Almansa in 1707, Philip V abolished its Furs by the Nueva Planta decrees, absorbing it into Bourbon Spain.

kingdom-of-mide.t: The midland kingdom around the sacred hill of Uisnech, ruled by the Clann Cholmain kings who often held the kingship of Tara.
kingdom-of-mide.o: Mide formed in the 6th century as the southern Ui Neill dynasties established themselves in the Irish midlands. The Clann Cholmain branch, descended from Colman Mor, emerged as its dominant line by the 8th century, ruling in what is now Westmeath with Uisnech as its symbolic centre.
kingdom-of-mide.r: Clann Cholmain kings alternated the kingship of Tara with the northern Ui Neill. Mael Sechnaill mac Maele Ruanaid and Mael Sechnaill mac Domnaill were among the most powerful kings in Ireland. The kingdom contained great monasteries such as Durrow and Clonard, and royal sites at Lough Ennell.
kingdom-of-mide.e: After Brian Boru's rise, Mide was repeatedly partitioned by rival provincial kings. In 1172 Henry II granted it to Hugh de Lacy, creating the Lordship of Meath, and the native line survived only as minor lords.

kizzuwatna.t: Kizzuwatna, a Hurrian-Luwian kingdom of the Cilician plain, through whose priests Hurrian gods and rituals entered Hittite religion.
kizzuwatna.o: Kizzuwatna arose in the plain of Cilicia and the Taurus mountains after the Hittite Old Kingdom weakened in the 16th century BCE. Its kings ruled from Kummanni and other centres such as Adaniya and Lawazantiya, and balanced between the Hittites and the Mitanni Empire.
kizzuwatna.r: Its kings, such as Isputahsu, Pilliya and Sunassura, concluded treaties with Hittite rulers and with Idrimi of Mukish. The population mixed Luwian and Hurrian elements, and its temples of Teshub and Hebat and its priests specialised in purification rituals.
kizzuwatna.e: Around 1400 BCE Sunassura accepted Hittite overlordship, and Kizzuwatna was soon absorbed into the Hittite Empire. Its cults passed to the Hittite court; Queen Puduhepa was a priest's daughter from Lawazantiya. The region later became Que.

kingdom-of-elmet.t: Small British kingdom around Leeds that held out against the Angles until Edwin of Northumbria expelled its king Ceretic around 617.
kingdom-of-elmet.o: Elmet emerged after Roman rule ended as a British kingdom in the area of modern West Yorkshire, between the Pennines and the Vale of York. It is remembered in place names such as Sherburn-in-Elmet and Barwick-in-Elmet, and a 6th-century memorial stone at Llanaelhaearn in Gwynedd names a man of Elmet.
kingdom-of-elmet.r: Very little is known of its government. Welsh poetry praises a king Gwallawg, possibly of Elmet, who fought alongside Urien of Rheged against the Angles. The kingdom survived surrounded by the growing Anglian powers of Deira and Mercia, perhaps protected by its wooded and marshy terrain and by dyke systems such as those near Barwick.
kingdom-of-elmet.e: The Historia Brittonum records that Edwin of Northumbria seized Elmet and expelled its king Ceretic, usually dated around 617. The district appears in the Tribal Hidage as the Elmetsæte, and its people were absorbed into Northumbria.

kingdom-of-sumenep.t: The kingdom of eastern Madura, whose first ruler Arya Wiraraja helped found Majapahit and whose princes ruled until 1883.
kingdom-of-sumenep.o: Tradition dates Sumenep's founding to 1269, when Kertanegara of Singhasari appointed Arya Wiraraja as its adipati. Wiraraja is a well-known figure in Javanese chronicles: he advised Jayakatwang and then helped Raden Wijaya defeat him and expel the Mongols in 1293, opening the way for Majapahit.
kingdom-of-sumenep.r: Sumenep was a dry land of salt pans, cattle and seafaring traders. Its rulers converted to Islam in the 16th century and later accepted the overlordship of Mataram and, from 1705, the Dutch East India Company. Panembahan Somala built the Great Mosque and the palace in the late 18th century, and Sultan Abdurrahman was a noted scholar of Javanese and Sanskrit texts.
kingdom-of-sumenep.e: Sumenep's princes served the Dutch as regents, supplying troops for colonial wars. In 1883 the colonial government abolished the royal title and ruled through ordinary regents. The palace and mosque remain landmarks of Madurese culture.

kingdom-of-dahomey.t: Fon kingdom of the Abomey plateau, famed for its female soldiers and royal palaces, and a major power of the Atlantic slave trade.
kingdom-of-dahomey.o: Dahomey arose in the early 17th century when a branch of the royal family of the Kingdom of Allada settled on the Abomey plateau among the Fon. Under Houegbadja in the mid-17th century the kingdom was consolidated with Abomey as its capital. King Agaja conquered Allada in 1724 and the Kingdom of Whydah in 1727, gaining access to the coast.
kingdom-of-dahomey.r: The king ruled through an exceptionally centralised administration, with a female corps of soldiers known to Europeans as the Amazons, a royal monopoly on the slave trade and annual customs honouring the royal ancestors. Dahomey paid tribute to the Oyo Empire from the 1730s until Ghezo ended it in 1823. After the slave trade declined, palm oil plantations grew.
kingdom-of-dahomey.e: King Behanzin fought France from 1890 and surrendered in 1894. France installed a puppet king and absorbed the kingdom into French Dahomey, which became independent in 1960 and took the name Benin in 1975. The Royal Palaces of Abomey are a World Heritage Site.

kaga-domain.t: The richest domain of Tokugawa Japan, held by the Maeda family at Kanazawa and famed as the million-koku domain of Kaga.
kaga-domain.o: Maeda Toshiie, a comrade of Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, received northern Kaga after the defeat of Shibata Katsuie in 1583 and moved into Kanazawa castle. His son Toshinaga sided with Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1600 and was rewarded with lands covering Kaga, Noto and Etchu.
kaga-domain.r: Assessed at over a million koku, the domain was second only to the shogun's own holdings. As outside (tozama) lords the Maeda were watched carefully, and they spent heavily on culture rather than armies to reassure the shogunate. Maeda Tsunanori patronised scholarship and crafts, and Kanazawa became a centre of gold leaf, Kutani porcelain and Kaga yuzen dyeing, with the Kenroku-en garden.
kaga-domain.e: The domain stayed cautious during the Boshin War and joined the new government. It was abolished in 1871, becoming the core of Ishikawa Prefecture, and Kanazawa remains a cultural centre.

kingdom-of-dumnonia.t: Post-Roman British kingdom of Devon and Cornwall, with its high-status site at Tintagel, which slowly gave way to the West Saxons.
kingdom-of-dumnonia.o: Dumnonia grew from the Roman civitas of the Dumnonii after Roman rule ended around 410, covering Cornwall, Devon and parts of Somerset. In the 6th century Gildas denounced its king Constantine for murder and sacrilege. Many Britons from the region emigrated to Armorica, where the district of Domnonée in Brittany carries the same name.
kingdom-of-dumnonia.r: Little is recorded of its government. Imported Mediterranean pottery and glass at Tintagel, and at sites such as Bantham, show trade with the Byzantine world, probably for tin, in the 5th and 6th centuries. Christianity was organised around local saints and monasteries, and inscribed memorial stones in Latin and ogham mark the burials of its elite.
kingdom-of-dumnonia.e: The West Saxons pushed westward through Somerset and Devon in the 7th century, and around 705 Aldhelm wrote to King Geraint urging Roman practice on Easter. In 710 Ine of Wessex fought Geraint, and Devon was gradually absorbed. A smaller British kingdom of Cornwall survived until the 9th century.

kingdom-of-breifne.t: A Gaelic kingdom of the drumlin country of Leitrim and Cavan, ruled by the O'Rourkes, whose king Tigernan Ua Ruairc helped bring about the Norman invasion of 1169.
kingdom-of-breifne.o: Breifne emerged in the 8th century among the Ui Briuin of Connacht, whose branch, the Ui Briuin Breifne, settled the lakes and hills of later Leitrim and Cavan. The O'Rourke family became its leading dynasty by the 10th century.
kingdom-of-breifne.r: Breifne was an upland kingdom of cattle, lakes and crannog dwellings. Its kings occasionally claimed the kingship of Connacht. Tigernan Ua Ruairc, ruler from about 1124 to 1172, fought Diarmait Mac Murchada of Leinster, who had abducted his wife Derbforgaill; their feud helped bring the Normans to Ireland. Tigernan was killed at Tlachtga in 1172.
kingdom-of-breifne.e: After the death of its king in 1256, Breifne split between the O'Rourkes of West Breifne and the O'Reillys of East Breifne. Both survived until the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

kingdom-of-africa.t: The Norman Kingdom of Sicily's string of coastal conquests in Ifriqiya, a short-lived Christian dominion over Muslim ports from Tripoli to Mahdia.
kingdom-of-africa.o: Under Roger II, the Kingdom of Sicily exploited famine and the collapse of the Zirid emirate to seize the North African coast. His admiral George of Antioch took Tripoli in 1146, and in 1148 Mahdia, Sousse and Sfax fell as the Zirid ruler al-Hasan fled. Gabès and other towns accepted Sicilian overlordship, forming what Roger styled his realm of Africa.
kingdom-of-africa.r: The Normans ruled indirectly, as they did with the Muslims of Sicily. Local qadis and governors stayed in place, Islamic law and worship continued, and the towns paid tribute to Palermo. Garrisons held the ports, and the aim was control of grain and the sea lanes between Sicily and Africa rather than settlement or conversion.
kingdom-of-africa.e: After Roger's death in 1154 the towns revolted, starting with Sfax in 1156. The Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min marched east, besieged Mahdia and took it in January 1160, ending Christian rule. The episode foreshadowed later European footholds on the Maghreb coast.

kingdom-of-lundu.t: A Manganja kingdom of the lower Shire valley, a southern offshoot of the Maravi confederacy linked to the feared Zimba warriors.
kingdom-of-lundu.o: The Lundu title was held by a branch of the Phiri ruling clan of the Kingdom of Maravi, which settled in the lower Shire valley among the Manganja. By the late 16th century the Lundu was a powerful independent ruler, and Portuguese writers associated him with the Zimba, warrior bands that attacked Portuguese posts on the Zambezi and coastal towns.
kingdom-of-lundu.r: The Lundu controlled routes carrying ivory from the interior to the coast near Quelimane and Mozambique Island and drew tribute from Manganja chiefs. Religious authority was closely tied to the Mbona rain shrine at Khulubvi, a cult the Lundu dynasty is said to have taken over and reshaped.
kingdom-of-lundu.e: The kingdom was brought back under Maravi overlordship by Kalonga Masula in the early 17th century and gradually lost power to chiefs and Afro-Portuguese prazo holders. By around 1800 it had broken up, and 19th-century Kololo and Yao incursions completed its decline.

khanate-of-khiva.t: The Uzbek khanate of Khwarazm, ruled from the walled city of Khiva for four centuries, notorious for its slave markets and finally a Russian protectorate.
khanate-of-khiva.o: In 1511 Ilbars and Balbars, descendants of Arab Shah of the Shibanid line, took Khwarazm after the Safavids had briefly seized it from Muhammad Shaybani. The Arabshahid dynasty ruled at first from Urgench and later from Khiva, which became the capital in the 17th century as the Amu Darya changed course.
khanate-of-khiva.r: The khanate ruled Uzbek tribes, Turkmen and settled Sarts along the irrigated lower Amu Darya. The khan and historian Abu'l-Ghazi Bahadur wrote a genealogical history of the Turks. Slave trading of Persians and Russians captured by Turkmen raiders was central to the economy. From 1804 the Qungrat dynasty, whose founders had been inaks, ruled as khans, building much of Itchan Kala.
khanate-of-khiva.e: Russian forces captured Khiva in 1873 and made it a protectorate. In 1920 the Red Army and the Young Khivans deposed the last khan, Said Abdullah, creating the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic.

kingdom-of-tiryns.t: Mycenaean citadel near the Argolic Gulf whose Cyclopean walls, among the most massive of the Bronze Age, so impressed later Greeks that they credited them to giants.
kingdom-of-tiryns.o: Tiryns stands on a low rock near the coast of the Argolid, settled from the Early Bronze Age, when a large circular building was erected on its summit. Mycenaean rulers built a fortified palace from c. 1600 BCE, and in the 14th and 13th centuries BCE the citadel was enclosed by walls up to 8 metres thick, with vaulted galleries.
kingdom-of-tiryns.r: The palace had a megaron with painted floors and frescoes of women in procession and boar hunts. Tiryns probably served as the harbour and partner, or subordinate, of nearby Mycenae. A few Linear B tablets and inscribed jars show palace administration. Greek myth tied it to Perseus and to Heracles, who served King Eurystheus.
kingdom-of-tiryns.e: The palace was destroyed c. 1200 BCE, but unlike most centres Tiryns continued, with a large lower town and a rebuilt hall into the 12th century BCE. It later became a small city absorbed by Argos c. 470 BCE. Its walls are a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with Mycenae.

kingdom-of-taxila.t: The kingdom of King Ambhi, who welcomed Alexander the Great to Taxila in 326 BCE and joined him against his rival Porus.
kingdom-of-taxila.o: After Achaemenid control of the Indus region faded in the 4th century BCE, a local kingdom emerged around Taxila, the old capital of the Kingdom of Gandhara, between the Indus and the Jhelum. Its ruler, known to the Greeks as Taxiles and in Indian tradition as Ambhi, was at odds with the neighbouring Paurava kingdom.
kingdom-of-taxila.r: Taxila was a wealthy city on the trade route from Bactria to the Ganges and a famous centre of learning; tradition says Chanakya, adviser to Chandragupta Maurya, taught there. Greek writers described its customs, including the exposure of the dead to vultures and the sale of girls in marriage markets. When Alexander arrived in 326 BCE, Ambhi submitted with gifts and provided troops and elephants for the campaign.
kingdom-of-taxila.e: Alexander confirmed Ambhi as ruler under Macedonian oversight. After Alexander's death the Greek commanders left the region, and around 317 BCE Taxila was absorbed by Chandragupta's Maurya Empire, becoming the seat of its north-western province.

kingdom-of-kyamutwara.t: A Haya kingdom west of Lake Victoria that split around 1800, giving rise to the kingdoms of Kianja and Bugabo.
kingdom-of-kyamutwara.o: Kyamutwara arose in the 17th century in the Kagera region, near today's Bukoba, among the Haya people. Traditions describe a dynasty of the Bankango clan later displaced by the Hinda, who were related to the rulers of the Kingdom of Karagwe.
kingdom-of-kyamutwara.r: The kingdom had the sacred kingship, chiefs and banana-and-coffee farming economy shared by the Haya states. Around 1800 succession disputes split it, and the Kingdom of Kianja and the Kingdom of Bugabo became separate states, leaving a reduced Kyamutwara.
kingdom-of-kyamutwara.e: The remaining kingdom passed under German East Africa and then British Tanganyika Territory as a native authority. The chieftaincies were abolished by independent Tanganyika in 1963.

kingdom-of-bugesera.t: A small kingdom between Rwanda and Burundi whose lands were divided between its two powerful neighbours in the late 18th century.
kingdom-of-bugesera.o: Bugesera lay in the lake-strewn lowlands around Lakes Cyohoha and Rweru, on today's border between Rwanda and Burundi. Its royal clan, the Bahondogo, are remembered in Rwandan and Burundian traditions as rulers of one of the older kingdoms of the region, dating to at least the 16th century.
kingdom-of-bugesera.r: Little is known of its government beyond royal rituals and drums similar to those of its neighbours. It was a land of cattle and farming, and its rulers engaged in alliances and wars with the Kingdom of Rwanda and the Kingdom of Burundi.
kingdom-of-bugesera.e: Bugesera was conquered and partitioned around the end of the 18th century, with the northern part absorbed by Rwanda and the southern by Burundi. Bugesera survives as a district name in Rwanda.

kingdom-of-avanti.t: The kingdom of Malwa with its capital at Ujjain, ruled by the fierce Chanda Pradyota and one of the four great powers of the Buddha's time.
kingdom-of-avanti.o: Avanti occupied the Malwa plateau of western central India, with Ujjain in the north and Mahishmati on the Narmada in the south. By the 6th century BCE it was one of the four leading kingdoms alongside Magadha, Kosala and Vatsa. Puranic tradition says the Pradyota dynasty seized the throne after the last king of an older line was killed by his minister Pulika.
kingdom-of-avanti.r: Chanda Pradyota Mahasena, a contemporary of the Buddha, was remembered as violent and ambitious; he threatened Rajagriha and fought Udayana of Vatsa, who eloped with his daughter Vasavadatta. Ujjain grew rich on the routes linking the Ganges plain with the western ports, and Avanti later became a centre of Buddhism through the monk Mahakaccana, a native of Ujjain.
kingdom-of-avanti.e: Around 400 BCE Avanti was conquered by Shishunaga of the Kingdom of Magadha, ending its independence. Ujjain remained a provincial capital under the Mauryas, where Ashoka served as viceroy, and later became the seat of the Western Satraps.

kingdom-of-bosnia.t: Medieval Bosnian kingdom of the Kotromanić dynasty, briefly the strongest Balkan state, until the Ottomans conquered it in 1463.
kingdom-of-bosnia.o: Ban Tvrtko I of the Banate of Bosnia, having won lands in western Serbia, was crowned king of the Serbs and Bosnia in 1377 at Mile near Visoko, claiming descent from the Nemanjić dynasty.
kingdom-of-bosnia.r: Tvrtko expanded to the Adriatic, taking Kotor and much of Dalmatia and Croatia by his death in 1391. Royal power then weakened as great nobles such as Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić and Stjepan Vukčić Kosača, whose lands became Herzegovina, made and unmade kings. Silver from Srebrenica supported the state, and the Bosnian Church, Catholicism and Orthodoxy coexisted. Carved tombstones called stećci mark the burials of the period.
kingdom-of-bosnia.e: The Ottomans took parts of the kingdom from the 1430s. In 1463 Mehmed II invaded, captured Bobovac and executed the last king, Stephen Tomašević, at Jajce. Most of Bosnia became an Ottoman province, while Hungary briefly held a northern banate.

kazallu.t: An Amorite-era city-kingdom of northern Babylonia, an early rival of Babylon whose walls were torn down by Sumu-la-El.
kazallu.o: Kazallu lay in northern Babylonia, near Marad and Kish; its site has not been found. Under the Neo-Sumerian Empire it was a province, and its governor Puzur-Numushda defied Ibbi-Sin in the last years of Ur. In the 19th century BCE it became the seat of an independent kingdom tied to the Amorite Mutiabal tribe.
kazallu.r: Kazallu is known mainly through the year names and inscriptions of its neighbours, which record wars and alliances with Larsa, Isin, Uruk and the new Amorite dynasty of Babylon. Kings such as Yahzir-El briefly controlled the region, and the city's position on the Euphrates canals gave it influence over northern Babylonia's grain lands. Its own institutions are almost undocumented.
kazallu.e: Sumu-la-El of Babylon defeated Kazallu and destroyed its walls in the early 19th century BCE, and it was absorbed by Babylon. Its Mutiabal population later rose against Hammurabi, but by about 1800 BCE the kingdom had ceased to exist.

kingdom-of-kalinga.t: The ancient kingdom of the Odisha coast, whose bloody conquest by Ashoka in 261 BCE turned the Maurya emperor towards Buddhism.
kingdom-of-kalinga.o: Kalinga, the coastal plain between the Mahanadi and Godavari rivers, appears in the Mahabharata and in Buddhist texts, which name Dantapura as an early capital. Its people controlled harbours facing the Bay of Bengal. According to the later Hathigumpha inscription, a Nanda king took a Jain image from Kalinga, which suggests a period of Magadhan control in the 4th century BCE.
kingdom-of-kalinga.r: Kalinga's strength lay in maritime trade with Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, rice farming in the Mahanadi delta and a large army; Greek sources reported that its king kept many war elephants. Jainism had a strong following there. Little is known of its rulers, and the government was probably a monarchy centred on Tosali, near modern Bhubaneswar.
kingdom-of-kalinga.e: Around 261 BCE the Maurya emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga. His Rock Edict XIII records 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported and expresses his remorse, a turning point in his commitment to dhamma. Kalinga regained independence after the Mauryas under the Mahameghavahana dynasty.

kingdom-of-wuli.t: Mandinka kingdom of the upper Gambia river, visited by Mungo Park on his journey into the interior in 1795.
kingdom-of-wuli.o: Wuli was one of the Mandinka kingdoms founded along the Gambia river as the influence of the Mali Empire spread westward. It occupied the north bank of the upper river and is traditionally dated to around the 16th century.
kingdom-of-wuli.r: The mansa of Wuli ruled from Medina with a council of lineage heads and Muslim clerics. Wuli controlled caravan routes between the Gambia and the upper Senegal and Niger, through which slaves, gold and cloth passed. Mungo Park stopped there in 1795, and the king gave him permission to continue east.
kingdom-of-wuli.e: In the 19th century Wuli was disrupted by wars between Muslim reformers and traditional rulers. The Anglo-French boundary agreement of 1889 divided the area, and Wuli became a district of the Gambia Colony and Protectorate.

kingdom-of-carchemish.t: Neo-Hittite Carchemish, the leading Iron Age kingdom on the Euphrates, heir to Hittite royal tradition and famed for its sculpted walls.
kingdom-of-carchemish.o: When the Hittite Empire fell c. 1180 BCE, the Viceroyalty of Carchemish survived, and King Kuzi-Teshub took the title great king. His descendants and their successors ruled a kingdom astride the Euphrates crossing, in what is now the Turkish-Syrian border.
kingdom-of-carchemish.r: Kings of the house of Suhi, and later Astiru and the regent Yariri, recorded their deeds in Luwian hieroglyphs on basalt reliefs lining processional ways, the Long Wall of Sculpture. Carchemish grew rich on river trade and textiles. British Museum excavations from 1911, with Leonard Woolley and T. E. Lawrence, uncovered much of the city.
kingdom-of-carchemish.e: The kingdom paid tribute to the Assyrian Empire from the 9th century BCE. In 717 BCE Sargon II deposed King Pisiri for plotting with Phrygia and turned Carchemish into a province. In 605 BCE the city saw Nebuchadnezzar's victory over Egypt.

kantoli.t: A Sumatran trading kingdom known only from Chinese records of its 5th- and 6th-century embassies, often seen as a forerunner of Srivijaya.
kantoli.o: Known only from Chinese dynastic histories, Kantoli sent envoys to the southern Chinese courts in 441, 455, 502, 518 and 563. Historians usually place it in southern Sumatra, around Jambi or Palembang, though its exact site is unknown.
kantoli.r: Chinese texts describe a Buddhist king who exported cotton cloth, areca nut and aromatic woods. In 502 a king called Gautama Subhadra sent tribute, followed by his son Vijayavarman. The embassies suggest a ruler eager for Chinese recognition to attract merchants to his port on the route between India and China.
kantoli.e: Kantoli disappears from the records after 563. Its role as a Sumatran gateway to China passed to the Melayu Kingdom and above all to Srivijaya, which rose at Palembang in the late 7th century.

katyuri-kingdom.t: An early medieval kingdom of the Kumaon and Garhwal hills, builders of the temples of Jageshwar and Baijnath.
katyuri-kingdom.o: The Katyuris emerged in the central Himalaya, modern Uttarakhand, around the 7th or 8th century, perhaps after the decline of the Kuninda Kingdom and other hill states. Their early capital was Kartikeyapura, probably near Joshimath, later moved to the Katyur valley around Baijnath.
katyuri-kingdom.r: The dynasty is known from a handful of copper-plate inscriptions of kings such as Lalitashuradeva, written in Sanskrit, and from local tradition. The kings were Shaivas, and the temple groups at Jageshwar and Baijnath are associated with their rule. They controlled routes into Tibet and the pilgrimage centres of the upper Ganges.
katyuri-kingdom.e: From around the 11th century the kingdom fragmented into local principalities ruled by Katyuri branches. The Chand dynasty took over Kumaon, and the Parmar kings united Garhwal. Katyuri chiefs survived as local rulers, notably at Askot.

kingdom-of-majorca.t: A Christian kingdom created after James I's conquest of Majorca, independent under its own dynasty from 1276 to 1344 and a realm of Aragon thereafter.
kingdom-of-majorca.o: James I of Aragon conquered Majorca from the Almohads in 1229, then Ibiza in 1235, and established a separate kingdom. On his death in 1276 he left Majorca, Roussillon, Cerdanya and Montpellier to his younger son James II, creating an independent dynasty.
kingdom-of-majorca.r: The kingdom was a Mediterranean trading state, with Palma and Perpignan as royal seats, merchant fleets reaching North Africa and a famed school of cartographers who made the Catalan Atlas. Ramon Llull, philosopher and missionary, was its most famous son. Its kings were forced to accept vassalage to the Crown of Aragon.
kingdom-of-majorca.e: Peter IV of Aragon seized the kingdom in 1343-1344, and James III was killed at Llucmajor in 1349 trying to retake it. Majorca remained a separate realm within the Crown until the Nueva Planta decree of 1715.

kingdom-of-huahine.t: A kingdom of the Leeward Society Islands that defeated a French landing in 1846 and stayed independent until the 1890s.
kingdom-of-huahine.o: Huahine, two islands joined by a narrow channel in the Leeward group of the Society Islands, was settled by Polynesians perhaps a thousand years ago. Around Lake Fauna Nui at Maeva, its chiefly families built one of the largest concentrations of marae in Polynesia. By the 18th century the island and nearby Maiao were ruled by a single royal line.
kingdom-of-huahine.r: Huahine's ruling family was closely tied by marriage to the Kingdom of Tahiti; Teriitaria II, queen from 1815, was also a wife of Pōmare II. James Cook visited in 1769 and in 1777 left the traveller Mai, who had been to England, settled there. The London Missionary Society arrived in 1818 and most islanders became Protestant. Islanders lived from breadfruit, taro, fishing and provisioning ships.
kingdom-of-huahine.e: In 1846 Huahine's warriors defeated French marines who tried to impose a protectorate, and the Jarnac Convention of 1847 recognised its independence. France proclaimed annexation of the Leeward Islands in 1888, completed on Huahine in 1895, and it is now part of French Polynesia.

kurume-domain.t: The Arima domain of Chikugo in northern Kyushu, known for its indigo kasuri cloth and a scholar lord who wrote on mathematics.
kurume-domain.o: After the Tanaka family who held Chikugo died out, the shogunate divided the province, and in 1621 Arima Toyouji, who had fought for Tokugawa Ieyasu, received Kurume with about 210,000 koku.
kurume-domain.r: The Arima ruled until 1871 from Kurume castle on the Chikugo river. Kurume kasuri, a dyed cotton fabric, became a famous product in the 19th century, and the domain promoted rice and wax. In the 18th century Arima Yoriyuki published works on Japanese mathematics. Heavy taxes provoked a large peasant uprising in 1754. In the 1860s the Suitengu priest Maki Izumi became a leading loyalist.
kurume-domain.e: Kurume joined the imperial side in 1868. Radical retainers involved in anti-government plots were purged in 1871, the year the domain was abolished; it became part of Fukuoka Prefecture.

kingdom-of-hanover.t: North German kingdom tied to the British crown until 1837, then ruled by its own kings until Prussia annexed it in 1866.
kingdom-of-hanover.o: The Congress of Vienna raised the Electorate of Hanover to a kingdom in 1814, with George III as king, and enlarged it with East Frisia, Hildesheim and Osnabrück. It continued in personal union with Great Britain under George III, George IV and William IV, governed by a viceroy.
kingdom-of-hanover.r: When Victoria became British queen in 1837, Salic law excluded her and her uncle Ernest Augustus became King of Hanover. He revoked the liberal constitution of 1833, and seven Göttingen professors who protested, including the Grimm brothers, were dismissed. The kingdom was largely agrarian, though railways and the port of Harburg developed. George V, blind from youth, became king in 1851.
kingdom-of-hanover.e: George V sided with Austria in 1866. His army won at Langensalza but surrendered two days later. Prussia annexed Hanover as a province, and the Guelph party long campaigned for restoration.

kingdom-of-illyria.t: Austrian crown land formed from the former French Illyrian Provinces, uniting Slovene and Adriatic lands under one title for three decades.
kingdom-of-illyria.o: When Austria recovered Napoleon's Illyrian Provinces, it kept the name and in 1816 created the Kingdom of Illyria as a crown land of the Austrian Empire. It comprised Carniola, Carinthia, Gorizia and Gradisca, Istria and Trieste, and for a few years Civil Croatia south of the Sava, which returned to Hungary in 1822.
kingdom-of-illyria.r: The kingdom was mainly an administrative label: it was divided into two governorates, at Laibach and Trieste, each run by Austrian officials under the system of Metternich, with provincial estates of little power. Laibach hosted the congress of 1821 on revolutions in Italy. Slovene cultural life grew, with the poet France Prešeren writing in Laibach in the 1830s and 1840s.
kingdom-of-illyria.e: After the revolutions of 1848, the 1849 constitution dissolved the kingdom into separate crown lands: Carniola, Carinthia and the Austrian Littoral. The emperor kept the title King of Illyria until 1918.

kingdom-of-thessalonica.t: Crusader kingdom created for Boniface of Montferrat after the Fourth Crusade, which lasted only twenty years before falling to Epirus.
kingdom-of-thessalonica.o: Boniface of Montferrat, leader of the Fourth Crusade, lost the election for Latin emperor in 1204 but received Thessalonica and much of Macedonia and Thessaly. He married Margaret of Hungary, widow of Isaac II, and invaded central and southern Greece, granting fiefs such as the Duchy of Athens and the Marquisate of Bodonitsa to his followers.
kingdom-of-thessalonica.r: The kingdom was ruled by Lombard nobles from northern Italy over a Greek population, under nominal homage to the Latin Empire. A Latin archbishop replaced the Orthodox metropolitan. Boniface was killed by the Bulgarians of Kaloyan in 1207, leaving his infant son Demetrius under a regency; the Lombard barons' revolt of 1208-1209 was suppressed by Emperor Henry.
kingdom-of-thessalonica.e: Weakened by internal divisions and Bulgarian attacks, the kingdom was gradually conquered by Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus, who took Thessalonica itself in 1224 and founded the Empire of Thessalonica. The title survived among Western claimants.

kingdom-of-deira.t: The Anglian kingdom of the Yorkshire Wolds and York, whose boys in a Roman slave market are said to have inspired Pope Gregory's mission to the English.
kingdom-of-deira.o: Deira developed from Anglian settlement in east Yorkshire, perhaps taking over a British territory whose name it kept. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle names Aelle as its first king from 560. Bede tells how Gregory the Great, seeing Deiran slave boys in Rome, punned that they were not Angles but angels.
kingdom-of-deira.r: Deira's centre lay around York and the Wolds. Edwin, son of Aelle, ruled all Northumbria from 616, accepted baptism from Paulinus at York in 627 and built the first church on the site of York Minster. After his death in 633 Deira had its own kings again, including Oswine, killed on the orders of Oswiu in 651.
kingdom-of-deira.e: Bernician kings repeatedly dominated Deira. Its last sub-king, Oethelwald, supported Penda against Oswiu and disappeared after the Winwaed in 655. Deira became the southern half of the Kingdom of Northumbria, its name surviving in later sources.

kingdom-of-the-iberians.t: The kingdom of the Georgian Bagratids in Tao-Klarjeti, a land of great monasteries whose rulers prepared the unification of Georgia.
kingdom-of-the-iberians.o: Early in the 9th century the Bagratid prince Ashot I moved from Kartli to the south-western borderland of Klarjeti, where he rebuilt Artanuji and the family won Byzantine titles. In 888 his grandson Adarnase IV took the title king of the Iberians, restoring the royal title in Georgia after three centuries.
kingdom-of-the-iberians.r: Several Bagratid branches shared rule over Tao, Klarjeti and Shavsheti, with titles granted by the Byzantine Empire. Monks led by Grigol of Khandzta founded monasteries, and great churches rose at Oshki, Ishkhani and Khakhuli, centres of Georgian learning. David III Kouropalates of Tao made the region powerful and helped Byzantium against the rebel Bardas Skleros.
kingdom-of-the-iberians.e: When David III died in 1000, Basil II annexed his lands of Tao to Byzantium. The remaining Bagratid holdings passed to Bagrat III, who in 1008 united them with Abkhazia and Kartli in the Kingdom of Georgia.

kingdom-of-the-lombards.t: Germanic kingdom that ruled most of Italy from 568 until Charlemagne's conquest in 774, shaping its regions and its law.
kingdom-of-the-lombards.o: The Lombards, a Germanic people settled in Pannonia, crossed into Italy under King Alboin in 568, just after the Gothic Wars had exhausted the peninsula. They overran the north and much of the centre and south, took Pavia in 572 after a long siege and made it their capital, leaving the Byzantines with Ravenna, Rome and the coasts.
kingdom-of-the-lombards.r: The king ruled with powerful dukes, some nearly independent, such as those of Spoleto and Benevento. Under Queen Theodelinda the Lombards began to move from Arian to Catholic Christianity. Rothari issued a written law code, the Edict of Rothari, in 643. Liutprand strengthened royal power and in 728 gave Sutri to the Pope, a step towards the Papal States. Lombard art survives at Cividale.
kingdom-of-the-lombards.e: When Aistulf took Ravenna in 751 and threatened Rome, the popes turned to the Franks. Pepin the Short defeated Aistulf, and Charlemagne besieged Pavia and captured King Desiderius in 774, taking the title King of the Lombards. The region of Lombardy keeps their name.

kalachuris-of-mahishmati.t: A short-lived but wide-ruling dynasty of western India whose silver coins circulated across the Deccan and whose era lasted for centuries.
kalachuris-of-mahishmati.o: The Early Kalachuris rose in the mid-6th century in Malwa and the northern Deccan as the Gupta Empire and the Vakataka dynasty faded. Their kingdom centred on Mahishmati on the Narmada and stretched over Gujarat, Malwa, the Konkan and northern Maharashtra. They used the era of 248 later called the Kalachuri-Chedi era.
kalachuris-of-mahishmati.r: Three kings are known: Krishnaraja, whose silver coins circulated widely, his son Shankaragana and grandson Buddharaja. They were devotees of Shiva in the Pashupata tradition. Some historians attribute the great Shiva cave at Elephanta and early caves at Ellora to their patronage, though this is debated.
kalachuris-of-mahishmati.e: Around 600 to 610 Buddharaja was defeated by Mangalesha of the Chalukyas of Badami, and Pulakeshin II completed the conquest of the Kalachuri lands. Later dynasties, notably the Kalachuris of Tripuri, claimed descent from them.

kachchhapaghata-dynasty.t: A Rajput dynasty that held the fortress of Gwalior and built its Sas-Bahu temple in the 11th century.
kachchhapaghata-dynasty.o: The Kachchhapaghatas emerged in the 10th century in the region of Gwalior, Narwar and Dubkund in northern Madhya Pradesh, probably as feudatories of the Gurjara-Pratihara or the Chandela dynasty. According to a Gwalior inscription, Vajradaman took the fort of Gopadri, Gwalior, from the Pratiharas around 977.
kachchhapaghata-dynasty.r: Several branches of the family ruled from Gwalior, Narwar and Dubkund. They were often vassals of the Chandelas and fought the Paramara dynasty; Kirttiraja is said to have defeated an army from Malwa. Mahipala completed the great Sas-Bahu temple at Gwalior fort in 1093, and the Dubkund branch built Jain temples, showing patronage of both faiths.
kachchhapaghata-dynasty.e: In the 12th century the Kachchhapaghatas lost Gwalior to a Pratihara family, and the region was later taken by Iltutmish of the Delhi Sultanate in 1232. Later Kachhwaha Rajputs of Amber claimed descent from them.

kingdom-of-vannius.t: A Roman client kingdom of the Quadi north of the Danube, set up to house the followers of the fallen kings Maroboduus and Catualda.
kingdom-of-vannius.o: After Maroboduus and his successor Catualda were driven out in 19, their followers were settled by Rome north of the Danube between the March (Morava) and Váh rivers. Drusus the Younger installed Vannius, of the Quadi, as their king, creating a buffer state opposite the Roman frontier in Pannonia and Noricum.
kingdom-of-vannius.r: Vannius ruled for some thirty years as a client of Rome. Tacitus says he was at first respected, then grew arrogant, enriching himself through raiding and tolls on traders. The kingdom grew wealthy on commerce along the Amber Road between the Baltic and Carnuntum, and Roman goods reached its elite graves.
kingdom-of-vannius.e: In 50 Vannius was overthrown by his nephews Vangio and Sido with the help of the Hermunduri and Lugii. Emperor Claudius refused to intervene but gave him refuge in Pannonia. The nephews divided the kingdom and stayed loyal to Rome; Sido fought for Vespasian in 69.

kingdom-of-lesotho.t: The independent mountain kingdom of the Basotho, entirely surrounded by South Africa, since 1966.
kingdom-of-lesotho.o: Basutoland became independent on 4 October 1966 as the Kingdom of Lesotho, a constitutional monarchy within the Commonwealth with Moshoeshoe II, a descendant of Moshoeshoe I of the Basotho Kingdom, as king and Leabua Jonathan of the Basotho National Party as prime minister.
kingdom-of-lesotho.r: Jonathan annulled the 1970 election he was losing and ruled by decree until a military coup in 1986. Moshoeshoe II was exiled in 1990 and replaced by his son Letsie III, then briefly restored before his death in 1996. The economy relies on mine wages from South Africa, textiles and the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, which sells water to Gauteng.
kingdom-of-lesotho.e: A disputed election in 1998 led to rioting and intervention by South African and Botswana troops under SADC. Since 2002 Lesotho has held regular elections under a mixed electoral system, with Letsie III as king.

kingdom-of-strathclyde.t: British kingdom of the Clyde, first centred on Dumbarton Rock and later at Govan, which outlasted the other northern Brittonic realms until absorbed into Scotland.
kingdom-of-strathclyde.o: The kingdom grew from the British people of the Clyde, descendants of the Damnonii, after Roman influence ended. Its early king Ceretic, probably the Coroticus whom St Patrick rebuked for slave-raiding in the 5th century, ruled from Alt Clut, the fortress on Dumbarton Rock.
kingdom-of-strathclyde.r: Rhydderch Hael, a king of the late 6th century, appears in the lives of Columba and Kentigern, the patron saint of Glasgow. In 642 Owain son of Beli defeated and killed Domnall Brecc of Dál Riata at Strathcarron. Society rested on cattle farming, and its people spoke Cumbric, a northern form of Brittonic. After 870 the royal centre moved to Govan, where a fine collection of carved stones survives.
kingdom-of-strathclyde.e: In 870 Viking kings from Dublin took Dumbarton after a four-month siege. The renewed kingdom, often called Cumbria, expanded south into Cumbria in the 10th century. Its last known king, Owain the Bald, may have died around 1018, and it was absorbed into the kingdom of Scotland during the 11th century.

kingdom-of-asebu.t: Fante coastal kingdom that invited the Dutch to the Gold Coast, sending envoys to the Netherlands in 1611.
kingdom-of-asebu.o: Asebu was a small Fante kingdom on the coast east of Cape Coast, with its port at Moree. It existed by the time Portuguese traders arrived in the late 15th century and resented Portuguese control of the gold trade from Elmina.
kingdom-of-asebu.r: Seeking new partners, Asebu's ruler sent envoys to the Dutch Republic in 1611, and in 1612 the Dutch built Fort Nassau at Moree, their first fort on the Gold Coast. Asebu then grew rich on gold and later the slave trade, while competing with neighbouring Fetu and the Fante states.
kingdom-of-asebu.e: Asebu was absorbed into the wider Fante group of states in the 18th century and joined the alliances against the Ashanti Empire. It came under British rule with the creation of the Gold Coast Colony in 1874 and remains a traditional area in Ghana.

kingdom-of-phrygia.t: Phrygia, the Iron Age kingdom of Gordion in central Anatolia, home of King Midas and the Gordian knot.
kingdom-of-phrygia.o: The Phrygians, probably migrants from the Balkans after the Late Bronze Age collapse, settled the plateau west of the Kızılırmak. By the 9th century BCE they had built a fortified capital at Gordion on the Sakarya river, with a citadel of megaron halls. Assyrian texts call the people Mushki.
kingdom-of-phrygia.r: Phrygian kings ruled from Gordion and built huge burial mounds; Tumulus MM held a king with bronze vessels and fine wooden furniture. Midas, the Mita of Assyrian records, was a rival of Sargon II and sent gifts to Delphi. The Phrygians wrote in an alphabet adapted from Greek and worshipped the mother goddess Matar, later Cybele.
kingdom-of-phrygia.e: Cimmerian invaders sacked Gordion in the early 7th century BCE, and Greek tradition says Midas killed himself. Phrygia then fell under the Kingdom of Lydia and the Achaemenid Empire, though its language and cults survived for centuries.
