kelantan-sultanate.t: North-east Malay sultanate, long a tributary of Siam, now a state of Malaysia known for its strong Malay and Islamic identity.
kelantan-sultanate.o: Kelantan had been ruled by various local princes for centuries, often under the influence of Pattani and Siam. In 1762 Long Yunus, of a Pattani-linked family, unified the territory and founded the line of rulers that still holds the throne, and in the early 19th century his successors adopted the title of sultan.
kelantan-sultanate.r: Kelantan was a populous rice-growing state on the delta of the Kelantan river, with fishing, weaving and metalwork. Its rulers sent the bunga mas to Siam while keeping internal autonomy, and Sultan Muhammad II strengthened royal power from Kota Bharu in the mid 19th century. Wayang kulit, kite flying and Islamic schools were prominent.
kelantan-sultanate.e: The Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909 placed Kelantan under British protection as one of the Unfederated Malay States. After Japanese and Thai occupation it joined the Federation of Malaya, and today it is a state of Malaysia whose sultan, Muhammad V, served as king from 2016 to 2019.

kong-empire.t: A Dyula Muslim trading state in northern Ivory Coast, built by Seku Wattara around the city of Kong, a centre of commerce and Islamic learning.
kong-empire.o: Kong was already a Dyula market town when, around 1710, Seku Wattara seized power from its earlier rulers and launched campaigns that extended its influence north towards the Black Volta and the middle Niger. The Wattara (Ouattara) family became the ruling dynasty, and their armies relied on cavalry and imported firearms.
kong-empire.r: Kong was more a commercial network than a centralised empire. Dyula merchants traded gold, kola nuts, cloth and slaves between the forest and the Sahel, and the town had mosques and Qur'anic schools of wide reputation. The warrior estate, the Sonangi, did the fighting while Muslim scholars and traders ran the city. After Seku's death about 1745 the realm fragmented and his relative Famagan founded the Kingdom of Gwiriko.
kong-empire.e: Kong declined into a regional trading town. The French explorer Louis-Gustave Binger arrived in 1888, and a French treaty followed in 1889. Samori Toure sacked and burned Kong in 1897, and the area was absorbed into the French Ivory Coast.

kingdom-of-atholl.t: A Pictish kingdom in the central Highlands whose name, 'New Ireland', hints at Gaelic influence, later a Scottish earldom.
kingdom-of-atholl.o: Atholl, Athfotla, appears in Irish annals from the 8th century, when a king of Atholl was drowned by Oengus son of Fergus, king of the Picts, in 739. The name is usually interpreted as 'New Ireland', suggesting Gaelic settlement or influence in the Pictish highlands of Perthshire. Fotla is also one of the seven Pictish provinces.
kingdom-of-atholl.r: Atholl seems to have had its own kings within the Pictish overkingship. Its lands in the valleys of the Tay, Tummel and Garry were pastoral and thinly peopled. Dunkeld, on its edge, became a major church centre in the 9th century.
kingdom-of-atholl.e: Atholl was absorbed into the Kingdom of Scotland as a mormaerdom and later an earldom. Its rulers produced Crinan, abbot of Dunkeld, father of King Duncan I, linking Atholl with the royal house.

kingdom-of-henan.t: A short-lived kingdom around Luoyang, one of Xiang Yu's Eighteen Kingdoms, whose king Shen Yang surrendered to Liu Bang in 205 BCE.
kingdom-of-henan.o: In Xiang Yu's settlement of 206 BCE, Shen Yang, a former official of Zhao and associate of Zhang Er, was rewarded for welcoming Chu forces at the Yellow River by being made King of Henan, with his capital at Luoyang.
kingdom-of-henan.r: The kingdom held the strategic Luoyang basin, the gateway between the Guanzhong region and the eastern plain. It lasted too briefly for any distinctive government to develop.
kingdom-of-henan.e: When Liu Bang emerged from the west in 205 BCE, Shen Yang surrendered without a fight, and his kingdom became Henan Commandery. Its loss opened the route east for Liu Bang's ill-fated march on Pengcheng, capital of Western Chu.

kingdom-of-seisyllwg.t: A Welsh kingdom of Ceredigion and Ystrad Tywi, named after King Seisyll, which merged with Dyfed to form Deheubarth.
kingdom-of-seisyllwg.o: Seisyllwg was created when Seisyll ap Clydog of Ceredigion added Ystrad Tywi, the Tywi valley, to his realm in the 8th century. The new territory was named after him. Little else is known of its early rulers beyond genealogies.
kingdom-of-seisyllwg.r: The kingdom covered much of later Cardiganshire and Carmarthenshire, a land of upland pasture and coastal farms with important churches such as Llanbadarn Fawr. Its last native king, Gwgon, drowned in 871, and it passed by marriage to Rhodri the Great of Gwynedd, whose son Cadell inherited it.
kingdom-of-seisyllwg.e: Cadell's son Hywel Dda united Seisyllwg with Dyfed around 920, creating the Kingdom of Deheubarth. The name Seisyllwg fell out of use, though Ceredigion persists as a county.

kingdom-of-morgannwg.t: A south-east Welsh kingdom formed by the union of Glywysing and Gwent, whose name survives in Glamorgan.
kingdom-of-morgannwg.o: Morgannwg, 'Morgan's land', is traditionally named after Morgan Hen ab Owain, who united the older kingdoms of Glywysing and Gwent around 942. Earlier rulers of the region are known from the charters of the Book of Llandaff.
kingdom-of-morgannwg.r: The kingdom covered the fertile vale and uplands between the Tywi and the Wye, with churches such as Llandaff and Llancarfan. Its kings dealt with English rulers, and Morgan Hen attended Aethelstan's court. After his death in 974 Gwent and Glywysing separated again at times, and the kingdom was later ruled by Gruffydd ap Llywelyn and then Caradog ap Gruffydd.
kingdom-of-morgannwg.e: Iestyn ap Gwrgant, the last native ruler, was overthrown around 1090 by the Norman Robert Fitzhamon, who created the Lordship of Glamorgan. The name survives in the counties of Glamorgan.

kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.t: Tiny Welsh kingdom between the Wye and the Ithon whose rulers claimed descent from Vortigern, the British ruler blamed for inviting the Saxons.
kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.o: Gwrtheyrnion means 'the land of Gwrtheyrn', the Welsh form of Vortigern. The Historia Brittonum, written in 829 or 830, says that after Vortigern's fall his son Pascent was granted Buellt and Gwrtheyrnion by Ambrosius, and that its ruler in the author's day, Fernmail, descended from him. The territory lay around Rhayader in what became Radnorshire.
kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.r: Almost nothing is known of its government beyond this genealogy. It was a small upland territory of river valleys and hill pasture, often ruled together with the neighbouring Kingdom of Buellt, and its dynasty used its link with Vortigern, whatever its truth, to assert ancient legitimacy.
kingdom-of-gwrtheyrnion.e: Gwrtheyrnion was absorbed by more powerful Welsh kingdoms, probably in the 10th century, and later formed a cantref of the Middle March between Wye and Severn, held by Welsh and Anglo-Norman lords such as the Mortimers.

kingdom-of-capsus.t: A Berber principality of southern Tunisia under Antalas, who fought the Vandals, allied with Byzantium and then turned against it.
kingdom-of-capsus.o: In the early 6th century, as the Vandal Kingdom lost control of the interior, Berber chiefs of the Frexes and neighbouring tribes built a power base in southern Byzacena around Capsa (Gafsa). Its best-known leader, Antalas, son of Guenfan, defeated a Vandal army sent by King Hilderic around 530.
kingdom-of-capsus.r: What is known comes from Procopius and Corippus. Antalas led a tribal confederation of herders and oasis farmers on the desert edge. He sided with the Byzantines after their conquest of 533 to 534, receiving subsidies, but rebelled in 544 after the general Solomon executed his brother. That year his forces killed Solomon at Cillium, and he briefly allied with the Byzantine mutineer Stotzas.
kingdom-of-capsus.e: Antalas was defeated by John Troglita, the general of the Praetorian Prefecture of Africa, and submitted around 546 to 548, fighting thereafter as a Byzantine ally against the Laguatan. His principality then disappears from the record.

kingdom-of-hejaz-and-nejd.t: The dual kingdom of Ibn Saud, uniting the holy cities with Najd, and the immediate forerunner of Saudi Arabia.
kingdom-of-hejaz-and-nejd.o: After conquering the Kingdom of Hejaz, Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud was proclaimed King of the Hejaz in Mecca in January 1926 while remaining Sultan of Nejd. In 1927 Nejd was also raised to a kingdom, and the two realms were ruled in personal union.
kingdom-of-hejaz-and-nejd.r: The Hejaz kept its own administration and consultative council under Ibn Saud's son Faisal as viceroy, while Najd was ruled directly. The Treaty of Jeddah in 1927 brought British recognition of full independence. The Ikhwan, angry at modern innovations and limits on raiding, rebelled; Ibn Saud defeated them at the Battle of Sabilla in 1929 and crushed the revolt by 1930.
kingdom-of-hejaz-and-nejd.e: On 23 September 1932 a royal decree unified the dual kingdom as the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, named after the ruling family.

kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.t: A small Anglian sub-kingdom on the Welsh border in Herefordshire and Shropshire, ruled by Merewalh's dynasty under Mercia.
kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.o: The Magonsaete, perhaps named after Magnis (Kenchester), emerged in the mid 7th century in the borderlands west of the Severn. Their first known ruler was Merewalh, whom later tradition made a son of Penda of the Kingdom of Mercia, though this is uncertain.
kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.r: Merewalh's family was noted for piety: his daughter Mildburh founded the abbey of Much Wenlock, and other children became saints. A bishopric at Hereford served the people. The rulers were sub-kings under Mercian overlordship, and the population included many Britons.
kingdom-of-the-magonsaete.e: The dynasty disappears from record in the 8th century, and the territory was absorbed directly into Mercia. Its outline survived as the diocese of Hereford.

kingdom-of-limerick.t: A Norse town-kingdom on the Shannon estuary whose fall to the Dal Cais opened the way for Brian Boru's rise.
kingdom-of-limerick.o: Vikings had raided the Shannon since the 9th century, and in 922 Tomrair mac Ailchi established a permanent fleet base at Limerick, Hlymrekr. The settlement competed with the Kingdom of Dublin for control of the Irish Sea trade and raided deep into Connacht and Munster.
kingdom-of-limerick.r: Limerick was a fortified trading port on an island in the Shannon, dealing in slaves and plunder. Its kings were rivals of Dublin's dynasty, losing a war with them in 937. In the 960s Ivar of Limerick allied with Irish kings of Munster against the rising Dal Cais.
kingdom-of-limerick.e: Mathgamain and Brian Boru of the Dal Cais defeated the Norse at Sulcoit in 967 and sacked the town. Brian killed Ivar and his sons on Scattery Island in 977. Limerick became the O'Brien capital and later the seat of the Kingdom of Thomond.

kuban-peoples-republic.t: A Cossack republic on the Kuban, proclaimed in 1918, that sought union with Ukraine and fought the Bolsheviks while quarrelling with the Whites.
kuban-peoples-republic.o: After the Russian Revolution the Kuban Cossack Host, descended partly from the Black Sea Cossack Host, set up its own Rada in Yekaterinodar. In January 1918 the Rada proclaimed an independent Kuban People's Republic, with a population split between Ukrainian-speaking Black Sea Cossacks, Russian line Cossacks and non-Cossack settlers.
kuban-peoples-republic.r: The Bolsheviks took Yekaterinodar in March 1918, and the government retreated with the Volunteer Army, which recaptured the city in August. The republic had its own ataman, Alexander Filimonov, and a Rada in which a Ukrainian-minded faction under Mykola Ryabovol and Luka Bych pushed for federation with Ukraine. This brought conflict with General Denikin, who wanted a united Russia.
kuban-peoples-republic.e: Ryabovol was assassinated in 1919, and in November Denikin had the Rada member Kulabukhov hanged and the Rada purged. Demoralised Kuban units deserted, and the Red Army took Yekaterinodar in March 1920, ending the republic.

kingdom-of-vientiane.t: The central Lao kingdom formed when Lan Xang split in 1707, destroyed by Siam after King Anouvong's revolt of 1826 to 1828.
kingdom-of-vientiane.o: When Lan Xang's succession dispute erupted, Setthathirath II, with Vietnamese backing, took power at Vientiane around 1707, while Luang Prabang broke away. Vientiane kept the old capital and much of the Lan Xang heritage, including the Emerald Buddha.
kingdom-of-vientiane.r: The kingdom ruled the central Mekong valley and much of the Khorat plateau, but it was weakened by wars with Luang Prabang. In 1779 the Thonburi Kingdom captured Vientiane and carried off the Emerald Buddha to Bangkok, and Vientiane became a Siamese vassal. King Anouvong built Wat Si Saket and tried to restore Lao power.
kingdom-of-vientiane.e: In 1826 Anouvong rebelled against the Rattanakosin Kingdom and marched toward Bangkok, but was defeated. In 1828 Siamese armies razed Vientiane, deported much of its population to the Khorat plateau and later executed Anouvong. The kingdom was abolished, and Vientiane was refounded under French rule.

keonjhar-state.t: A Bhanja dynasty state in the forested hills of northern Odisha, known for the Bhuyan risings of 1868 and 1891 against its Raja.
keonjhar-state.o: Tradition holds that Keonjhar was founded in the 12th century by a younger brother of the ruler of Mayurbhanj, so that both states were ruled by branches of the Bhanja dynasty. The capital was Keonjhargarh.
keonjhar-state.r: Keonjhar was hilly and wooded, with a large population of Bhuyan and Juang peoples, whose obligations to the Raja caused tension. Disputed successions and harsh exactions led to Bhuyan revolts in 1868 and 1891, the second led by Dharanidhar Naik, both suppressed with British help. The state was later known for its iron ore.
keonjhar-state.e: Keonjhar merged into Orissa on 1 January 1948 and is now a district of Odisha.

kingdom-of-cambodia-1953-1970.t: Independent Cambodia under Norodom Sihanouk, who kept the kingdom neutral and peaceful through the 1950s and 1960s while war raged next door.
kingdom-of-cambodia-1953-1970.o: King Norodom Sihanouk's campaign against French rule won full independence on 9 November 1953, confirmed by the Geneva conference in 1954. In 1955 he abdicated in favour of his father Norodom Suramarit to enter politics, founding the Sangkum Reastr Niyum movement, which won every seat in the national assembly.
kingdom-of-cambodia-1953-1970.r: Sihanouk dominated politics as prime minister and, after his father's death in 1960, head of state. The Sangkum promoted Buddhist socialism, built schools, hospitals and modern buildings in Phnom Penh, and pursued neutrality in the Cold War. In 1965 Sihanouk broke with the United States and tacitly allowed North Vietnamese forces to use Cambodian territory, while repressing the left.
kingdom-of-cambodia-1953-1970.e: A deteriorating economy, a peasant revolt at Samlaut in 1967 and growing hostility from the right weakened him. On 18 March 1970, while Sihanouk was abroad, the national assembly deposed him, and Lon Nol proclaimed the Khmer Republic.

kingdom-of-brittany.t: Breton kingdom forged in the 9th century by Nominoe and his successors, who won independence from the Carolingian Franks.
kingdom-of-brittany.o: Louis the Pious appointed the Breton noble Nominoe as his representative in Brittany in 831. After Louis's death Nominoe broke with Charles the Bald, defeating him at Ballon in 845. His son Erispoe won again at Jengland in 851, and the Treaty of Angers recognised him as king with Rennes, Nantes and the Pays de Retz.
kingdom-of-brittany.r: The kingdom united Domnonée, Cornouaille and Broërec with the Frankish marches. Salomon, who killed Erispoe and took the throne in 857, gained the Cotentin and Avranchin in 867. The kings ruled through local machtierns and monasteries such as Redon, and set up a Breton church province at Dol.
kingdom-of-brittany.e: After internal conflict Alan the Great defeated the Vikings at Questembert around 888, but after his death in 907 Vikings overran Brittany. Alan Barbetorte returned from England in 936 and expelled them by 939, ruling as duke and founding the Duchy of Brittany.

kerma.t: The first great kingdom of Nubia, centred on Kerma at the Third Cataract and for centuries a rival to pharaonic Egypt.
kerma.o: Kerma culture developed in Upper Nubia from about 2500 BCE, with its centre at Kerma near the Third Cataract of the Nile. The town grew from a farming and cattle-herding settlement into the capital of a kingdom that Egyptian texts called Kush, controlling the river trade in gold, ivory, ebony and cattle.
kerma.r: The rulers lived in a walled city dominated by the Western Deffufa, a massive mud-brick temple. Kings were buried under huge circular tumuli, some with hundreds of sacrificed attendants. Kerma potters made distinctive polished black-topped red ware. At its height, in the 17th century BCE, Kerma raided as far as Elkab in Egypt and allied with the Hyksos of the Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt against Thebes.
kerma.e: The New Kingdom pharaohs struck back. Thutmose I sacked Kerma around 1500 BCE, and Egypt annexed Nubia as the Viceroyalty of Kush. Kerma traditions survived beneath Egyptian rule and fed into the later Kushite Empire of Napata and Meroë.

kothi-state.t: A small Baghel Rajput principality of Baghelkhand that branched off from the Sohawal ruling family.
kothi-state.o: Kothi emerged as a separate holding from Sohawal State, whose rulers were a cadet branch of the Baghel house of Rewa. The register dates it from 1600, but the details of its separation are known mainly from family tradition.
kothi-state.r: The Raja ruled a few dozen villages in the upland country west of Rewa. In the British period Kothi was a non-salute state under the Baghelkhand Agency of Central India, and little else of its internal history is widely recorded.
kothi-state.e: Kothi was merged into Vindhya Pradesh in 1948, which became part of Madhya Pradesh in 1956. Its lands lie in today's Satna district.

kingdom-of-barwe.t: A Shona kingdom of central Mozambique whose rulers, the Makombe, resisted Portuguese conquest into the 20th century.
kingdom-of-barwe.o: Barwe emerged around 1500 between the Mutapa lands and the Kingdom of Manyika, ruled by a dynasty related to the Mutapa house. Its rulers, titled Makombe, controlled routes between the Zambezi and the gold-bearing highlands.
kingdom-of-barwe.r: The Makombe was a sacred king whose installation required ritual approval, including holy water sent from the Kingdom of Uteve, and spirit mediums held great influence. The kingdom traded with Portuguese posts at Sena and Tete and frequently fought Afro-Portuguese prazo holders and neighbouring states. In the 19th century it fought off the Gaza Nguni and the warlords of the Zambezi.
kingdom-of-barwe.e: After repeated campaigns, Portuguese forces occupied Barwe in 1902, ending its independence. A major rising in 1917, led by Barwe nobles and spirit mediums, was crushed, and the area was absorbed into Portuguese Mozambique.

kingdom-of-fiji.t: A short-lived constitutional monarchy under Seru Cakobau that briefly united Fiji before debt and disorder led to cession to Britain.
kingdom-of-fiji.o: Seru Epenisa Cakobau of the Kingdom of Bau claimed the title Tui Viti, king of Fiji, but faced rivals such as Enele Maʻafu of the Tovata Confederacy and American debt claims. A cotton boom during the American Civil War brought hundreds of European planters to Fiji, and in 1871 settlers at Levuka helped Cakobau form a national government with a constitution.
kingdom-of-fiji.r: The kingdom had a cabinet dominated by Europeans, among them John Bates Thurston, and a legislature in which settlers held great influence. Maʻafu joined as viceroy for Lau, uniting the main chiefly powers. The government struggled to tax settlers, who often refused to recognise its authority, and to control the brutal labour trade that brought Pacific Islanders to the plantations.
kingdom-of-fiji.e: Bankrupt and unable to keep order, Cakobau and the leading chiefs offered Fiji to Britain. The Deed of Cession was signed on 10 October 1874, creating the Colony of Fiji. Cakobau's war club was later returned to Fiji as the mace of its parliament.

kasepuhan-sultanate.t: Senior branch of the divided Cirebon Sultanate in West Java, whose palace preserves one of the oldest royal compounds on Java.
kasepuhan-sultanate.o: When Panembahan Girilaya of Cirebon died as a hostage at the Mataram court in 1662, his sons were freed in 1677 with help from the rebel Trunajaya and the Banten Sultanate. Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa of Banten divided Cirebon among them, making the elder, Pangeran Martawijaya, Sultan Sepuh, the senior sultan, of Kasepuhan.
kasepuhan-sultanate.r: Kasepuhan held the old Pakungwati palace founded by Sunan Gunung Jati, whose shrine made Cirebon a centre of Javanese Islam. The sultan shared Cirebon with the Kanoman Sultanate, and from 1681 both accepted Dutch East India Company protection. Court culture blended Javanese, Sundanese, Chinese and Islamic elements, visible in batik and mask dance.
kasepuhan-sultanate.e: Herman Willem Daendels and then the British during British Java stripped the Cirebon sultans of governing power, and by 1815 they had become pensioned nobles. The Keraton Kasepuhan remains the seat of a ceremonial sultan and a major heritage site.

koch-kingdom.t: The Koch kingdom of Biswa Singha and Nara Narayan, which briefly dominated north-east India in the 16th century before splitting into Koch Bihar and Koch Hajo.
koch-kingdom.o: After the Bengal Sultanate destroyed the Kamata Kingdom around 1498, Biswa Singha, a leader of the Koch people, united the local chiefs and founded a new state around 1515, centred on the Cooch Behar area. He adopted Hindu kingship and Brahmin rituals.
koch-kingdom.r: Under Nara Narayan (r. 1540–1587) and his brother and general Chilarai, the Koch defeated the Ahom kingdom and forced tribute from the Kachari kingdom, Jaintia, Manipur and Tripura. Nara Narayan rebuilt the Kamakhya temple and patronised the Vaishnava saint Sankardev and Assamese and Sanskrit literature.
koch-kingdom.e: In 1581 Nara Narayan divided the kingdom with his nephew Raghudev, creating Koch Bihar in the west and Koch Hajo in the east. Koch Bihar continued as Cooch Behar State; Koch Hajo was later absorbed by the Mughals and the Ahoms.

kalabhra-dynasty.t: Rulers of the Tamil country during a poorly documented period between the Sangam age and the rise of the Pallavas and Pandyas.
kalabhra-dynasty.o: The Kalabhras are known mainly from later sources hostile to them. The 8th-century Velvikudi copper plates of the Pandyas say a Kalabhra king overthrew the Tamil kings and seized the land, ending the rule of the Early Pandyas, Early Cholas and Early Cheras around the 3rd century. Their origins are unknown; they may have come from the hill country to the north.
kalabhra-dynasty.r: Very little is known about their rule. Later Hindu sources accuse them of suppressing Brahmin grants, which may reflect patronage of Buddhism and Jainism; the Buddhist writer Buddhadatta mentions a king Accuta Vikkanta of the Kalabhra family in the Kaveri region. Much Tamil ethical literature, possibly including parts of the Tirukkural tradition, is often dated to this period.
kalabhra-dynasty.e: In the late 6th century the Pandya king Kadungon and the Pallava king Simhavishnu expelled the Kalabhras, founding the First Pandyan Empire and expanding the Pallava dynasty.

kingdom-of-new-galicia.t: The Spanish kingdom of western Mexico, centred on Guadalajara, created by a brutal conquest and enriched by the silver of Zacatecas.
kingdom-of-new-galicia.o: Nuño de Guzmán led a notoriously violent campaign through western Mexico in 1529-31, founding towns and naming the territory Nueva Galicia. Guadalajara was founded in 1532 and, after several moves, settled at its present site in 1542.
kingdom-of-new-galicia.r: New Galicia had its own audiencia from 1548, seated in Guadalajara from 1560, giving it a degree of autonomy within New Spain. The Mixtón War of 1540-42, a major indigenous uprising, nearly ended Spanish rule there. From 1546 the silver mines of Zacatecas made the region rich and drew settlers north. Ranching and agriculture fed the mining towns.
kingdom-of-new-galicia.e: In 1786 the kingdom became the Intendancy of Guadalajara. With independence in 1821 it passed to the First Mexican Empire, and its territory became the states of Jalisco, Nayarit, Aguascalientes and parts of others.

kingdom-of-ruhuna.t: The southern kingdom of ancient Sri Lanka, base of rebels and liberators, from which Dutugemunu and Vijayabahu I set out to reunite the island.
kingdom-of-ruhuna.o: According to the Mahavamsa, Ruhuna was founded in the 3rd century BCE by Mahanaga, a brother of Devanampiya Tissa of the Anuradhapura Kingdom, who settled in the south-east of the island and built Mahagama, modern Tissamaharama. Its rulers formed a branch of the Sinhalese royal line, sometimes independent, sometimes subordinate to Anuradhapura.
kingdom-of-ruhuna.r: Ruhuna's dry south-east depended on reservoirs such as Tissa Wewa, while ports like Godavaya linked it to Indian Ocean trade. Its kings patronised Buddhist monasteries, and the shrine at Kataragama made it a pilgrimage region. Rugged and distant from the capital, it served for centuries as a refuge for princes and resistance against invaders; King Kavantissa ruled there, and his son Dutugemunu marched north to defeat Elara around 161 BCE.
kingdom-of-ruhuna.e: When the Chola Empire occupied northern Sri Lanka in the 11th century, Ruhuna became the centre of Sinhalese resistance. Its prince Vijayabahu I drove out the Cholas in 1070 and founded the Polonnaruwa Kingdom, which reabsorbed Ruhuna, though it rebelled again in the 12th century.

kurin-khanate.t: A khanate created by Russia in the Lezgin lands of southern Dagestan, which lasted until the end of the Caucasian War.
kurin-khanate.o: In 1812 the Russian authorities formed the Kurin Khanate from Lezgin communities in the Samur river area of southern Dagestan, which had been free societies. They placed it under Aslan Khan, a member of the Kazikumukh ruling family, as a Russian ally, with its seat at Kurakh.
kurin-khanate.r: The khanate governed Lezgin villages of farmers and herders under Russian supervision. Its khans held Russian military rank and pensions, collected taxes and supplied troops. Aslan Khan also gained the Kazikumukh Khanate, and the two were often ruled together. Kurakh had a Russian fort, and the khanate remained loyal during the wars with the Caucasian Imamate.
kurin-khanate.e: After the defeat of Shamil and the stabilisation of Dagestan, the Russian Empire abolished the khanate in 1864 and incorporated it into the Kyurin district of the Dagestan Oblast. The area remains the heartland of the Lezgin people in southern Dagestan.

kanyok-kingdom.t: A Luba-related kingdom of the southern Kasai, long a rival of the Luba Empire, whose history is known mainly from oral tradition.
kanyok-kingdom.o: The Kanyok lived between the Lubilash and Mbuji-Mayi rivers in the southern Kasai and shared many institutions and origin stories with their Luba neighbours. A centralised kingship under the Mwen a Kanyok had formed by the 17th century, according to oral traditions.
kanyok-kingdom.r: The Mwen a Kanyok was a sacred ruler who governed through titled officials and village chiefs. Kanyok traditions recall repeated wars with the Luba Empire, sometimes as rival and sometimes as tributary. In the 19th century the kingdom was drawn into regional trade and raiding linked to the Chokwe and other slave traders.
kanyok-kingdom.e: The Congo Free State extended its authority over the Kanyok in the 1890s, ending the kingdom's independence. Its history has been reconstructed by historians largely from oral traditions collected in the 20th century.

kingdom-of-mema.t: Soninke kingdom on the western edge of the inland Niger delta, a successor to the Ghana Empire that sheltered the young Sundiata Keita.
kingdom-of-mema.o: Mema lay west of Lake Debo in present-day Mali, a region of lakes and pasture once far wetter than today. It was a province of the Ghana Empire and emerged as an independent kingdom as Ghana declined after the 11th century. Archaeological survey around Akumbu shows a dense cluster of settlements and iron-smelting sites.
kingdom-of-mema.r: Little is recorded of its government. In the Sundiata epic, the exiled Mande prince found refuge with the king of Mema, who gave him horsemen for his campaign against the Sosso kingdom. Mema's Soninke elite traded along the Niger and kept horses, a source of military strength.
kingdom-of-mema.e: Mema became a province of the Mali Empire in the 13th century and was later absorbed by the Songhai Empire, around the middle of the 15th century. A drying climate drove much of its population away, and the region is now sparsely inhabited.

kingdom-of-kotte.t: The last Sinhalese kingdom to unite all of Sri Lanka, under Parakramabahu VI, before its kings became clients of the Portuguese.
kingdom-of-kotte.o: Parakramabahu VI took power in 1412 after the fall of the Alakeshvara family of the Kingdom of Gampola, possibly with Chinese backing following Zheng He's intervention. He moved the capital to the fortified town of Kotte near Colombo, which the Alakeshvaras had built as a defence against the Jaffna Kingdom.
kingdom-of-kotte.r: Parakramabahu VI reigned for over five decades and briefly unified the island, conquering the Jaffna Kingdom and subduing the Vanni chieftaincies. His reign was a golden age of Sinhala poetry, with the monk-poet Sri Rahula. Kotte controlled the cinnamon-growing west coast, whose trade attracted the Portuguese, who arrived in 1505 and soon built a fort at Colombo.
kingdom-of-kotte.e: In 1521 the kingdom split into Kotte, the Kingdom of Sitawaka and the Kingdom of Raigama. Kotte's king Dharmapala converted to Christianity and in 1580 bequeathed his realm to the King of Portugal; on his death in 1597 it became part of Portuguese Ceylon.

kingdom-of-bugabo.t: A small Haya kingdom on the western shore of Lake Victoria, formed when Kyamutwara split around 1800.
kingdom-of-bugabo.o: Bugabo emerged around 1800 from the division of the Kingdom of Kyamutwara in the Kagera region of north-western Tanzania, one of several small Haya states created by succession disputes among royal lines.
kingdom-of-bugabo.r: Little is recorded of its history. Like its neighbours it was a banana and coffee farming kingdom ruled by a mukama with chiefs and royal rituals.
kingdom-of-bugabo.e: Bugabo became a native authority under German East Africa and later British Tanganyika Territory. Its chieftaincy was abolished in 1963.

kazikumukh-shamkhalate.t: The leading Muslim state of medieval Dagestan, ruled by shamkhals from the Lak village of Kumukh, which later divided into Tarki and Kazikumukh.
kazikumukh-shamkhalate.o: The Laks of Kumukh were among the first peoples of mountainous Dagestan to adopt Islam, and their village became a religious centre. By the 14th century a ruler with the title shamkhal, claiming descent from early Arab commanders, headed a state there that spread its authority over neighbouring communities and the Kumyk plain.
kazikumukh-shamkhalate.r: The shamkhals ruled with Lak and Kumyk nobles, promoting Islam among neighbours and leading campaigns against Georgian and Circassian lands. The state lived from herding, crafts and trade and was tributary to the Golden Horde before Timur's invasion of 1395. In the 16th century it was the strongest power in Dagestan, courted by the Ottomans and Safavid Empire.
kazikumukh-shamkhalate.e: Internal quarrels and pressure from Persia weakened it, and by about 1642 the shamkhals had moved their seat to Tarki on the Caspian coast, founding the Shamkhalate of Tarki, while Kumukh itself became the Kazikumukh Khanate.

kingdom-of-ireland.t: The kingdom created when Henry VIII took the title King of Ireland in 1542, ruled by English monarchs until the Act of Union of 1800.
kingdom-of-ireland.o: The Crown of Ireland Act of 1542, passed by the Irish Parliament, replaced the Lordship of Ireland with a kingdom. Henry VIII pursued 'surrender and regrant', converting Gaelic chiefs into earls, while the Tudor and Stuart conquests extended English authority across the island.
kingdom-of-ireland.r: Ireland was governed by a lord deputy or lord lieutenant at Dublin Castle and its own Parliament. Plantations in Munster and Ulster settled English and Scottish Protestants. After the Williamite war of 1689 to 1691, the Penal Laws excluded Catholics from land and office, creating the Protestant Ascendancy. Grattan's Parliament gained legislative independence in 1782.
kingdom-of-ireland.e: After the United Irishmen rebellion of 1798, the Acts of Union of 1800 merged Ireland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1 January 1801.
kingdom-of-ireland.re: Christianity; Catholic majority, Anglican established church

kutlehr-state.t: A tiny Rajput hill state in the lower Himalaya near Kangra, one of the minor principalities absorbed by the Sikh Empire in the early 19th century.
kutlehr-state.o: The ruling family claimed descent from Brahmins who became Rajputs and came from the plains; tradition places the foundation around 750. Its seat was the fort of Kot Kutlehr, between the Beas and the Sutlej.
kutlehr-state.r: Kutlehr was one of the smallest of the Kangra group of hill states, a few villages and forts under a Raja who was often a dependant of Kangra State or other larger neighbours. Few records of its internal history survive.
kutlehr-state.e: Ranjit Singh's Sikh Empire annexed the state in 1825, leaving the family a jagir. After 1846 the British confirmed the family in a smaller jagir. The territory is now in Himachal Pradesh.

kingdom-of-cappadocia.t: Cappadocia, a Hellenistic kingdom of the central Anatolian plateau ruled by Iranian-descended kings who became loyal allies of Rome.
kingdom-of-cappadocia.o: Ariarathes, the Persian satrap, defied Alexander's successors until Perdiccas killed him in 322 BCE. His adopted son Ariarathes II regained the land c. 301 BCE, and his heirs took the title king, ruling the plateau from Mazaca beneath Mount Argaeus.
kingdom-of-cappadocia.r: The Ariarathid kings ruled a rural country of large estates and temple domains, such as the shrine of the goddess Ma at Comana. Iranian traditions mixed with Greek culture; Ariarathes V was a patron of philosophers. The kingdom supplied horses, slaves and grain and allied with Rome against the Seleucid Empire.
kingdom-of-cappadocia.e: After Pontic interference, Rome installed Ariobarzanes I in 95 BCE. The last king, Archelaus, was summoned to Rome by Tiberius and died there in 17 CE, and Cappadocia became a Roman province.

kingdom-of-karasahr.t: The oasis kingdom of Agni on the northern Silk Road, one of the homes of the Tocharian languages and of Central Asian Buddhism.
kingdom-of-karasahr.o: Karasahr, called Yanqi in Chinese and Agni in its own documents, grew around the Bosten Lake oasis on the north-eastern edge of the Tarim Basin. It enters Chinese records in the 2nd century BCE as one of the city-states of the Western Regions, alternating between Xiongnu and Han control.
kingdom-of-karasahr.r: Its people spoke Tocharian A, an Indo-European language preserved in Buddhist manuscripts. Ruled by its own kings, Karasahr lived from irrigated farming, fishing, salt and Silk Road trade, and its monasteries at Shikshin followed the Sarvastivada school. The pilgrim Xuanzang passed through in 630. The Han general Ban Chao subdued it in 94, and the Tang Dynasty conquered it in 644 and made it one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi.
kingdom-of-karasahr.e: After Tang power in the Tarim faded in the late 8th century, Karasahr passed under Tibetan and Uyghur influence. Uyghurs fleeing the fall of the Uyghur Khaganate in 840 settled there, and the region became part of the Kingdom of Qocho, where Tocharian gave way to Old Uyghur.

kingdom-of-gwiriko.t: A Dyula-ruled kingdom around Bobo-Dioulasso in western Burkina Faso, founded by a branch of the Wattara family of Kong.
kingdom-of-gwiriko.o: Gwiriko was created around 1714 by Famagan Wattara, a kinsman of Seku Wattara of the Kong Empire, who led Dyula warriors into the region of the upper Black Volta. He established his rule over the Bobo, Bwa and other farming peoples, with Sya, later Bobo-Dioulasso, as the main centre. After Seku's death it became independent of Kong.
kingdom-of-gwiriko.r: The Wattara and their Dyula allies formed a Muslim ruling and trading class over largely non-Muslim farming villages, collecting tribute and controlling trade in kola, salt, gold and slaves. After Famagan's reign the kingdom fragmented into rival branches, and in the 19th century it was weakened by revolts of subject peoples and wars with Kenedougou.
kingdom-of-gwiriko.e: By the 1890s Gwiriko was a loose collection of chiefdoms. Samori Toure's armies passed through the region, and in 1897 the French occupied Bobo-Dioulasso. The area became part of French Sudan and later French Upper Volta.

kamta-rajaula-state.t: A small Chaube jagir of Bundelkhand, one of the estates granted to the former Brahmin governors of Kalinjar in 1812.
kamta-rajaula-state.o: Kamta-Rajaula was created in 1812 as one of the shares given to the Chaube family, who had held the fort of Kalinjar for the rulers of Panna, in return for surrendering it to the British.
kamta-rajaula-state.r: The estate covered a few villages near Kamta, the hill sacred to Rama at Chitrakoot, under the Bundelkhand Agency. Little else of its history is recorded.
kamta-rajaula-state.e: After independence Kamta-Rajaula was merged into Vindhya Pradesh with the other Bundelkhand states and absorbed by 1950.

kingdom-of-undi.t: The western Chewa kingdom of the Undi, an offshoot of Maravi whose lands held gold mines worked by Portuguese traders.
kingdom-of-undi.o: The Undi dynasty was founded in the 17th century by a member of the Phiri ruling clan of the Kingdom of Maravi who, according to tradition, quarrelled with the Kalonga and led followers west. He established his capital at Mano near the Kapoche river, on the borderlands of present-day Mozambique, Zambia and Malawi.
kingdom-of-undi.r: The Undi ruled through kin and territorial chiefs who sent tribute and recognised his ritual primacy, including over rain shrines. The kingdom traded ivory and cloth with the Portuguese at Tete and Zumbo, and in the 18th century Portuguese and Goan miners worked gold deposits in Undi territory under licence. Chewa culture, including the Nyau masked societies, flourished.
kingdom-of-undi.e: Decline set in during the 19th century as Afro-Portuguese warlords and, from the 1830s, Ngoni invaders raided its lands. By around 1880 central authority had collapsed. The Undi title survives as a Chewa paramount chieftaincy in Zambia.

kingdom-of-yauri.t: Small kingdom on the middle Niger, among the 'outer' Hausa states, that survived the 19th century jihad with its dynasty intact.
kingdom-of-yauri.o: Yauri grew up along the Niger above the Bussa rapids among the Reshe and other river peoples, with a ruling house that adopted Hausa language and institutions. It was counted among the Banza Bakwai and is traditionally dated to around the 15th century.
kingdom-of-yauri.r: Yauri controlled river crossings and trade between Hausaland, Borgu and Nupe. It was frequently subject to stronger neighbours, including the Kingdom of Kebbi and the Songhai Empire, and adopted Islam at court. After the jihad of the early 19th century its rulers accepted the suzerainty of the Gwandu Emirate within the Sokoto Caliphate.
kingdom-of-yauri.e: Internal disputes led to the founding of a new capital at Yelwa in the 1880s. Yauri came under the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria around 1901 and survives as the Yauri Emirate in Kebbi State.

kingdom-of-the-ouarsenis.t: An obscure Berber kingdom of the Ouarsenis mountains in Algeria, known mainly from its monumental Djedar tombs.
kingdom-of-the-ouarsenis.o: After Roman and Vandal authority faded in the interior of Mauretania Caesariensis in the late 5th century, a Berber kingdom emerged in the Ouarsenis mountains and high plains around Tiaret. Procopius mentions a ruler named Mastigas who, in the 530s, held most of Mauretania except the coastal city of Caesarea.
kingdom-of-the-ouarsenis.r: Very little is known of its government. The Djedars, thirteen great stepped pyramid tombs near Frenda and Tiaret, built between the 5th and 7th centuries, are attributed to its rulers. Their Latin inscriptions and Christian symbols show a Romanised, Christian Berber elite ruling over pastoral and farming tribes.
kingdom-of-the-ouarsenis.e: The kingdom disappears from the record by the late 6th century, and its lands later came under the Arab conquerors and Berber Islamic states such as the Rustamid imamate, whose capital Tahert lay close by.

kingdom-of-hungary-1920-1946.t: Interwar Hungarian kingdom without a king, ruled by Regent Miklós Horthy, which sought to undo the Treaty of Trianon and was drawn into the Second World War.
kingdom-of-hungary-1920-1946.o: After the fall of the Hungarian Soviet Republic, a national assembly restored the monarchy in 1920 but, with the Habsburgs barred, elected Admiral Miklós Horthy regent on 1 March. The Treaty of Trianon in June 1920 took two-thirds of the former Kingdom of Hungary (1867-1918). Former king Charles IV twice tried to return in 1921 and failed.
kingdom-of-hungary-1920-1946.r: Prime Minister István Bethlen stabilised the conservative regime in the 1920s, with restricted voting and dominance of landowners. Revision of Trianon was the central aim, and through the Vienna Awards of 1938 and 1940 Hungary regained southern Slovakia and northern Transylvania with German and Italian support. Antisemitic laws began with the numerus clausus of 1920 and tightened from 1938.
kingdom-of-hungary-1920-1946.e: Hungary joined the war against the Soviet Union in 1941. Germany occupied it in March 1944, and around 437,000 Jews were deported, most to Auschwitz. Horthy's attempt to leave the war in October 1944 led to Ferenc Szálasi's Government of National Unity. The monarchy was abolished in February 1946.

kingdom-of-elymais.t: A semi-independent kingdom of Khuzestan and the Zagros under Parthian rule, known for its rock reliefs and for killing the Seleucid king Antiochus III.
kingdom-of-elymais.o: Elymais (from Elam) covered the mountains of eastern Khuzestan and, at times, the plain of Susa. Its people resisted the Seleucid Empire: Antiochus III was killed in 187 BCE while plundering a temple of Bel there. Around 147 BCE a local ruler, Kamnaskires I, took Susa and issued coins as king.
kingdom-of-elymais.r: Elymais mixed Iranian, Mesopotamian and Greek traditions, worshipping Bel, Nanaya and Artemis at rich temples. Its kings, often called Kamnaskires or later Orodes, minted bronze coins and ruled as vassals of the Parthian Empire, sometimes in revolt. Rock reliefs at Hung-e Azhdar, Tang-e Sarvak and Hung-e Kamalvand show rulers and nobles in Parthian dress, and the bronze statue from Shami belongs to this world.
kingdom-of-elymais.e: Ardashir I of the Sasanian Empire conquered Elymais around 221 CE, ending the dynasty. Its lands became part of the Sasanian province of Khuzestan.

kingdom-of-cyrene.t: The Greek kingdom of the Battiad dynasty in eastern Libya, enriched by silphium, horses and grain.
kingdom-of-cyrene.o: According to Herodotus, colonists from the island of Thera, sent by the oracle of Delphi, founded Cyrene around 631 BCE under a leader who became King Battus I. The site, on a fertile plateau above the coast of Cyrenaica, was shown to them by local Libyans, with whom the settlers intermarried.
kingdom-of-cyrene.r: Eight kings, alternately named Battus and Arcesilaus, ruled for nearly two centuries. Battus II brought new settlers and defeated an Egyptian army sent by Apries at Irasa around 570 BCE, and the reformer Demonax of Mantinea later limited royal power. The economy rested on silphium, a medicinal plant shown on the city's coins, and on horses and grain. Cyrene paid tribute to the Achaemenid Empire from 525 BCE.
kingdom-of-cyrene.e: Royal power provoked repeated conflict, including Barca's secession. Arcesilaus IV, whose chariot victory at Delphi in 462 BCE was celebrated by Pindar, was overthrown around 440 BCE, and the monarchy gave way to the Republic of Cyrene.

kingdom-of-moray.t: A powerful northern Scottish realm whose rulers, styled kings or mormaers, contested the Scottish throne, most famously through Macbeth.
kingdom-of-moray.o: Moray emerged in the 10th century in the lands around the Moray Firth after the decline of the Pictish kingdom of Fortriu. Its ruling family, probably from Cenel Loairn by later genealogies, sometimes appear in Irish annals as kings of Alba, reflecting their claims to the Kingdom of Scotland.
kingdom-of-moray.r: Moray's rulers commanded a rich coastal plain and highland hinterland. Macbeth, mormaer of Moray, killed Duncan I in 1040 and ruled Scotland until 1057, making a pilgrimage to Rome. His stepson Lulach briefly succeeded him. The house of Moray clashed repeatedly with Norse earls of Orkney and with the line of Malcolm III.
kingdom-of-moray.e: After Angus of Moray died in battle at Stracathro in 1130, David I annexed the province, planting burghs and Flemish settlers. Revolts by MacWilliam claimants continued into the 13th century.

kingdom-of-hadramawt.t: The frankincense kingdom of south Arabia, ruling the Wadi Hadramawt from Shabwa and controlling the Dhofar groves and the port of Qana.
kingdom-of-hadramawt.o: Hadramawt is named in Sabaean inscriptions of the 7th century BCE, when it was first an ally and then a rival of the Kingdom of Saba. Its kings ruled the long Wadi Hadramawt and its tributaries from Shabwa, a walled town where all incense had to be brought for taxing before caravans set off west.
kingdom-of-hadramawt.r: Its wealth came from frankincense, gathered in Dhofar where Hadramawt founded the port of Sumhuram (Khor Rori), and shipped through Qana on the Indian Ocean coast, a port described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea. The kingdom worshipped the moon god Sayin and wrote Hadramitic, a south Arabian language. It absorbed much of the Kingdom of Qataban in the 2nd century CE.
kingdom-of-hadramawt.e: In the early 3rd century CE Saba sacked Shabwa, and around 300 CE the Himyarite Kingdom under Shammar Yahrish conquered Hadramawt outright. The name survived as a region, and the valley's later sultanates, such as the Kathiri Sultanate and the Qu'aiti Sultanate, inherited it.

kotah-state.t: A Hada Chauhan Rajput state on the Chambal river, separated from Bundi under Shah Jahan and famed for its school of painting.
kotah-state.o: Kota was separated from Bundi State in 1631, when the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan granted it to Madho Singh, a son of Rao Ratan Singh of Bundi, as a reward for service. The Hada rulers continued as Mughal mansabdars.
kotah-state.r: The Maharaos ruled the fertile Chambal valley. In the late 18th century the regent Zalim Singh Jhala dominated the state, and in 1838 the British created Jhalawar for his descendants out of Kota lands. The court fostered the Kota school of painting, noted for its hunting scenes. It was a seventeen-gun salute state.
kotah-state.e: Kota joined the Rajasthan union in 1948, and Maharao Bhim Singh II became its Rajpramukh. Kota is now a major city of Rajasthan.

kingdom-of-jembrana.t: Small, thinly peopled kingdom of western Bali, notable for its Bugis Muslim settlers and its position facing Java.
kingdom-of-jembrana.o: Jembrana occupied the forested western tip of Bali, facing Java across the Bali Strait. Its early history is poorly documented: a local dynasty emerged around 1700, and the area was repeatedly dominated by its more powerful neighbours, especially the Kingdom of Buleleng and the Kingdom of Badung.
kingdom-of-jembrana.r: With little irrigated land, Jembrana was poorer than the southern Balinese kingdoms. Bugis seafarers from Sulawesi settled at Loloan near Negara in the 17th and 18th centuries, adding a Muslim trading community to the Hindu Balinese population and linking the kingdom to the shipping routes of the Java Sea.
kingdom-of-jembrana.e: Jembrana came under Dutch control together with Buleleng after the 1849 expedition and was placed under direct colonial administration in 1882. It later became a regency of Bali province in Indonesia.

koti-state.t: A small Rajput hill state just north of Shimla, a feudatory of Keonthal and one of the Simla Hill States.
koti-state.o: The ruling family claimed Rajput descent, and tradition dates the state to around 1500. Little is reliably known about its origins.
koti-state.r: Koti was a small mountain state near Mashobra and was a feudatory of Keonthal State. Like its neighbours it was occupied by Gurkhas of the Kingdom of Nepal in the early 19th century and restored under British protection after 1815. Little detail of its history is recorded.
koti-state.e: Koti merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now part of Shimla district.

kingdom-of-the-moors-and-romans.t: A post-Roman Berber kingdom in western Algeria whose king Masuna called himself ruler of both Moors and Romans.
kingdom-of-the-moors-and-romans.o: As Vandal control of the interior weakened in the late 5th century, Berber leaders in the former Mauretania Caesariensis set up their own states. An inscription at Altava (Ouled Mimoun) dated 508 names Masuna as 'king of the peoples of the Moors and Romans', the best evidence for this kingdom, which probably arose in the 470s or 480s.
kingdom-of-the-moors-and-romans.r: The kingdom combined Berber tribal leadership with surviving Roman towns, Latin inscriptions and Christian communities, and kept Roman provincial dating. Masuna allied with the Byzantine general Solomon against other Berber rulers in 535, as Procopius records. Its exact borders are unknown, but it was centred on the Tlemcen region and the Oran plain.
kingdom-of-the-moors-and-romans.e: Garmul, a later king, attacked Byzantine Africa in the 570s and was killed by the general Gennadius in 578. Power in the region then passed to the Kingdom of Altava, which survived until the Arab conquest.

kingdom-of-mustang.t: The small Tibetan Buddhist kingdom of Lo in the high valleys of northern Nepal, whose walled capital Lo Manthang survives intact.
kingdom-of-mustang.o: Ame Pal, a Tibetan warrior, unified the upper Kali Gandaki valley around 1380 and founded the walled city of Lo Manthang as his capital. The kingdom of Lo controlled one of the main trade routes between the Tibetan plateau and the Indian subcontinent.
kingdom-of-mustang.r: Lo prospered from the trade in salt from Tibet and grain from the south, and its kings built great monasteries such as Thubchen and Jampa in Lo Manthang, whose murals are among the finest in the Tibetan world. The Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism predominated. Lo paid tribute in turn to western Tibetan rulers, the Kingdom of Jumla and later Nepal.
kingdom-of-mustang.e: After the Gorkha conquests in the late 18th century, Lo became a tributary of the Kingdom of Nepal while keeping its own king. The monarchy lost its status when the Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal abolished royal titles in 2008. The last king, Jigme Dorje Palbar Bista, died in 2016.

kathrota-state.t: A minor chiefship of the Kathiawar peninsula, one of its many small estates.
kathrota-state.o: Kathrota was a small estate in Kathiawar held by a local chiefly family from around 1700. Its origins are poorly documented.
kathrota-state.r: The ruler held a handful of villages and, after 1807, came under British supervision in the Kathiawar Agency. Standard references record little else.
kathrota-state.e: Kathrota merged into the United State of Saurashtra in 1948 and became part of Gujarat in 1960.

kingdom-of-boussouma.t: Mossi kingdom east of Ouagadougou, one of the smaller independent Mossi states of the Burkina Faso plateau.
kingdom-of-boussouma.o: Known mainly from Mossi oral tradition. Boussouma was founded by a branch of the Mossi royal family, probably in the 17th century, on lands east of the Kingdom of Ouagadougou, and its rulers bore the title Dima.
kingdom-of-boussouma.r: The Dima of Boussouma ruled with ministers and village chiefs over Mossi farming communities, with local earth-priests keeping the rites of land. The kingdom kept its independence from Ouagadougou and was a frequent rival of the Mogho Naaba.
kingdom-of-boussouma.e: Boussouma came under French control in 1896 and became part of French West Africa, later French Upper Volta. The Dima of Boussouma remains a traditional ruler in Burkina Faso.

kingdom-of-lithuania-1918.t: A short-lived monarchy declared by the Council of Lithuania in 1918, which elected a German prince as King Mindaugas II.
kingdom-of-lithuania-1918.o: Germany recognised Lithuanian independence in March 1918 on condition of close ties with the German Empire, and plans circulated to unite the crown with Prussia or Saxony. To avoid this, the Council of Lithuania on 11 July 1918 proclaimed a constitutional monarchy and invited Prince Wilhelm of Urach, a Catholic from Wurttemberg, to be king.
kingdom-of-lithuania-1918.r: Wilhelm accepted and took the name Mindaugas II, after the medieval king of the Kingdom of Lithuania, but he never came to Lithuania and the German authorities did not recognise his election. In practice the country remained under German military occupation, while the council prepared Lithuanian institutions.
kingdom-of-lithuania-1918.e: As Germany's defeat approached, the Council revoked the election on 2 November 1918 and adopted provisional republican principles. The state continued as the Republic of Lithuania (1918-1940). Wilhelm never set foot in the country, and the episode is remembered as a curiosity of Lithuanian state-building.

kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia.t: The leading western Rus' state after the Mongol invasion, whose ruler Daniel was crowned King of Rus' and founded the city of Lviv.
kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia.o: In 1199 Roman Mstislavich of the Principality of Volhynia took Halych and united it with his own lands. After his death in battle in 1205 Galicia fell into decades of strife involving Hungary and Poland. His son Daniel won back both lands by 1238 and made the state one of the most powerful in Eastern Europe.
kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia.r: Daniel submitted to Batu Khan in 1245 but looked to the West for help, and in 1253 he was crowned King of Rus' by a papal legate at Dorohychyn. He founded Kholm and Lviv, which he named after his son Leo, and welcomed German, Armenian and Jewish settlers to the towns. Orthodox, Catholic and steppe influences met in its court.
kingdom-of-galicia-volhynia.e: The direct dynasty ended in 1323, and Yuri II Boleslaw, a Masovian Piast, was poisoned by boyars in 1340. Poland and Lithuania then divided the kingdom, with Casimir III taking Galicia by 1349 and the Duchy of Volhynia going to Lithuania.

kingdom-of-spain.t: Spain's present parliamentary monarchy, built through the peaceful transition from Franco's dictatorship to democracy.
kingdom-of-spain.o: Two days after Franco's death, Juan Carlos I was proclaimed king on 22 November 1975, ending Francoist Spain. With Prime Minister Adolfo Suárez he dismantled the dictatorship: the Law for Political Reform of 1976, free elections in June 1977 and the Constitution of 1978, approved by referendum.
kingdom-of-spain.r: Spain became a parliamentary monarchy divided into 17 autonomous communities, recognising Catalan, Basque and Galician identities. The king's stand against the coup attempt of 23 February 1981 secured democracy. Felipe González's Socialists governed from 1982 to 1996, joining NATO and the European Economic Community in 1986. The 1992 Barcelona Olympics and Seville Expo marked modernisation.
kingdom-of-spain.e: Spain remains a parliamentary monarchy. ETA declared an end to violence in 2011, Felipe VI succeeded his father in 2014, and the Catalan independence crisis of 2017 tested the constitutional order.

kingdom-of-kebbi.t: Hausa kingdom founded by the rebel Songhai general Kanta, which briefly dominated Hausaland in the 16th century.
kingdom-of-kebbi.o: Around 1516 Muhammadu Kanta, a commander serving the Songhai Empire under Askia Muhammad, quarrelled over the spoils of a campaign against Agadez and rebelled. He established an independent kingdom in the Kebbi region of north-western Hausaland and built fortified capitals at Surame and later Birnin Kebbi.
kingdom-of-kebbi.r: Kanta defeated Songhai and the Kanem-Bornu Empire and made Kebbi the dominant power in western Hausaland, taking tribute from Katsina, Zamfara and others. After his death Kebbi lost much of its empire but remained a strong military state, a member of the Banza Bakwai. Its people, the Kebbawa, are farmers and fishermen of the Rima and Niger valleys.
kingdom-of-kebbi.e: In 1805 jihadists of the Sokoto Caliphate took Birnin Kebbi. The Kebbi dynasty fought on from the marshes and in 1831 established the Argungu Emirate, which resisted Sokoto until British rule. The name lives on in Kebbi State.

kushan-empire.t: An empire of Yuezhi origin stretching from the Amu Darya to the Ganges, a crossroads of Rome, China and India that carried Buddhism into Central Asia.
kushan-empire.o: Kujula Kadphises, chief of the Kushan branch of the Yuezhi, united the five Yuezhi chiefdoms of Bactria in the 1st century CE and pushed south across the Hindu Kush, taking lands from the Indo-Parthians and Indo-Greeks. His successors Vima Takto and Vima Kadphises extended rule deep into northern India.
kushan-empire.r: Under Kanishka the Great in the 2nd century, the empire was ruled from Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura, using Bactrian written in Greek script. Gold coins showed Greek, Iranian and Indian gods side by side. The Kushans controlled Silk Road trade between Han China, Parthia and Rome, and patronised Gandharan and Mathuran art, which produced some of the earliest images of the Buddha. Mahayana Buddhism spread northward under their rule.
kushan-empire.e: In the 3rd century the Sasanians conquered the western lands, creating the Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom, while the Gupta Empire and local rulers took the Indian territories. Small Kushan kingdoms lingered in Gandhara and Kashmir until overrun by the Kidarite Kingdom in the 4th century.

kingdom-of-sanwi.t: An Anyi kingdom on the Aby lagoon in south-eastern Ivory Coast, ruled from Krinjabo, which was among the first states on that coast to sign a treaty with France.
kingdom-of-sanwi.o: Sanwi was founded around 1740 by Anyi migrants from Aowin, who left their homeland after the Ashanti Empire overran it. Under their leader Amon Ndoufou I they settled around Krinjabo and the Aby lagoon, subjecting the Eotile and Essouma peoples of the coast, including those of the trading town of Assinie.
kingdom-of-sanwi.r: Sanwi followed Akan forms of rule, with a king from a royal matrilineage, a court of chiefs and an elaborate regalia of gold and royal stools. The economy rested on gold, farming and trade with Europeans at Assinie, where French and other merchants exchanged guns, cloth and spirits for gold, ivory and slaves.
kingdom-of-sanwi.e: In 1843 Sanwi's rulers signed a treaty with the French naval officer Louis Edouard Bouet-Willaumez, and Assinie became a French post. Sanwi was absorbed into the French Ivory Coast, though its kings remained and in 1959 attempted a brief secession.

kingdom-of-ergyng.t: A small British kingdom in the Wye valley around the Roman town of Ariconium, whose name survives in Archenfield, a Welsh-speaking district of Herefordshire.
kingdom-of-ergyng.o: Ergyng emerged after Roman rule ended, its name derived from Ariconium, an iron-working town near Ross-on-Wye. It appears in the 6th and 7th centuries in the charters of the Book of Llandaff, which name local kings such as Peibio, associated in legend with the birth of Saint Dubricius.
kingdom-of-ergyng.r: Ergyng was a Christian British kingdom in which churches and monasteries, many linked to Dubricius, held land through royal grants. Its rulers were at times linked to the dynasties of Gwent and Glywysing. Little else is reliably known of its government.
kingdom-of-ergyng.e: From the 7th century the kingdom was absorbed by Gwent, and English settlement from Mercia advanced into the area. By the 10th century it was the district of Archenfield, under English lordship but still Welsh in law and speech; Domesday Book recorded its Welsh customs.
